Georgia: Ambassador D’Antuono Visits the Dmanisi Archaeological Site
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:46:54 CEST
21:46:54 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Georgia, Massimiliano D’Antuono, visited Dmanisi, an open-air museum and one of the world’s most important archaeological sites, featuring evidence of human settlements dating back 1.8 million years. Research at the Dmanisi prehistoric site is being conducted by an international, multidisciplinary team coordinated by the National Museum of Georgia, with long-standing participation from the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Florence.
                                    
                                       
				   Ambassador D’Antuono was hosted by David Lordkipanidze, director of the National Museum of Georgia, and by Prof. Lorenzo Rook of the University of Florence, who leads the mission funded by the Italian Ministry of Education, Universities, and Research (MAECI) and has been working at the Dmanisi paleontological site for years.
                                    
                                       
				   The Dmanisi site, one of the milestones of modern paleoanthropology, has provided evidence of a crucial moment in human evolution: the out-of-Africa migration. In the 1990s, human and animal remains dating back 1.8 million years were discovered in the countryside surrounding this village, located about 80 kilometers from the Georgian capital; the hominid fossils are considered the oldest ever discovered outside the African continent. 
   The Italian research team is working to thoroughly study the rich fossil fauna associated with the human remains, with the aim of obtaining genetic information of extraordinary interest and reconstructing, in as much detail as possible, the environment and ecosystem of which our ancient ancestors were a part.

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. The TKB-1167 air target engagement system can be operated by crews without in-depth engineering training, the High Precision Systems Holding Company (part of the Rostec state corporation) told TASS at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 in Egypt.

3 cities submit bids to host Estonia's multisport arena by deadline

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09

3 cities submit bids to host Estonia's multisport arena by deadline
Pärnu, Tallinn and Tartu submitted bids by the deadline to host the major arena planned by the Estonian Olympic Committee (EOK).
All three cities seeking to host the multifunctional arena submitted applications to the Estonian Olympic Committee (EOK) by the September 1 deadline.
More specifically, Pärnu, Tallinn and Tartu submitted proposed locations along with additional documentation, allowing the bids to now be compared, EOK multifunctional arena project manager Helen Veermäe told ERR.
"The aim is to ensure that all potential locations are assessed on a comparable basis and, above all, according to their substantive characteristics and potential," she said.
Tallinn proposed the Ülemiste freight terminal area as the location for the arena. Pärnu's preferred site is near the future Rail Baltica terminal, in Veterans Park next to Papiniidu Bridge on the banks of the Pärnu River. The City of Tartu has reserved a plot of land for the arena on Roosi tänav, near the Estonian National Museum.
The selection process will now begin. In May, the EOK and the Ministry of Culture formed an expert committee that will oversee the selection process and ultimately submit a recommendation, together with its reasoning, to the government.
As a first step, however, the expert committee will soon select an independent expert to conduct an economic impact analysis, Veermäe said.
"The independent expert selected will prepare a comparative economic impact analysis based on the materials submitted by the cities, gather additional data where necessary and conduct interviews with representatives of the cities and other key stakeholders," she said.
Once the expert committee has approved the expert who will conduct the analysis, the economic impact analysis will take approximately three months to complete. The expert committee will then prepare a summary and submit its recommendation on the most suitable location to the government, Veermäe said.
The government will make the final decision on which city the arena will ultimately be built in. Once that decision has been made, it will also become clear when construction could begin and when the arena could be completed.
The EOK began the arena project's preparatory phase last November. Among other things, representatives have visited Finland to study the business model of a multifunctional arena.
Plans for the arena began to be pursued more seriously after Estonia secured the right to host the 2029 European Basketball Championship. Estonia's largest indoor arena at present is Tallinn's Unibet Arena, which can accommodate up to 7,000 spectators.
The government is currently discussing next year's state budget and the state budget strategy for the next four years. Economy Minister Erkki Keldo told "Aktuaalne kaamera" on Tuesday that some investments will have to be dropped in order to reduce the budget deficit.
"We will also have to drop investments that might have been possible in better times — buildings and other construction projects. We cannot afford them when such a large share is going toward defense investments," Keldo said. Estonia aims to spend at least 5 percent of its GDP on national defense in the coming years.

====================================================================================================

EU seeks to transform procurement into €600B driver of industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:42:29 UTC
21:42:29 KST

The proposal also spells out how public authorities can favor EU goods and services — a power that they enjoy under existing rules but rarely use. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The EU wants to transform public procurement into a powerful tool of industrial policy by channeling hundreds of billions of euros spent on infrastructure, schools, energy or health toward European businesses.
In its Public Procurement Act unveiled on Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission is following up on recommendations by economic reform guru Mario Draghi to give a lift to struggling European industry while shielding the bloc from external risks in an increasingly uncertain world.
The sums involved are huge. Public procurement represents up to 15 percent of the EU’s GDP — or around €2.5 trillion a year. Of that, some €600 billion is governed by EU rules, Executive Vice President Stéphane Séjourné told reporters.
Advertisement
“This is public money, which must also serve our collective goals,” the French commissioner said. “It’s the equivalent of a yearly recovery plan and about four to five times the EU budget in terms of spending.”
The Commission is also promising annual cost savings of €650 million for public authorities as three old directives and two dozen sectoral laws — spanning 900 pages — are boiled down into a single regulation running to just 200 pages. That ties in with von der Leyen’s broader second-term agenda of cutting red tape through a series of “omnibus” administrative reforms.
To harness public procurement to its strategic goal of strengthening European industry, the EU executive is betting on quality as the main driver in the awarding of public tenders. This would set a minimum quality weighting of 30 percent, rising to 50 percent for labor-intensive contracts. Environmental, social, innovation, security and resilience considerations would all count as quality.
Public authorities could still deviate from the rule if they can justify using price alone on the grounds that quality is guaranteed through technical specifications.
While public authorities can already put green or social criteria at the center of procurement, Commission research found that their use was neither optimal nor consistent across the bloc. Some contracting authorities, for example, fear litigation if they turn down the lowest-price offer.
European preference
The proposal also spells out how public authorities can favor EU goods and services — a power that they enjoy under existing rules but rarely use. Under the new rules, authorities could restrict participation, impose origin requirements, and reject tenders where EU or “covered” content accounts for less than 50 percent of the tender’s value.
Advertisement
The Commission’s goal is to provide greater clarity regarding how these rules are applied so that authorities can better evaluate European bids and, if necessary, exclude bids from non-covered countries, Séjourné said.
“In any case, it won’t be the European Commissioner’s fault if public procurement agencies choose Chinese buses over European ones, since everything is spelled out in the text and currently allows for the preference of European buses,” he added.
Séjourné described the procurement bill as “an act of radical simplification.” The Commission chose a regulation instead of a directive — over the objections of a majority of member countries. A regulation reduces the scope for divergent national transposition of EU procurement rules, making implementation in national law simpler and avoiding “gold-plating” by capitals.
The Public Procurement Act would also make it easier for companies to find and participate in tenders across the EU by introducing a network of digital platforms. There are currently 123 platforms across the bloc — either at national or at local level — and the Commission wants to make sure they all communicate with one another.
Different procedures are also simplified and boiled down to two.
Advertisement
The first is a standard, open procedure with offers being assessed before awarding the contract to the winning bid. The second is a “dynamic” procedure where a public authority pools companies that meet its criteria and later invites them to participate in a tender or negotiate for individual procurement opportunities.
Procuring innovation
The Commission is also seeking to address the longstanding EU problem of homegrown research failing to reach the market.
The bloc is a research powerhouse, but innovators and startups often can’t obtain the funding they need in the EU to market their products and scale up within the bloc. They turn to the U.S. for funding instead, or end up in the “valley of death,” which is when a company already has a viable product, but not the funding to market it.
The Commission’s answer is its proposed European Innovation Act, also announced on Wednesday, which aims to turn governments into major buyers of pre-commercial solutions.
“Innovative ideas developed in Europe too often fail to reach the market, scale across borders or generate new growth sectors,” it states.
The Innovation Act has been led by Bulgarian Research Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva, and was initially more ambitious. But the scope of the law was narrowed down after two negative opinions from the Commission’s quality watchdog, according to documents seen by POLITICO.
Advertisement
The EU massively lags other regions in governments procuring research or early-stage prototypes, with the proposal claiming that other regions are investing between five and eight times more than the EU in the public procurement of R&D.
One way to correct this is to create an EU-wide framework for pre-commercial procurement. Harmonizing the procedures should also allow for joint procurement by several public buyers across borders.
The Innovation Act will also seek to help companies to market their intellectual property, by establishing a new competence center in the EU’s Intellectual Property Office.
Finally, the Commission will also come up with a so-called innovation challenge. The idea is to let public authorities start with a problem rather than a product and pitch a “societal challenge” to the market.

Hong Kong Medical Council rejects proposal on time frame for handling complaints
In written submission to Legislative Council, watchdog also rejects proposed reforms to its disciplinary sentencing, supervision and membership
Hong Kong’s medical watchdog has said a target time frame for handling complaints will not be necessary as it presented its rebuttal against a government proposal that includes major reforms to its operations, disciplinary sentencing, internal supervision and membership make-up.
In a written submission to the Legislative Council’s bills committee on the medical registration amendment bill, dated Tuesday and uploaded to the Legco website the next day, the Medical Council’s chairwoman Professor Grace Tang Wai-king said a dedicated working group had been established to study the details of the bill and assess its implications for the watchdog’s operations.
Among the government’s proposed amendments was requiring the watchdog to make public the target time frames for specific steps in its complaints procedure, and set up milestone dates for submissions of documents and inquiries.
“There is no need to stipulate the requirement for the Medical Council of Hong Kong to set target time frames for specific steps in the law,” the council stated in the submission.
“Instead, this can be handled administratively by [the council] as [has been] the practice of government departments and other statutory bodies.”

Malaysia’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition has doubled down on its pledge to stamp out corruption, as all eyes turn to the country’s Pardons Board, which is reportedly set to discuss the possible release of disgraced former leader Najib Razak at a meeting this week.
The Pardons Board, chaired by the country’s king, is expected to meet on Friday to discuss potentially granting Najib clemency from his ongoing jail sentence for corruption linked to the multibillion-dollar 1MDB scandal, according to local news reports.
The revelation adds a fresh spin to the drama surrounding Najib’s earlier attempt at securing a court order to complete his sentence in his home after his 12-year jail term was halved and his fine reduced from 210 million ringgit (US$51.6 million) to 50 million ringgit following a decision by former king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah in 2024.
Should the pardons board, led by current king Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, grant Najib a full pardon, it would mean his immediate release from prison and his records wiped clean of all existing criminal records, similar to when Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was freed from a sodomy conviction in 2018.
In an apparent response to a news report on the Pardons Board meeting by local Chinese daily Sin Chew Daily, the PH secretaries’ council said the coalition continued to reject corruption and abuse of power, and that any individual found guilty of such offences, especially in high-profile cases, “must complete their sentences in full”.
“Pakatan Harapan was built on the support of Malaysians … who placed high hopes on our Reform agenda and the creation of a country that is clean, with integrity and responsible,” the secretaries’ council said in a statement on Wednesday.

They praised his lifelong love for the country and Hong Kong, as well as his broad vision and firm stance that contributed to the city's smooth and stable return to the motherland.
The condolence message added that Tung's time in office marked the pioneering stage in which the theoretical concept of "one country, two systems" was put into practice.
"He united the SAR government and society in a spirit of solidarity and perseverance, calmly tackled a series of complex political, economic and social challenges, while steadfastly safeguarding the nation's sovereignty, security and development interests and maintaining overall stability in Hong Kong," the message read.
Even after stepping down as Chief Executive, Tung continued to prioritise the fundamental interests of the nation and Hong Kong, dutifully serving as vice‑chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference National Committee, the offices noted.
"Tung Chee-hwa's life is one defined by patriotism, hard work and dedication," the message added, saying he set a shining example for the world and will forever be respected and missed.
Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macao Studies, described Tung as someone who was "very kind and upright", while possessing a strategic mindset that is lacking in many politicians in Hong Kong.
The former head of the government's central policy unit praised Tung's introduction of the accountability system as "visionary", especially when the government did not have sufficient recognition or experience at the time.
Lau disclosed that Tung established a think tank and foundation in the later years after feeling the need to address issues in society such as an adverse political climate, infighting and sluggish economic diversification.

Trump gives ethically dubious $45,000 cash gifts to Natalie Harp, White House aides - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:38:22 UTC
21:38:22 KST

US President Donald Trump gave $45,000 cash gifts to three young, loyal White House employees "for the holidays," including executive assistant Natalie Harp, the Washington Post reported on Tuesday, citing financial disclosures released by the Trump administration.
The three women all earn $150,000 salaries from their White House positions, according to an annual report to Congress.
Former chief White House ethics lawyer for then-president George W. Bush, Richard Painter, told WaPo that the payments may violate a federal statute prohibiting the supplementation of federal employees' salaries from outside sources.
“He’s clearly trying to make it easier for them financially to work in government service at the White House. You can't do that,” Painter told WaPo.
Former acting director of the Office of Government Ethics (OGE) during the Obama administration said that the payments may not have violated the prohibition, and would only have done so if Trump made the gifts in order to keep one of the employees after they expressed that they couldn't live on what they were making and would move to the private sector, according to the report.
White House claims payments part of longstanding practice
The White House pushed back on the idea that the payments violated any rules.
“The president has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector,” WaPo cited White House spokesperson Davis Ingle as saying.
“The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.”
While there are rules against employees giving gifts to superiors, a large payment to an employee from a superior is “not a circumstance that OGE ever really envisioned,” Fox said. "This just doesn't happen."
According to WaPo's report, there have been no other public incidents of US presidents giving White House staff large cash payments, and government ethics experts said they were unaware of any other payments of this scale from a superior to a subordinate government worker.
Aides all worked for Trump between terms
Harp, Trump's 35-year-old aide, known as the 'human printer' due to her carrying around a portable printer to provide Trump with hard copies of news articles and social media posts, came under public attention after it was reported that she was among the few staffers who accompanied Trump on a catering truck transporting him between planes leaving Turkey following a potential Iranian assassination threat.
In addition to Harp, 31-year-old communications advisor Margo Martin, who, according to WaPo, often gets closer to Trump than his Secret Service security detail to film him for social media, and 26-year-old Chamberlain Harris, a White House aide who serves as Trump's executive assistant, according to the report.
Harris was appointed to the US Commission of Fine Arts, which oversees Trump's White House ballroom and other Washington-area construction projects in February.
Director of Oval Office Operations Walt Nauta received a $20,000 gift from Trump, according to the report.
Nauta served as a valet in the first Trump administration and was a key witness and co-defendant in the Justice Department's probe of Trump's handling of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago.
All four employees worked for Trump between his first and second terms and have ties to Trump dating back to his first administration.

Unknown Publisher

Mohammed Sameai and Sahin Demir
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Nearly 1,400 families were displaced in a single day in western Yemen amid escalating fighting between government forces and the Houthi group, authorities said Wednesday.
The government-run Executive Unit for the Management of Displaced Persons Camps said 1,367 families were newly displaced on Sept. 8 in the provinces of Taiz, Al-Hudaydah and Lahj, according to a statement carried by the official Saba news agency.
The new displacement brought the total number of families recorded as displaced across the three provinces to 6,145 since the beginning of September.
The agency attributed the displacement to continued military escalation and growing concerns over civilian safety.
Field teams are continuing to register displaced families, verify their locations and assess their humanitarian needs, while coordinating with local authorities, aid organizations and partners, it said.
The unit called on humanitarian organizations and donors to expand their response, warning of growing needs for shelter, food, water, basic supplies and health services and the possibility of further displacement.
The displacement comes as fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has intensified in recent weeks on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda, alongside airstrikes targeting Houthi positions.
On Wednesday, government forces and the Houthis also reported clashes across Taiz, Al-Bayda, Al-Dhale and Al-Hudaydah, while government-aligned forces sent reinforcements to the strategic western coastal city of Mocha near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Russia hopes US-mediated Ukraine peace talks resume soon: Kremlin

Unknown Publisher

21:37:05 KST

Russia hopes that US-mediated peace talks on ending the war in Ukraine will resume soon, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has said.
No such talks between Russia and Ukraine have taken place since February, but President Donald Trump sent his negotiators to Moscow and then Kiev at the weekend in a bid to relaunch the stalled process.
Peskov on Wednesday was responding to a comment by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that it may be possible to draw up a roadmap to restart talks and work towards an acceptable outcome for both sides.
A huge gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the 4-1/2-year war, with Kiev rejecting Moscow's demands that it give up more territory.
Peskov said Moscow would not publicly discuss any specifics of a potential settlement, but there was a "confirmed political will" to resume talks.
"We hope that these negotiations will resume in the foreseeable future, and we remain in contact with our American counterparts," he said, a day after Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone.
Peskov added that the issue of exchanging prisoners between Russia and the US was "a constant item on the agenda", including between the two presidents. He noted that Russia had released one American prisoner, Robert Gilman, at Trump's request last month.
The two countries have traded prisoners at several points in the past few years.
The biggest such deal was in August 2024, when Russia got back eight prisoners held in the West, including a member of its FSB security service convicted of murder in Germany.
In exchange, 16 people were released from Russian and Belarusian jails. Among those freed by Moscow were prominent Russian dissidents and three US citizens, including Wall Street Journal correspondent Evan Gershkovich.

Estonian‑co‑produced film gets 7‑minute standing ovation in Venice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

Estonian‑co‑produced film gets 7‑minute standing ovation in Venice
The Estonian‑co‑produced feature "Woman Unknown" premiered Sunday at the ongoing Venice Film Festival's main competition, and got a seven‑and‑a‑half‑minute standing ovation.
"Woman Unknown" (Danish: Kvinde ukendt) is directed by Danish filmmaker May el‑Toukhy and is a psychological drama filmed primarily in Latvia. Of the 28 shooting days, 25 took place in Riga, with Estonia's Nafta Films among the co‑producers.
Esko Rips, CEO of Nafta Films and a co‑producer, said the film's selection among the 21 titles in the main competition is important recognition of the Estonian company's three years of work, which was a truly pan-Baltic states affair as it began in Lithuania and culminated in filming in Riga.
"For us, this confirms that operating in all three Baltic states gives us an advantage in producing international films. It allows us to find the best solution for each film in terms of financing, filming locations and creative needs," Rips said.
The Danish-Swedish-Latvian-Estonian co‑production was locally managed by Nafta Films' Latvian team, with co‑producers including Rips and Latvia's Madara Kalniņa.
"Woman Unknown" stands out in this year's competition also because el‑Toukhy is one of just two women directors from among the 21 competing films, ironically enough given women's invisibility and the limits imposed on them by society are central themes of the film itself.
"My film is about the invisibility of women. On the one hand, about objectification, and on the other, about how women are neither seen nor listened to," el‑Toukhy said at a film festival press conference.
"Woman Unknown" is set in Denmark at the end of World War Two. The story centers on Marie, a young nanny and housekeeper preparing to marry her wealthy employer, Christian, an older widower. A dark secret from her past — an intimate relationship with a German soldier during the Nazi occupation of Denmark — threatens her new life.
The film explores society's control over women's choices, their bodies and pasts, showing that the end of the war did not necessarily spell an end to all violence and condemnation.
Mathilde Arcel Fock ("Second victims," "Special Unit: The First Murder") stars in the lead role. The cast also includes Carsten Bjørnlun ("Barracuda Queens," "The Shooter").
The Venice Film Festival runs to Saturday.

Iran moves to accelerate UN Narcotic Drugs Commission membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:35:54 UTC
21:35:54 KST

Iran moves to accelerate UN Narcotic Drugs Commission membership
TEHRAN – Iranian officials have discussed ways to expedite the country’s membership in the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs and strengthen regional cooperation in this regard.
During the second meeting of the expert committee on international narcotics relations held on Monday, Brigadier General Hossein Zolfaqari, the secretary general of the Drug Control Headquarters (DCHQ), and Kazem Gharibabadi, the newly appointed chair of the expert committee on international narcotics relations, reviewed the reports on consultations conducted with the member states of the United Nations Economic and Social Council (UNESOC), underlining the need to continue diplomatic efforts in Tehran, Vienna, and New York, Mehr news agency reported.
They underscored the significance of raising international support for the country’s candidacy for membership of the Commission on Narcotic Drugs through holding meetings with the ambassadors of the targeted countries, and expounding on the country’s experiences, capacities, and achievements in the fight against narcotics.
The second expert meeting also focused on the current status of the building of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and the ways and frameworks for sustaining cooperation between Iran and the UNODC.
The officials highlighted that the future activities of the UNODC have to proceed based on mutual interests, and that Iran’s participation should not be limited to covering costs; the cooperation should involve research projects in areas like prevention, treatment, and capacity building.
The UNODC office in Tehran has to play a more active role in fostering cooperation with neighboring and regional countries and to leverage its capacity to shape joint regional programs, the officials noted.
During the meeting, the participants also called for enhancing the operational capacity of the regional center for the study and treatment of substance use disorder to hold training courses and promote ties among countries in the region.
The officials explored potential for the development of collaborations with BRICS and Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) member states, as well.
Supporting Iran’s counter-narcotics work pays off beyond its borders
The UNODC has released a report, emphasizing the need to support Iran in the battle against narcotics.
Supporting Iran’s counternarcotics work pays off beyond its borders, the report highlighted, saying it keeps drugs from reaching other regions, cuts into the money that funds organized crime, and supports public health by slowing the spread of addictive synthetic substances.
The main seizure of methamphetamine in and around Middle East and South-East Asia over the past few years has been reported in Iran, according to the report, which was published on Thursday.
Iranian seizure of methamphetamine increased from 30,393 kilos in 2022 to 40,453 kilos in 2025, placing the country at the forefront of the fight against drug trafficking.
In the first quarter of 2026 alone, Iranian authorities have intercepted 3,663 kilograms of methamphetamines destined for Europe and the Persian Gulf.
These weren’t just street-level busts. These were five intelligence-led operations targeting industrial-scale shipments originating in Afghanistan, evidence that trafficking networks in the region are shifting toward synthetic drugs.
While international attention has primarily focused on the vast region’s declining opium production, advanced criminal drug trafficking networks have successfully shifted toward manufacturing and exporting synthetic drugs such as methamphetamine, commonly known as meth. West Asia is now the epicenter of a synthetic drug boom.
Iran is strategically positioned along the “Afghanistan-West Asia corridor,” which serves as the primary trafficking route for these illicit commodities. The clear signal from Tehran is that these substantial shipments are being intercepted before they can reach international markets. Yet, sustained success will require enhanced international cooperation and support.
Each interception reduces the illicit financial flows that fund organized crime and slows the spread of synthetic drugs into new markets. These shipments are not merely statistics. Each seizure disrupts a supply chain that would otherwise put methamphetamine on the streets of Europe and the Persian Gulf, while cutting into the earnings of organized criminal networks.
Through its Country Partnership Programme as well as the Cooperation Framework with the Islamic Republic of Iran, UNODC supports the country's efforts in advancing border technology with the procurement of detection scanners, strengthening labs' forensic capabilities to identify new synthetic compounds, as well as regional intelligence sharing.
Sustained donor investment is critical to prevent this route from becoming a gateway for synthetic drugs. However, the scale of the challenge demands more than financial contributions—it requires a collective and sustainable approach by the international community. By supporting UNODC’s work in Iran, donor nations are investing in regional stability and international security, while also protecting their own borders from the flow of illicit substances.

Nurkulov’s detention term was due to expire on September 21. Consequently, Prosecutor Rimas Juodis asked the court last week to extend his detention for the maximum period of three months.
“The defendant no longer holds a residence permit in Lithuania, so if released, he would have to leave the country immediately. Furthermore, the offence he is charged with carries a mandatory prison sentence,” Juodis said.
The prosecutor told BNS that Nurkulov had arrived in Lithuania by plane just as his temporary residence permit was due to expire. He was detained at the airport in March, so he was unable to renew his permit, and it was automatically revoked.
Closing statements were due to be delivered in this case last week, but they had to be postponed when it emerged that some documents had been translated from Russian and Arabic not by a translator – who had been warned of the consequences of providing an inaccurate translation – but by a translation app.
It was therefore decided that the translations of the aforementioned documents, which will be carried out in accordance with the law, should be submitted at the next hearing.
Nurkulov faces up to 10 years in prison.

Explainer-Why is US ally Iraq unable to disarm Iran's militia allies?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:32:23 UTC
21:32:23 KST

Explainer-Why is US ally Iraq unable to disarm Iran's militia allies?
DUBAI/BAGHDAD, Sept 9 - Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi could face a credibility crisis if Iran-backed Shi'ite militias fail to heed his call to hand over their weapons to the state.
After a July meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, Zaidi pledged to disarm the powerful groups by September 30, the same date scheduled for the withdrawal of the remaining U.S.-led international coalition forces from Iraq.
But he faces strong resistance from Iran's proxies in Iraq, who have supported Tehran by attacking U.S. targets in the Middle East war.
WHY IS ZAIDI FACING OBSTACLES?
In 2025, several powerful Iranian-backed militia groups in Iraq indicated they were prepared to disarm for the first time to avert the threat of an escalating conflict with the U.S. Trump administration.
But their pledges never materialized, leaving Zaidi with the delicate task of trying to rein in these groups, who report to Iran's elite Revolutionary Guards, after he took office in May.
Zaidi, a multimillionaire, has received far more support from a U.S. president than many of his predecessors. But, like all Iraqi leaders, he also needs the backing of Iran, which has steadily gained vast influence in the country through its ties to Shi'ite militias and politicians. So he has to tread cautiously.
On August 17, special forces reporting directly to the prime minister arrested the intelligence chief of Harakat al-Nujaba, an Iran-aligned faction that the U.S. has designated a terrorist organisation, on accusations of involvement in drone attacks against U.S. interests, according to a security document reviewed by Reuters and three government sources.
The detention, which lasted 48 hours, triggered threats of retaliation from the group and prompted intervention by senior Shi'ite politicians who helped defuse tensions.
A week later, Iraqi special forces arrested four militia members, including a local commander, over allegations they facilitated attacks on U.S. interests, underscoring the political and security obstacles facing the prime minister's disarmament campaign.
Senior Shi'ite politicians have warned that tough measures against the militias will make disarmament impossible and could lead to instability. They argue that armed groups cannot hand in their weapons at a time when they are supporting Tehran in the war against the United States. Militias were also reluctant in the past, saying they could not surrender weapons as long as U.S.-led coalition forces remain in Iraq.
WHAT DO THE MILITIAS WANT?
Five Iran-aligned armed groups have categorically rejected the government's September 30 deadline to surrender their weapons, dissolve their organizations, and integrate into state security forces, according to four Shi'ite political sources and three security sources familiar with the disarmament effort.
In August, the most powerful militia, Kataib Hezbollah, issued a statement criticizing Zaidi and set conditions for dialogue, including guarantees that American forces would never return and measures that would rid Iraq of any U.S. influence on political or economic decision-making.
HOW POWERFUL ARE THE ARMED GROUPS?
The militias are part of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of about 10 hardline Shi'ite armed factions that collectively command about 50,000 fighters and arsenals that include long-range missiles and anti-aircraft weapons, according to two security officials who monitor militias' activities.
The Resistance group, a key pillar of Iran's network of regional proxy forces, has claimed responsibility for dozens of missile and drone attacks on Israel and U.S. forces in Iraq and Syria in recent years.
The militias have become increasingly sophisticated in carrying out precise drone attacks. These groups also have business interests in construction, real estate and currency exchange houses. REUTERS

Bank of Russia may keep key rate at 14% at its next meeting — consensus forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:31:58 UTC
21:31:58 KST

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia’s Board of Directors may keep the key rate unchanged at 14% per annum at its upcoming meeting on September 11, according to 18 of 19 experts surveyed by TASS. Analysts noted that accelerating underlying inflation, fuel shortages, a weaker ruble, and uncertainty over budget parameters are limiting the scope for further monetary policy easing.
At its previous meeting in July, the Bank of Russia cut the key rate for the fifth consecutive time since the beginning of the year, lowering it by 0.25 percentage points to 14% per annum. The regulator said that the acceleration in price growth during the summer months was largely attributable to one-off factors, while underlying inflation indicators remained within an annualized range of 4-5%. At the same time, the Bank of Russia raised its 2026 inflation forecast to 6-7% and noted the need for a more gradual reduction in the key rate.
In late August, Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Alexey Zabotkin noted that the room for a rate cut had already narrowed in July and that further decisions would depend on the actual situation. Adviser to the Bank of Russia Governor Kirill Tremasov also said that the situation on the fuel market should become clearer and more predictable by the regulator’s October meeting, while it was still too early to draw conclusions.
According to analysts expecting a pause, the available data taken together point toward keeping the rate at 14%. A 25-basis-point cut remains the alternative.
"The balance of factors currently does not favor further easing. The acceleration in core inflation that began in July continued in August. Judging by weekly data, the current pace of price declines is not yet sufficient to reach the 4% target. Corporate lending has accelerated again. M2 money supply growth remains at around 13%, compared with the Bank of Russia’s forecast range of 7-12%, while the ruble has weakened by more than 8% against the dollar and the yuan since the beginning of August," portfolio manager at Alfa Capital Management Company Alexey Kornev said.
According to him, the situation on the fuel market remains an additional pro-inflationary factor. "At its previous meeting, the regulator proceeded from the assumption that the fuel shortage was temporary, but it cannot yet be said that the situation has fully normalized," Kornev added.
Inflation limits room for rate cuts
Sovcombank Chief Analyst Mikhail Vasilyev pointed to an acceleration in both headline and core inflation. "The Bank of Russia reported that seasonally adjusted inflation stood at 11.6% in July after 11.4% in June, while core inflation rose to 7% in July from 5.3% in June. Judging by weekly data, we forecast that seasonally adjusted inflation will be around 7% in August. As a result, three-month seasonally adjusted inflation for June-August is currently running at around 10%," he noted. According to Vasilyev, another argument in favor of a pause is money supply growth of around 13% year-on-year, exceeding the Bank of Russia’s 7-12% forecast.
Olga Belenkaya, head of macroeconomic analysis at Finam Financial Group, believes that the main arguments in favor of a pause could include insufficient data to reassess the future rate trajectory and a certain increase in pro-inflationary risks. "The gradual pass-through of higher transportation costs and the weaker ruble into prices, the Bank of Russia’s conclusion that the underlying component of inflation also increased based on July data, and signs of elevated price pressure in the manufacturing sector" also support a pause, she noted.
The regulator’s decision could be complicated by the lack of complete inflation data for August. "Rosstat will publish the data on the same day, but later, at 7:00 p.m. Meanwhile, it is full-month data covering a broad sample of goods and services that the Bank of Russia considers the most representative and reliable, particularly for assessing underlying inflation," Belenkaya added.
Freedom Global Lead Analyst Natalia Milchakova estimates the probability of the rate remaining at 14% at around 60%, compared with a 40% probability of a cut to 13.75%. According to her, factors supporting a pause include the fuel situation, persistently high inflation expectations among households and the weakening ruble.
A minimal cut remains on the table
The only survey participant to name a rate cut as the baseline scenario was Dmitry Kulikov, Senior Director of the Sovereign and Regional Ratings Group at ACRA. In his view, the Bank of Russia could take the opportunity to lower the rate by 25 basis points to 13.75% before new budget projections are published.
"Before the new budget plans are published, the Bank of Russia has an opportunity to take another 0.25-percentage-point step downward without having to provide an additional detailed explanation of its response to fiscal stimulus. It seems to me that this opportunity will be used," Kulikov noted.
Analysts expecting a pause also see arguments in favor of a cautious cut. Gazprombank Chief Economist Pavel Biryukov pointed to a possible slowdown in core inflation in August and weaker consumer demand. "Preliminary estimates of core inflation in August look better than the Bank of Russia’s projected trajectory. In July, seasonally adjusted annualized core inflation accelerated to 7% from around 5% in May-June. However, according to our estimates based on Rosstat’s weekly data, core inflation may have returned to 5% in August," he noted.
"Household inflation expectations corrected to 13.7% in August after the July spike. Growth in retail lending slowed to 0.5% month-on-month in July from 0.9% in June. Leading indicators point to a possible weakening in demand dynamics in the second half of the year," Biryukov added.
According to T-Investments Chief Economist Sofia Donets, the economy has returned to a slowdown since the July meeting, business sentiment has remained weak, and wage growth has fallen below 10% for the first time since 2021. "Inflation and inflation expectations are moving in line with the Bank of Russia’s forecasts, but risks are being amplified by a renewed fuel shortage, geopolitical tensions, uncertainty surrounding the budget and an 11% weakening of the ruble. Therefore, we expect the key rate to remain at 14% on September 11, with a cut to 13.75% as the most likely alternative," Donets noted.
Expectations of a rate cut
Anatoly Aksakov, Chairman of the State Duma Committee on the Financial Market, told TASS that the likelihood of a 0.25-percentage-point key rate cut at the September meeting had increased amid the current slowdown in inflation. In his view, such a move would be cautious but would send a clear signal to the market.
Earlier, on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum, Sberbank CEO Herman Gref forecast that the key rate would decline in increments of 25-50 basis points to 13-13.5% by the end of this year. VTB CEO Andrey Kostin told reporters that he did not expect a pause at the September meeting and believed the rate would continue to decline gradually.
VTB Group Chief Economist Rodion Latypov, however, considers a pause at the September meeting more likely, although he expects the rate-cutting cycle to continue over the medium term. In his view, inflation currently exceeding target levels is due to temporary supply shocks. "We consider them temporary, so we expect the key rate-cutting cycle to continue over the medium term. A pause at the September meeting is possible and currently appears more likely, but the Bank of Russia will also consider the possibility of a 25-basis-point key rate cut," he noted.
Another half-point by year-end
Most analysts expecting a pause in September believe that the Bank of Russia will be able to resume rate cuts at its key policy meeting on October 23, when more information will be available on budget parameters and the impact of the fuel shortage on inflation.
"By the end of the year, the key rate could decline to 13.5% - we expect the regulator to continue gradually easing monetary policy in order to minimize the risks of excessive cooling of the economy. Such a trajectory is also consistent with the Bank of Russia’s own baseline scenario published in July," Senior Interest Rate and Debt Market Strategist at SberCIB Investment Research Igor Rapokhin said.
Sovcombank’s Vasilyev has a similar assessment. "In our baseline scenario - assuming no change in the geopolitical situation, no deterioration in the fuel market and no negative surprises from the budget - we expect the Bank of Russia to cut the key rate by 25 basis points to 13.75% at its next meeting on October 23. We forecast that the key rate will decline to 13.5% by the end of the year," he noted.
At the same time, according to Vasilyev, the risks are skewed toward a higher rate. In a risk scenario, the Bank of Russia could keep it at 14% through the end of the year in the event of a deterioration in the geopolitical situation, a prolonged fuel shortage, further ruble weakness or a more significant widening of the budget deficit.
Sergey Klisenko, Managing Director of the National Rating Agency’s Rating Service, also believes that a rate cut could be postponed until October or December. In his assessment, another wave of fuel shortages in August is delaying the normalization of supply and the restoration of production capacity compared with forecasts made one to one and a half months ago. "We believe the Bank of Russia will refrain from cutting the rate in September, postponing it either until the key policy meeting in October, when its medium-term forecast will also be updated, or until December," he concluded.

New Trajan's Baths museum opens: restored Great Mosaic and Painted City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:31:15 UTC
21:31:15 KST

Trajan’s Baths in Colle Oppio will host a new museum where visitors can admire two major Roman works, the Great Mosaic and the Painted City. Entries will be limited to protect them.
From the weekend of 12 and 13 September, visitors in Rome will be able to admire the largest partially intact Roman-era fresco and mosaic ever discovered, in the heart of Trajan's Baths, where the new museum will be inaugurated.
The announcement was made by Rome's mayor, Roberto Gualtieri, at Colle Oppio, at the conclusion of restoration work on the large exedra and the underground gallery that houses the two previously unseen works.
The project was carried out as part of the PNRR – Caput Mundi programme.
These are the large mosaic "The Muse and the Philosopher" and the fresco "The Painted City", described by Gualtieri as a unique ensemble, a stratification that recounts more than a century of archaeological history, from the Neronian-Flavian age to that of Trajan.
The Painted City and the Great Mosaic
Trajan's Baths were designed by Apollodorus of Damascus at the request of Emperor Trajan. Inaugurated on 22 June AD 109, they covered around 60,000 square metres and included bathing facilities, porticoes and spaces for physical and cultural activities and leisure time. The construction also incorporated older structures, including part of the Domus Aurea, which make it possible to trace the complex archaeological stratification.
The Painted City is a ten-square-metre fresco belonging to a building that predates Trajan's Baths, dating from the first century AD, depicting a city seen from above. Discovered in 1998, it is "perhaps the largest surviving wall-fresco representation of a view of a city, with its insulae and a series of features of outstanding beauty but also of great historical and documentary importance", the mayor explained.
In the monumental wall mosaic "The Muse and the Philosopher", located in a large hall overlooking a nymphaeum, a Roman harbour is depicted in detail. It is not known whether it is real or imaginary, although some scholars have suggested it could be the harbour of Claudius.
Already partially visible, after restoration the exposed section, which allows visitors to admire "the philosopher and other figures of extraordinary artistic quality", as Gualtieri put it, reaches five metres in height. However, finds made beneath the decoration have made it possible to reconstruct an original space that was much taller, with walls that must have risen to around twelve metres.
The mayor added: "These are the two star attractions, truly unique, which will be on display while their surroundings continue to be excavated, because the Superintendency will carry on with its research work".
Restricted visits to preserve the artistic heritage
To assess the impact of visitor numbers on the conservation of the works, the first visits will be organised on an experimental basis for small groups at weekends only, with free guided tours by reservation, starting on 12 and 13 September. From 2 October the site will be open to visitors from Friday to Sunday. There will be six time slots a day, with a maximum of 15 people at a time.
During the restoration, panoramic rest areas and new pedestrian routes were also created within the complex, along with a new tiered seating system designed to host concerts, conferences and events.

====================================================================================================

El Niño 2026-27: How extreme weather could hit the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:31:07 UTC
21:31:07 KST

Breadcrumb
A 'supercharged' El Niño is coming: How it could hit the Middle East
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up." This is the sharp warning issued by the United Nations’s Secretary-General, António Guterres, following a seasonal forecast published by the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) on September 3.
The WMO, a UN agency, is "the world's most authoritative source of information for governments and decision-makers" on global weather patterns. Its seasonal updates aggregate findings shared by meteorologists and experts around the globe.
And they all point in one direction: the coming months will unfold under the looming shadow of a "supersized" meteorological event, El Niño, which could spark extreme weather worldwide, including floods and landslides.
According to the WMO, this natural phenomenon, which cyclically affects global weather patterns, could be the strongest in 70 years.
In the Middle East and North Africa, analysts warn that this supersized El Niño could compound existing humanitarian crises.
Sudan, Palestine, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen are all at "high risk" of facing humanitarian knock-on effects linked to floods and excess rainfall.
Elsewhere in the Levant and the Gulf, other countries will face above-average temperatures and rainfall, which could also lead to floods.
What is El Niño?
Once every few years, a climate phenomenon known as “El Niño” develops over the tropical Pacific. It is is caracterised by higher-than-usual sea surface temperatures and a change in dominant winds.
Its effects vary from one occurrence to the next, but generally, El Niño pushes weather patterns around the world to extremes.
In certain regions, it causes and intensifies droughts, while in others, it leads to stronger typhoons and floods.
While El Niño is generally the bearer of bad news, this year it is more feared than usual.
According to the WMO, this year's El Niño is "fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific". Sea surface temperatures were already 2.2 to 2.6 degrees Celsius above average in the Pacific Ocean by mid-August, while below-water temperatures reached more than 8 degrees Celsius above average.
This anomaly in temperatures is enough to convince meteorologists, with an "exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100%", that El Niño will last until February 2027 at least.
It should strengthen during the fall of 2026 and peak towards "the end of the year," but its climate impacts will last "well into 2027."
"This exceptional El Niño demands exceptional preparation and response," warned the WMO Secretary General, Celeste Saulo, in a press release.
"Never before in the 50-year history of the World Meteorological Organisation have we launched such a major mobilisation."
What does this mean for the Middle East?
Given the unusual intensity of this year's episode, experts fear exceptional impacts. According to the WMO’s forecasts, sea surface temperatures in the Pacific could eventually reach 4 degrees Celsius above average, making it the most intense El Niño recorded since the 1950s.
"El Niño should not be considered in isolation," explains Vanessa Cardamone, a climate analysis consultant with the humanitarian think tank ACAPS.
"It interacts with climate change and global warming. This year, we have abnormally high temperatures across land, oceans and seas, and this is something that also contributes to influencing precipitation patterns and extreme precipitation events."
But El Niño’s impact will vary greatly by region, and local effects are difficult to anticipate.
What we know for sure is that temperatures will be above average everywhere, including the Middle East, from September to November 2026.
According to Vanessa Cardamone, these abnormally high temperatures can increase the risk of tropical-like formations forming above the Mediterranean Sea.
Known as "Medicanes", these Mediterranean mini-hurricanes can have a big impact, as the one that recently hit Libya in March 2026 did.
But beyond this, it’s hard to say what impact El Niño will have specifically in the Middle East.
"Evidence about the impact of El Niño in the region is pretty recent and scattered," Cardamone adds.
Recent studies on Morocco show that it typically leads to reduced precipitation, with an associated decrease in wheat production (around 30%).
On the contrary, the Levant region is expected to receive significantly more water than usual, especially in Syria and Iraq.
This can mean good news for farmers, as more rain can lead to better harvests. But it could also cause natural disasters.
"Based on experience, when we see this pattern, we can anticipate some related hazards, mainly floods," says Cardamone.
In Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Iran, authorities and humanitarian actors should prepare for an at-risk winter.
"In regions that still host internally displaced persons and refugees, I would flag an increased risk of waterborne diseases because floods typically destroy sanitation infrastructure," adds Cardamone.
What about the Gulf and the Horn of Africa?
Countries in the Gulf should also receive more rain than usual.
Yemen is particularly exposed to flood risk, as it lies at the intersection of the Gulf and the Horn of Africa, where even more extreme precipitation is expected.
"We know that the rainy season could be particularly destructive this year. We anticipate floods between October and December. Coastal areas of Yemen, particularly the southwest, could also experience flooding," explains Cardamone.
A recent analysis released in July 2026 by ACAPS lists the main humanitarian impacts that El Niño could have in the region.
Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan are among the countries considered at highest risk worldwide, because in countries that are already dealing with the fallout of armed conflict, ACAPS foresees that "environmental pressures from climate extremes will intersect with conflict, displacement, and socioeconomic crises, creating cascading shocks and increasing the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance."
Finally, the region as a whole could also be affected by the indirect effects of El Niño, such as rising food prices linked to a global decline in food production.
In 2015-2016, an El Niño episode "triggered the worst drought in southern Africa in 35 years, cutting regional maize production by roughly 25% and worsening food insecurity," the WMO notes.
Anticipating this risk, the World Food Programme warns that "this 2026-2027 El Niño could push at least 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027."
As of early August 2026, the World Food Programme did not list any country in the Middle East or the Gulf among the 22 countries "at high risk" of experiencing severe droughts or floods, though Sudan, South Sudan, and Somalia are on the list.
But if the global production of food staples dives down, effects will likely be felt everywhere.
Lyse Mauvais is a freelance journalist based in southern France, after four years in the MENA region covering Jordan, Syria and Iraq. She focuses on environmental and climate issues around the Mediterranean

Across China: In Tianjin, summer cool comes with greener way of life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:30:59 CST
21:30:59 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Tuane van der Merwe came to north China's Tianjin Municipality with her parents looking for a break from the summer heat. What the South African family found was more than cool air.
From city parks and mountain retreats to electric vehicles and convenient transport options, Van der Merwe found that greener choices were simply part of everyday life.
Van der Merwe, an English teacher who has lived in China for three and a half years, was showing her parents around Tianjin during one of their regular visits.
In the city, pocket parks dot street corners, greenways wind through neighborhoods, and public green spaces are never far from where people live.
"In the cities here, you can see the city and nature together as one," Van der Merwe said. "That makes the air cleaner and makes the environment healthier."
The greenery took on a different form when the family traveled north to Jizhou District, where city streets gave way to wooded hills and rural homestays.
For Van der Merwe, preserving such places is important, even as cities bring more nature into everyday life. "There has to be some space for city people to come and relax," she said.
Official data show that green coverage in China's urban built-up areas has exceeded 43 percent, while per capita park green space has reached 15.91 square meters. In the first half of this year, construction began on more than 2,800 pocket parks and 2,450 kilometers of urban greenways, while about 7,500 hectares of urban parks and green spaces were renovated or upgraded.
What stood out was how greenery extended beyond parks and scenic spots. Wherever she went, Van der Merwe said, nature seemed to be incorporated into the surroundings.
"Nature is a big part of it," she said.
Nature, however, was only one part of the family's search for summer comfort. Back at their homestay in Jizhou, they switched on the air conditioner. The room quickly cooled.
"China is hot for us in summer, but the air-conditioning system works perfectly," Van der Merwe said. "I'm not overheating."
Behind that everyday comfort is a power system increasingly accommodating renewable energy.
"Reliable grid support is essential to this kind of 'air-conditioning freedom,' as is the growing supply of green electricity," said Liu Chang, an official responsible for new energy trading management at the Tianjin Power Exchange Center.
As power grid technology improves and green electricity trading expands, more clean electricity is entering the power system and serving households and businesses, Liu said.
By the end of July, Tianjin had traded 15.77 billion kilowatt-hours of green electricity in 2026, accounting for 41.46 percent of its directly traded electricity.
China is seeking to make its power system greener and less reliant on fossil fuels. Under a plan for the 2026-2030 period issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration in July, non-fossil energy is expected to account for 50 percent of the country's electricity generation by 2030, with the power system capable of integrating more than 2.8 billion kilowatts of installed new-energy capacity.
For the Van der Merwes, the greener experience continued once they were back on the road.
On Tianjin's streets, new energy vehicles are common and electric buses pull quietly into stops. For shorter journeys, shared bicycles are readily available. Subways, buses and ride-hailing services offer other choices, while high-speed rail links Tianjin with cities further afield.
Van der Merwe said the variety itself stood out, with these options helping reduce emissions while making urban life more convenient and green travel easier.
"You don't have to have your own car. You don't have to pay a lot of money to get to a place," she said. "You can rent a bike from the street, you can use the bus, you can go by subway, or you can just order a (ride-hailing car from) Didi."
More than 200 million passenger trips are made by green modes of transport each day in China, according to the Ministry of Transport. They include around 100 million trips by urban rail transit, another 100 million by bus and 24 million by shared bicycle.
Across the journey, many of the greener choices the family encountered were already part of ordinary daily life. Parks sat close to residential communities, public transport was readily available, and reliable electricity supported everyday comfort.
The family came to Tianjin in search of relief from the summer heat. By the end of the trip, their memories of "cool" extended beyond mountain breezes and air conditioning to the greener everyday scenes they had encountered along the way. ■

UNESCO warns of continued rise in attacks on schools worldwide

PARIS, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) expressed its concern Wednesday over the continued rise in attacks on schools around the world, with the latest global data revealing an alarming escalation in such attacks in 2025.
On the occasion of the International Day to Protect Education from Attack, UNESCO said in a press release that 1,680 attacks on schools were verified by the United Nations in 2025, an increase of 33 percent compared to 1,265 attacks in 2024.
More broadly, an estimated 258 million children and adolescents have had their education disrupted by crises worldwide, including 93 million who are entirely out of school, UNESCO said.
Nearly 80 percent of all out-of-school crisis-affected children, some 74 million, live in just 20 countries facing the world's most severe crises, UNESCO said. The organization noted that barriers to learning are steepest for the most vulnerable within these settings, with 74 percent of refugee children, 52 percent of internally displaced children and 45 percent of children with disabilities out of school.
UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany said schools and universities must always be protected, calling on all parties to conflicts to respect international law and ensure that education can continue in safety and dignity, even in the midst of crisis.
The International Day to Protect Education from Attack was established by a unanimous decision of the United Nations General Assembly in 2020, with September 9 designated as the annual observance. ■

Letter from China: The pulse of black soil, where every grain counts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:30:38 CST
21:30:38 KST

by Xinhua writer Ji Hang
HARBIN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- As our buses rolled across the endless plains of northeast China's Heilongjiang, golden-green rice paddies along the road stretched to every horizon. Harvest was still about three weeks away, yet the fields already hummed with anticipation.
Last week, I joined a reporting trip to explore the province's agriculture, visiting farms and agricultural enterprises.
Before arriving, I was told that one in every nine bowls of grain eaten across China comes from Heilongjiang, China's top grain-producing province for 16 consecutive years. I kept wondering: what is the secret behind its output?
During the trip, what struck me most was not the scale, but something intelligent: smart agriculture; something innovative: customized farming; and something invisible: an attachment to the land.
The province's rise to the top did not happen overnight. Behind this record is a highly mechanized farming system, with the comprehensive mechanization rate for plowing, sowing and harvesting reaching 99.28 percent.
Now, the province is taking the next step toward smarter farming. From AI-powered crop monitoring and drones to upgraded agricultural machinery, technology is helping farmers make more precise decisions and boost efficiency.
Traditionally, farming meant being out in the fields, rain or shine. Farmers walked the paddies, pinching soil between their fingers to guess its moisture, squinting at leaves for signs of blight.
But today, agricultural service apps, serving as digital agronomists and helpers, enable farmers to monitor crop growth, soil moisture and pest risks, and even manage watering from their living rooms.
Farmers can get an AI diagnosis in seconds by uploading a photo of a yellowing leaf. When they need machinery, apps match them with nearby harvesters, which they told me they could summon as easily as hailing a taxi online.
Heilongjiang's rice breeders describe seeds as "the chip of agriculture." For years, they faced what they called an "impossible triangle": varieties tasted wonderful but yielded poorly and lacked resistance; high-yielding and resilient varieties, however, often tasted bland.
To break through this bottleneck, the province has spent years refining its seed selection and breeding, successfully developing a new generation of varieties that are flavorful, resilient and high-yielding.
What I have seen so far shows how deeply Heilongjiang cares about growing rice well. Yet, to truly sell it well, the province is stepping up its game, relying on customized models and upgrading the industrial chain.
"I have a plot in Heilongjiang" and "You name it, we'll grow it" were phrases I heard many times during this trip. Clearly, Heilongjiang is betting on demand-driven, custom-tailored farming.
For decades, the routine was simple: consumers bought whatever was planted. Now, a growing number of enterprises are securing orders even before a single seed is sown.
At Qiaofu Dayuan Agricultural Co., Ltd. in Wuchang, a renowned rice-growing area in the province, I walked past rows of paddies where each plot reserved for customized orders carried a marker with the client's name.
Qiao Wenzhi, head of the company, explained that, from paddy to plate, customers can follow their rice at every major stage of production through video check-ins and a traceability system.
Qiao added that the company redesigned its offerings last year so that consumers can easily customize a plot size that aligns with their actual consumption.
For the province, which recorded its 22nd consecutive bumper harvest with a record-breaking grain output of 82 million tonnes last year, the goal is clear: maximize the value of every single grain across the entire industrial chain.
Stepping into the exhibition room of Heilongjiang Heliang Agriculture Co., Ltd., I found the array of coarse grains, packaged in various shapes and sizes, nothing short of astonishing.
To cater to modern lifestyles, the company has developed over 800 products from more than 70 varieties of grains. From ready-to-eat congee to functional multigrain meals tailored for fitness enthusiasts, the offerings are designed for convenience and health.
The company's vice president, Su Meili, told us it produces over 1,000 packaging designs a year, blending visual appeal with taste. "We want people to see the packaging and instantly feel that the food will be delicious," she said.
Hu Jinyou, a professor at China Agricultural University who joined our trip, told me that as a new generation of well-educated farmers enters the fields, digital management and innovation are gradually becoming the norm.
Zhang Fang, head of Heliang Agriculture, perfectly embodies this wave. After graduating from university, she returned to her hometown's black soil. The post-80s native has since amassed over 17 million followers online, where she frequently shares stories about rice, coarse grains, and the land that raised her.
Her attachment to the black soil is far from unique. During the trip, I kept sensing the same pull among locals: "This land is in our blood."
To draw more people, especially the younger generation, closer to agriculture, the province is going well beyond product innovation and transforming vast paddies into thriving tourism destinations.
Across the fields, sprawling rice paddy art has turned farmland into open-air galleries, while hands-on farming experiences invite visitors to transplant seedlings and harvest rice.
It is a simple but powerful idea: let people see and touch the land, and the connection will follow.
Standing atop the observation tower at dusk, watching the golden light bathe the living canvas below, I felt, for a moment, the same attachment to the land that so many here share. ■

What 13 minutes in Nepal can teach us about acting before disaster strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:30:33 UTC
21:30:33 KST

Share & more
Rajendra Dawadi had to make a decision in an instant. Warned that floodwaters were racing towards his school in Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, the headmaster had no way of knowing how much time he had, nor whether the floodwaters would reach his school. He did not hesitate and evacuated more than 900 students and 16 staff to higher ground.
Approximately 13 minutes later, a wall of water, mud, and debris swept through the area, destroying the school.
Dawadi acted before he knew for certain what was coming. His calculation was simple. If the warning proved wrong, his students would miss a day of school. If it was right and he did nothing, hundreds of children could die.
The instinct to act while there is still time, despite uncertainty, is at the heart of anticipatory action. Investing ahead of known risks has been shown to save lives and reduce losses. But acting ahead requires accepting that some forecasts will never provide complete certainty, and that waiting to act can carry far higher consequences.
Nepal shows what formal systems can and cannot do
Nepal is hardly a newcomer to acting ahead of disasters. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology introduced the flood early warning system in the 1990s, combining both high-tech river level monitoring stations with simpler community-based systems for detecting rising waters and disseminating warnings.
In 2022, the government held the first national dialogue on anticipatory action, and this year endorsed a national policy. Humanitarian organisations have been experimenting with anticipatory approaches for more than a decade, releasing pre-arranged emergency funding at least twice for flood response.
The August disaster, however, fell outside of the mainly weather-related monsoon flooding that these mechanisms were designed to anticipate and warn against. A huge section of glacier and surrounding bedrock collapsed high in Tibet, sending ice, rock, and debris into the river system and generating a catastrophic flood that travelled nearly 100 kilometres downstream. Automatic monitoring stations along the upper Bhotekoshi River were meant to detect rising water and alert communities downstream, but the flood moved so quickly that monitoring stations inside Nepal were destroyed before they could transmit a warning. The community-level river gauges that gradually measured river behaviour were also too slow for a flood travelling at an average speed of 193 kilometres per hour.
Some of these limitations were already understood. A 2023 review of Nepal’s anticipatory action experience raised concerns about the reliability of forecasts and called for greater flexibility to combine scientific triggers with human judgement and changing conditions on the ground. A later study in 2025 found their early warning messaging system frequently did not prompt the necessary actions to save lives and protect assets.
What happened at Dawadi’s school shows why this matters. The warning that saved Dawadi’s students did not come through the formal monitoring or early warning system. A relative upstream called the school accountant. Teachers received calls from family and friends. A parent arrived to collect her child. Dawadi ordered the evacuation. Teachers, parents, and others then helped get the children uphill. Many others were not so fortunate. Elsewhere along the flood’s path, people had almost no time to react.
Forecasting and early warning technology remain essential, but they have to be matched by readiness at the community level – evacuation plans, trusted communication networks, prepared local institutions and people able to act when information arrives.
Those community connections are part of the infrastructure of disaster readiness. I saw their importance when I lived in Japan and studied how the country prepares for disasters in 2019. Japan is famous for its enormous investment in seawalls, flood defences, earthquake-resistant buildings and sophisticated warning systems. But some of its most important investments are far simpler.
Children learn about disaster risk from kindergarten. Communities practise evacuations. Families are encouraged to have a go-bag ready at all times. Residents identify neighbours who may need help. Survivors share their experiences with communities facing similar hazards.
Japan also shows the limits of relying too heavily on infrastructure and more formal warning systems. During severe 2018 flooding in Mabi, a district in western Japan situated near two rivers, embankments were overwhelmed and mobile-phone warnings failed to reach some of the elderly people most at risk. Research after the Mabi flood and the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and Tsunami found that some residents delayed evacuating because they believed physical defences would protect them.
Forecasting and early warning technology remain essential, but they have to be matched by readiness at the community level – evacuation plans, trusted communication networks, prepared local institutions and people able to act when information arrives. These investments may be less visible than satellites, monitoring stations or dams, but they can determine whether a warning actually saves a life.
Schools are an important part of that community readiness. My research on education and anticipatory action with the Geneva Global Hub for Education in Emergencies in 2024 found much the same thing that Dawadi’s experience demonstrates: Schools can play a critical role in turning early warnings into action. They reach children and families every day, while teachers are often trusted community leaders who can communicate risks, organise evacuations, and connect formal warning systems with local knowledge. Disaster education also gives children knowledge they take home and carry into adulthood, strengthening the ability of entire communities to respond to future crises.
Governments, donors, and aid agencies must become more comfortable spending money before they can be certain a crisis will unfold as forecast.
Scientists are still grappling with how to predict rock-ice avalanches like the one in Nepal. But as glacial flooding increases as a result of global warming, they warn that these events are expected to be more common around the world. Anticipatory approaches and funding will need to adapt to include these emerging risks while investing more in the local institutions and relationships that can turn warnings into action.
Yet humanitarian financing still runs overwhelmingly in the opposite direction. Ninety-nine percent of international humanitarian funding still flows after disasters happen and only about 12% of total anticipatory action funding between 2022 and 2023 involved those organisations closest to communities. In a time of collapsing budgets and hyper-prioritisation, it is urgent to rethink whether scarce resources are being deployed where – and when – they can have the greatest effect.
Some actions may prove unnecessary. Sometimes, supplies will be moved for a flood that changes course. Cash may be released ahead of a drought that proves less severe than expected. Schools may close for storms that never arrive. That does not make those decisions bad ones. Governments, donors, and aid agencies must become more comfortable spending money before they can be certain a crisis will unfold as forecast. The cost of acting unnecessarily can be far smaller than the cost of acting too late.
Dawadi understood that tradeoff.

Cantonal police confirmed to local media that a "serious workplace accident" had occurred at the plant, resulting from "an event that affected part of the structure" and causing "serious injuries to two people".
Initial reports indicated that a section of the building had collapsed, with two individuals caught in the incident. The cause of the explosion remains under investigation.
The old Ritom power plant, originally built in 1917, was undergoing renovation as part of a broader redevelopment project for the facility. New electrical machinery had recently been installed in the old section where the accident occurred. The construction site for the new power plant is expected to be completed in the coming months.
A major emergency response was launched, with firefighters, paramedics and a REGA (Swiss Air Rescue) rescue helicopter deployed to the scene. Police have cordoned off the area. Externally, no visible damage to the structure has been reported.
Authorities continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding the explosion. Further updates are expected as the inquiry progresses. ■
