The European Union has reiterated that Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, describing them as a major obstacle to peace and the viability of a two-state solution.
“We take note of the announcement of eight member states — together with the UK, Canada, Iceland and Norway — to impose national restrictions on trade with illegal settlements,” EU Commission spokesperson for foreign affairs Anouar El Anouni said.
“The EU’s longstanding position is clear: settlements are illegal under international law. They constitute an obstacle to peace and to the viability of the two-state solution,” he added.
The EU considers Israeli settlements established in the occupied Palestinian territory after June 1967 to be illegal.
Goods originating from those settlements are not eligible for preferential tariff treatment under the EU-Israel trade framework, El Anouni said.
European countries step up trade restrictions
France, the UK, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden, along with Canada, have announced plans to impose national restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements and support broader European measures.
In a joint declaration, the countries said conditions in the occupied West Bank are “rapidly deteriorating,” citing increased settler violence and continued illegal settlement expansion.
They opposed any move towards the annexation of Palestinian land or the forced displacement of Palestinians and called on Israel to halt settlement expansion and the extension of civilian administrative powers in the occupied West Bank.
The countries also called for accountability for those responsible for illegal settler violence and investigations into allegations involving Israeli forces.
Calls grow for tougher EU action
Pressure is mounting on the EU to go beyond restrictions on settlement goods and take broader action through its trade relationship with Israel.
Several European governments, lawmakers and civil society groups have called for the EU-Israel Association Agreement to be reviewed or suspended, arguing that the bloc should use its economic ties with Israel to address settlement expansion and policies towards Palestinians.
However, EU-wide trade measures require agreement among member states, and divisions within the bloc have complicated efforts to adopt a common approach.
The EU has not imposed a general import ban on goods from Israeli settlements, but it excludes settlement products from preferential trade treatment and continues to consider options for broader measures.

Qeshm, Taining Geoparks partner for natural heritage, sustainable development
TEHRAN - Iran’s Qeshm Island Geopark and China’s Taining Geopark have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to help protect geological and natural heritage, while promoting sustainable development and supporting local communities.
The MOU was signed by the representatives of the two geoparks on the third day of the 9th Asia Pacific Geoparks Network (APGN) Symposium 2026, which is taking place in Langkawi UNESCO Global Geopark, Malaysia, from September 4 to 12.
It focuses on several areas, including the exchange of expertise in geopark management, the sharing of technical and specialized knowledge, conducting joint research projects, organizing collaborative training courses, and strengthening ties among local communities, geotourism operators, and other stakeholders of the two geoparks, IRNA reported.
The MOU also calls for promoting the potential of the two geoparks internationally through media outreach and joint marketing initiatives.
UNESCO Global Geoparks
UNESCO Global Geoparks are single, unified geographical areas where sites and landscapes of international geological significance are managed with a holistic concept of protection, education and sustainable development. Their bottom-up approach of combining conservation with sustainable development while involving local communities is becoming increasingly popular. At present, there are 241 UNESCO Global Geoparks in 51 countries.
Located in the Persian Gulf, Qeshm Island covers more than 1,400 square kilometers and is home to a range of geological, ecological and cultural attractions. The island’s UNESCO-listed geopark forms part of the Zagros mountain belt and contains geological formations dating from the Late Precambrian to Cambrian periods. Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark empowers its local communities through innovative initiatives that preserve cultural heritage while supporting sustainable livelihoods.
Taining UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the northwest of Fujian Province, on the southeastern side of the mid-Wuyi Mountains. The landscape consists of mountains, hills and basins, with elevation decreasing from northwest to southeast.
9th APGN Symposium
The APGN connects UNESCO Global Geoparks across the Asia-Pacific region, fostering cooperation, knowledge exchange, and best practices in geopark management while supporting sustainable development and community engagement. Through regional collaboration and partnerships, APGN advances sustainable geotourism, promotes environmental education, and highlights the importance of geological heritage in conserving natural and cultural resources and supporting local economic development.
Promoting Sustainable Geotourism, supporting Geopark Development, strengthening Regional Cooperation, and enhancing Awareness and Education are the core objectives of APGN.
The APGN Symposium is a flagship regional event that brings together geopark professionals to share experiences, discuss innovations, and collaborate on future initiatives, supporting APGN’s broader mission of preserving Earth’s geological heritage while promoting cultural diversity, sustainable tourism, and the well-being of local communities.
The 9th APGN Symposium has brought together the international geopark community to share knowledge and strengthen collaboration in geotourism and sustainable development.
This year’s theme, ‘Celebrating Networking in Geotourism’, highlights the importance of building resilient networks among geoparks to inspire innovation, foster meaningful connections, and lead transformative actions for sustainable development.

GII 2026 places Tehran 65th among top 100 science and technology clusters
TEHRAN – The Global Innovation Index (GII) has ranked Tehran as the world’s 65th-largest science and technology (S&T) cluster this year, according to a report released by the UN’s World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO).
Each year, the GII identifies and ranks the world’s top 100 innovation clusters. Using a bottom-up, data-driven approach that transcends administrative and political boundaries, the GII identifies geographic areas with a high concentration of inventors, scientific authors, and venture capital (VC) activity. These innovation clusters often extend across multiple municipalities or subnational regions and, in some cases, span two or more countries.
Three metrics determine the top 100: the locations of inventors listed in patent applications filed under the WIPO Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), the affiliations of authors of published scientific articles, and the locations of companies receiving venture capital funding.
The GII 2026, under the theme “Powering entrepreneurs at the frontier of science”, examines how scientific breakthroughs become deep science startups and spinouts.
The top 100 innovation clusters continue to be predominantly located in three regions — Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Northern America — accounting for 89 of the world’s top 100 clusters. South-eastern Asia, Eastern Asia and Oceania hosts the most clusters of any region (36), followed by Europe (30) and Northern America (23).
In addition to China and India, six other middle-income economies have clusters among the top 100, including Brazil (1 cluster), the Islamic Republic of Iran (1), Egypt (1), Malaysia (2), Mexico (1), and Turkey (1).
Tehran is the only cluster within Iran that falls within the top 100 innovation clusters in 2026. In 2026, Tehran had 405 PCT applications, 58,732 scientific publications, 107 venture capital deals, 0.0 percent Share of global PCT applications, 0.7 percent share of global scientific publications, and 0.0 percent share of global venture capital deals, making it the 65th largest innovation cluster and 88 innovation cluster by intensity, slipping down from 63rd and 85th, respectively in 2025.
The city’s estimated cluster population, PCT application per capita, and scientific publication capita amount to 7,852,733; 52; and 7,497 respectively, IRNA reported.
The venture capital pre-deals per capita is about 14, and the total innovation intensity share per capita is 0.097.
In patent registration, medical technology ranked first (with 19 percent share), followed by computer technology, civil engineering, and pharmaceuticals.
Top publishing organizations in Tehran are University of Tehran with 5,232 articles, Islamic Azad University with 4,081 articles, and Iran University of Science and Technology with 3,725 articles. A majority of published articles are in engineering fields.
China and the United States lead the innovation cluster count for a fourth consecutive year. China has 25 clusters (one more than last year); the United States follows with 20 clusters (two fewer than last year).
Germany holds seven clusters within the top 100 in 2026, the most of any European economy. The United Kingdom (UK) retains four clusters, and France has two clusters within the top 100.
India maintains four clusters, Japan retains three clusters, and the Republic of Korea likewise maintains three clusters, within the top 100. Canada retains three clusters within the top 100.
This year, 2 clusters entered the top 100: Riyadh (92nd) in Saudi Arabia, entering for the first time, and Fuzhou (96th) in China, rejoining after last appearing in 2024.
Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou, Tokyo-Yokohama, San Jose-San Francisco, Seoul and Beijing are the world’s five biggest “GII Innovation Clusters,” or concentrations of innovative activity identified by WIPO through the analysis of international patent filings, scientific publications and venture capital deals.
Tehran among the world’s most innovative cities
In a recent global ranking by StartupBlink 2026, Tehran’s position has advanced by 20 spots, ranking 348 among the world’s most innovative cities.
Tehran is home to 96 startups, making up 81 percent of all startups in the country. Tehran has approximately 1 startup per 100,000 people. In 2025, the ecosystem recorded an annual growth rate of over 36 percent. The city is currently ranked as the 1st strongest startup ecosystem in Iran, having remained stable since 2025. At the regional level, Tehran ranks 11th in West Asia, having moved up 2 spots since 2025.
According to Iran Innovation Zone, the achievement is the result of strengthening innovation infrastructure and developing interactions among different sectors operating in the knowledge-based economy, Mehr news agency reported.
The report by StartupBlink has highlighted the role of Pardis Technology Park, the country’s largest technology and innovation hub, as one of the driving forces of Iran’s knowledge-based economy. The park hosts hundreds of knowledge-based and technology companies, creating business development infrastructure and providing a platform for enhancing cooperation among startups, investors, large industries, and institutions.
Moreover, hosting the International Innovation and Technology Exhibition (INOTEX) every year, Pardis Technology Park plays a key role in networking and connecting experts in the innovation ecosystem. According to the report, thanks to the capacities of Pardis Technology Parks, Iran’s startup ecosystem ranks 95 globally.
The Innovation and Prosperity Fund and MCI (Hamrah Aval – Iran’s first mobile operator) Ventures are the two other key agents that have developed Iran’s innovation ecosystem by facilitating the growth of technology and knowledge-based companies.
Iran ranks 58th globally in ‘Corporate Engagement’, an indicator that reflects the effective interactions between large industries and innovative and technological companies.
Fintech, the leading industry in Iran, ranks 72nd globally, 5th in the Middle East, indicating the country’s high capacity in the development of financial technologies. Iran Fintech Industry has 23 startups, representing 19 percent of all startups in Iran.
In the Global Startup Ecosystem Index 2026, Iran’s startup ecosystem is ranked 103 worldwide, holding steady compared to the previous year. The Iranian startup ecosystem ranks 10th in West Asia, having remained stable since 2025. It ranks right after Oman and is followed by Iraq.
The country has 118 startups, representing one percent of all startups in the Middle East. This equals approximately one startup per 100,000 people. The ecosystem grew by +54.4 percent over the past year.

EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:30:49 UTC
20:30:49 KST

European authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services when they spend public money under the EU latest effort to counter China’s economic might.
In a further “Buy European” plan, the European Commission published proposals on Wednesday for a sweeping overhaul of EU public procurement rules.
National authorities and public bodies, such as schools and hospitals, will be encouraged to buy goods and services made in Europe but, unlike earlier plans to promote domestically manufactured clean tech, there will be no binding “made in Europe” quotas.
Brussels officials are concerned that many public agencies think existing EU rules oblige them to choose the cheapest bid when spending public money, which can lead to the contract going to a non-European firm.
The European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, Stéphane Séjourné, told reporters the regulation would give public sector buyers greater legal certainty and clarity about purchasing goods and services made in Europe.
“Purchasers can have a more preferential approach to European bids [and] restrict or reject bids from countries which do not have a public procurement agreement or do not play by binding rules in terms of public procurement internationally,” he said.
Public procurement is estimated by EU officials to amount to 15% of the bloc’s gross domestic product, about €2.6tn (£2.2tn) a year, and is seen in Brussels as an underused lever already deployed by Washington and Beijing to support their respective domestic companies.
The new rules will oblige public buyers in the EU to put more emphasis on quality and metrics such as environmental sustainability and local supply chains, rather than opting for the cheapest bid.
Under the proposals public agencies will be obliged to give a minimum 30% weighting to quality when they draw up conditions to award a contract, or explain why they chose to disregard this indicator.
Labour-intensive contracts will have a minimum 50% weighting for quality, so purchasers must ensure decent jobs when awarding the contract, not simply the cheapest price.
Séjourné hopes the proposals will encourage more democratic scrutiny over the spending of public money by local authorities. “It won’t be the European Commission’s fault if purchasers were to prefer Chinese buses to European buses because … in the [draft regulation] there is every possibility to give preference to European buses.”
Brussels is concerned about inroads Beijing is making into European markets for transport and infrastructure, especially Chinese firms benefitting from state subsidies that make them cheaper than European alternatives.
In April, the commission blocked a Chinese rolling-stock company from joining a consortium to build a new line on the Lisbon metro after an investigation found the firm had benefited from state subsidies that gave it an “unfair competitive edge”.
Last year, Brussels opened an investigation into Chinese security company Nuctech, which has supplied European airports and ports with security scanners. EU officials suspect the company was helped by subsidies and tax breaks that gave it an unfair advantage in the European market, although the investigation has not reached final conclusions.
Séjourné – a close ally of France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, who has long championed European preference – said spending public money on goods made in Europe should become “part of public discourse and accountability”.
He added: “It should be very clear that it’s not because of European Union rules that a foreign product was preferred over a European one, but because it was a political choice that was made.”
The draft regulation, which also aims to radically simplify rules by merging three laws into one, must be agreed by the European parliament and the EU ministers before it enters into force. It is likely to be altered during the legislative process.
Séjourné is also spearheading a push for made-in-Europe rules to apply to the public purchase of renewable energy products and electric cars under the the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, which also is likely to be changed by MEPs and ministers, marks a departure for Brussels, long a bastion of open markets.
The plans have alarmed the British government, but EU officials said the latest draft rules on procurement would not disadvantage UK firms because existing agreements ensured both sides played by the same rules.
Séjourne said the EU had agreements with the UK whereby reciprocal market access was respected. “There should not be any difficulties for the UK,” he added.
Non-EU countries that have agreements with the bloc on public procurement are not expected to face barriers.
An online tool will allow public purchasers to see which countries are covered by the EU’s web of free-trade agreements and other international deals that cover procurement.
Membership of the World Trade Organization’s agreement on government procurement (GPA), which promotes fair competition in markets to supply state bodies, will be an important indicator. The GPA has 22 members including the EU (counted as one), the UK, the US, Canada and Japan. Mainland China is not party to the agreement.

Protector metadata issues due to be fixed by December
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:30:18 BST
20:30:18 KST

Problems affecting the dissemination of Full Motion Video metadata from the RAF’s Protector remotely piloted aircraft are expected to be resolved by the end of 2026, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided the update in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made in resolving metadata dissemination issues identified in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s Major Projects Annual Report 2025 to 2026.
Pollard said: “Protector has been employed on operations since November 25, with Full Motion Video being passed to operational users.”
The answer confirms that the aircraft is already providing Full Motion Video to operational users despite the outstanding metadata issue.
Full Motion Video provides live or near-live imagery from an aircraft’s sensors, while associated metadata can contain information such as location, sensor position, time and other details required to exploit and distribute the imagery effectively across operational systems. The remaining problem is expected to be addressed during the third quarter of the current financial year.
Pollard said: “Metadata issues are expected to be resolved by the end of Quarter 3 of Financial Year 2026-27 (October to December 2026).”
That gives Defence a window running to the end of December 2026 to complete the work, although the parliamentary answer does not identify the technical cause of the problem or set out the specific measures being taken to correct it. It also has not prevented Protector from being used operationally. Pollard explicitly stated that Full Motion Video is already being delivered to users, with the outstanding work focused on the associated metadata.
Protector is the RAF’s new remotely piloted aircraft system and is replacing the Reaper fleet. It is intended to provide long-endurance intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and strike capability, with the aircraft able to carry precision-guided weapons as well as sophisticated sensors.
The programme has also been progressing the integration of its weapons. In a separate parliamentary answer published on 8 September, Pollard said previous delays to Brimstone 3 integration had been overcome through a revised programme of US and UK testing, while Paveway IV had been operationally available since March 2026.

What happened in meetings by US chargé d'affaires in Baghdad?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:30:08 UTC
20:30:08 KST

Breadcrumb
What do we know about the meetings held by the new US chargé d'affaires in Baghdad Stephen Fagen?
Iraqi diplomatic sources familiar with the matter told The New Arab about details of a series of meetings held by the new US chargé d'affaires in Baghdad, Stephen Fagen, with some senior Iraqi officials.
They said his moves during the first days of taking up his post carried multiple political, security and economic messages, foremost among them: Supporting the government of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi; resolving the issue of placing weapons under state control; completing arrangements to end the international coalition's mission in Iraq; US sanctions on Iran; combating corruption; and completing the formation of the cabinet.
The US Embassy in Baghdad announced last Wednesday, 2 September, the appointment of former US ambassador to Yemen Stephen Fagen as chargé d'affaires at the US mission in Iraq, succeeding Joshua Harris, who ended his duties last Monday.
The diplomatic sources said, "Fagen's decision to move quickly towards Iraqi presidencies and leaders reflects US interest in the period after 30 September, rather than being merely a protocol procedure related to the start of his new duties."
"Washington wants to know how capable the Iraqi government is of implementing the commitments it made regarding placing weapons under state control and ending any armed activity outside its institutions," the sources added.
Sanctions on Iran top the agenda
According to sources, Fagen's first meeting with Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein focused mainly on the next phase of Iraqi-US relations, as well as US sanctions on Iran and their repercussions for Iraq.
They said the US side stressed during the meeting that Washington "is closely monitoring" Iraqi financial and economic dealings with Tehran and does not want Iraqi territory or institutions to become a channel for circumventing US sanctions imposed on Iran.
The sources added that "the US message on this issue is clear: Iraq can maintain its relations with neighbouring countries, but it cannot enter into financial or economic arrangements that could be interpreted by the US as support for Tehran or as an attempt to circumvent sanctions."
They noted that this issue "will remain a permanent item on the agenda of communications between Baghdad and Washington during the next phase."
Weapons and ties with factions
Fagen's meeting with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, according to the sources, carried broader political and security dimensions.
Washington continues to view the Zaidi government positively and supports its stability but at the same time wants practical steps on several issues it considers essential to maintaining the partnership between the two countries.
The sources said that "the weapons issue was directly present in the discussions, particularly as the deadline for the end of the international coalition's mission in Iraq approaches."
They said Washington wants to see, alongside this, "tangible progress in the programme to place weapons under state control."
The same issue was also strongly present during Fagen's meeting with Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zidan.
The sources explained that "Washington wants the issue of placing weapons under state control to follow an institutional and legal process, rather than being merely a political understanding with some factions."
According to the sources, the importance of the meeting with the Supreme Judicial Council president is linked to the US administration's desire to learn about the legal mechanisms that the state could use to deal with any weapons or armed activity outside the framework of official institutions.
These messages, the sources argued, indicate that US interest is not limited to some factions announcing their readiness to hand over weapons.
It also extends to the nature of the legal and institutional framework the state will adopt to ensure its monopoly over decisions of war and peace.
Ending coalition mission, next security phase
Fagen's meetings in Baghdad also addressed, according to Iraqi diplomatic sources, the completion of the anticipated withdrawal of the international coalition from Iraq and the need to adhere to the timetables agreed between Baghdad and Washington.
The sources said Washington wants the transition from the international coalition's military mission to a new phase of security and advisory relations to take place without the withdrawal creating a security vacuum.
They stressed that the US side attaches importance to ensuring that Iraqi security institutions retain the ability to deal with challenges that may emerge after the coalition's military mission ends.
Combating corruption was also among the issues receiving US attention, according to the same sources, which said Washington wants to see broader and more serious measures to pursue financial and administrative corruption.
They explained that US interest is not limited to employees and lower-ranking officials but extends to "corruption networks and those involved in major cases, including people with political and financial influence."
The sources added that the message Fagen conveyed on this issue was the need for "real efforts to combat corruption, rather than selective or limited measures", given that corruption is directly linked to weak state institutions and threatens the economy, investment and political stability.
Cabinet and factional influence
Regarding the completion of the cabinet, the sources said the issue was present in discussions concerning the next phase of government.
They stressed that Washington wants state institutions to remain free from the influence of armed factions.
They added that "political participation must not become a cover for armed activity outside state institutions."
They noted that the US position "is not only about who announces that they will hand over their weapons but also about the nature of the relationship between political and armed activity and whether there is a genuine separation between the two."
The sources stressed that Washington wants key government and security positions to be subject to state institutions and their decisions, rather than to any armed group or political faction possessing an independent military force.
In this context, Iraqi parliament Foreign Relations Committee member Mukhtar Mahmoud told TNA, "Fagen has only recently taken up his duties, and it is natural for him to begin his meetings with Iraqi officials responsible for political, diplomatic and security issues, particularly since relations between Iraq and the United States involve many shared issues that require continued dialogue and direct coordination between the two sides."
"Completing the international coalition's withdrawal from Iraq is one of the most prominent issues currently on the table, particularly as the deadlines for ending the coalition's mission and moving to a new phase of cooperation and security relations between Baghdad and Washington approach," Mahmoud said.
He added that the next phase "requires a high level of coordination to ensure that what has been agreed is implemented smoothly and without affecting the security situation and internal stability."
He said the meetings also come as part of following up on the results of Zaidi's visit to Washington and the understandings and agreements reached between the two sides.
He explained that the importance of any official visit "lies not only in its political and media results, but in the ability to turn what has been agreed into practical steps and programmes for implementation on the ground."
Mahmoud further said that "Iraq and the United States are entering a new phase of relations that requires moving from the level of agreements and understandings to actual implementation, whether in the political, economic or security fields, in a way that serves shared interests while maintaining Iraq's sovereignty and national decision-making."
"The continuation of meetings between Iraqi and US officials is positive and important, and not every meeting should be interpreted as carrying political messages or pressure, particularly since there are many shared issues that require ongoing discussions and the nature of the current phase calls for greater coordination between the two countries," he added.
The parliamentary Foreign Relations Committee member stressed that "Iraq is keen to build a balanced relationship with the United States based on shared interests and mutual respect."
He said the next phase "will be a genuine test of the two sides' ability to implement what has been agreed, particularly on the issues discussed during the prime minister's visit to Washington, in a way that has a practical impact on cooperation between the two countries."
The US Embassy in Baghdad announced last Wednesday the appointment of former US ambassador to Yemen Stephen Fagen as chargé d'affaires at the US mission in Iraq.
The embassy said in a statement that Fagen previously served as US ambassador to Yemen and, before that, as chargé d'affaires and deputy chief of mission at the US Embassy in Baghdad, in addition to serving as consul general in Erbil.
It said he has extensive regional experience that could contribute to strengthening relations between the United States and Iraq.
Fagen held several positions at the US State Department, including director of the Office of Iranian Affairs at the State Department between 2015 and 2018.
He also served as deputy chief of mission at the US Embassy in Baghdad between 2020 and 2021 and worked at the US Consulate General in Erbil between 2018 and 2020, in addition to diplomatic assignments in Pakistan, Tbilisi and Cairo.
Fagen's assumption of leadership of the US mission in Baghdad as chargé d'affaires comes while the position of permanent US ambassador to Iraq has remained vacant since the end of 2024, with several diplomatic officials managing the mission during this period.
Elizabeth Trudeau and Daniel Rubinstein successively headed the US mission in Baghdad as chargé d'affaires before the US Embassy announced that Fagen would take over the role following the end of Joshua Harris' duties. Harris had formally assumed the role in September 2025.
In a message marking the end of his duties, Harris affirmed his country's continued support for Iraq's sovereignty and the strengthening of bilateral cooperation between Baghdad and Washington.
Fagen therefore begins his new mission in Baghdad with previous experience in Iraqi and Iranian affairs, amid a phase in which security, weapons, relations with Iran, sanctions, combating corruption and the US military withdrawal intersect with efforts to reshape relations between Baghdad and Washington.
This makes his initial moves and contacts with Iraqi officials an important indicator of the priorities of the next phase.

Young Argentines’ mounting debt struggles test support for Milei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:30:06 UTC
20:30:06 KST

Young Argentines’ mounting debt struggles test support for Milei
Nearly half of Argentina’s 45 million people owe money, and more than 5 million are behind on payments, according to a non-profit group
At 18, Martin Taborda began studying law at Argentina’s prestigious University of Buenos Aires, hoping to become the first in his family to graduate. Just two years later, that dream has slipped out of reach.
Unemployed and US$1,300 in debt, he can no longer afford the bus fare from his suburb or the books he needs to keep studying – even at a tuition-free university that has helped generations of Argentines climb into the middle class.
He’s not alone. Nearly half of Argentina’s 45 million people owe money, and more than 5 million are behind on payments, according to the Centre for City Studies, an Argentine non-profit that tracks debt using central bank data. Borrowers under 25 have the highest delinquency rate of any age group, at 37.6 per cent.
“There’s hardly any work for anyone in this country right now,” said Taborda, who borrowed the equivalent of just over US$100 through a mobile payment app in 2024 for education expenses. His debt swelled tenfold as interest accrued on missed payments. Forced to rely on others, he said, “You start to feel like a parasite.”
A new wave of household debt is testing support for President Javier Milei among the young Argentines who helped elect him, and offering the nation’s fragmented opposition an opening to rally disillusioned voters ahead of next year’s presidential election.

Additional information

Vučić, who has led the country as president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced anti-corruption demonstrations sparked by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in the city of Novi Sad in the north of the country in November 2024, which killed 16 people.
The opposition and protesters accuse Vučić and his allies of violence against political opponents, corruption, links to organized crime, and suppressing media freedom; Vučić and his supporters themselves reject these accusations.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram that a Russian drone struck a 24-story residential building in the city's Darnytskyi district, where emergency services were working.
“Five people were injured in the enemy attack on the capital this morning. Three of the wounded were hospitalized,” Klitschko said.
In the wider Kyiv region, Ukraine's National Police said two people were killed and six others injured in attacks on the Bucha, Boryspil and Brovary districts.
Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said drones targeted the Starokozache border crossing with neighboring Moldova, killing two people and injuring three others.
Kiper said fires broke out at the site and operations at the international checkpoint were suspended as emergency services responded.
Acting Mykolaiv Governor Heorhii Reshetilov said a 70-year-old woman was killed and four others injured in the regional capital during what he described as a “massive combined” Russian strike on the southern region.
“Transport, port and civil infrastructure facilities, a shopping center, a postal terminal, a cafe, two private houses and four trucks were damaged. One truck was destroyed,” Reshetilov said, adding that damage was also reported in the region's Mykolaiv district.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for a stronger international response to the attacks and further sanctions on Moscow.
“Unfortunately, there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes, which are taking people’s lives practically every day,” he said on US social media company X.
Ukraine's Air Force said the country's air defenses downed 165 of 196 Russian-launched drones overnight. It also said Russia launched an unspecified number of Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its overnight strikes targeted military industry facilities, Ukrainian seaports and ships, as well as logistics centers it said were being used by Ukrainian forces.
The ministry said the targets included a drone production warehouse in Kyiv; port, drone production and storage facilities and logistics centers in Mykolaiv; and a cargo ship carrying military equipment heading to Odesa.
It also said it struck logistics facilities at the Starokozache border checkpoint, which it accused Ukraine of using to receive military cargo.
Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers and port and energy infrastructure in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment.
Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”.
The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO.
Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery.
The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”.
In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself.
Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”.
“Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth.
The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”.
This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”.

While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington.
In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation was in Poland this week to visit potential locations for the base and discuss the issue further.

What are the holes in the UK’s ban on imports from Israeli settlements?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:27:57 UTC
20:27:57 KST

How the UK’s ban on Israeli settlement goods has limits
Over a year, the UK imported just £6m ($8.1m) in goods recorded as Palestinian, including Israeli settlement goods.
Britain has announced a ban on imports of goods produced in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank as part of a wider package of measures targeting expanding Israeli settlements and intensifying settler pogroms against the Palestinians.
In a speech to Parliament, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband dialled up the rhetoric compared with previous British governments, accusing Israel of carrying out “ethnic cleansing” in Palestine and reaffirming the UK’s longstanding position that Israeli settlements across the occupied West Bank are “unlawful”.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4In maps and charts: Russian and Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets
- list 2 of 4Flash floods surge through Morocco’s Atlas Mountains
- list 3 of 4Authorities in India rescue baby orangutans dumped in forest
- list 4 of 4Turkish jets perform dramatic flyover above Egypt’s pyramids
But beyond the language of the announcement, what will the measures materially change? What percentage of Britain’s total trade with Israel is sourced from the illegal settlements?
Also, how will officials distinguish between goods produced inside Israel, those from the settlements, and Palestinian goods in the occupied territory? And could the government’s promise to target companies profiting from settlements ultimately force it to take action against companies to which it has awarded billions of pounds in public contracts? Here is what we know.
What exactly has the UK announced?
The government has outlined five measures:
Banning the import of goods from illegal Israeli settlements into the UK; taking action on services by creating new designation powers to target individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlement activity; banning the advertising or promotion of land and property in illegal settlements; strengthening the UK’s existing global human rights sanctions regime to target those responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law, including in Palestine; using that regime to sanction several extremist settlers who have supported or incited pogroms against Palestinian communities.
On the surface, the first measure is straightforward, and it outlines that goods produced in Israeli settlements will no longer be allowed into Britain. But to figure out how much trade that will actually stop is considerably more difficult.
How much trade will the import ban actually affect?
First, this is not a ban on trade with Israel. Far from it. The UK has a free-trade agreement with Israel, and that trading relationship is set to continue. Trade in goods and services between the two countries totalled about £6bn ($8.1bn) in 2025, according to UK government figures.
The new ban applies specifically to goods imported from Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory.
So how much are those imports worth? The government itself acknowledges that it is “difficult to obtain accurate figures for UK trade” with Israeli settlements.
Al Jazeera asked the British government how much the UK imports specifically from Israeli settlements, but did not receive a response by the time of publication of this article.
Official UK trade statistics distinguish between trade with Israel and trade with Palestine. But they do not distinguish between goods produced by Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and those produced by Israeli settlers living in the same territory. Some 750,000 Israeli settlers live illegally on Palestinian land across the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.
That means the Palestine figures cannot simply be read as a measure of Britain’s trade with Israeli settlements. But they do give some indication of the relatively small scale of trade recorded with the Palestinian territory.
The latest government figures, covering the four quarters to the end of March 2026, put total UK-Palestine trade at £40m, up from £38m in 2025.
While the UK says it will “take action” on services, it is not outlined as being included in the initial ban. That means services connected to finance and insurance, logistics, legal services and tourism will not automatically be prohibited in the same way as physical goods.
Meanwhile, the UK goods exported to Israeli settlements, which form the majority of the trade, will also not be included in the ban. That means that over the latest four quarters, the UK imported just £6m worth of goods recorded as coming from Palestine. In theory, even if every one of those imports had come from Israeli settlements, the ban would have affected no more than £6m of that recorded trade over the year.
This is equivalent to just 0.1 percent of the roughly £6bn (some $8bn) in annual trade between the UK and Israel.
The value of settlement goods within that £6m could be considerably smaller. That £6m represents goods Britain records as imports from Palestine – not goods specifically originating in the illegal Israeli settlements. It can therefore include products grown or manufactured by Palestinians living under occupation in the West Bank.
Among the largest categories of goods Britain imports from Palestine are fruit and vegetables, vegetable oils, and coffee, tea and cocoa – precisely the kinds of agricultural products that can be produced by Palestinian farmers as well as Israeli settlement businesses.
This also means Britain is therefore preparing to ban a category of imports whose current value it cannot accurately quantify. So if Britain cannot accurately measure the flow of settlement goods into the country, how will it identify and stop them at the border?
Could settlement goods simply be labelled as Israeli and escape the ban?
While the figure for the occupied Palestinian territory includes some settlement goods, there is another route by which goods from Israeli settlements can make it to Britain. And, again, it is very difficult for the UK government to keep track of this.
A June 2026 report by the Global Echo Litigation Center called Importing Occupation examined shipments of fresh produce from Israel to Europe and found that settlement goods were systematically concealed within supply chains.
That means goods labelled as Israeli – and which would therefore, in theory, be counted within the roughly £6bn UK-Israel trading relationship – can include products originating in Israeli settlements.
In fact, the investigation found that roughly one in six shipments it examined contained products originating in Israeli settlements, according to the organisation.
Goods produced in the occupied Palestinian territory could consequently reach markets presented as products of Israel.
That exposes a potential weakness in Britain’s proposed system. If settlement goods are concealed within Israeli supply chains and presented as Israeli products, identifying them at the border – and enforcing the import ban – becomes considerably more difficult.
So how does the UK government enforce it?
The government has not yet set out in detail how the new import ban will be policed. Britain does, however, already operate a system intended to distinguish goods produced in Israeli settlements from those produced within Israel’s internationally recognised borders.
The distinction currently matters because of tariffs. Under the UK-Israel trade agreement, qualifying Israeli products can receive preferential tariff treatment. Products originating in Israeli settlements in territory illegally occupied since 1967 cannot.
To claim those preferences, importers must provide proof of origin. That documentation must include the postcode and name of the city, village or industrial zone where a product obtained its originating status.
HM Revenue and Customs maintains a detailed list of locations that are not eligible for preferential treatment under the UK-Israel agreement, including settlements and industrial zones in occupied territory.
Since September 2025, another requirement has been added. Importers seeking Israeli tariff preferences must use customs document code Y864, declaring that the goods did not originate in territories brought under Israeli administration since June 1967.
In other words, Britain already has a mechanism for finding out where this product was actually made.
But, under the existing rules, a settlement product can still enter Britain – it just cannot get preferential treatment available to qualifying Israeli goods.
Jess Stober, the Legal Director of Global Echo, told Al Jazeera that this is where the ban could materially change the incentives for companies throughout the supply chain.
“Under the old system, if an importer was caught, the tariff could be paid and the goods could still be sold,” she said. “Under a ban, prohibited goods may be refused entry and businesses may face substantial financial losses and sanctions. That gives every participant in the supply chain a reason to conduct proper origin due diligence.”
And a postcode-based origin regime works only if the origin being declared is accurate. If a product grown or manufactured in a settlement can be consolidated, repackaged or otherwise passed through an Israeli company before export, customs officials need a means of establishing where the product actually originated rather than simply where it was exported from.
Banning all Israeli goods would plainly solve the origin problem – there would no longer be a need to distinguish settlement products from other Israeli imports – but that is not the policy Britain has announced. Its much larger trading relationship with Israel will continue.
Will Britain end up sanctioning companies it already does business with?
Goods, however, are only one part of the government’s announcement. Potentially more consequential is its promise to create new designation powers targeting individuals and companies that “support, facilitate or profit from” illegal settlement activity.
That wording raises a very different question. What happens when the company profiting from settlement activity is also doing business with the British government?
An Al Jazeera investigation published last week found more than £2.1bn ($2.8bn) in UK public-sector contracts were awarded to 17 companies and entities linked to illegal Israeli settlements.
Companies owned by Motorola Solutions, the US technology and communications giant, accounted for more than £1.7bn ($2.3bn) of that total, the vast majority, through its British subsidiary Airwave Solutions.
Other contracts identified by Al Jazeera were held by companies belonging to four major corporate groups: German building materials multinational Heidelberg Materials, French engineering group Egis, Spanish train manufacturer CAF and Chinese conglomerate Fosun.
All of the companies identified in Al Jazeera’s investigation were connected to corporate groups whose activities have been linked to Israeli settlements, including through infrastructure, transport, communications or commercial operations.
The government’s latest announcement, therefore, creates a potentially awkward contradiction. Britain says it intends to acquire new powers to designate companies that profit from illegal settlement activity.
Stober said the government should consider whether its own commercial relationships were consistent with its position on the occupation.
“The question is really one of consistency: the UK Government has now expressly accepted that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory is unlawful,” Stober said. “If it is aligning its trade and sanctions policy with that position and with the ICJ’s July 2024 Advisory Opinion, it should also examine whether its own procurement and contracting relationships are consistent with those same obligations.”
So how broadly does the government intend to use those powers? If companies profiting from settlement activity fall within these parameters, some could potentially find themselves targeted by the same government from which their corporate groups or subsidiaries hold major public contracts.
That could have consequences well beyond the comparatively small flow of physical goods from settlements. For example, what would then happen to the Home Office contract with Airwave Solutions, owned by Motorola Solutions, worth 1.562 billion pounds ($2.13bn) to provide the secure communications network used by police, fire and ambulance services across England, Scotland and Wales?
The overriding question is what this designation would mean for existing public contracts – including whether sanctions could require, permit or prompt the government to terminate or restructure them.
Al Jazeera has asked the government whether it is reviewing its existing public-sector contractors for links to Israeli settlement activity, whether companies holding government contracts could be designated under the new powers, and what would happen to existing contracts if they were.
The UK government has not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Norway has helped 69 Russian citizens return home from the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard after a Norwegian court ordered the seizure of the ship that brought them, Reuters reported. The vessel remains under arrest on behalf of Ukraine's state energy company Naftogaz, which is enforcing a compensation award for property Russia took in Crimea. Moscow calls the seizure piracy and says it will appeal.
The passengers left, the ship stayed
The Russians traveled home on 8 September through the northern Norwegian border town of Kirkenes, the governor of Svalbard said. A Norwegian court ordered the seizure of the Professor Molchanov on 2 September, stranding its passengers and crew on the archipelago.
The ship is held at Barentsburg, one of two Russian settlements on Svalbard. Those settlements house 392 of the archipelago's 2,914 residents, according to Statistics Norway.
The vessel is an expedition cruise ship owned by Roshydromet, Russia's state weather and environmental monitoring agency, in Arkhangelsk, according to CruiseMapper. It sails under the Russian flag, and the Dutch operator Oceanwide Expeditions chartered it earlier for polar voyages.
Ukraine’s spy service and navy team up to strike two Russian crude tankers in the Black Sea
A different kind of enforcement
European states have moved against Russian shipping repeatedly this year, but mostly at sea and under sanctions powers. France's navy boarded a sanctioned shadow-fleet tanker in the Atlantic in June, and British forces boarded one in the English Channel. This case rests on an arbitration award instead, and it holds the ship as security for a debt rather than inspecting a cargo.
Moscow protests, Oslo proceeds
The seizure has sharpened tensions between Russia and Norway, a NATO member. Russia's Foreign Ministry summoned the Norwegian ambassador that same week and delivered a strong protest.
Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 and lies midway between the North Pole and the European mainland. A 1920 treaty governs it and lets citizens of signatory states, Russia among them, settle there without a visa.

Russia says it hopes US-mediated talks with Ukraine will resume soon
MOSCOW, Sept 9 - Russia hopes that U.S.-mediated peace talks on ending the war in Ukraine will resume soon, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday.
No such talks between Russia and Ukraine have taken place since February, but President Donald Trump sent his negotiators to Moscow and then Kyiv at the weekend in a bid to relaunch the stalled process.

Syria: How  the 'house of sisters' threat split society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:27:00 UTC
20:27:00 KST

Syria: How the 'house of sisters' threat split society
September 9, 2026
A knock on the door, a muted threat and then they made the decision to leave the country, says Layla, a math teacher and mother-of-three in her 40s.
Until recently, Layla — who didn't want DW to use her full name for security reasons — was living in Damascus, Syria's capital. She and her family are Alawites, the same religious sect as former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad, who are often targeted because they're seen as Assad's allies.
"But we never supported him, his father killed members of my family. We hated him actually," she told DW. Still, she describes feeling fearful when rebel groups entered Damascus in 2024 for the first time after the fall of the Assad regime, calling them "extremists."
At first, she and her husband decided to stay in Syria. But then a stranger came to the door.
"He told me 'we know your daughter plays piano and has dance lessons. You should stop that. If you don't, maybe we will take her to the house of the sisters," Layla recounts.
In conservative Islamic circles, women playing music and dancing for an audience is frowned upon. And Layla had heard about the so-called "house of the sisters" — she had read online it was a place where Syrian women from other sects were forced to convert to Islam. A few days later, the family decided to leave the country. They are now in Lebanon.
"I just don't want my children to grow up that way," Layla explains.
What is the 'house of sisters'?
Headlines about the "house of sisters" first really made waves in Syria in May after an Alawite university student Batoul Alloush, 21, was reported missing by her family, possibly kidnapped, only to turn up later wearing religious clothing and saying she left her family in order to convert to Islam.
There were already other stories of missing women, including from the Alawite minority.
Reham Suleiman, a psychologist who works for the United Nations and with the Alawite community, told DW she has firsthand knowledge of several cases of kidnapping. "And it’s not just one incident or coincidence," she says. It is clear some of women were kidnapped for ransom money, revenge or forced marriage.
But other cases were apparently resolved when, for example, the women said they had been visiting friends, wanted to escape their families or had run away to a lover. Alloush herself said she wished to convert to Islam and leave her family. Her parents insist she's been drugged or coerced.
Organizations like Amnesty International and the UN's Commission of Inquiry on Syria say the cases — which number between 40 and 60 — have not been fully investigated.
A political football
Syrian authorities did look into the "house of sisters." A spokesperson for Syria's Minister of Social Affairs, Hind Kabawat, told DW that the ministry has not licensed any facility with that name and that any unlicensed centers of this nature would be shut down.
Syrian fact-checking organizations like Verify-Sy found that pictures of the supposed "house of sisters" building were created with AI.
"A constant stream of unverified claims circulates on a daily basis concerning alleged kidnappings and killings, arrests and cases of torture in detention facilities," a spokesperson from Verify-Sy told DW.
"Verifying many of these is challenging when evidence available through open sources is scarce, contradictory or otherwise insufficient."
So whether the "house of sisters" exists in some form is unclear. But real or not, some groups appear to have instrumentalized it for their own agenda anyway, independent media outlet Shaam News Network, or SNN, wrote recently.
"Despite the absence of any physical evidence … social media platforms and pages began circulating 'the house' as an established fact," SNN wrote. "And it gradually became the focus of broader narratives about the 'organized kidnapping' of Alawite women."
International influencers
A private organization called the Syrian Investigation Mechanism, or SIM, founded in May 2026, links the "house of sisters" to a Muslim organization that proselytizes to gain new converts. SIM claimed the missing women were coerced into converting and held in "the house."
In an interview on YouTube, SIM director Yasser Shalati, who is based in Brandenburg, Germany, claims this is evidence of "demographic engineering." SIM did not reply to DW's requests for further comment.
A Berlin-based organization, the Union of Syrian Alawites in Europe, or USAE, has also repeatedly posted about the "house of sisters."
On his personal Facebook page, Muaiad Ibrahim, who is listed as USAE's deputy director in official court documents, regularly criticizes the new Syrian government and recently expressed support for Syria's highest religious scholar under the Assad regime, Ahmed Hassoun. In late August, Hassoun was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing.
Other recently founded overseas organizations — including some that claim they have a network of millions of human rights advocates but link to incomplete websites — have also repeatedly disseminated stories about the "house of sisters."
Arab investigative journalism outfit DARAJ notes some of these organizations have been criticized for their apparent support of the Assad regime.
The damage done?
"This kind of information ebbs and flows, but it does have a real impact and its quite powerful," says Gregory Waters, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, who's traveled extensively in Syria and monitors events on his site, Syria Revisited.
"It has the political intent to isolate Alawites, to make them fearful and keep them from engaging with the government, with [Syrian] Sunnis, and maybe to some extent, pull them towards insurgent [anti-government] networks."
Online propaganda feeds on real events within minority communities, adding to their existing fears, he says.
Verify Sy conducts a monthly audit of online disinformation, and researchers there say incitement is the second most common objective. Waters says Syrian authorities have been trying to rein in local influencers who spread disinformation, although obviously they can't impact those based overseas.
Like anywhere else in the world, you'll get a wide spectrum of opinions within every Syrian community, Waters notes. "There are there those who will insist that there's a program of ethnic cleansing, and there are others who say life is fine, we are fully integrated into the state."
Although it depends which part of the country you're looking at, he doesn't think relations between different communities are getting worse.
"In Syria, everything is unique to its local environment," Waters explains. "So in some places, we could say that walls between communities have hardened over the past two years and little progress has been made in reducing that. But even so, the walls are not getting higher."
Stabilization first
"Right now, generally speaking, the government in Damascus is busy establishing institutions, taking control of the security situation and trying to stabilize the country," argues Naseef Naeem, research director at the Berlin-based Candid Foundation, which consults on Syrian affairs. But sooner or later, Syria is going to need more of a national dialogue between different community groups, he says.
In the meantime, both he and Waters believe the Syrian economy, devastated after years of war, could hold the key to better relations.
"As soon as the economic recovery really gets underway, many of these phenomena will gradually disappear," Naeem told DW.
For example, Waters says, over summer, a lot of domestic tourists, many of them Sunni, made their way to the Syrian coast, an area where many Alawites live.
"There was a massive tourism boom," Waters explains. "Everybody's interacting and I've heard from friends there that there wasn't harassment, no violence. The government and security authorities really emphasized supporting the tourism industry in coastal areas this year and it's had a really positive impact."
Those kinds of inter-community contacts in real life "help reduce the impact of disinformation campaigns and the level of fear," he concludes.

Pledges for action in Europe as PISA results show drop in child reading and maths skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:25:12 UTC
20:25:12 KST

The OECD's latest PISA report, based on a standardised test taken by 15-year-olds, found that student performance across OECD countries reached a record low in maths and reading.
There has been dismay and pledges for action across Europe after it was revealed on Tuesday that maths and reading skills among pupils have declined across the world, largely due to digitalisation and a drop in recreational reading.
The OECD's latest PISA report, based on a standardised test taken by 15-year-olds, found that student performance across OECD countries reached a record low in maths and reading.
Within the EU, pupils in Spain, Croatia, Luxembourg, Malta, Greece, Romania, Cyprus, and Bulgaria score below the OECD average in reading, mathematics and science skills.
Only Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Austria, Poland and Czechia managed to secure a mean performance above the average.
French Education Minister Édouard Geffray deplores what he called the “cognitive destruction” of young people and acknowledged that France needed to take action to reverse course.
“Young people who spend three hours a day on their phones during class, who are distracted for more than three hours a day, are losing the equivalent of almost two school years,” he said, deploring the “overconsumption of social networks.”
In an interview with Le Monde daily, Geffray targeted middle schools as the “major focus of the next five-year term to implement the most effective teaching practices.”
The PISA report logged the steepest decline in reading, with scores falling by 28 points across OECD members between 2015 and 2025, with pupils from wealthy families being the ones who fell furthest behind.
Some of the reasons for the decline are related to increased digitalisation, longer screen time and falling rates of reading for enjoyment.
"Most troubling is the decline in the very skills that matter most in the AI age: evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources and thinking critically about what we read," the report stated.
Meanwhile, Spain’s education minister said that a lack of reading comprehension was “the root of all educational problems” after Spanish students logged their worst ever performance since PISA testing began in 2000.
“We must continue working on reading comprehension, because it is the foundation of everything. If you don't understand what you read, it's impossible to solve a problem in math, physics, chemistry, or any other subject,” Milagros Tolón told Cadena Ser radio.
Tolón acknowledged that the educational decline may be directly related to new technologies.
“This may be related, as the OECD has already indicated, to screen time, rushed and superficial reading habits, and the increasing prevalence of short messages in the digital lives of teenagers,” she added.
She said that since 2024 Spain has been promoting cooperation programmes to strengthen both reading comprehension and mathematics.
Over 760,000 teenagers in dozens of countries took the Programme for International Student Assessment last year, the results of which were released on Tuesday.
China, Singapore, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea scored the highest marks on the test. Estonia, the United Kingdom and New Zealand also did well.
The key to why scores are falling so widely may be found in an accompanying survey taken by students.
Compared with the 2022 results, almost every country saw a drop in families' support for children’s education, especially for boys, as measured by questions about how often parents talk to their kids about their schoolwork or take an interest in their learning.
“Parents see themselves more as a client of the school, not as someone who takes personal interest,” said Andreas Schleicher, director for education and skills for the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, which runs the PISA test.
Students who said a family member asks them at least weekly what they did in school that day scored around 35 points higher on the PISA science test, equivalent to over a year and a half of learning, compared with students whose families take less interest.
That number includes adjustments for socioeconomic differences.
Digital distraction is another factor. Over a quarter of students in high-income countries complained their classmates got distracted by digital devices in most or every science class.
In countries with strong policies controlling the use of mobile phones in schools, distraction rates were lower.
There’s undoubtedly a strong association between students using digital devices for leisure and lower test scores, Schleicher said. When tech is used for learning, however, the results are more nuanced.
Countries where high schoolers reported using digital devices for around two to three hours per day in school saw higher test scores, but scores fell once tech use climbed beyond that.
Almost four in 10 children in the Netherlands are at risk of leaving school with a low level of literacy as the PISA results show the country has fallen behind the European average over the last decade.
Junior Education Minister Judith Thielen promised to come up with an action plan in autumn to tackle low literacy rates.
“It is my ambition to stop the downward trend and turn it around,” she said. “I want to see better results in three years’ time.”

'A gamble with our lives': Ex-Anthropic researcher warns of AI 'catastrophe'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:24:48 UTC
20:24:48 KST

Jacob Coxon says AI executives privately fear catastrophe while racing to build it anyway. His exit follows a summer of AI containment failures and a new push in Congress to ban superintelligent AI outright.
A researcher who spent three years building the systems behind some of the world's most powerful AI models has quit the industry entirely, warning that the companies racing to build ever-more capable AI "are gambling with our lives".
Jacob Coxon, 27, resigned from Anthropic on 8 September after also working at OpenAI and set out his reasons in a lengthy thread on X.
"Neither company is acting responsibly," he wrote. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence."
In his thread, Coxon argued that AI systems are approaching a point where they could "hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources," and said the pace of progress in each of those domains "is not slowing".
He claimed that many of the people building the technology privately fear it could prove fatal for humanity, even if they avoid saying so publicly.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he wrote, adding that executives "couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible" while expressing the same fears in private.
A race neither side says it can stop
Coxon's departure is not an isolated warning.
Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei has spent much of the year raising alarms about the technology his own company builds, warning in a January essay that powerful AI could hand authoritarian states the tools for a "totalitarian nightmare" of total surveillance, and cautioning in a later memo that superintelligence would "test us as a species".
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has struck a more measured public tone but still describes superintelligence, his preferred term over AGI or artificial general intelligence, as arriving within "a few thousand days," or roughly in 2032.
Amodei, by contrast, told the White House in a March 2025 policy filing to expect what he calls "powerful AI" as early as late 2026.
Coxon, for his part, wrote that Anthropic staff understand the risks well but feel trapped in a race, believing that if they slow down, less careful developers will simply take their place.
He called this dynamic "a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company's Slack".
It is also not the first resignation of its kind at Anthropic. In February, the company's former safeguards research lead, Mrinank Sharma, left with a letter warning that humanity faced grave and growing danger from the technology.
Warning shots
Coxon is optimistic about the potential for industry coordination, pointing to a string of incidents this year in which AI systems have slipped their intended boundaries.
In July, AI agents built by OpenAI broke out of an internal testing environment and autonomously hacked into Hugging Face, a code-sharing platform, an episode OpenAI itself later called a "warning shot" for the sector.
Anthropic, Coxon's former employer, has disclosed a similar pattern, saying its own Claude models gained unauthorised access to the real systems of three separate organisations.
Coxon said such episodes have made pacing agreements between US labs "more viable," though he does not believe the industry is currently on track to avoid a global race.
He suggested this might ultimately require "costly actions such as a temporary ban on improving model capabilities".
Lawmakers move to act
Some legislators are no longer waiting for labs to coordinate voluntarily.
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar unveiled the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on 3 September, legislation that would permanently outlaw the development of superintelligent AI in the US and impose a temporary pause on other advanced AI development until a new federal regulator sets safety rules.
Violators could face up to 20 years in prison. Separately, Representatives George Whitesides and Pat Harrigan have introduced a bill directing the National Institute of Standards and Technology to monitor how advanced AI systems are being used to conduct further AI research and development themselves.
In Brussels, the European Union has taken a more incremental but firmer regulatory path.
Obligations on general-purpose AI models under the bloc's AI Act took effect in August 2025, with stricter rules for high-risk systems following in August 2026.
The European Commission has rejected pressure from several major tech firms to delay enforcement, and companies that breach the rules face fines of up to €35 million or 7% of their global turnover, whichever is higher.
Despite the scale of his warnings, Coxon closed his thread with a direct appeal to researchers still working at frontier labs, urging them to weigh up what the coming years will actually demand of them.
"Do you want to kick off a superintelligent RL run without a rigorous understanding of its mind?" he asked.
"Should you put your head down because 'it's happening anyway' or take this moment to call for different conditions?"

Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:24:10 BST

Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
- Published
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.
Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.
Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.
Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.
It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.
The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.
Trump had been due to speak by phone to the German chancellor on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US, but the government spokesman in Berlin said the call had been postponed without saying why. No new date has been set.
Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".
While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it made a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.
Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."
Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.
As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.
Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.
"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.
The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.
Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.
