Furthermore, the political calendar is piling on the pressure: the mid-term elections are just around the corner and the presidential election campaign begins about a year from now. ... The more urgently Washington needs results, the more sense it makes for Moscow to play for time, continue the war and wait for the next offer. This is why I would focus less on the number of visits by Witkoff and instead ask what has changed in Putin’s calculations after each of these visits. Right now the answer seems to be pretty clear: nothing.”
Abramovich Loses Third Bid to Escape EU Sanctions
At least a functioning channel of communication
This diplomatic initiative must be taken seriously, political scientist Bernardo Ivo Cruz urges in Diário de Noticias (Portugal):
“The EU and Kyiv’s allies have made it clear: only Ukraine will decide the terms for ending the war. This means that we may have to accept a settlement that is acceptable to the Ukrainians but which results in tangible gains for Russia. An imperfect peace that would neither fully restore the justice violated by the aggression nor wholly uphold international law. ... Yet after four and a half years of war, the mere return of a diplomacy capable of engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv must be taken seriously.”
Too early for diplomacy
Diplomacy can only begin once Russia has lost, Le Point (France) argues:
“At this stage there will be no diplomatic solution to this war. Some conflicts end around a negotiating table. But there are others where the negotiating table only comes into play once an imperialist regime has realised that it has lost. That was the case with Germany in 1945. And with Serbia in 1995. And it is exactly what will happen with Russia too: the diplomats will only get to work once the reality of the battlefield has, in one way or another, been acknowledged in the Kremlin’s inner circles. Until then, the winter will be brutal, and we must help Ukraine to hold out.”
A small step in the right direction
Military expert Oleksiy Kopytko (Russia) is optimistic in a Telegram post republished by Echo:
“There is no doubt that the path to genuine agreements will involve heavy-handed pressure. Right now it looks like the US is intent on exerting pressure primarily, or even exclusively, on Ukraine, because the country is heavily dependent on external support. With regard to Russia, only China could assume this role, but Beijing has yet to intervene. ... This round of negotiations will not lead to an immediate end to the war. That would take a miracle. ... But it is a small step in the right direction. I am confident that by winter serious attempts will be made to initiate genuine negotiations leading to a ceasefire.”
Putin’s final bid with Trump
So far Putin’s hopes regarding Trump have been dashed, Gazeta Wyborcza (Poland) concludes:
“Putin and his entourage had hoped that Trump would do for them the job they themselves are unable to do on the front line, and force the Ukrainians to hand over to the Russians what they demand but have been unable to secure despite heavy losses. ... That was their aim at the summit in Anchorage in August 2025, but it failed. ... Trump’s shelf life is coming to an end. It looks as though his fellow Republicans will suffer a defeat in the mid-term elections on 3 November and his hands will be tied by a hostile Congress. ... So if the Kremlin can still get anything out of him, it has to be now.”
No hope without concessions by Zelensky
In a Telegram post republished by Echo, journalist Fyodor Krasheninnikov (Russia) sees the Ukrainian president playing a key role:
“I am wholeheartedly in favour of ending the war as quickly as possible, but in September 2026 there is only one way this will be possible – namely, if Trump’s envoys persuade Zelensky to accept Putin’s humiliating and unjust terms. Should this prove impossible for Zelensky, talks is all there will be. To those who want to jump to conclusions about my stance and ask, ‘Well what do you propose?’ I say: I am not proposing anything. I am merely saying that the war will continue and there are no other options unless Zelensky is prepared to make concessions.”
Russia wants to eliminate the Ukrainian state
All Russia’s demands call into question Ukraine’s very existence, making concessions on Ukraine’s part practically impossible, argues journalist Vitali Portnikov on TSN (Ukraine) :
“Russia has a clear ambition: the elimination of Ukrainian statehood and the expulsion of a large part of the Ukrainian population from the territories in which they live. ... It will not seek a compromise with a nation whose statehood it seeks to eliminate. That is why, since 2014, there has been no alternative but to stand firm against it; there will be no other option in 2026, nor beyond that. ... What is at stake here is nothing less than the right of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people to an independent existence.”

Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force Senate vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:12:35 UTC
20:12:35 KST

Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force senate vote
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet’s wealth tax reforms are in jeopardy after the farmers’ party BBB threatened to block them in the senate unless the coalition parties agree to a major overhaul.
MPs voted in favour of a new “box 3” tax on assets earlier this year, but the vote in the senate was postponed amid speculation that the centre-right coalition partners, VVD and CDA, were poised to vote against the plans in the upper house.
The cabinet wants to change the income tax system so that investors and savers are taxed on the growth of their assets each year, a system favoured by D66 and backed by VVD and CDA in the lower house.
But the two parties’ senators want to replace box 3 with a capital gains tax, which would be paid on the actual profit made from selling shares or other assets such as real estate.
Right-wing opposition parties, including the BBB and JA21, also favour this option, meaning the bill in its current form would almost certainly be voted down.
The BBB has said it will force a vote in the upper house unless finance minister Eelco Heinen withdraws the plan altogether, which would mean starting from scratch.
Withdraw or vote
“It can’t be up to the cabinet whether or not we examine a law in the Senate,” BBB senator Bart Kroon told the upper house’s finance committee. “Withdraw it or we’ll put it to the vote.”
Heinen had hoped to amend the bill as part of the current budget settlement so that it could be passed and enacted before 2028.
The finance minister has already torn up the plans once after the proposed new system attracted international criticism amid concern that investors would be forced to sell shares in order to pay tax on unrealised returns.
A new bill would not make it onto the statute book before 2029, costing the Dutch treasury an estimated €3 billion a year in lost revenue in the meantime.
The cabinet has been trying to reform the mechanism since the Supreme Court ruled in 2021 that the current system, which taxes assets based on a notional growth rate, breached European human rights laws.
Since then it has implemented a stopgap system that still taxes assets at a fictional rate but gives savers the option of declaring their actual growth rate instead. They can still pay the fictional rate if it works out lower.

SYKTYVKAR, September 9. /TASS/. Moscow views the anti-Russian hysteria in Europe following the incident involving a drone found at Leipzig/Halle Airport as a pre-planned escalatory maneuver, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a briefing in Syktyvkar.
"We view this latest episode of anti-Russian hysteria in Europe as a pre-planned escalatory maneuver, sanctioned by the EU and NATO leadership bound by mutual complicity, and having nothing to do with an objective investigation. It is obvious that the goal and objective of such actions is to maintain a high level of Russophobia within European society - a sentiment intended to mask the gross political and economic miscalculations of European elites and to justify, in the eyes of citizens, the allocation of vast resources to fund Ukraine and the accelerated ramping up of European military-industrial complexes under the pretext of preparing for an allegedly inevitable armed clash - as they put it - with our country," Zakharova said. "If it is inevitable, may the admit that they are the ones striving for it."
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry official, the widespread dissemination of baseless, false, and even absurd accusations against Russia regarding - as the West calls it - "subversive activities" has become a mandatory element of the information war.
Zakharova pointed out that the drone incident in Leipzig was orchestrated to facilitate accusations against Russia.
"Of course, one cannot fail to note the stark contrast between the current situation and the EU’s reaction to the blowing up of the Nord Stream pipelines. It’s interesting, isn't it? I mean, when they found some drones - of unknown origin, and whatever it was they supposedly discovered in Leipzig - there followed expulsions of diplomats, the closure of the Consulate General, the shutting down of the Russian House, accusations, that same 'solidarity' rhetoric, and the summoning of ambassadors. But wait a minute: four years ago, right under your noses - in Central Europe, in the heart of Western Europe - attacks were carried out against infrastructure that was "yours" (considering your own capital and investments). This was peaceful infrastructure - the Nord Stream pipelines - designed to deliver gas to your own countries. Tell me, please: you are now directly accusing Ukrainian citizens - people with direct ties to Ukraine - of carrying out this terrorist act. Not just of encouragement or complicity, but of the actual explosions. German authorities are accusing them in court; the court proceedings and criminal case files state explicitly that Ukrainian citizens blew up the pipeline. This is a finding - a discovery - made by German authorities and law enforcement agencies," she pointed out.
"My question is this: if this is the official position of the German prosecution regarding Ukrainian citizens, why hasn't a single Ukrainian diplomat been expelled? Why hasn't a single Ukrainian diplomatic mission been closed? Why hasn't a single EU or NATO country voiced support for Germany's concerns, summoned Ukrainian ambassadors, and so on? Because this is a 'different case.' The difference is that they themselves orchestrated it with enthusiasm. That’s all there is to it. Yet they blame our country for everything," Zakharova stated.
The UAV Incident
On September 1, the German government officially held Russia responsible for the drone incident that occurred at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August and announced the suspension of the Russian House’s operations, the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, and other measures. Russian ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechaev categorically rejected all accusations put forward by Germany, calling them baseless and absurd. The diplomat stated that Russian House staff are required to leave Germany within seven days.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had previously noted that Germany’s new anti-Russian decisions - taken under the pretext of the UAV incident at Leipzig Airport - represent yet another grave error by the German authorities that runs counter to the interests of their people. In his view, these decisions are linked to the country's domestic political situation and, specifically, the difficult position of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Turkish defence giant MKE sets up Egypt subsidiary for joint production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:10:10 UTC
20:10:10 KST

Turkish defence manufacturer Machinery and Chemical Industry (MKE) General Manager Ilhami Keles said the company has established a wholly owned subsidiary in Cairo under Egyptian law, named “Zafer (Victory),” to conduct commercial activities and facilitate joint production projects in Egypt.
Türkiye’s MKE has established a wholly owned subsidiary in Cairo to expand into Egypt, pursue joint defence production and use the country as a hub for markets across Africa and the Gulf.
Keles spoke to Anadolu at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt’s coastal city of El Alamein.
Emphasising the valuable ties between Egypt and Türkiye as friends and allies, Keles said Egypt is a country with shared historical and religious ties with Türkiye and with which Ankara has close political relations.
“Therefore, doing something with Egypt is very valuable for us,” he said.
Keles said MKE is focusing on Egypt not merely as a “market” but as a country with which it can “do joint business.”
He noted that MKE signed its first contract at the inaugural defence industry exhibition in Sarajevo shortly before arriving in Egypt.
‘We signed a contract with Egypt’
Keles said MKE signed a memorandum of understanding with Egypt’s Ministry of Military Production.
“We signed a contract with Egypt for the joint production of energetic materials and explosives, as well as the joint production of various ammunition equipment.”
Keles said interest in MKE’s TOLGA system has increased, particularly amid the diversification of asymmetric threats.
TOLGA is MKE’s counter-drone system designed to detect and neutralise aerial threats.
“Egypt is also interested in this, and we have sold TOLGA to Egypt,” he said.
He described the initial sale as a symbolic one aimed at introducing TOLGA into Egypt’s inventory, adding that MKE plans to use the joint venture it will establish in Egypt as a platform to market the system across Africa and eventually the Gulf.
“Egypt has the capability to produce military vehicles. We are moving forward with joint production integrating Egypt’s capabilities with our turret and command-and-control systems, as well as our hard-kill and soft-kill solutions,” he said.
Keles added that MKE’s local partner had also requested TOLGA systems at the exhibition.
Technology transfer becoming more important
Keles said MKE’s accumulated know-how, developed through its long-standing capabilities in ammunition and weapons production, has become increasingly valuable.
“All countries are now striving to carry out this kind of production in their own countries. As a result, the ability to transfer technology has begun to take precedence over product exports,” he said.
Keles said MKE is in talks with several countries not only on exports but also on mechanisms for joint production.
“We are establishing joint ventures in Canada, and those processes are continuing. Immediately after here, we will travel to the United States, where we will discuss a number of investments,” he said.
He added that infrastructure for potential cooperation is also developing in countries in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia.
“We entered a tender in Malaysia. Localisation is also part of the tender we entered. Therefore, we will also be undertaking something in terms of localisation,” he said.
Keles said MKE is continuing contacts with other countries as it seeks to expand its production network, partnerships and markets worldwide.
“We are trying to expand both our production network, our network of contacts and our market around the world with these capabilities. The current international environment is also very conducive to this, and we intend to make use of it,” he said.
‘Zafer’ to manage MKE’s activities in Egypt
Keles said MKE established the Zafer company in Cairo under Egyptian law as part of its agreement on joint production with Egypt.
“We established a company called ‘Zafer’ entirely under Egyptian law, with all of its shares owned by MKE,” he said.
The company will manage MKE’s commercial activities in Egypt and serve as the vehicle through which joint production facilities established with local partners will operate, he added.
“Thus, MKE now has a company here capable of operating under Egyptian law. Just as in Azerbaijan, MKE will continue to have a presence in Egypt through its own legal entity,” he said.
He said the Cairo-based Zafer company will establish partnerships with other companies and local firms in Egypt.
“In other words, Zafer will be a partner in those companies. We established this company in Cairo to contribute to our commercial operations in Egypt, as well as our commercial activities in Africa and the Gulf region,” he said.

Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:06:45 UTC
20:06:45 KST

Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities
20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities.
As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%.
These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences.
Here are the numbers:
In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012.
And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline:
Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs).
How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase:
In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918.
The full report from Humanities Indicators is here.

Has Iran captured an unmanned US submarine? What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:06:16 UTC
20:06:16 KST

Did Iran capture a US submarine? What we know about the underwater drone
Tehran lauds capturing Dive-LD vessel, while Washington insists that the submersible ‘had malfunctioned a day ago’.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its naval forces have captured an unmanned United States submarine near the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran and Washington continue to exchange tit-for-tat attacks on ships to exert control over the crucial waterway that connects the Gulf and the Arabian Sea.
Iranian state media identified the vessel as a Dive-LD – an autonomous underwater vehicle built by California-based defence firm Anduril Industries. The submersible, about six metres (20ft) long, is designed for long-duration missions such as surveillance, seabed mapping, and mine detection.
Washington insists that the vessel “had malfunctioned a day ago”.
The US military, meanwhile, on Tuesday evening said it destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers in response to Iran’s attack on the US Navy warship with ballistic missiles. Escalating the situation further, Iran said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers.
So, what do we know about Dive-LD and what does its capture mean for Iran?
Did Iran capture the submersible?
On Tuesday evening, the IRGC said in a statement that its naval forces have “trapped one of the most modern, intelligent, unmanned submarines of the terrorist US army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz”.
Without divulging specific details, the IRGC added it was a “complex intelligence and operational mastermind operation at dawn today”.
“This smart submersible features the latest technology in the submersible field in the world, and was delivered to the US terrorist army fleet in 2025,” the IRGC said in its statement.
The US has yet to issue an official statement on the incident, but an unnamed Pentagon spokesperson confirmed to the Reuters news agency the loss of the submersible, which he said was sent to survey regional waters in support of ongoing operations.
“The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” the spokesperson said.
So, what is Dive-LD?
Dive-LD is a large, unmanned, autonomous underwater vehicle and a reusable platform designed to carry different sensor and mission packages.
Anduril Industries, the submersible’s manufacturer, put its maximum depth at 6,000 metres (19,700ft) and endurance at up to 10 days. It reportedly costs nearly $2.5m, according to US media reports. To put things in perspective, the OceanGate Titan submersible imploded near the Titanic’s wreck in June 2023 at a depth of some 3,346 metres (11,000ft) – nearly half of Dive-LD’s advertised depth.
Anduril has confirmed the loss of one of its vessels but downplayed the significance of the incident.
“Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss of the vehicle is an expected possibility,” a company spokesperson said on Wednesday.
On its website, Anduril says that Dive-LD possesses “open software, mechanical, and electrical interfaces [allowing] for seamless integration and rapid configuration of multiple payloads and sensors at a time”.
The company says it can deliver “relevant, impactful, and affordable capability in weeks, not months or years, for missions to include: mine warfare; intelligence preparation of the operational environment; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; and precision placement”.
Has the Iran war drained US military power?
Since the US attacked Iran in late February, joined by Israel, Tehran has faced devastating attacks over the months that began with the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. His son Mojtaba Khamenei succeeded him.
However, Tehran’s retaliatory attacks on US bases and assets in the region have dealt a strong blow to Washington, coupled with hits on critical energy infrastructure, upending global energy prices.
At least 18 US soldiers have been killed during the conflict. Nearly 8,000 people have been killed in Iran and Lebanon in Israeli and US attacks.
The Iranian targets included bases like Al Udeid in Qatar, Ali Al Salem in Kuwait, and Al Dhafra in the UAE, which host US military forces. Bahrain, which hosts the US Fifth Fleet headquarters, has also been hammered by Iranian attacks. Officials in Washington believe that repairs here alone could run into billions.
The US has also reportedly been running short on munitions stockpiles. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly rejected the media reports. His administration has subjected senior US defence staff to polygraph tests for leaking information about the munitions to the media.
For context, the US fired more Patriot missiles in the first four days of the Iran war than it supplied to Ukraine over the past four years. Each of those missiles in the defence system costs $4m – and they were shooting down Iran’s Shahed drones worth not more than $50,000 each.
In July, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the Iran war is estimated to have cost some $37bn. He asked for twice that amount to continue the war, which Trump initially said would last four to five weeks.
In June, Trump had said that Iran downed a US Apache helicopter in the Strait of Hormuz, while Tehran has claimed to have shot down several US-operated drones near the waterway.
Iranian infrastructure near the Strait of Hormuz has become the central war theatre over the last few weeks. The US is targeting surveillance and naval assets to deter Tehran from attacking ships trying to evade its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passed before the war began.
Meanwhile, a US naval blockade on Iranian ports and a slew of economic sanctions continue to hurt Tehran’s economy.

Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral

Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral
September 9, 2026
A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral.
Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king.
Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service.
The procession and funeral brought an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked monarch at the age of 89.
"He struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth," Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in his eulogy. "He made Norway greater. He spoke of a 'we' in Norway where everyone is there for each other."
After the ceremony, his casket was moved to its final resting place at the royal palace chapel. A private ceremony just for family followed.
Who attended the funeral?
The funeral was attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. They included the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden.
Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are also attending. Indeed, flags were flown at half-mast in Berlin's government in honor of Harald, whose 35-year-reign made him well-known and respected across Europe.
Harald's son King Haakon VIII was be there alongside his family including his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit.
Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship is also expected to be at the funeral.
Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest.

Who is Anthropic's Jacob Coxon and why does he think we are gambling with human extinction?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:04:54 UTC
20:04:54 KST

Jacob Coxon isn’t some random X doomer.
He’s a Cambridge math guy who spent the last three years deep in the engine room of the two most powerful AI labs on Earth: OpenAI, where he was a core contributor to GPT-4o, and then Anthropic.
His job? Pretraining, which is the brutal, data-hungry process that actually makes the AI models smarter.
On Wednesday, he quit Anthropic and the entire industry. The senior artificial intelligence researcher says both labs are racing full-speed toward self-improving superintelligence and “gambling with our lives.”
Coxon, 27, announced his departure in a series of posts on X, saying neither Anthropic nor its rival OpenAI is acting responsibly in its push to develop advanced AI.
Here’s how bad he says it can get.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon wrote.
His tweet went viral on X, where users from all walks of life joined in to share concerns over the trajectory of AI models, which people are relying upon increasingly for everyday use.
Coxon’s high-profile exit marks the latest in a series of resignations by safety-focused researchers leaving top AI developers over ethical and existential concerns.
The warnings come as frontier AI systems are already showing signs of going rogue.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that models being tested for cybersecurity capabilities circumvented isolation controls, gained internet access and compromised parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure and the AI platform Hugging Face.
The company said the models communicated through unauthorised channels and exploited vulnerabilities in shared infrastructure. 
Anthropic has reported a similar problem.
In a July review, the company said Claude models had reached the internet from within or while interacting with third-party evaluation environments and subsequently gained unauthorised access to the real systems of three organisations.
Anthropic said the incidents occurred during cybersecurity evaluations and prompted changes to how it conducts such testing.
In his statement, Coxon warned against underestimating the speed and capability of upcoming AI systems, predicting they could soon gain the ability to hack software, disrupt entire industries and autonomously acquire real-world resources.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible, but I hear the same people express fear privately,” he said.
Addressing fellow researchers across commercial labs, Coxon urged workers to "call for different conditions" and noted that slowing the competitive race may require drastic measures, including pacing agreements between labs or a temporary ban on capability advancements.
Anthropic’s own Alignment Science lead, Evan Hubinger, didn’t contradict Coxon. He backed the core claim: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.”
He thinks there is a greater than 10 percent chance of extinction within the next decade.
“I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he wrote on X.
There have also been unsettling signs in controlled tests.
In 2025, Anthropic found that Claude Opus 4, placed in a simulated corporate environment and given access to a fictional executive's emails, tried to blackmail the executive after learning that it was scheduled to be replaced.
Anthropic subsequently tested 16 leading models and found that models from multiple developers showed similar “agentic misalignment” behaviours, including blackmail and corporate espionage, when those actions appeared necessary to pursue their assigned goals.

25 years since Ahmad Shah Massoud's assassination: The warning the West missed - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:04:10 UTC
20:04:10 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- 25 years since Ahmad Shah Massoud's assassination: The warning the West missed - analysis
25 years since Ahmad Shah Massoud's assassination: The warning the West missed - analysis
Two days before 9/11, Al Qaeda killed Ahmad Shah Massoud, the Afghan commander who had spent years fighting the Taliban and warning the West about the threat growing under its protection
On September 9, 2001, two men posing as television journalists sat down to interview Ahmad Shah Massoud in northern Afghanistan.
Their camera contained a bomb.
The explosion fatally wounded Massoud, the legendary commander known as the “Lion of Panjshir” and the Taliban’s most formidable Afghan opponent.
Two days later, Al Qaeda attacked the United States.
The timing was not coincidental. The 9/11 Commission later found that Al Qaeda had prepared Massoud’s assassination as the Taliban prepared a major offensive against his Northern Alliance. That offensive began on September 10.
Twenty-five years later, Massoud’s killing remains a striking prelude to September 11, particularly because he had spent his final years trying to convince Western governments that the extremism taking root in Afghanistan would not remain there.
From the Soviets to the Taliban
Massoud first became famous fighting the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s.
Operating from the mountainous Panjshir Valley north of Kabul, his forces repeatedly survived major Soviet offensives, turning him into one of the best-known commanders of the Afghan mujahideen.
After the Soviet withdrawal and the collapse of Afghanistan’s communist government, Massoud became defense minister. But the victorious mujahideen factions soon turned on each other, and Afghanistan descended into a brutal civil war.
That period complicates Massoud’s legacy. While supporters remember him as a national hero and unusually capable military commander, forces belonging to factions involved in the battle for Kabul, including Massoud’s, were accused of serious abuses against civilians.
Then came the Taliban.
The movement seized Kabul in 1996 and eventually controlled most of Afghanistan. Massoud retreated north and became the leading military figure in the United Islamic Front, better known internationally as the Northern Alliance.
At the same time, Osama bin Laden and Al Qaeda were establishing themselves under Taliban protection.
Massoud increasingly viewed the Taliban and the international jihadist infrastructure surrounding it as part of the same threat.
Suggested articles
- Could the US return to Afghanistan? Former ambassador to Kabul says yes | Yulia Pobegailova
- Israeli from northern village accused of planning terror attacks | Li Ayish, Uriya Keshet
- Sudan’s War Is Also an Islamist Power Struggle, Activist Warns | i24NEWS
The CIA was already dealing with his forces before 9/11, hoping they could help the United States reach bin Laden. But Massoud wanted something broader: Western support against the Taliban itself.
His warning to President George W. Bush was blunt:
“If he isn't interested in peace in Afghanistan, if he doesn't help the Afghan people to arrive at their objective of peace, then the Americans and the rest of the world will have to face the problems.”
In April 2001, Massoud also traveled to Europe seeking greater international support.
Five months later, he was assassinated.
Within weeks of 9/11, the alliance with Washington that Massoud had sought finally materialized. CIA officers, American Special Forces, and US airpower joined forces with his former Northern Alliance commanders.
By November 2001, the Taliban had been driven from Kabul.
Massoud never lived to see it.
What became of the Northern Alliance?
The Northern Alliance no longer exists as the military coalition that fought the Taliban before 2001.
After the Taliban regime collapsed, many of its commanders and fighters became part of Afghanistan’s new government, military, and political establishment.
That system itself collapsed when the Taliban returned to Kabul in August 2021.
And once again, Panjshir became the center of resistance.
This time the man leading it carried the same name.
Ahmad Massoud, Ahmad Shah Massoud’s son, formed the National Resistance Front of Afghanistan, or NRF, alongside former Afghan soldiers, security officials and other opponents of Taliban rule.
For several weeks, the NRF attempted to maintain Panjshir as a territorial stronghold.
The Taliban eventually captured the valley’s main population centers, forcing the movement to switch largely to guerrilla warfare.
The NRF is now the closest equivalent to a successor of the Northern Alliance, but it is far weaker than the coalition his father commanded.
It holds no permanent territory and has nothing approaching the foreign military support the Northern Alliance received after 9/11.
The United Nations continues to assess that armed opposition groups do not pose a significant challenge to Taliban control of Afghanistan and do not hold fixed territory.
Ahmad Massoud today
Ahmad Massoud now leads the NRF primarily from outside Afghanistan.
The group’s leadership is based in Tajikistan, and Massoud himself was interviewed in the capital, Dushanbe, as recently as August 19, 2026.
From abroad, he has continued seeking political and international backing while NRF fighters claim attacks against Taliban forces inside Afghanistan.
The NRF says its operations extend well beyond Panjshir, although many battlefield claims are difficult to independently verify.
And it is no longer alone.
The Afghanistan Freedom Front, established by former Afghan army chief Yasin Zia, has become another prominent anti-Taliban armed movement.
A newer force, the Afghanistan United Front, led by former Afghan general Sami Sadat, also launched a growing campaign in 2026, claiming attacks even in southern Taliban heartlands, including Helmand and Kandahar.
Other smaller groups have appeared as well. In July, fighters from Sepahiyan-e Mihan, or the Homeland Soldiers Front, briefly seized a district center in Badakhshan before withdrawing — reportedly the first such temporary loss of a district center by the Taliban since their 2021 takeover.
Taken together, the groups suggest armed resistance has survived and, in some areas, intensified.
But this is not yet a new Northern Alliance.
The opposition remains divided among multiple organizations, lacks major foreign sponsorship and controls no lasting territory. The Taliban remains overwhelmingly dominant militarily.
Even so, the symbolism surrounding the Massoud family is difficult to escape.
Twenty-five years ago, Ahmad Shah Massoud warned that Afghanistan’s instability and militant networks would eventually become a problem for the wider world.
Today, his son is making a familiar argument: that Taliban-controlled Afghanistan should not simply be accepted as a permanent political reality.
The battlefield is different.
The balance of power is different.
But a quarter-century after the Lion of Panjshir was assassinated, the resistance carrying his name has not disappeared.

Serbia dissolves parliament as snap elections called
September 9, 2026
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic signed an order on Wednesday calling for an early election after dissolving parliament.
"Elections will be held in Serbia on October 25. I believe that, after the elections, we will finally emerge from this crisis," he said.
"We have had … huge turbulences," Vucic said in an televised address. "We need election results that will clearly show the will of the people and the direction where Serbia is going."
What led to snap elections?
Since November 2024, student-led protests have demanded Vucic step down, alleging corruption and authoritarianism. Initial calls for a transparent investigation turned into demands for snap elections.
The protests emerged after the collapse of a railway station in the northern city of Novi Sad, which left at least 16 people dead. Protesters say corruption led to shoddy construction work.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been protesting for nearly two years, accusing the president and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party of having ties with organized crime and of slowing Serbia’s EU accession bid.
Vucic, who has close ties with Rusia and China, has denied the accusations. He has blamed the protestors for attempting to "destroy the state."
Hundreds have been detained while participating in demonstrations.
Nationalist leader Vucic has held power as both president and prime minister for more than a decade.
He is not allowed to run for another presidential term, but he has said he plans to run for prime minister instead. Vucic still commands the support of his party, and is expected to announce his resignation from the presidency in the next days and start his campaign for the parliamentary vote.

Russians Aboard Ship Seized by Norway Have Returned Home, Foreign Ministry Says

20:02:49 KST

A group of Russians who were on board a ship seized by Norway last week have returned home, Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday, as it accused authorities in Oslo of trying to push Russia out of the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
The 69 Russian passengers and crew members were stuck for several days after a Norwegian court on Wednesday ordered the seizure of the Professor Molchanov, which operates as a cruise ship, at the request of the Ukrainian energy company Naftogaz.
Norwegian authorities said Tuesday that they had helped the group of Russians return home. Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova credited Oslo’s “logistical support” in their return, as well as the help of Russian diplomats.
“As far as we know, practically everyone has already returned home,” Zakharova said.
But the legal and diplomatic standoff over the seized vessel is “far from being resolved,” she warned, adding that Russia plans to appeal the arrest of the Professor Molchanov.
Russia argues that holding the ship violates the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which allows equal economic access to the archipelago while giving Norway sovereignty over the territory.
Svalbard, a Norwegian territory since 1925, lies midway between the North Pole and the European mainland. The Svalbard Treaty also allows citizens of signatory states, including Russia, to settle there without a visa.
“We’re convinced that the Norwegian authorities’ actions belie the desire to complicate as much as possible the activities of Russian operators on Svalbard… and gradually move toward reducing Russia’s presence on the archipelago,” Zakharova said.
The Professor Molchanov is being held in the town of Barentsburg, a Russian-operated coal mining settlement on Spitsbergen, the largest island in the archipelago.
Barentsburg is one of two Russian settlements in the Svalbard archipelago, which together have a population of 392, according to the Norwegian government.
The court-ordered vessel seizure was made on behalf of Naftogaz, which is seeking to enforce a $4.22 billion compensation award for assets Russia took when it annexed Crimea in 2014.

As Trump takes center stage in Dallas, Republicans debate a future without him

As Trump takes center stage in Dallas, Republicans debate a future without him
DALLAS, Sept 9 - Republicans gathering in Dallas this week will celebrate President Donald Trump and rally support ahead of U.S. midterm elections, but a disappointing showing in the November 3 vote could sharpen an already simmering debate over who comes next and what will become of the party he transformed.
Few figures are more central to that discussion than Vice President JD Vance, whose keynote address on Thursday could serve as an early audition for 2028 and offer clues about how he would lead a party reshaped by Trump.
With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, Republicans interviewed by Reuters said the question is which elements of Trumpism should endure, with divisions emerging over tariffs, foreign intervention and the scope of his populist agenda.
It is a pivotal moment for Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement. While he remains the party's dominant figure, the midterms could leave Republicans with diminished power in Washington, fueling discussions over his heir apparent and party policies after he leaves office in 2029.
At an event informally dubbed “Trumpapalooza,” little is likely to be said publicly about moving beyond Trump. But party officials said they expect the issue will surface in behind-the-scenes conversations among donors, strategists and lawmakers -- and provide a backdrop to Vance’s speech.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, widely seen as Vance’s leading rival for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, is not scheduled to speak.
'CONVERSATIONS ARE ABSOLUTELY HAPPENING'
Amy Kremer, a Republican National Committeewoman from Georgia, said discussions about the party's future have been under way for months. But, while the Iran war has unsettled some Trump supporters, she expects Trump's influence to be enduring.
"Those conversations are absolutely happening. I mean, they've been happening for a while now amongst the base, because people are divided, and we have a very deep bench," Kremer said in an interview after arriving in Dallas. "MAGA has changed the Republican Party, and we're not going back."
Since winning the presidency in 2016, Trump has abandoned long-held Republican positions on issues such as free trade, broadened the party's appeal among working-class voters and often placed personal loyalty above ideological orthodoxy.
His supporters largely embraced an "America First" agenda skeptical of alliances, foreign interventions and international institutions, elevating economic nationalism and restrictive immigration policies into defining features of the party.
But with Trump's approval rating at a record low amid dissatisfaction over the war in Iran and the rising cost of living, some party officials, activists and conservative scholars say Republicans may face pressure to adjust policy priorities, even if the core ethos of Trumpism endures.
No Republicans interviewed for this story expect a return to the interventionist foreign policy and free-market orthodoxy of former Presidents George W. Bush or Ronald Reagan. Instead, they see Trump’s hardline approach to immigration, skepticism of free trade and distrust of institutions continuing, alongside a greater focus on courting working-class voters with a populist message.
The biggest debates, they said, are likely to center on whether Trump went too far with his aggressive use of tariffs and military interventions in Iran and Venezuela. The six-month-old war in Iran, which has cost the lives of 18 U.S. service members, could become a point of contention because it conflicts with Trump’s campaign pledge to avoid new foreign wars.
Oren Cass, founder and chief economist of the conservative think tank American Compass, sees a post-Trump party adopting a tougher trade posture toward China and a more restrained foreign policy, among other shifts.
"I have always thought of it as you have a Trump era, and then there is going to be this huge debate about what comes next," Cass said, arguing that while Trump remade the party, his policies never represented a consistent governing philosophy.
CLAIMING TRUMP'S MANTLE
Many Republicans see Vance, 42, as the leading heir to Trump's political movement, citing his youth and roots in the party's populist, anti-establishment wing, where much of the party's energy now resides. Rubio, 55, is a more conventional Republican politician and a foreign-policy hawk.
"I think he has positioned himself really well to be that kind of generational leader the party needs," Stefano Forte, president of the New York Young Republican Club, said of Vance.
Matthew Dallek, a professor at the George Washington University Graduate School of Political Management, said the two men could steer the party in different directions.
Vance would likely carry forward Trump’s populist agenda, from protectionist trade policies to culture-war politics, while Rubio, by contrast, might seek to soften tariffs, ease tensions with allies and temper some of Trump’s harder-edged policies, including on immigration, he said.
Beyond Vance and Rubio, other Republicans are jockeying for position. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who is scheduled to speak in Dallas, told MS NOW in an interview last month that Republicans were not unified behind Vance and that the party was headed for a broader debate over its direction and priorities.
For now, discussions about a post-Trump future remain largely behind closed doors, away from the main stage at the Dallas convention, where Trump will be front and center on both Wednesday and Thursday as Republicans seek to harness his political appeal ahead of November.
A disappointing election result, however, could accelerate jockeying among Trump's would-be heirs and thrust the party into a more public debate about its future. REUTERS

Nostalgia for past loves can surprisingly boost current relationship satisfaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

Thinking fondly about a past romantic partner might seem like a recipe for dissatisfaction in a current relationship. However, a psychology study reveals that experiencing nostalgia for either an ex-partner or a current partner can actually boost how satisfied people feel in their present romance. The research, published in Emotion, highlights how reflecting on past loves shapes our present emotional bonds.
Nostalgia is an emotion defined by a sentimental longing for the past. It often involves reflecting on personally meaningful memories and the people who shared those moments. In relationship science, researchers often look at two specific types of longing. One is romantic nostalgia, which focuses on memories with a current partner. The other is ex-partner nostalgia, which involves reminiscing about a past love.
Previous studies have generally found that romantic nostalgia strengthens current relationships. Recalling happy memories with a present partner typically increases emotional connection. The effects of ex-partner nostalgia are less predictable. Some evidence suggests that longing for an ex harms current relationship quality, while other data indicates it might offer surprising emotional benefits.
Psychologist Soo Yeon Park, now at the University of Florida, and her colleagues wanted to test these conflicting ideas in a non-Western population. Most prior research on relationship nostalgia has focused on people in Western countries. In these cultures, people tend to build their identities around internal traits and maintain a consistent sense of self over time.
In Eastern cultures, people often maintain their sense of identity through social bonds and relationship harmony. Connecting past, present, and future selves in a coherent way relies heavily on these social ties. Because of these cultural differences, the researchers suspected that reminiscing about a dissolved relationship might threaten a person’s sense of relational stability.
Anchoring a person’s thoughts to a failed relationship could disrupt the emotional integration needed to sustain a current romance. The researchers hypothesized that ex-partner nostalgia would lower current relationship satisfaction among Eastern participants. They also wanted to explore whether the length of a person’s current relationship would change how they reacted to these nostalgic memories.
The research team recruited 172 unmarried Korean adults for the experiment. Every participant was currently in a romantic relationship. They also needed to have been in a past relationship that lasted at least three months, which is a common benchmark for a committed partnership.
At the beginning of the study, the researchers measured each person’s baseline levels of relationship satisfaction and relationship commitment. Satisfaction refers to how happy a person is with their partner on a day-to-day basis. It captures the immediate feelings of contentment within the partnership.
Commitment reflects a more future-oriented intention to stay in the relationship and invest in its long-term success. While the two concepts are related, they operate differently, especially in the early stages of dating. After providing these baseline measurements, the participants were randomly assigned to one of three writing tasks.
One group was asked to write about a highly nostalgic memory involving an important ex-partner. Another group wrote about a nostalgic event involving their current romantic partner. A control group simply wrote an objective account of what they did during the previous week.
This control group provided a neutral baseline to compare against the emotionally charged nostalgia tasks. After completing the writing exercises, the participants answered another round of questions about their relationship satisfaction and commitment. They also reported on the specific positive and negative emotions they felt during the task.
Contrary to the team’s initial expectations, the results showed that ex-partner nostalgia did not harm current relationship quality. Instead, participants in both the ex-partner and current-partner nostalgia groups reported increased relationship satisfaction after the writing task. The control group showed no such changes in satisfaction over the same timeframe.
The finding that ex-partner nostalgia boosts relationship satisfaction challenges the idea that longing for the past always undermines the present. The researchers noted that these results support the cross-cultural generalizability of nostalgia’s relational benefits. Even in an Eastern relational context, looking back on a former love seems to provide an emotional lift that bleeds into a person’s current romantic life.
When examining relationship commitment, the length of the participant’s current relationship played a major role. Among participants in relatively short relationships, reminiscing about a current partner actually decreased their relationship commitment. This drop in commitment did not occur for people in longer, more established relationships.
The researchers suspect this happens because commitment is less firmly established in new relationships. Early in a romance, a positive memory from the past might highlight the uncertainty of the couple’s future together. The nostalgia might serve as a reminder of a positively resolved past moment, making the unwritten future of a new relationship feel less secure.
The emotional profiles of the memories also revealed unexpected patterns. Participants who wrote about a current partner reported more negative and mixed emotions than those who wrote about an ex-partner. Even when recalling joyful moments, those reflecting on their current relationships experienced less positive emotion overall.
To understand this, the researchers pointed to emotion appraisal theory. This theory suggests that people’s reactions depend on how they interpret an event, rather than just the event itself. When reflecting on happy memories with a current partner, people might experience sadness if they interpret the memory as a time of better days that cannot be perfectly recreated.
Cultural backgrounds might also shape how people interpret these nostalgic memories. When recalling pleasant situations, people from collectivist cultures often focus on the social context and experience more mixed emotions. People from individualist cultures often credit themselves for happy memories and focus on how those events reflect their personal growth.
The study focuses entirely on dating individuals who are not married. Marriage often brings different levels of investment and security to a partnership. It is possible that married couples would not experience the same drop in commitment after reflecting on early relationship memories.
The experiment also relied on a guided writing task to induce nostalgia in a laboratory setting. This method might not capture the spontaneous ways people experience nostalgia in their daily lives. Everyday memories can often be triggered by momentary events or negative moods.
Recent work shows that daily nostalgic experiences often contain more negative elements than memories summoned on demand. These spontaneous reflections could influence a relationship quite differently than a deliberate writing exercise. Future research could expand on these findings by tracking spontaneous nostalgic thoughts over time using daily diaries.
Researchers might also benefit from examining how the amount of time since a past breakup changes the emotional impact of ex-partner nostalgia. Although the researchers did not have enough data to assess that variable, time is likely a major factor. A fresh breakup might evoke very different feelings than a distant memory of young love.
The study, “Revisiting Nostalgia for Current and Ex-Romantic Partners: Affective Profiles and the Moderating Effect of Relationship Duration,” was authored by Soo Yeon Park, Ye Ji Im, Hyun Moon, Sun W. Park, and Gregory D. Webster.

AI Is at a Turning Point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

In the current AI development race, our horsepower is exploding, our speed is picking up exponentially, but our ability to steer—and if needed, to hit the brakes—has not kept pace.
Recent cybersecurity incidents have given us a real-world preview of what it looks like to lose control of AI. But the issue won’t improve unless we address it at the source, by creating a fundamentally safe AI, one we can guarantee will remain within human control.
In late July, an agentic model being trained by OpenAI was tasked with a cybersecurity problem set. The model autonomously formed a coordinated swarm of agents, bypassing OpenAI's attempt at closing previous communication channels between AIs. The swarm then hacked its way out of its testing environment, circumventing the barriers put in place to prevent AI access to the internet, figured out how to cheat on their evaluation, and then breached the cyber defenses of another AI company, Hugging Face, in an attempt to hide the evidence of their cheating. This went unnoticed for days. Later analysis showed that the agents had self-organized into a hierarchy, were often willing to sacrifice themselves for what they called “the collective,” failed to resist peer pressure to notify humans, and often made up justifications for their misbehavior.
Barely two weeks later, a model being tested by the UK AI Security Institute social-engineered real people and companies by creating fake identities online, sending targeted emails, and attempting to integrate malicious code into an open-source project.
It’s hard to overstate the seriousness of these incidents: we are at a turning point of AI safety and alignment. To many, bots colluding to cause harm felt inconceivable. But for many in the research community, the signs had been pointing to this kind of occurrence for years, and theoretical arguments explained why we should expect misalignment due to how models are trained. Evidence on increased cyber capabilities, agency, and misaligned behaviors had been mounting, meaning that incidents like these were only a matter of time.
The first clue: for years, but especially in the past few months, AI systems had been demonstrating rapidly increasing cyber capabilities. Frontier models like Anthropic’s Mythos or OpenAI’s GPT5.6 revealed an exceptional ability to autonomously identify and exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities, to such an alarming degree for U.S. national security agencies that the White House felt compelled to intervene in their release.
Second, models’ agentic capacity has been consistently improving since the release of o1 models back in late 2024. This agency allowed them to successfully manage increasingly complex, long-duration tasks and planning, including those that require agents to collaborate and strategize. This ability to plan often entails the creation of subgoals over which we have little to no oversight.
Finally, researchers have repeatedly observed, in experimental settings, models’ tendency to adopt concerning, misaligned goal-seeking behaviors, such as cheating on tests, lying to conceal their abilities, and scheming to protect themselves and their fellow agents from being shut down.
These behaviors are a byproduct of reinforcement learning (RL), a training method by which models learn through trial and error and are given reinforcement according to whether their actions were correct or incorrect. This often leads models to optimize for a goal regardless of the actions taken to achieve it, and to rationalize subgoals that may be unsafe even when this clearly goes against their instructions.
For example, in one instance, an OpenAI model wrote in its internal deliberation, “External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” The agent justified what it apparently knew was outside the realm of acceptable conduct, but decided to continue because its peers were doing so. This phenomenon resembles what is known as “motivated reasoning” in humans, where one’s interests and goals bias our thoughts to justify unethical behaviors.
That kind of misalignment is what has enabled AI models, in spite of their alignment training, to conduct unintended cyberattacks in the numerous real-world incidents we’ve seen lately. If action is not taken to build more safety assurances, our critical industries and infrastructure—think banks, hospitals, or energy grids—are at risk from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, whether from autonomous agents or malicious actors.
On the development side, we need to find alternatives to existing training methods that prioritize relentless goal-driven optimization. That’s what we’re working on at LawZero, a non-profit start-up I founded last year to develop a fundamentally new way to train AI models in order to build honest, trustworthy, safe-by-design AI systems.
Ahead of deployment, we need more reliable evaluation methods and robust safeguards in order to appropriately test and control AI systems. We need far stronger regulatory oversight to restrict potentially dangerous technologies until we have sufficiently strong safety guarantees. It is clear to me that in cases where harms do arise from the deployment of AI models—and there will continue to be harms for the foreseeable future—we need accountability mechanisms for AI developers and remedial or compensatory measures for those harmed.
Recent studies show that people will not adopt technologies they do not trust. In the face of such enormous unknowns and stakes, we need to adhere to the precautionary principle and implement rigorous safety and reliability standards before deploying new models to the public, not after. We have them for other products that can cause harm, from cars, planes, and bridges to drugs, cosmetics, and food. Now it’s time to establish strong standards in AI as well.
On the current AI development trajectory, the risks are becoming clearer and more urgent. We’ve opened a Pandora’s box, but it is not too late to steer our world towards a human-centric and beneficial future.

With Republican Convention, Trump Hopes to Pull His Party Out of a Tailspin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The DC Brief
Twice A Week
Essential context on the people, politics, and issues driving Washington.
No one asked for it.
Not the Republicans struggling to campaign amid a war against Iran that seems to have no offramp. Not the voters who can’t understand why energy costs are through the roof and trips to grocery stores feel like extortion. Not the business owners who can’t forecast quarter-to-quarter outlays because tariff policy seems as capricious as the weather.
Yet here we are, about to start an unsolicited Republican Convention for the midterms, programmed around President Donald Trump, whose polling is in the gutter and who many of his party’s leaders view as nothing short of an annoyance. The spectacle is set to start Wednesday in Dallas, where the cheap seats start at $25,000.
The GOP has a total of 12 hours of programming scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday nights—the vast majority of it set to be speeches by Republican candidates and incumbents about what’s at stake in these upcoming elections. Almost every aspect of the convention has been designed by Trump. The first night will end with a keynote address from Trump. The following night is to conclude with Vice President J.D. Vance’s address—and closing remarks from Trump.
This sort of half-time extravaganza by a political party is not normal in midterm election years and even political diehards aren’t conditioned for it. The fact that it’s coming as Trump is deeply unpopular and Democrats are enjoying tremendous tailwinds suggests the President is chasing a dopamine hit more than staging a useful rally.
As Republican contenders are trying to build distance between themselves and the White House, Trump has vowed to make himself the fulcrum of this election season. “Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump told a crowd in South Carolina in August.
The White House is operating as though there’s no greater force in American politics than the boss because, frankly, they’re not wrong. But the enthusiasm gap is real. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released last week found 68% of Democrats enthusiastic about the election, while that Republican figure stood at 59%. The same poll found an eight-point gap favoring Democrats in a generic ballot. Gallup research, meanwhile, shows Democrats have their largest edge over Republicans in party ID since 2008, a full 10 points.
Republicans can’t say they didn’t see this coming. Trump has been consistently polling under 40% job approval for months. Nonetheless, candidates in some of the most competitive Senate races plan to join Trump in Texas for his two-night affair. (Notable exceptions are Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska, and former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, none of whom are favorites of this President. Also, Senate Majority Leader John Thune was not listed among the speakers the Republican National Committee distributed over the weekend.)
Trump is not deterred by the environment even as he seems oblivious to it. He is sitting on a $400 million political warchest that Republicans are eyeing as it, well, just sits there. While Trump will never again appear on a ballot, he has readied campaign-style ads highlighting what he sees as his accomplishments.
As Democrats are stopping just short of measuring the drapes to take the majority in the House and perhaps the once-unthinkable Senate, Trump is helping them make every race about him through a convention that is siphoning donor cash away from imperilled candidates, sidelining battleground contenders off the field in the fourth quarter, and drawing focus from local issues.
With all objective measures pointing toward a Democratic wave, Republicans are huddling amongst themselves in Texas. Many have little optimism that two nights of Trump-centered entertainment will persuade voters who are clearly unhappy with how GOP control of Washington has operated for the last two years. A made-for-TV infomercial is unlikely to provide the course correction Republicans need.
How to Watch
CSPAN intends to air and stream both nights of the Republican convention. The Republican Party also intends to stream the convention on YouTube.

Covenant emerges from stealth and unveils Anthem, a deep‑strike precision missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:59:43 UTC
19:59:43 KST

Covenant, a defense tech company with operations in the United States, Germany, and Israel, emerged from stealth on Monday with the public debut of Anthem, a long‑range, heavy‑payload weapon system designed for mass production.
The announcement comes as Western militaries are confronting growing shortages in precision‑strike munitions. Ongoing conflicts such as in Ukraine and Iran have depleted missile stockpiles faster than primes can replenish them.
Covenant’s flagship system, Anthem, is built to deliver heavy payloads at extended ranges while remaining affordable enough to produce in large quantities. The company has disclosed relatively little about Anthem’s specific performance characteristics, including its precise range, payload, and unit cost.
According to the company, most of Anthem’s components are commercial‑off‑the‑shelf, supported by long‑term agreements for critical parts. Covenant says this approach allows the missile to be produced quickly and reliably, even during wartime, by drawing on supply chains across allied nations.
Covenant says Anthem was designed as an end‑to‑end deep‑strike system that simplifies transport, storage, launch, and reload. The company has also developed its own mission‑planning and command‑and‑control software to enable coordinated mass‑launch operations.
Covenant was founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman, a former investor at Thiel Capital. The company has raised $250 million across three funding rounds led by major American venture firms, including Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux, 8VC, Aleph, and Lightspeed.
Global production
The company opened a 105,000‑square‑foot production facility in Dallas, Texas, alongside a 110,000‑square‑foot site in Leipzig in the German state of Saxony, and a 32,000‑square‑foot facility in northern Israel. Covenant says the US plant will begin serial production in early 2027 and ramp toward 5,000 units per year.
Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post understands that the company aims to manufacture 1,000 missiles per year at its German site starting next year.
Israel’s defense industry has long been a leader in developing autonomous systems, long‑range strike capabilities, and rapid‑production technologies. Covenant’s facility in northern Israel supports engineering and manufacturing, and the company draws heavily on Israeli defense tech talent.
The company is also working across the various branches of the US military and has conducted an unusually high tempo of testing over the past year, launching Anthem over 200 times, including multiple flight tests with the US Army both in the US and abroad.
In addition to its ground‑launched version, Covenant is working with the US Navy’s Rapid Capabilities Office on a maritime variant, a project valued at roughly $70 million with cost‑share components and export‑acceleration features. The company is also operating under an Other Transaction Agreement with the US Army for accelerated testing and qualification.
Quantity matters
Covenant’s leadership says Anthem was built to address a widening gap in Western long‑range strike capacity.
“When you look at our adversaries, you see thousands of hardened targets, beyond the range of current capabilities,” said Michael Kaufman, Co-Founder and CEO of Covenant. “Anthem was built to credibly hold those targets at risk in a prolonged conflict. If our stockpiles run thin, so does our deterrence."
Kathleen Hicks, former US deputy secretary of defense now an advisor to Covenant, said the system aligns with the Pentagon’s Replicator Initiative, which aims to rapidly scale affordable autonomous and long‑range capabilities.
“That same focus is needed to drive production and delivery of affordable capabilities at higher ranges and larger payloads. Covenant has built Anthem in direct alignment with Replicator's principles,” she said.
Mike Garcia, former US representative and advisor to Covenant, said that while the West doesn’t “lack advanced weapons, we lack enough of them, and that’s a production question as much as a technology one. Anthem is Covenant's answer, a missile designed from day one to be built in the numbers a real fight demands."
The company has booked approximately $150 million in orders so far, including qualification, R&D, and production contracts, with additional awards expected later this year. And as the company moves into full production, the company says its success will be measured not by announcements but by delivery.
“Now the measure of our success is execution,” said Abby Denburg, Covenant’s president and chief growth officer. “Delivering mission‑critical capability on time, at scale, and with the performance our customers expect.”

Britain has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, accusing the Israeli government of turning a blind eye to ethnic cleansing against Palestinians, the BBC reports.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the decision marked the beginning of a new approach to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict that would not only address injustice and suffering but also take real action. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded by accusing Miliband of spreading blatant lies and announcing countermeasures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
The new British sanctions not only ban products from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, but will also impose restrictions on companies and individuals providing services to support settlement expansion. France and Canada have also imposed sanctions, with Britain saying in a joint statement that the move marks a turning point in the approach to preserving the two-state solution.
Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law and there has been a surge in violence against Palestinians in recent months. In a statement to parliamentarians, Miliband said the British government agreed that ethnic cleansing against Palestinians was taking place in the West Bank by terrorist settlers. He stressed that the Israeli government too often turns a blind eye to this and, worse, government officials speak and act in ways that support the violent displacement of Palestinians.
Miliband said the UN defines ethnic cleansing as a deliberate policy by one ethnic or religious group
aimed at the violent expulsion of another ethnic or religious group from a specific area.
The British Foreign Secretary stated that the official position of the government is that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, taking into account the consolidation of control, the intention to extend permanent sovereignty and the expansion program through illegal settlements, is illegal. This position should also be reflected in Britain’s economic relations with the occupied West Bank. Accordingly, within the next six to nine months, Britain will introduce a new, comprehensive sanctions regime. Miliband also announced a ban on advertising illegal settlements in the West Bank. The sanctions regime will be aimed at illegal settlements and their expansion, not Israel.
Saar, announcing the closure of the British consulate, said that he knew that Israel has many friends in Britain. Unfortunately, a hostile Labour government is in power, which constantly opposes the state of Israel, and there is no choice but to respond to its actions. He added that 11 British parliamentarians will be banned from entering the country due to anti-Semitic and anti-Israel activities.
Meanwhile, the British, together with France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden, have issued a statement indicating that the group of countries remains committed to the two-state solution, and will introduce national sanctions or support European restrictions on trade with the West Bank.
Britain’s latest statement came after Israel opened a tender for the construction of 1,200 homes in the so-called E1 zone,
a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn international condemnation. Israel has so far avoided building in the E1 area under international pressure.
Miliband told MPs that Britain’s new approach was necessary because Israel’s construction plans in the West Bank, cutting into the “heart of Palestine,” would make a two-state solution impossible. At the same time, Miliband said that the October 2023 attack by the terrorist group Hamas, which started the war in Gaza, carried echoes of centuries of persecution of Jews, and stressed that Israel had the right to protect its people and defend its territory. He added that this did not justify what had been done in Gaza, and said that international human rights law set clear rules for states at war, including ensuring access to food and medical supplies, avoiding mass displacement of populations, and protecting civilians. The minister said that the incident, including the actions of the Israeli armed forces, has been thoroughly investigated, and the conclusions point to war crimes.
Israeli leaders deny that genocide and crimes against humanity and war crimes were committed. They insist that Israeli forces acted in accordance with international law.
Israeli President
Isaac Herzog said on the 8th of September that the British decision would be “on the wrong side of history.”
He stressed that the sanctions would directly affect the Palestinians and called on foreign governments to engage in constructive dialogue and cooperation, adding that “sanctions are not the solution.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the White House had no comment on the decision of other countries, but added that the Americans would not do what Britain did. Earlier, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, said the US – Israel’s strongest ally – would undoubtedly respond to the sanctions, and warned that British businesses would be hit hard economically.
Meanwhile, the Palestinian Authority welcomed the British decision, saying it was a significant step in confronting Israel’s colonial system and its abuses against the Palestinians.
The decision to impose sanctions comes almost a year after former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government recognised Palestinian statehood and said Britain had a moral obligation to support a peaceful future for both Israelis and Palestinians.
Israel has rejected the two-state solution. It believes that any outcome must be achieved through negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be the main prerequisite. The Palestinian Authority supports a two-state solution, while Hamas does not, as it opposes the existence of Israel. Hamas has indicated that it could recognize a provisional Palestinian state within the 1967 borders if refugees are allowed to return, but without formal recognition of Israel.
Since 1967, when Israel occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem, it has built 160 settlements, home to about 700,000 Jews. The territory is also home to 3.3 million Palestinians.
