Why Switzerland is still not ready to face heatwaves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Why Switzerland is still not ready to face heatwaves
Several Swiss cities have strengthened their measures against heatwaves through alerts, awareness campaigns and climate shelters. However, a nationwide strategy is still lacking.
“It may sound paradoxical, but I suffer more from the heat in Switzerland than in Spain,” says Ana Maria Vicedo CabreraExternal link, an environmental epidemiologist and professor at the University of Bern.
The Spanish researcher studies the effects of climate change on human health. “Spain is certainly hotter than Switzerland, but we have become accustomed to living with these conditions. In Switzerland, we have not yet adapted,” she told Swissinfo.
This summer is likely to be the hottest ever recorded in Switzerland. Daily temperatures have exceeded the long-term average by 5°C to 10°C. In several places, the mercury approached 40°C, and heatwave alerts remained in effect for weeks. In Lugano, in southern Switzerland, 49 tropical nights were recorded, during which temperatures never dropped below 20°C, setting a record since measurements began in 1865.
Several Swiss cities have introduced measures to protect the most vulnerable people, especially the elderly. These range from awareness campaigns to climate shelters. Heat isn’t just a meteorological phenomenon, but a public health issue, Cabrera notes.
However, protection against the effects of heatwaves in Switzerland remains insufficient, according to her. Measures vary considerably from one city to another, there is no coordinated national strategy, and some at-risk groups remain largely excluded.
“In the past, heat was seen as a problem limited to a few days a year and to a few cantons. That is no longer the case. The effects of heatwaves are now felt, directly or indirectly, throughout Switzerland,” says Cabrera.
Free access to swimming pools and a map of shaded benches
The canton of Ticino, in Italian-speaking Switzerland, and the city of Geneva were the first in the country to adopt tools and action plans against heatwaves, in 2004 and 2007 respectively. These strategies include early warning systems, coordination between social and healthcare services, and access to cool places like green spaces or air-conditioned cinema theatres.
High temperatures can cause fatigue and heatstroke, dehydration, worsen a range of medical conditions and, in severe cases, lead to death. Older people, individuals with chronic illnesses, pregnant women and young children are particularly vulnerable.
In Geneva, residents aged 65 and over can access two municipal swimming pools free of charge in the morning and three air-conditioned cinemas in the afternoon during the hottest days. Around 8,600 people took advantage of these freebies between June 18 and August 5.
The effectiveness of such interventions on public health is still being assessed, says Cabrera. Nevertheless, the idea of establishing climate shelters is particularly relevant in Switzerland, where most homes do not have air conditioning and are not thermally insulated against heat.
Another advantage of these spaces is their potential to encourage social interaction, which is especially important in the context of increasingly long heatwaves.
“You cannot ask older people to remain indoors for five or six consecutive days. They need to be able to go shopping, maintain social relationships and engage in physical activity, otherwise their health may deteriorate,” Cabrera notes. She says clear alternatives are needed to the oft-repeated advice of avoiding the hottest hours of the day or drinking enough water.
In recent years, other municipal and cantonal authorities have also strengthened their heat protection measuresExternal link. Bern and Lucerne maintain daily contact with older residents during heatwaves, while Zurich offers free home support services. Neuchâtel, for its part, created a mapExternal link this summer showing benches located in shaded areas.
Critics of Switzerland’s heat protection measures
Swiss cities’ steps to address extreme heat still lag behind cities such as Paris, Barcelona and various locations in the United States, says Cabrera.
The French capital, for example, is preparing for an extreme heat scenario (“Paris at 50°CExternal link”) through a network of cool spaces accessible to residents, increased vegetation and water features in public areas, as well as urban planning measures designed to limit the urban heat island effect.
Eleni Myrivili, the United Nations’ leading expert on extreme heat, recently criticised Switzerland’s inadequate adaptation to climate warming. In an interview with Schweiz am WochenendeExternal link, she argued that a country like Switzerland should have much stronger protection systems for vulnerable groups and that the roughly 200External link heat-related deaths recorded at the beginning of the summer could have been prevented.
The first major heatwave of this summer coincided with an increase in mortality among older people in Switzerland, according to preliminary data from the Federal Statistical Office. Between June 22 and June 28, the number of deaths was approximately 15% higher than expected for that time of year.
However, it is not possible to attribute these deaths directly to heat. Determining the actual causes of death and confirming the link will likely not be possible until 2028. During the summer of 2015, excess mortality reached about 18%.
A studyExternal link led by Ana Maria Vicedo Cabrera estimates that heat caused 623 deaths in Switzerland between June and August 2022, one of the hottest years on record. Of these, 370 deaths could have been avoided in the absence of human-induced climate change.
Across the rest of Europe, the heat also had severe consequences for mortality. According to provisional data reported by The GuardianExternal link, the four heatwaves that struck this summer caused at least 35,000 deaths. In Germany, France and Spain alone, more than 25,000 deaths are estimated to have been attributable to high temperatures.
According to the World Health Organization, heat-related mortality in Europe has increased by 30% over the past 20 years.
In Myrivili’s view, issuing heat alerts is not enough. Authorities must ensure that information reaches older people living alone and that support networks are in place to contact them, assist them and accompany them to cooler locations.
“We need to be more ambitious in implementing more advanced measures that can reduce or mitigate heat exposure,” agrees Cabrera.
She adds that greater attention should also be paid to vulnerable groups that have so far received little consideration in prevention strategies, such as people with mental health disorders. As part of a research projectExternal link supported by the insurance company Mobiliar, her team is developing specific recommendations and guidelines to improve protection for this group during heatwaves.
A studyExternal link conducted in the canton of Bern found that the risk of hospital admission among people with mental health conditions rises significantly as temperatures increase. Research has also identified a correlation between heat and an increase in suicide ratesExternal link.
Changing habits during heatwaves
Adapting to heat is an issue for everyone, Cabrera stresses, which is why some daily habits will gradually need to be reconsidered, from the way buildings are insulated and cooled to travel patterns and the organisation of schedules and activities during the summer months.
The expert points to schools as an example. In several cantons, classes resume at the beginning of August, which this year coincided with a heatwave.
“We should ask ourselves whether it is appropriate to modify the school calendar,” she says.
Cabrera also highlights the need to strengthen protection for people who work outdoors. In her view, clearer rules are needed to determine when and under what conditions work can continue during heatwaves, along with closer monitoring of the health of workers who are most exposed to high temperatures. The city of Geneva’s heatwave action plan, for example, requires the suspension of outdoor activities that are directly exposed to sunlight from 1:00 p.m until sunset.
A national strategy to protect everyone from heat
Today, heat-protection measures vary considerably from one city and canton to another, depending on available resources and local political priorities.
Cabrera argues that the Swiss government should step in with a national strategy and provide clearer guidelines, greater resources and financial support that would enable cantons and municipalities to develop interventions tailored to the needs of their populations.
“Everyone should benefit from a minimum level of protection, regardless of where they live,” she says.
Similar demands are being made by the Swiss alliance “No 50-Degree Summers!External link”, which brings together around 70 organisations active in the fields of climate, health, environment and agriculture. The coalition is also calling for a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels and a substantial reduction in greenhouse gas emissions across all sectors.
More
What Switzerland needs to learn from earlier and longer heatwaves
‘Climate change is no longer a future threat’
Heatwaves and drought are also set to become increasingly prominent political issues. An urgent debate is expected during the autumn session of the Swiss parliament, which opens on September 14.
For Cabrera, this summer should serve as a wake-up call. “We must learn from what has happened and clearly recognise that climate change is no longer a future threat but a reality we are already facing,” she says.
“It is important not to forget the problem as soon as temperatures fall. Preparation for next summer must begin now.”

Kaja Kallas under fire from EU capitals when she needs them most
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:54:16 UTC
15:54:16 KST

The EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas is on a collision course with European capitals at a time when her institutional role is being increasingly challenged.
The European Union's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, suffered another political defeat when member states torpedoed her latest initiative to set up an expert group on European defence, at a time when her diplomatic service is under growing pressure to reform.
On Sunday, the European External Action Service (EEAS) cancelled, at the last minute, the launch of a new high-level group tasked with producing a report on how to boost the EU's defence capabilities by identifying strategic investment gaps.
Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, had announced the initiative just days earlier, saying it aimed "to have some of the brightest minds on security and defence come together and really provide out-of-the-box solutions."
"We have decided not to proceed with the initiative," an EU official told Euronews, asking not to be named. "Some member states felt this was not the right path to pursue at this moment."
The episode underscores how Kallas at times attempts to push forward without the necessary political support, even as backing from member states – especially smaller ones – is her best bet to keep the EEAS relevant.
Diplomatic misstep
Italy led the charge against the initiative with a firm no, after the group included a representative seen as a major political opponent of Defence Minister Guido Crosetto.
According to the Italian press agency ANSA, the person in question was Roberta Pinotti, who previously served as defence minister under the centre-left governments of Matteo Renzi and Paolo Gentiloni – both of the opposite political colour to the current Italian executive.
France and several other countries also objected to the expert group, stressing it had not been discussed at ministerial level and had caught most European governments by surprise.
The pressure was such that it forced the EEAS to cancel the initiative.
For the EEAS, the expert, advisory nature of the initiative meant not all countries needed to be represented, and that former political and military officials were the obvious choices.
Still, the initiative drew opposition on multiple fronts: from the countries that were represented, over the names chosen; and from the countries left out, who resented not having a seat at the table.
Three EU officials, who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the topic, described the initiative as a "mismanagement," "unfortunate" and "a f***-up" respectively – reflecting widespread frustration over how things had unfolded.
Sense of urgency
For the diplomatic service, the EU needs to speed up its defence preparedness or risk being caught flat-footed, but some member states appear to be dragging their feet rather than proposing new ideas.
The intent had been to create a sense of urgency, accelerating efforts to fill Europe's defence capacity gaps and set a clear direction ahead of the Munich Security Conference in February, as the US government prepares its troop review by year's end.
"Everyone agrees about the urgency of the topic, but the whole choreography was just a bit unfortunate," an EU diplomat said.
At the same time, the EEAS is frequently criticised for not being efficient enough, which runs counter to the argument that European capitals need to be constantly consulted, even to appoint experts for an advisory body.
"As a former prime minister, she is underestimating how much member states want to be consulted on foreign policy matters," a second diplomat said, noting that the episode shows how some countries are hypersensitive about the procedure.
Ironically, such lack of consultation with her constituency comes at a time when Kallas's role is being increasingly challenged by Brussels and other key European capitals.
Pressure to reform
The EU foreign policy chief has repeatedly clashed with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over who steers the bloc's foreign policy. Von der Leyen has pursued what she dubbed a "geopolitical Commission" and periodically tested her own footing on international affairs, with relations with Israel emerging as a key flashpoint.
This personal and institutional clash has increasingly intersected with recurring calls to reform EU foreign policy-making, with the latest Franco-German proposal considering placing the EEAS under the Commission's remit, albeit with a bolstered portfolio.
Following an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland last week, Kallas pushed back against the proposal, saying there was broad support for the current institutional setup, even if all agreed it could be better implemented.
"The problem that was mentioned by many member states is that, if we then move everything to the Commission, then especially the small member states lose control of the foreign policy," Kallas said.
"The member states were clear that they don't want to lose the steering wheel of the foreign policy."
Small countries' scepticism
Streamlining the bloc's external action and centralising it under the Commission would mean only the largest member states could meaningfully shape decisions made in Brussels.
Kallas' role was precisely designed with this duality in mind, serving simultaneously as a Vice-President of the Commission and as EU High Representative following the political direction of the member states, thus giving every country a seat at the table.
Yet while small member states are the ones currently shielding Kallas' institutional role from being absorbed into an all-powerful Commission, her latest blunder has managed to draw the ire of precisely that constituency.
"The member states want to see the EEAS as a service for them, not as an institution with its own mind that takes initiatives that were not previously discussed," a third EU diplomat from a small country sceptical of the reform told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
It was not the first time Kallas had appeared to press forward without the necessary political backing from member states. Last year, she pitched a €40 billion military support package for Ukraine that was rejected by EU leaders.
A row of incidents
Kallas is no stranger to diplomatic faux pas. In May, she said the US had evacuated its embassy in Kyiv amid warnings of an imminent Russian attack, only for the claim to be disputed by Washington. That same month, she also triggered a backlash after appearing to compare China to a disease.
In June, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar cut off all contact with her, after media reports that she had privately compared Israel to apartheid-era South Africa – a move that drew mixed reactions from EU leaders.
The High Representative has also raised eyebrows over her insistence on using frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine, and over her strained relations with the US administration.
However, as large member states and a Commission increasingly centralised are calling into question the current institutional setup, any further stumbling that could alienate support from the member states might prove fatal for Kallas and her institution.
"There is overall dissatisfaction with how VP Kallas is handling issues like that," a fourth EU diplomat said.

====================================================================================================

Transit ban could cost hundreds of millions – stevedoring companies urge Saeima not to rush
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:54:10 UTC
15:54:10 KST

In connection with the draft Saeima decision “On the immediate suspension and future prevention of imports into Latvia, including transit through Latvia, of grain originating from the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus”, the Latvian Stevedoring Companies Association (LSA) is urging lawmakers to assess the practical, economic and legal consequences before taking a decision and to discuss them with the industry.
“Latvia in this case is only one link in an international food supply chain. Grain transported through Latvia’s transport infrastructure is owned by major global agricultural commodity traders, including companies from the United States and other countries that are Latvia’s strategic partners, while the final recipients are located in third countries, including Nigeria, Senegal, Cameroon, Mozambique, Egypt, Tanzania, Congo and Kenya.
If Latvia, as one link in this chain, halts or substantially changes transportation conditions through a political decision, the consequences will affect not only Latvian companies but also international cargo owners, carriers and final recipients.
If grain transit through Latvia were banned, there is a high risk that claims amounting to several hundred million euros could be brought against Latvian companies, including state-owned enterprises, for failure to fulfil existing obligations,” the Association stresses.
At the same time, according to the industry’s preliminary estimates,
the state budget and state-owned enterprises could lose several hundred million euros more in planned revenue.
Therefore, when taking such a political decision, it is essential to fully assess its fiscal impact in advance and recognise the state’s responsibility for the consequences caused by a sudden change in the rules governing an international supply chain, the Latvian Stevedoring Companies Association explains.
The Association also calls for the European Union’s common approach to be taken into account. EU sanctions are not directed against international trade in food and agricultural products between Russia and the rest of the world. Even when the EU introduced significantly higher tariffs on imports of Russian and Belarusian grain, transit through the EU to third countries was maintained in view of global food security and food availability considerations.
“As an EU member state, Latvia must assess whether national decisions are consistent with the EU’s common approach, how effective they would be, and what consequences they could have for Latvia’s economy and international obligations,” the Association stresses.
The LSA and port companies already cooperate with all state institutions involved in cargo controls,
including the Customs Board of the State Revenue Service and the Food and Veterinary Service, and comply with established requirements for checking cargo and accompanying documentation.
Cargo is already subject to strict controls, and if the competent authorities conclude that control mechanisms need to be strengthened further, the industry will support legally justified and proportionate measures. Port companies are interested in ensuring that the control system is sufficiently effective to prevent sanctioned, illegal or unverifiable-origin cargo from entering Latvia’s transport system, the LSA stresses.
“The state’s task is not only to impose restrictions but also to create a safe, predictable and competitive business environment. Decisions taken by the Saeima affect both the public interest and companies and international partners that have entered into long-term commitments in reliance on the existing regulatory framework. A significant and sudden change in the rules of the game also affects Latvia’s reputation as a reliable, predictable and legally stable partner in international markets,” the Association warns.
The LSA says it will comply with any legally adopted decision by the Latvian state and the European Union. However, before such a significant decision is taken, it urges lawmakers to hear the industry’s position and fully assess the consequences, taking into account not only the political objective but also the economic, fiscal and reputational cost to Latvia.

Occupied territory or colonial remnant? The nuance behind the British bases in Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:53:29 UTC
15:53:29 KST

Experts say that it's too emotive to refer to the British Overseas Territories of Akrotiri and Dhekelia in Cyprus as an 'occupation', instead they are colonial remnants that provide mixed benefits to both sides.
The British overseas territories of Akrotiri and Dhekelia on the island of Cyprus have generated a buzz online in recent days, after a social media post by a French politician claimed that the UK was "occupying" Cyprus.
The X post by French MEP Manon Aubry, of the far-left France Unbowed party, was originally published in February but resurfaced after being reposted and quoted by social media users last week.
Aubry's post contains a video of herself in Akrotiri — known officially as the Sovereign Base Area of Akrotiri — in which she says its presence in Cyprus, as well as that of Dhekelia, shows that part of the country is still "occupied by the British Army".
She adds that the bases are being used to provide intelligence about the Gaza Strip to Israel and that, as NATO bases, they are ultimately under the command of US President Donald Trump.
"Stop colonialism!" Aubry says in the text of her X post.
In response, social media users attached a community note to the post, explaining that Akrotiri and Dhekelia are covered by the 1960 treaty that Cyprus signed to establish its independence from the UK.
They added that this is unlike the north of the country, which the vast majority of the international community considers to be under Turkish military occupation in an issue known as "the Cyprus problem".
Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974, ultimately dividing the island with Turkish forces controlling the north of the island, about 36% of its territory, to this day. Self-proclaimed "Northern Cyprus" is recognised only by Turkey.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, spoke to experts to break down some of the nuance surrounding the British bases in Cyprus, whether they bear any similarities to the Turkish occupation, and whether Aubry's claims hold any weight.
A colonial relic
Simply put, the question about the status of the bases is a complex one, according to scholars.
They said that, legally speaking, the UK is not "occupying" Cyprus, because the base areas are recognised under international law, including by Cyprus itself.
"We can look at the definition of occupation, which includes the presence of a military force without a territory's consent," said Peter Clegg, professor of politics and international relations with a specialisation in British Overseas Territories, at the University of the West of England.
"In this case, there is consent," he said. "There is agreement from the Cypriot government that the bases can exist."
Clegg pointed to the vast aspects of civilian daily life that are overseen in the base areas by the Cypriot government, such as education and social welfare, and the fact that the government has not challenged the legality of the independence treaty since it was drawn up.
Under the terms of the agreement, the UK promises "not to develop the Sovereign Base Areas for other than military purposes" and "not to set up and administer 'colonies'" there.
It also says that Cypriots have full access to the area surrounding the bases, that their rights will be fully protected, and that laws applicable to the Cypriot population who live there "will be as far as possible the same as the laws of the Republic [of Cyprus]".
The importance of consent was also noted by Costas M Constantinou, professor of international relations at the University of Cyprus, although he highlighted that the situation is not so clear-cut.
"I wouldn't call it occupation, but rather an ingenious development of colonialism," he told The Cube. "The main difference from occupation is that Cypriots formally agreed to it when they signed the Treaty of Establishment in 1960, which also established the bases."
"But they were basically coerced, as decolonisation of the island was made conditional on accepting the 'sovereign bases'," he added. "This raises questions about the legality of the bases today."
Neophytos Loizides, professor of international conflict analysis at the University of Warwick, said that the Cypriot people were not consulted when Akrotiri and Dhekelia were left behind as part of the independence deal and that the UK, as the colonial power, used its leverage to hold on to the territories.
"The agreement was signed under duress," he said. "Cypriot leaders did not have the same power as the UK, so the UK could impose its will."
Responding to Manon Aubry's use of language directly, he said that it's more accurate to call the bases a "colonial remnant" rather than an "occupation", which is an "emotive use of words".
"This is different to the occupation happening in the north of Cyprus," he said. "A Cypriot person is unlikely to say the British are occupiers, but they wouldn't necessarily say they're there legitimately either."
For Constantinou, the key word is "ambivalence".
"Greek Cypriots and certainly the Cypriot government don't view the bases as something that is equivalent to the Turkish occupation in the north," he said. "Those Cypriots who live inside the base areas and may still consider it a colonial remnant don't necessarily or always see it negatively, as many economically benefit from working in the bases and some also feel that the British army provides security vis-a-vis the Turkish army, in areas such as the Achna Forest village in the Dhekelia base."
As for Aubry's claims that the UK was using the bases in Cyprus to assist Israel, Clegg said they were incorrect.
"There have been some surveillance flights in and around Gaza, but the UK has made clear, and it's likely true, that the flights were unarmed and were used to help identify the location of the hostages following the 7 October attacks," he said.
He added that there was limited or no information sharing with Israel or the US, but there were humanitarian aid flights from the bases to Gaza.
"There's a discussion to be had about how the bases are being used, but I don't think everything being thrown at them is entirely true and fair," he told The Cube. "It's likely somewhere in between."
The UK government insists that the surveillance flights over Gaza were conducted solely for hostage location, that it maintained strict control over the information it gathered and that only data directly related to the whereabouts of any hostages was given to Israel.
However, certain investigative outlets have cast doubt on whether this intelligence sharing extended into broader Israeli military operations, accusing the government of a lack of transparency for refusing to reveal exactly what information was shared and potential complicity in Israel's war.
What's next for the bases?
Akrotiri and Dhekelia made headlines earlier this year when a drone hit the former in March during the wider war between Iran and both Israel and the US. More drones launched in the following days were intercepted.
The strikes reignited the debate about the bases' future in Cyprus, which, unlike the UK, is not a NATO member. Protesters argued that ordinary Cypriots would pay the price if anything bad happened to them, while President Nikos Christodoulides demanded talks with London about the future of the "colonial" military bases.
Rather than directly challenging British sovereignty, however, Nicosia has shifted towards a phased, technical approach, proposing joint committees on how both sides can work together and launching high-level diplomatic dialogue.
"From the Cypriot perspective, the return of the territory would be welcome, but they'd also like to see a better functional relationship," Loizides said. "The British bases cannot perpetually put at risk the Cypriot population on the island."
"In the future, it may be that the British maintain the bases but under a protection framework, so that Cyprus benefits from it, and the colonial status changes into a more modern security framework," he added, noting that the relationship between both sides has "improved dramatically" in recent decades.
Any such change is unlikely to happen anytime soon, though, according to Clegg, who described the recent comments from Cyprus as "genuine concern, but more rhetorical than trying to bring about real change."
The UK briefly considered whether it was beneficial to keep the bases amid the Turkish invasion in the 70s, but pressure from the US pushed London to keep the status quo.
"The bases are British, there's close cooperation with Cyprus, but there's a US interest too; there's a triangular relationship," Clegg said. "This has been at the heart of how they've been administered."
A change in status could come as part of a wider peace settlement regarding the Cyprus problem, according to Loizides, explaining that the British bases could factor into the equation as part of a security framework in the region.
"If the Cyprus problem were fixed, there'd be an opportunity to further develop the European defence mechanisms in the Middle East and east Mediterranean," Loizides said. "The entire region could benefit from the British bases; they could provide security to Cyprus and the EU, so there's a basis for a good agreement for the Brits here too."
The future of the bases came under legal scrutiny after the International Court of Justice handed down an advisory opinion in 2019, in which it said that the UK's detachment of the Chagos Islands from Mauritius during decolonisation in the 1960s violated the right to self-determination and territorial integrity.
Some Cypriot officials and legal experts say that this is similar to how the UK carved out Akrotiri and Dhekelia during Cyprus' transition to independence, although other analysts say the cases are distinct, because while the indigenous population of Chagos was expelled, the British bases in Cyprus were baked into the 1960 treaty, with formal recognition from the new republic.
London has since agreed to hand over sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, but the necessary legislation has stalled following pushback from Trump.
Nevertheless, in the Cypriot case, the UK has consistently maintained its commitment to and sovereignty over Akrotiri and Dhekelia under the 1960 agreement. Al Carns, former armed forces minister, told The Telegraph in April that their legal status is "non-negotiable", dismissing any suggestion of transferring control of them.
The government of Cyprus did not respond to a request for comment as of the time of publication.

Night train service between Brussels and Milan starts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:52:29 UTC
15:52:29 KST

A new night train service from Brussels starts today. The Belgo-Dutch rail company European Sleeper is launching a service between the Belgian and Flemish capital and Milan, in northern Italy.
The first train on the new route will depart from Milan at around 4.45 pm on Wednesday and arrive in Brussels shortly before midday on Thursday. En route, the train will stop at destinations including Como (Italy), Lugano, Aarau (Switzerland) and Cologne (Germany). In Belgium, the train will also stop at Verviers (Liège Province).
In the opposite direction, departure from Brussels is scheduled for 7.10 pm, with arrival in Milan the following day at 11.40 am. The train will run three times a week in each direction.
The plan is to change the route between Brussels and Cologne from mid-December. The night train will then run from Brussels to Antwerp and the Dutch cities of Breda and Eindhoven, and on to Cologne – and will therefore no longer travel via Verviers and Aachen.
Other night train options from Brussels
European Sleeper also operates night trains from Brussels via Amsterdam to destinations including Berlin, Dresden and Prague, and from Paris via Brussels to Hamburg and Berlin. The Austrian railway company ÖBB also operates night trains between Brussels and the Austrian capital, Vienna.
From mid-December to the end of March, Travelski, a subsidiary of Compagnie des Alpes, will run a weekly night train from the Netherlands, via Antwerp and Brussels, to the French Alps and back. Compagnie des Alpes is the parent company of the Bellewaerde and Walibi theme parks in Belgium.
European Sleeper previously announced that it hopes to launch a night train service from Brussels and Amsterdam to Copenhagen (Denmark) and Malmö (Sweden) in 2028. The company is also looking at a service to Barcelona (Catalonia).

Tehnopol kicks off autumn season by bringing alumni and active teams together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:52:29 UTC
15:52:29 KST

Tehnopol’s Accelerator community came back together on August 27 for the autumn season kick-off, bringing founders, alumni and the Tehnopol team out of summer mode and into a night of trivia, panel discussion and networking.
Turnout was strong, drawing alumni and current teams from across Tehnopol’s accelerator programmes. It was the first time Tehnopol has organized this kind of kick-off explicitly designed to mix alumni and current cohorts together, rather than keeping each programme’s community in its own lane.
The evening opened casually, with arrivals easing into a trivia round – played individually, giving people an excuse to bounce between conversations instead of huddling with whoever they walked in with. Food and drinks kept flowing as the room filled, setting a relaxed tone before the night’s main event: a panel putting some of startup land’s favourite assumptions on trial.
Testing startup “truths” against 2026
The evening’s centrepiece was a panel titled “Still Valid or Outdated?”, built around a simple premise: a lot of what counted as settled startup wisdom a few years ago has been knocked around by AI, shifting investor expectations, new sales models and geopolitics. The panel ran through a list of once-common assumptions, with each panellist first calling a verdict – still valid or outdated – before making their case.
The lineup brought together four different vantage points: Anne-Liisa Elbrecht, Head of Tehnopol Accelerator; Natalja Napsep, co-founder and COO of Bidrento; and Kristjan Lind, founder and CEO of Bikeep, with Triin Hertmann – angel investor and Fomo.Observer co-founder – moderating. Between an investor’s read on the market, a founder’s ground truth, and Tehnopol’s view from inside the accelerator, the panel promised more disagreement than consensus – exactly the point of the format.
What’s next this season
Tehnopol isn’t wasting time to follow up the kick-off: applications are now open for its AI Accelerator, a 6-month programme for early-stage startups and spin-offs building AI technologies, with mentor-led support to get to market faster. The call is deliberately wide, too: alongside typical early-stage startups, Tehnopol is inviting students, researchers and SMEs already working with AI, including past programme alumni looking to launch a product or spin up a new business line.
A new DeepTech Accelerator cohort is also in the works, with applications opening 1 October. The programme is built for Estonian deep tech startups validating their business models and chasing initial growth, backed by training, mentoring, development funding and introductions to international investors – the goal being to turn science-based ideas into competitive businesses faster. It’s a joint effort, run by Tehnopol together with Sparkup Tartu Science Park, with activities spanning both Tallinn and Tartu.
Rounding out the season is the Film and Multimedia Pre-Accelerator, IDA Hub, open to anyone with a promising idea in film or multimedia, or no idea at all, since first-timers are welcome to just try their hand at being a film entrepreneur under mentor guidance. It centres on a two-day TECH Bootcamp of workshops and mentoring.
There’s also a hackathon on the calendar with unusually high stakes: the City Resilience Hack runs 24–25 September in Tallinn, organised by the City of Tallinn and Tehnopol, with a €75,000 prize fund on the table. Teams spanning business, tech, defence, data, cybersecurity, logistics and design will tackle real resilience challenges posed by partner cities Helsinki, Valencia, Dnipro and Lviv, from crisis communication tools to critical infrastructure monitoring. Winners get more than cash: access to pilot projects in partner cities and a shot at joining Tehnopol’s acceleration programme. Applications close 10 September.

Gallery: New Tallinn exhibition explores queer belonging and family

Gallery: New Tallinn exhibition explores queer belonging and family
In a new show in Põhja-Tallinn, artists August Kilmi and Ly-Ann Kõllo explore the family ideal and what happens when queer people feel they don't fit into it.
Opened at Krulli SAAL on Saturday, Kilmi and Kõllo's "Who Gets a Seat at the Table" explores the dream of the ideal family, expectations formed in childhood, and the disappointment that follows when someone feels there is no place for them within that dream.
The artists examine family and home, and how a queer person fits — or doesn't fit — into these spaces.
The exhibition features a four-channel video installation and four additional installations drawing on familiar household furniture either recreated or dismantled.
"In the video work, we meet the expected family members — a father, a mother, a son and a daughter — and see a queer person's attempt to take on these roles," the artists said.
"Who Gets a Seat at the Table" will remain on view at Krulli SAAL through September 20.

Child among four killed by Ukrainian drone attacks – Russian governor
Four people, including a child, were killed overnight in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Russian Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk, Krasnodar Region Governor Veniamin Kondratyev has said.
Another 29 people were injured across the city, the official said on Wednesday morning. Three of the victims are in a serious condition, he added.
Novorossiysk is a key hub for Russian maritime trade, which Kiev has been trying to disrupt with regular long-range attacks on ships and port infrastructure.
Kondratyev stressed that only civilian sites were targeted by Ukrainian forces. A church and a kindergarten were damaged, as well as three private homes and five apartment blocks, he reported. Gelendzhik, another resort town in Krasnodar Region to the southeast of Novorossiysk, came under what Mayor Aleksey Bogodistov described as a “most massive and lengthy” drone raid. He did not report any casualties.
Russian air defenses intercepted 596 Ukrainian drones in 12 hours overnight into Wednesday, the Defense Ministry said.
In June, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky ordered mass attacks on Russian ships, which was part of Kiev’s bid to cause more economic damage. Moscow responded to Zelensky’s “40-day pressure campaign” by ramping up its own long-range strikes, leaving Ukraine effectively cut off from maritime trade.
On Tuesday, Zelensky reiterated his calls for a pause in hostilities in the Black Sea, claiming it would come as a relief for the entire world. Both nations are major exporters of wheat, a key food commodity.
A Türkiye-mediated agreement that ensured free shipping in the Black Sea and provided for inspections of incoming cargo ships to ensure that they were not carrying weapons existed in the early phase of the conflict. Moscow ultimately pulled out of the deal after accusing Kiev of using designated safe routes to launch naval kamikaze drones at Russian ports.

Trump did not oppose UK sanctions on West Bank settlements, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:47:40 UTC
15:47:40 KST

The Trump administration did not oppose Britain’s sweeping new economic measures targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, Axios reported early Wednesday, citing U.S. officials, despite a warning from the U.S. ambassador to Israel that London could face American retaliation.
According to the report, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with U.S. President Donald Trump before announcing the measures Tuesday and briefed him on the plan. Two sources familiar with the conversation said Trump did not object or attempt to persuade Burnham to change course.
U.S. officials also told their British counterparts that Washington shares some of London’s concerns about the policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in the West Bank, even though the United States does not support the specific sanctions Britain announced, according to Axios.
The apparent lack of opposition from Washington is significant as Israel faces mounting international pressure over settlement expansion in the West Bank, territory Palestinians seek as the heartland of a future independent state.
Britain was joined Tuesday by 11 countries — Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden — in issuing a joint statement warning that Israeli policies in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a two-state solution.
“The Government of Israel’s actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-state solution,” the countries said, calling on Israel to immediately halt settlement expansion and changes to civilian administrative powers and ensure accountability for settler violence.
The countries also announced their intention to impose restrictions on trade with settlements they consider illegal under international law. Most of the international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.
Britain’s measures went further, including sanctions against five Israelis it described as “extremist settlers,” measures targeting organizations involved in settlement construction and a ban on imports of goods from Israeli settlements.
Israel responded sharply. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar ordered the closure of the British Consulate in East Jerusalem, the removal of British representatives from the Gaza coordination headquarters in the southern city of Kiryat Gat and an end to British involvement in training Palestinian Authority security forces in Ramallah.
Israel also barred 12 Britons from entering the country, accusing them of involvement in antisemitic and anti-Israel activities and of denying Israel’s right to exist.
White House distances itself from Huckabee warning
The White House also distanced itself from remarks by U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who had warned Britain that its actions could provoke an American response, according to Axios.
Huckabee told the BBC that if Britain imposed sanctions on Israeli settlements, it could face a U.S. response that would affect its ability to do business.
Huckabee said such action could come at the federal or political level and suggested it could have “a huge economic impact on British businesses.”
But a White House official told Axios that Huckabee’s comments had not been coordinated with either the White House or the State Department.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also declined Tuesday to condemn Britain’s decision.
“The president hasn't commented on this and neither have I. We were made aware that they are going to make this decision. We heard their arguments as to why,” Rubio said. "We share the goal of stability. We don't want to see an uptick in violence or tensions in the West Bank in a tenuous time in the region."
Burnham: ‘For too long, we hesitated to act’
Burnham later defended the measures in an extensive statement, saying successive British governments had been reluctant to take concrete action because of fears they would be characterized as hostile to Israel.
“For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel,” Burnham wrote in the Guardian.
Britain had advocated a two-state solution for years, he said, but “those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action.”
Burnham stressed that the measures were not directed at Israelis generally but at what he described as unacceptable policies pursued by Netanyahu’s government.
The British prime minister also addressed the war in Gaza, describing Palestinian suffering there as “a scar on the conscience of the world.” He said civilians, including children, continued to be killed and pointed to the supposed humanitarian crisis in the territory.
Burnham said that even before becoming prime minister, he had argued that Britain’s response had been too slow and inadequate. He said he had pledged upon entering 10 Downing Street to change the government’s approach.
“I will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution — the best hope for peace and stability in the region — comes under attack,” he wrote.
Burnham focused much of his criticism on Israeli construction in the West Bank, claiming that Netanyahu’s government had approved more settlements during its four years in office than had been approved during the previous two decades.
He singled out plans for the E1 area between Jerusalem and the Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim. The project has long drawn international opposition because critics say construction there could sever territorial links between Palestinian population centers in the northern and southern West Bank, making a contiguous Palestinian state more difficult to establish.
“The Israeli government has now approved 104 new settlements since it took office in December 2022, and ahead of the October elections in Israel, it is allowing tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement to go ahead,” Burnham wrote. “This would cut a swathe through the heart of the West Bank — snuffing out the hope of realizing a two-state solution. It cannot be allowed to happen.”
Israel argues that Jerusalem and Ma’ale Adumim are strategically linked and has rejected international demands that settlement policy be dictated from abroad.

BRICS leaders gather in India, but does the group have a clear purpose?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:47:00 UTC
15:47:00 KST

Does BRICS have a clear purpose?
September 9, 2026
In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members.
"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind.
"It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW.
For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible.
"India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there."
India takes host role
Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil.
At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi Jinping is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing.
"The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa.
She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member.
For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship.
However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend.
"In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh.
Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first".
However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times.
"With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the west as a whole.
"India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?"
Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned.
"India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics."
What is BRICS for anyway?
BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose.
The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP.
Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order.
"Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa.
She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues.
There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh.
What might happen this year
Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security.
While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO.
"India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely."
Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm."
He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve.
"With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

“Sun the Quilt” Wins the 2026 VELUX Light of Tomorrow Global Award with a Responsive Facade Inspired by Daily Rituals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

How can daylight tackle global challenges? This question lies at the heart of Light of Tomorrow by VELUX, a global student competition that encourages architecture students to explore the future potential of daylight in the built environment. In its 12th edition, the competition received hundreds of responses from around the world, culminating in eight finalist projects presented to an international jury at the UIA World Congress of Architects in Barcelona. The 2026 global winner, Sun the Quilt, developed by students from Xi'an University of Architecture and Technology in China, was chosen for its strong concept, design thinking, and innovative use of daylight that transforms an everyday domestic ritual into an innovative facade system shaped by daylight, climate, and care.
Responding to the competition theme, "Light of Tomorrow," the project reimagines the simple act of drying quilts, textiles, food, and household objects in the sun. The proposal combines a fully openable window, an operational ledge, and nested, extendable, and rotatable frames that support drying, shading, ventilation, and daylight modulation within a single architectural system.
The result is an adaptable facade that allows quilts and other household items to move outside while the resident remains safely indoors. By studying seasonal and daily solar patterns, they developed a responsive system that changes throughout the year. When deployed, a quilt becomes an external shading device; when retracted, daylight returns to the interior.
The project emerged from a personal observation. For many people living in dense urban environments, access to sunlight is negotiated through improvised everyday practices. Quilts are carried across courtyards; clothes hang from balconies, and household objects are placed wherever light and air can be found. What may appear as visual clutter became a starting point for architectural investigation.
Research conducted across the Yangtze River Delta documented the various poles, frames, balconies, and window-mounted devices used to dry quilts and clothing. Rather than dismissing these informal solutions, the team recognized them as evidence of an unmet architectural need. This led to a broader question: how can architecture better support rituals connected to sunlight, hygiene, comfort, privacy, and safety?
A key strength of the proposal is its ability to transform a modest act into a broader architectural idea without unnecessary complexity. Reflecting on the design process, the team leader, XU Qicheng, commented that, "For every component, we ask the same question: Does it make this everyday ritual safer and easier, or does it improve the relationship between daylight, the room, and the body. This really helped us keep the final design focused." The students explored questions of flexibility, stability, safety, and user experience, developing a system of tracks, pivots, clamps, and guided movements that support everyday use while enhancing the relationship between daylight, people, and space.
The jury praised the project for its poetic simplicity and strong connection to daily life. They highlighted how the facade system allows light to be modulated differently throughout the seasons while supporting textiles, food, and other domestic objects. Jury member Níall McLaughlin (IE) commented:
 The architects have gone through a problem, got to the bottom of that problem, worked it through, and then made it into something that can live and thrive in the world.
While rooted in the specific context of the Yangtze River Delta, the project offers lessons that extend well beyond China. People around the world negotiate access to sunlight, ventilation, and privacy in different ways. Rather than proposing a universal solution, Sun the Quilt presents a compelling principle: the facade can become a responsive, inhabitable boundary between inside and outside.
As Tina Christensen, Director of Light of Tomorrow by VELUX at the VELUX Group, noted, the winning project demonstrates "how daylight can be used with clarity and purpose to connect to real-world concerns, achieving meaningful impact through modest means."
The complete list of winning projects, jury selections, and competition materials from Light of Tomorrow by VELUX 2026 provides further insight into this year's proposals and the ideas the jury recognized. Highlights from the awards ceremony also document the finalists and the presentation of the global awards.

A 24-hour strike has brought most public transport in the Netherlands to a halt, with no trains and buses, trams or metros stopping in any main city. Only rides to and from Schiphol airport are still running.
The FNV union organised the strike in protest at the cabinet’s planned cuts to social security, which it says will hit unemployment and disability benefits that transport workers are more likely than most to need.
NS is running no regular trains for the whole day. The only exception is the airport sprinter between Amsterdam Centraal, Schiphol and Hoofddorp, which runs four times an hour.
It is the first nationwide 24-hour public transport strike since May 2019, when unions walked out over the state pension age.
International services, including the Eurostar, ICE and Eurocity, are also not running within the Netherlands, and the regional trains to Antwerp and Aachen are cancelled.
In Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague there are no buses, trams or metros, and Rotterdam’s metro stations are closed. The ferries across the IJ behind Amsterdam Centraal are not sailing either.
Regional bus companies such as Arriva, Qbuzz and Connexxion are running a reduced service depending on how many drivers turn up for work.
Why the unions are striking
 The strike is the latest in a series of actions against the cabinet’s plans to save €6.5 billion by cutting social security benefits over its four-year term, first set out in the coalition agreement between D66, VVD and CDA.
The original package included raising the state pension (AOW) age faster, halving unemployment benefit (WW) from two years to one and cutting disability benefits (WIA). The cabinet dropped the pension plan in April after it became clear it had no majority in either house of parliament.
Under the budget deal reached by the coalition parties on August 31, the cabinet has since scrapped most of the remaining cuts in an effort to win opposition support for its budget plan on September 15. The cuts to AOW are off the table and the halving of the WW has been postponed, according to details leaked to RTL Nieuws.
FNV said that is not enough, and that around 70% of the planned cuts still stand and the WW will still be halved and WIA payments still reduced, only later than planned. It wants the entire package withdrawn.
“It is unacceptable that the minority cabinet is cutting so much on social security,” FNV rail official Henri Janssen told NOS on Wednesday morning.
Janssen said he understood travellers’ frustration, but that they should direct their anger at the cabinet rather than the strikers. He did not rule out “tougher action”, including a wider strike beyond public transport, if the cuts are not dropped.

Why Vijay's gold ring scheme may miss its September 15 launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:42:15 UTC
15:42:15 KST

Under Vijay's gold ring scheme, every newborn delivered at a government health facility will receive a one-gram gold ring. At the current gold rate, the ring is worth around Rs 13,600.
NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay's gold ring scheme, which was scheduled to be launched on September 15, shall be deferred from its expected date. The announcement comes as the CM prepares for his first official overseas visit to London. Vijay is set to meet European industrialists during the visit and pitch Tamil Nadu as an investment destination.Vijay will leave Chennai for London via Dubai on Wednesday night and is expected to stay in the UK capital for a few days. He will travel on an Emirates Airlines passenger flight.
During the visit, Vijay is expected to invite European companies to set up businesses in Tamil Nadu and seek fresh investment commitments for the state. Senior officials from the industries and finance departments are also expected to travel to London. Some may leave ahead of the chief minister to prepare for his meetings with prospective investors.The visit comes soon after the ‘Vettri Tamil Nadu Investment Conclave 2026’, where the state government announced investment commitments worth Rs 1,02,514 crore through 104 memorandums of understanding (MoUs).Security and protocol arrangements for Vijay’s departure are also being finalised.
A high-level Advance Security Liaison meeting is reportedly scheduled at Chennai’s old airport on Wednesday to review the arrangements.Vijay’s London visit also comes amid key political developments in Tamil Nadu. Before leaving for the UK, he is scheduled to chair a second alliance coordination meeting at the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam headquarters in Panaiyur.The meeting is expected to discuss the structure of the ruling alliance and post-poll coalition arrangements. A Common Minimum Programme is also on the agenda, along with discussions on a steering committee and an official name for the alliance.Invitations have reportedly been sent to all alliance partners, including Congress, VCK, IUML, MDMK, CPI and CPM. Congress, VCK, IUML and MDMK have confirmed their attendance, while the Left parties are likely to stay away.
What is the gold ring scheme?
Vijay had announced the one-gram gold ring scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election. The initiative was planned as a symbolic gift to newborns and draws on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’.Under the scheme, every newborn delivered at a government health facility will receive a one-gram gold ring. At the current gold rate, the ring is worth around Rs 13,600.“Through this scheme, the government assumes the role of the maaman (uncle) for every child born in its institutions, presenting a gold ring as an enduring token of welcome,” a government order said.The scheme was originally scheduled to be launched on September 15, which coincides with the birth anniversary of former chief minister C N Annadurai.It will have retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday. The government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of the child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.The state has allocated around Rs 755.83 crore annually for the scheme, which will cover all newborns delivered at government institutions. There will be no restriction based on birth order and no gender-based discrimination.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings and supply them based on annual requirements. A project and programme management unit will also be established to oversee implementation and monitoring.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries each year, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or about 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.
The scheme is open to Tamil Nadu residents whose children are delivered at government institutions. Mothers will have to submit proof of residence, with documents such as ration cards, voter identity cards, Aadhaar, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates accepted.The government said the initiative was intended to combine cultural significance with public healthcare.“Gold carries profound cultural and emotional resonance in Tamil Nadu. Gifting gold to a newborn celebrates the baby’s arrival, honours the mother’s noble journey and transforms public health delivery into a source of immense community pride,” the order said.

Academia Historica president says democracy strengthened Taiwan government legitimacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:40:59 UTC
15:40:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Academia Historica President Chen Yi-shen (陳儀深) said Wednesday that democratization strengthened government legitimacy and gave people a greater political voice, CNA reported.
Speaking at the opening of an exhibition titled “Light and Shadow: Multiple Perspectives on Taiwan around 1945,” Chen said a government without full elections could be seen as an illegitimate foreign regime. He said ending martial law in 1987 and holding full legislative elections in 1991 and 1992 strengthened the government’s democratic legitimacy.
Chen said the democratic transition followed decades of efforts by local people seeking greater political representation. He linked that process to a 1950 statement by US General Douglas MacArthur that Taiwanese should have the power to determine their own future.
Chen said the 1943 Cairo Declaration showed that the leaders of China, the US, and the UK agreed that Taiwan and Penghu should be returned to China after World War II. However, he said Japanese forces surrendered to the Allied powers in October 1945, with the flags of China, the US, the UK, and the Soviet Union displayed at the ceremony.
Chen said the Republic of China government later changed the nationality of residents without full international recognition. He cited the UK government’s position at the time that Taiwan’s status could not be settled before a postwar peace treaty with Japan was signed.
The US position changed after the Korean War began in 1950, Chen said. He said historical records showed that the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty, which took effect in 1952, did not transfer sovereignty over Taiwan and Penghu to China.
Chen also described how public attitudes changed in the early postwar period. He said diaries by physician Wu Hsin-jung (吳新榮) and politician Lin Hsien-tang (林獻堂) showed that some people initially welcomed Chinese troops.
Those views changed as political repression intensified, Chen said. Wu was detained for more than 100 days after the 228 Massacre, while Lin moved to Japan in 1949 as martial law and authoritarian rule restricted political expression.
Chen said the government also played a role in Cold War cooperation with the US and Japan against communist expansion. Washington provided military and economic assistance and later signed a mutual defense treaty with the government.

Taiwanese companies join Arm's growing physical AI ecosystem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:40:44 UTC
15:40:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Several domestic companies have joined Arm's expanding physical AI ecosystem, as the development of AI-powered machines creates new opportunities for suppliers across the technology industry, CTEE reported.
Arm, a designer of chip architectures, said Tuesday that more than 80 companies are now involved in the initiative. They provide technologies and services across areas including chips, sensors, AI models, cloud services, and end-user systems.
Taiwanese companies including TSMC, Realtek Semiconductor Corp., Artery Technology Corp., Aaeon Technology Inc., EverFocus Electronics Corp., Nexcobot Co., and Insyde Software Corp. are among the listed partners. Their participation highlights the range of technologies needed to build physical AI systems, from computing and sensing to control and connectivity.
Artery develops microcontroller units, or MCUs, which are used to control individual functions in electronic systems. In robots, these chips can handle tasks such as controlling joint movement and collecting sensor data, along with other real-time functions.
As robots become more complex and gain more freedom, the number and performance requirements of control chips are expected to increase. Artery's role in Arm's initiative therefore points to potential opportunities for MCU suppliers as more smart machines adopt AI-enabled control systems.
Realtek's networking and Bluetooth technologies address the connectivity needs of physical AI systems. The company's chips can enable these devices to communicate with other machines, edge systems, and cloud platforms.
EverFocus, meanwhile, brings experience from the video surveillance market, where it has developed technologies related to image sensing and processing. Its expertise could support the development of robotic vision systems, which enable machines to interpret their surroundings and respond to what they see, according to CMoney.
Physical AI refers to AI technologies designed to operate in the real world, enabling machines to interpret their surroundings and perform tasks. Arm estimates that the physical AI computing market was worth about NT$786.4 billion (US$25 billion) last year and could exceed NT$6.29 trillion by 2030, according to LTN.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A drone intrusion temporarily halted flight operations at Taichung's Ching Chuan Kang Air Base on Tuesday evening, forcing eight indigenous defense fighter jets to divert to Hsinchu Air Force Base, per MNA.
Air Force Command said the drone was detected in the airspace around the base at 7:37 p.m. The tower notified aviation control authorities to suspend takeoffs and landings. Local police were also contacted.
Although historically and militarily known as Ching Chuan Kang Air Base, the site also serves as Taichung International Airport. It serves as a dual-use airfield for both military operations and commercial civilian travel.
The drone left the controlled airspace by 8:02 p.m., allowing flight operations to resume. The incident also affected two civilian flights, the Air Force said. It added that weather had improved Tuesday evening, allowing fighter jets to resume night-flight training, per UDN.
Taichung Airport Director Chang Jui-shu (張瑞澍) said the drone intrusion occurred at about 7:40 p.m. and was cleared at 8:02 p.m. During that time, a flight from Macau to Taichung was forced to circle before landing after the situation was resolved, per LTN.
Police from Chingchuan Police Station were dispatched after being notified of the drone intrusion. Officers found no trace of the drone, though they will continue patrolling the area and reviewing surveillance footage to try to identify the operator, according to police.
The Air Force said the incident has been referred to the Air Police Bureau for investigation. It pointed out that operating a drone inside controlled airspace is illegal and poses a significant risk to aviation safety.

Taiwan's AIDC expands into anti-drone systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:40:41 UTC
15:40:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation (AIDC) is developing cheaper anti-drone solutions to strengthen national defense.
The aerospace company is the only domestic firm that can design planes for civilian and military applications. Its executive Alex Tsai (蔡明晃) said constant drone disruptions in the Middle East highlight the importance of a domestic counter-drone network, especially with the People's Liberation Army using drones in its operations.
Tsai said the challenge is global, with traditional air-defense systems too inefficient and costly against swarms of small, cheap drones. He added that armed forces worldwide have pushed for specialized radar systems that can detect and remove compact threats before they reach the target.
Tsai described a two-way approach: soft kill disables drones by deception or signal jamming, while hard kill uses cheap flak or rockets to strike them down. He added a third option using another drone to intercept and collide with the other.
The government-funded think tank Research Institute for Democracy, Society, and Emerging Technology (DSET) said Taiwan's drone development also references Europe's use of sensors, real-time data, and communications technology.
Tsai said it all boils down to costs. He said conventional missiles were designed to engage high-value threats, not swarms of cheap drones.
On exports, DSET estimates that first-quarter drone exports to Europe for 2026 already exceeded the combined total for 2025. Tsai said overseas demand is strongest for Taiwan's motors and batteries as customers prefer buying from non-China sources, with growing interest in flight-control boards and AI modules.

The Russian exception: Why Moscow still has a role in Europe’s ITER fusion project despite EU sanctions
The European Union and Russia are geopolitical adversaries, with Russia under sweeping EU sanctions and its ties with the bloc severely curtailed. Is Belgium becoming a narco-state?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:39:12 UTC
15:39:12 KST

“If we do nothing, Belgium risks becoming a narco-state,” warns Belgian Drug Commissioner Ine Van Wymersch. Speaking on VRT TV she noted how criminal organisations are gaining ever greater control over Belgian society and sees only one way to turn the tide: "We must go after the money," she says. “Fortunately, everyone is now on the same page.”
Is Belgium becoming a narco-state?
“Is Belgium becoming a narco-state?” This is the opening question that VRT’s Fatma Taspinar posed to journalist Rudi Vranckx, who, together with his Dutch colleague Sinan Can, has produced a four-part documentary (“Drugsdelta”) centred on that very question.
“Belgium and the Netherlands are not narco-states,” is Vranckx’s brief reply, but he adds a warning. “We must be careful.” Drug Commissioner Ine Van Wymersch agrees with him. She fears that Belgium will indeed become a narco-state, “if we do nothing”.
Van Wymersch explains: “It is about more than just drugs: a narco-state is a parallel state in which criminal organisations, through corruption and intimidation, acquire enormous power over a country’s economic life, society and political authorities. It is a criminal alternative to a democratic society.”
The shootings in Brussels over recent weeks, months and years reveal that these organisations have already penetrated deep into Belgian society. Drug-related violence is also spreading beyond Brussels, Antwerp and Rotterdam.
Vranckx, too, notes that such criminal organisations have already penetrated very deep into Belgium society. Take the Port of Antwerp, for example. He speaks to a dock worker who explains how easy it is to ‘earn’ 75,000 euros in a matter of minutes.
Follow the money!
The drug commissioner is not surprised that people change their tune when such large sums of money are involved. “That is why we must ensure they are not tempted.” How? By disrupting the cash flows of criminal organisations, for example through the seizure of property and confiscations.
“Follow the money – that’s the only thing you can do,” agrees Rudi Vranckx. Criminal defence lawyer Sven Mary concurs. “Go after the money. Prison sentences of up to 20 years achieve nothing. Punish them but make them pay as well. 10 million euros or even 100 million euros. These are the sums we’re talking about.”
“In her last interview Belgian Justice Minister Verlinden said that she needs 1 billion euros. Well, you could easily raise that from those criminal organisations in the space of a year.”
Van Wymersch is pleased that “everyone is finally on the same page”. She fears that Belgium could well become a narco-state “if we do nothing”.
“Ideally, efforts should have started 20 years ago. We didn’t do that then, so we have to do it today. We have no other choice. We must take on that criminal money and reinvest it in the fight against drugs.”
