TEL AVIV, September 9. /TASS/. The UAE authorities warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of a potential large-scale attack by Hamas well before October 7, 2023, Haaretz reported.
The report is based on a new book, "Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment," written by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval after conversations with dozens of sources in Israel and around the world, including senior officials.
According to the journalists, about ten days before the October 7 attack, UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan called Netanyahu to warn him that Hamas leader in Gaza Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack on Israel.
The sources said the conversation had lasted about 45 minutes, with the UAE president expressing serious concern about Sinwar’s plans and warning that they could lead to bloodshed, destabilize the region and undermine the Abraham Accords between Israel and Arab countries. To his surprise, Haaretz reported, Netanyahu took the warning calmly, expressing confidence that Israel was in full control of the situation in Gaza. Netanyahu believed the threat could only come from the West Bank and reassured the UAE president that Israel was prepared for any scenario.
On October 7, 2023, armed members of Hamas and other Palestinian groups entered Israel from Gaza, killing residents of border communities and taking about 250 people hostage. Hamas described its attack as retaliation for the aggressive actions taken by Israeli authorities against the Al-Aqsa Mosque on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem’s Old City. In response, Israel imposed a total blockade on the Gaza Strip and launched air strikes on Gaza, as well as parts of Lebanon and Syria, before beginning a ground operation in the Palestinian enclave. The active phase of the operation continued intermittently for nearly two years.
On October 9, 2025, Israel and Hamas, mediated by Egypt, Qatar, the United States and Turkey, agreed to implement the first phase of a peace plan proposed by US President Donald Trump. The Gaza ceasefire took effect on October 10. Under the deal, Israeli forces withdrew to the so-called yellow line but retained control of more than 50% of the Strip’s territory. The second phase calls for the withdrawal of Israeli troops from the enclave, the deployment of international stabilization forces and the establishment of new administrative institutions in the Strip. Israel, however, demands that Hamas units first be disarmed, which has not yet happened.

Russia’s losses in the war against Ukraine have exceeded its combined losses in all wars over the past 80 years – General Staff
Kyiv • UNN
The losses of Russian troops killed and wounded have exceeded 1.5 million, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported. These are Russia’s largest losses since World War II.
The total combat losses of Russian forces since the beginning of the full-scale invasion have exceeded 1.5 million killed and wounded. These are the Russian army's largest losses in a single war since World War II, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the General Staff, this figure exceeds the combined losses of the Soviet and Russian armies in all wars and armed conflicts of the second half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century taken together.
In particular, Russia's current losses are approximately 100 times greater than the losses suffered by the USSR during 10 years of war in Afghanistan.
In addition, the figure of 1.5 million is approximately 125 times greater than Russia's officially acknowledged losses during the First and Second Chechen Wars.
The General Staff emphasized that the figure of 1.5 million includes both Russian military personnel killed and wounded since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.

"People don't know it's happening" — Deepfake crisis spreads across Finnish schools, workplaces and military
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
07:38:55 EEST
13:38:55 KST

Ella (not her real name) froze in disbelief when she discovered there were nude photos of her being circulated on pornographic websites.
"Can this really happen? It felt like a nightmare at first. Then the shock and panic hit," she recalled.
The nude images of Ella were not real, but instead someone had created them using artificial intelligence (AI) by manipulating photos taken from her social media accounts.
The phenomenon of so-called 'deepfake' images has spread rapidly in recent years, driven by the wide availability of many easy-to-use apps whose sole purpose is to strip clothes off women and girls.
Ella's case first came to light when Yle's verification team interviewed her for an article (in Finnish) in March this year on the hidden threat posed by deepfake imagery.
"We're talking about an epidemic"
Speaking to Yle News' All Points North podcast, Yle investigative journalist Johanna Vehkoo said that Finland is facing an "epidemic" of deepfake imagery.
"It's happening in schools. It's happening in workplaces, as I've just described. It's happening to well-known women, and it's happening to women who are not that well-known at all. It's happening to children. And it's happening in the army."
Vehkoo called on tech giants such as Apple and Google to 'deplatform' the websites and apps that facilitate the creation and distribution of deepfake imagery.
"They shouldn't be selling these apps on their app stores. But they are selling them. They're making money. They're profiting off this abuse," she noted.
She further added that Finnish society needs to wake up to the threat deepfake imagery poses to women and young girls.
"I'm pretty sure that most people don't even know that it's happening and that it's illegal," she said. "It's just so prolific and it's happening all the time, and it just needs to be stopped."
Yle journalist Johanna Vehkoo joined Ronan Browne in the APN studio to discuss the troubling trend of deepfake imagery in Finland. You can watch the full episode from the video below, on Yle Areena or on our YouTube channel.
More disturbing cases
Although there had been high-profile cases involving deepfake images in other parts of the world, Ella was one of the first people in Finland to speak publicly about the effect the misuse of the technology can have on victims.
Since then, many more disturbing cases have emerged.
In March this year, Yle revealed that one website contained over 1,500 sexually explicit deepfake images and videos of well-known Finnish women, including Finance Minister Riikka Purra (Finns) and Green Party leader Sofia Virta as well as athletes, musicians and actors.
The investigation uncovered the extent and scale of the problem, as one contributor to the website boasted to Yle that it is possible to create up to 200 deepfake pornographic images a day.
Yle's investigative team used a fake profile to communicate with the website's Finnish users, but were not able to identify them.
Under current Finnish law, the distribution of deepfake images is illegal, but creating them is not — unless the subject in the image is under 18 years old. This means there is very little deterrent to stop these users from creating deepfake images.
"LOL the worst that can happen is that some images get removed," one of the deepfake image creators wrote to Yle.
The ease of creating these deepfake images, and the lack of deterrent from doing so, is reflected in the number of cases that are slowly coming to light.
In June, Yle reported (in Finnish) that deepfake images of four women conscripts attached to the Kainuu Brigade had been spread by their male counterparts.
One of the victims described the experience as "humiliating and deeply offensive".
"It's just unbelievable that you can turn against a friend like this. Even those silent witnesses who just saw the images but didn't distribute them had plenty of time to come tell us about it," another said.
The case ended up in the Kainuu district court, where four male conscripts were fined after being found guilty on the charge of distributing sexual images.
Yle's investigative team also tracked down a man who allegedly manipulated photos of his female friends, relatives and co-workers, as well as evidence that a young boy created nude images of dozens of underage girls.
"We're in danger of this becoming normalised," Yle investigative journalist Johanna Vehkoo told the APN podcast. "And I think we can't let something like this just go on without a proper discussion and proper action."

The SAR's first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, made a virtual return to her alma mater on Wednesday morning, beaming in from the Tiangong Space Station for a live educational lecture that captivated students across Hong Kong and Macao.
The event, part of the "Tiangong Class" Hong Kong and Macao Designated Session, took place at Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College and gave young viewers a rare glimpse into life aboard the space station.
Alongside her Shenzhou-23 crewmates, Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan, Lai led a 90-minute interactive tour, showcasing in-orbit demonstrations and offering an intimate look at their daily routines.
As a payload specialist, Lai drew particular attention when she gave students a tour of her sleeping quarters and presented the surprisingly diverse menu available to the crew.
"The science and technology teams on the ground have prepared a wide variety of nutritious and well-balanced recipes for us. There are staple foods like rice, noodles, and bread, as well as dozens of speciality dishes like braised pork, Buddha Jumps Over the Wall, Kung Pao Chicken, black pepper beef fillet, and many more," she said. 
"There are also various types of dehydrated vegetables; after adding water, they look like this... very healthy and delicious. We also make our own yoghurt here. The variety of food is truly diverse."
During a lively question and answer session, one student asked what motivated her to apply for the national payload specialist programme. 
Lai admitted she hadn’t dreamt of becoming an astronaut as a child, but when she learned that mainland authorities were, for the first time, opening the selection process to candidates from Hong Kong and Macao, she knew she had to seize the chance.
"Looking back now, my educational background, scientific research training, and work experience, have all been important factors that enabled me to seize this opportunity," she said. 
"So I hope that students will always prepare yourselves well in your daily lives. When an opportunity comes, be brave and actively go after it."
Also present at the dialogue was Chief Executive John Lee, who noted that many students had written letters to Lai during her mission. 
Lai said that training and life in orbit can sometimes feel isolating and difficult, but she draws strength from the trust placed in her and is determined to complete her mission with full dedication.
In his opening remarks, Lee praised Lai’s achievement as proof that Hongkongers can play a direct role in national space endeavours — and that the dream of space flight is within reach for those bold enough to pursue it. 
He also reaffirmed the government’s commitment to strengthening science education and outreach, urging broader community participation in the city’s growing aerospace enthusiasm.

Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:35:01 UTC
13:35:01 KST

Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
- Date:
- September 9, 2026
- Source:
- Beijing Zhongke Journal Publising Co. Ltd.
- Summary:
- Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.
- Share:
A new study in Earth and Planetary Physics is changing scientists' understanding of when Central America and South America underwent one of the major tectonic collisions that helped shape the Americas. By examining the magnetic characteristics of volcanic rocks in Colombia's Northern Andes, researchers found evidence that the main phases of collision took place earlier than previously believed, before about 10 million years ago.
The research was led by Victor Piedrahita (first author) and J. Li (corresponding author), along with an international group of geoscientists. Their work centered on late Miocene volcanic rocks (approximately 12-6 million years old) from the Combia Volcanic Province in central Colombia. These rocks formed during a key period when the South American Plate was interacting with the continental portion of Central America.
Magnetic Clues Preserved in Volcanic Rocks
To reconstruct what was happening tectonically at the time, the researchers used magnetic fabric analysis. This technique studies the orientation of magnetic minerals inside rocks and can reveal whether their internal structure reflects original volcanic processes or later deformation caused by tectonic forces.
"Volcanic rocks can preserve a remarkably detailed record of geological processes," says Dr. Victor A. Piedrahita. "Their magnetic fabrics help us determine whether deformation occurred before, during, or after the rocks were emplaced."
The team found that many of the volcanic rocks still retain primary magnetic fabrics created by magma movement or volcanic debris flows. That suggests they experienced little or no major tectonic deformation during the late Miocene. Some locations did preserve signs of deformation, but those effects were relatively limited in both strength and geographic extent.
Major Tectonic Deformation Had Already Weakened
Taken together, the evidence indicates that the strongest crustal shortening and collision-related deformation in the Northern Andes had mostly ended before the late Miocene. In other words, by the time these volcanic rocks were forming, the most intense phase of tectonic compression had already passed.
"Our data indicate that the most significant collisional events between Central and South America occurred earlier than we previously thought, mainly during the Oligocene-middle Miocene," explain Piedrahita and Li. "By the time these volcanic rocks formed, tectonic deformation had become weaker and more localized."
The findings could help scientists improve models of how the Andes formed and better understand how interactions between tectonic plates influenced the geological development of the Americas. The study also highlights how magnetic techniques can be used to reconstruct ancient tectonic activity in volcanic regions.
The research was supported by grants from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), awarded to J. Li and Victor Piedrahita.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Beijing Zhongke Journal Publising Co. Ltd.. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- A. Piedrahita Victor, Chadima Martin, Ramírez Jackeline, Tabares Alejandra, I. Marín-Cerón Maria, Li JinHua. Magnetic fabric of the late Miocene extrusive rocks of the Combia Volcanic Province: Tectonic implications for the northern Andes. Earth and Planetary Physics, 2026; 10 (1): 44 DOI: 10.26464/epp2026011

Meta ran over 300 ads with suspected AI child abuse, NGO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:35:00 UTC
13:35:00 KST

Meta ran over 300 ads with suspected AI child abuse, NGO says
- Meta ran over 300 ads on Instagram and Facebook in 2026 showing suspected AI-generated child sexual abuse material, reaching more than 29,000 people, according to the Tech Transparency Project.
- Many ads promoted deepfake "nudify" apps linked to developers and Meta advertising partners in China, violating Meta's policies and US laws.
- Meta removed about half the ads by Sept 1 and took down the rest after being alerted, while continuing to improve detection amid growing global scrutiny and legal actions.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Meta Platforms Inc has run more than 300 advertisements on Instagram and Facebook containing suspected child sexual abuse material in 2026, according to a report on Sept 8 by the non-profit Tech Transparency Project.
The ads collectively reached more than 29,000 people and typically used artificial intelligence to depict young children being molested, TTP said.
Many served to promote deepfake “nudify” apps, which were the subject of an earlier report by the group, which tracked their source to app developers and a Meta advertising partner in China.
TTP is a research arm of the Washington DC-based nonpartisan corporate and government watchdog Campaign for Accountability.
The failure to prevent such material appearing on Meta’s services, used by billions globally, comes as the company faces unprecedented scrutiny for social media’s alleged harms to children.
The ads violate Meta’s own policies prohibiting child exploitation, abuse and nudity, along with US federal laws.
TTP said it reported the ads to the Congressionally mandated National Centre for Missing & Exploited Children.
“Content involving child sexual abuse is among the most serious that can be found online,” said Katie Paul, TTP’s director. “But this content isn’t hiding in dark corners of the internet. It’s being used in paid ads on Meta platforms.”
In one instance, TTP said it found ads that used a photo a young girl had posted to her Instagram account in which she was wearing a sports uniform.
The ad animated her image into a video in which she is depicted performing a sex act, TTP said.
Another ad showed a preteen girl removing her shirt, with accompanying text promising “dark” content.
“We don’t tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated,” Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Bloomberg News.
Many of the ads flagged had already been removed, he said.
Those behind such activity frequently shift tactics to circumvent Meta’s systems, and the company continues to strengthen its detection and enforcement, he added.
TTP in July reported Meta had shown thousands of sexually suggestive ads for nudification apps, which are designed to digitally remove clothing or place photos of real people into graphic images of videos.
The new findings pertain to ads that are more graphic, TTP says.
Meta as of Sept 1 had removed about half the offending ads from its ad library, TTP said.
The company removed the remaining ads after TTP shared its findings, it said.
Such content is often called child pornography, but law enforcement and experts also refer to it as child sexual abuse material, or CSAM, because it’s evidence of a non-consensual crime.
TTP’s report comes not long after Meta agreed to a landmark settlement to pay up to US$18 billion (S$22.76 billion) to resolve claims from US states over the alleged harms its apps caused to young people.
Australia and more than two dozen countries are implementing or pursuing bans on under-16s accessing social media like Instagram.
The UK government on Sept 8 said it will mandate that Apple Inc and Alphabet Inc’s Google – responsible for the iPhone and Android operating systems, respectively – stop children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their phones and tablets.
Beyond Meta, law enforcement groups in the US are struggling to deal with the proliferation of AI-altered explicit images and videos, due in large part to tools that make it simple to create illegal content.
The 332 ads TTP found reached those who may have been scrolling Instagram and Facebook in the European Union, the UK, the US, India and Australia.
Some of the individual ads reached just a handful of users, some reached hundreds, and two reached more than 2,500 in the EU alone.
Wired in August reported that Meta had run more than 50 ads containing CSAM.
TTP’s new research includes newly discovered material not previously reported.
Most of the ads flagged to Meta had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under US$5,000, Stone said.
Meta in the second quarter posted revenue of US$60.8 billion, and its services had an average of 3.6 billion daily active users as of June.
While Instagram and Facebook aren’t available in China, businesses based in the country use them as promotional platforms for reaching global audiences.
Meta has several advertising partners in China, some of which TTP said placed ads containing CSAM. BLOOMBERG

S. Korean banks' household loan growth slows in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:31:46 CST
13:31:46 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- South Korean banks' household loan growth slowed last month as tighter credit controls and a cooling stock market led to a downturn in non-mortgage lending, central bank data showed Wednesday.
Debt owed by households to deposit-taking banks totaled 1,198.3 trillion won (894.1 billion U.S. dollars) at the end of August, up 3.4 trillion won from a month earlier, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The August gain was lower than an expansion of 5.5 trillion won in the previous month, but it kept an upward trend for a sixth straight month.
The slowdown was caused by a slump in retail stock investments and bank's stricter credit management that stoked the downturn in non-mortgage lending.
Other loans, including credit loan, credit line and commercial real estate-backed loan, fell 0.6 trillion won in August from a month earlier, reversing from an increase of 2.0 trillion won in July.
Mortgage loans continued an upward trajectory, swelling 4.0 trillion won last month compared to a 3.5 trillion won growth in the prior month.
The mortgage demand was driven by a rise in property transactions and newly-built apartment move-in volume in Seoul and its surrounding areas.
The number of newly-built apartment move-in volume across the country advanced from 13,000 in June to 18,000 in July and 19,000 in August, while apartment sales in the capital region remained steady throughout the summer.
Corporate loans, extended by domestic banks, totaled 1,430.8 trillion won at the end of August, up 9.7 trillion won from a month earlier. It outpaced an increase of 7.7 trillion won in the previous month.
Lending to large corporations mounted 4.9 trillion won as banks aggressively promoted lending to big companies, which sought funds for corporate bond redemptions.
Loans to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) climbed 4.8 trillion won due to financial support programs for smaller businesses, rolled out by some banks. ■

The IMF is considering reforming pandemic response financing following the Ebola outbreak in the Congo

The IMF is considering reforming pandemic response financing following the Ebola outbreak in the Congo
Kyiv • UNN
The IMF is discussing financing pandemic preparedness in the Congo following the Ebola outbreak. A total of 6,686 cases have been confirmed, and 3,226 people have died.
The International Monetary Fund is considering including pandemic preparedness and response reforms in its financing program for the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The reason is the rapid spread of Ebola, which exposed weaknesses in the financing of the country's healthcare system, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
The Congo, together with the WHO and the World Bank, is working on measures that could be included in the IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Facility. In particular, the parties are discussing the creation of a separate financing strategy for pandemic prevention and response.
Health shocks in the DRC are more of a recurring than an exceptional phenomenon
IMF warns of risks to the economy
The fund considers the Congo's epidemic preparedness system to be "fragmented and incomplete." Cuts in international aid have further weakened the country's ability to detect and contain new outbreaks.
As of September 6, the number of confirmed Ebola cases had reached 6,686, of which 3,226 had resulted in death. The epidemic has spread to 6 provinces and remains uncontrolled.
According to estimates by the Congo and its partners, approximately $1.3 billion is needed to contain the outbreak over the next 6 months. The IMF warns that a prolonged epidemic could increase government spending and harm trade, transport, agriculture, and the logistics of the mining industry.

====================================================================================================

Australia breaks from international pack on Israeli sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:27:45 UTC
13:27:45 KST

analysis
The United Kingdom moves against Israeli settlers but for now, Australia stands still
It's almost 12 months since Prime Minister Anthony Albanese joined 10 other countries in recognising the state of Palestine at the United Nations General Assembly.
The move was dismissed by some critics as too late, or only symbolic, at the time.
And at that time, the prospects of a Palestinian state ever emerging were already pretty grim, with Gaza largely reduced to rubble and Israel in the process of expanding settlements in the West Bank at a record pace.
In the intervening year, with the world's attention distracted by the conflict with Iran, and by Israel's invasion of a vast swathe of Lebanon, the Israeli cabinet has defied growing criticism from the international community by only escalating its efforts to make a Palestinian state a physical impossibility.
The overnight move by the international community, spearheaded by the United Kingdom but including Canada, France and other European nations, is a significant escalation of attempts to stop Israel from doing that.
The move is not just significant because it escalates penalising actions into trade sanctions.
It is important because of what goes with that, as well as the changing context of Israel's actions.
Israel believes the West Bank 'belongs to us'
In the past, Israel has justified many of its moves to clear Palestinians from their homes — in Gaza, in Jerusalem or the West Bank — on specific security grounds: that houses and the people who lived in them were responsible for, or represented, a security threat.
Even many Israelis who are not fans of the settlement movement will say that, while they don't like them, their presence makes them feel more secure.
But settlers themselves tend to justify their takeover of Palestinian land in the West Bank on the grounds of an assertion of sovereignty, based in the Bible, rather than any immediate security threats emanating from any particular village.
Those past security concerns, and UK Labour's fraught history of allegations of antisemitism, have been part of the reason why Westminster has hesitated to adopt findings against Israel in the international criminal system.
As British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Tuesday, "For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel."
On Tuesday, local time, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the House of Commons that the British government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank — perpetrated by settler terrorists".
"And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians," he added.
"Now for a long time, the British government has rightly said settlements are illegal.
"But we have remained silent on the question of the legality of the occupation as a whole, which in 2024 the International Court of Justice concluded was unlawful.
"Today I announce that the official view of the British government is that the occupation is unlawful."
Loading...
The significance of this is that the UK — along with countries like Australia — previously legally separated the status of the settlements from the status of the military occupation of the West Bank as a whole.
The occupation was viewed as a temporary, unresolved political dispute — even though it has been in place since 1967 — to be settled via bilateral negotiations.
Miliband also foreshadowed the likelihood of the International Court of Justice making a finding of genocide against Israel, and that the UK would accept such a finding, and the possibility of further actions at the UN General Assembly in New York later this month.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his pledge at the time of the UN move last September, saying his government was "going to fulfil our promise that there will be no Palestinian state".
"This place belongs to us," he said.
In March this year, Israel announced another 34 settlements in the West Bank, as well as allocating billions of shekels to fast-track infrastructure, roads, and security connectivity for these sites.
In August, it provocatively pushed ahead with a development that Miliband described to the House of Commons on Tuesday as "crossing a long-standing red line": the issuing of tenders for more than 1,200 homes in a 12-square-kilometre tract of land immediately east of Jerusalem known as E1.
The proposed housing development would start to cut the West Bank — Palestinian territory — in half, and also cut it off from Jerusalem, destroying the prospect of a viable Palestinian state.
Sanctions significant, but may be difficult to implement
While settlements — and the increasing violence shown by settlers towards Palestinian landowners (tolerated or even sometimes perpetrated by the Israeli military) — are the most visible signs of Israeli actions in the West Bank, it is also in a state of virtual war on the West Bank economy.
While settlers physically attack Palestinians, they also uproot their trees and divert the water supplies of villages, which make them viable.
But on a larger scale, Israel has increasingly made economic life impossible.
Israel has withheld tariffs and revenue it collects on behalf of the Palestinian Authority — which is supposed to fund its provision of day-to-day services. It leaves the Palestinian banking system in a perpetual state of uncertainty by refusing to guarantee it will offer exchange services with the Israeli banking system.
It puts strict limits on how much paper money — even though it is Israeli shekels — can be exchanged between the Palestinian and Israeli economies.
The settlements themselves are often economically unviable. They are not just the odd caravan on a hill but often mini cities.
Though the Israeli government does consider informal settlements, known as outposts, illegal, they often later authorise them as formal settlements.
The Israeli government doesn't just tolerate the violence; it provides massive subsidies to encourage people to move to the settlements, including reduced income tax rates, security gear for unauthorised or "young" outposts as well as funds to purchase vehicles, drones, security cameras, generators, electric gates, and perimeter fences.
That's what makes the various economic trade sanctions announced overnight by the UK, France, Canada and 12 European countries both so significant and also so potentially difficult to implement.
They are also one of the reasons Australia has, on this occasion, broken from the pack of other nations in not adopting the trade sanctions against West Bank businesses.
Australia remains exposed, but may act further
The argument goes that it will be almost impossible for international companies to distinguish between Palestinian businesses in the West Bank and settler businesses, or between sanctions that only hurt settlers and those that might also hurt the Palestinian economy.
The Albanese government knows it remains exposed by its position, which one Labor source described as "rhetorically less impressive", but there are signs it may act further in the coming weeks and months.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the Senate on Tuesday that the "Netanyahu government's actions in the West Bank, the rapid expansion of settlements, the proposed E1 settlement development and flagrant settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution".
Australia is "not, at this time, pursuing a blanket style import ban", she said, because "we have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis".
Loading...
The real effectiveness of any blanket bans is likely to be in the realm of finance, rather than sanctions on, say, date farms in the West Bank.
A particular issue for the UK in recent months has been investor "expos" inviting people in Britain to come along and find out how they could invest in the West Bank, in illegally occupied land.
The UK signalled action "against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion", Mr Miliband said.
It will also ban the advertising in the UK of illegal settlements.
Just what specific actions France and Canada will take in support of the UK position are unclear, although they have said they will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements.
The Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway have already either banned goods or are in the process of doing so, while Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden also pledged to take further action overnight.
Loading
To date, the US has been notably quiet about the UK actions, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio not condemning the UK action but saying the US would "obviously" not be going along with it either.
"Obviously, we're not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don't have any comment on it right now," Rubio told reporters in Miami.
The US does not want to see "anything destabilising going on right now in the West Bank with so much going on in the region", he added.
"We were made aware that they were going to make this decision," he said.
"We heard their arguments as to why. But we share the goal of stability. We don't want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region."
Loading...
But there already has been more than an "uptick" in conflict on the West Bank, and little sign that the US-led peace initiative for Gaza is making any progress.
Some analysts have expressed concern that the Israeli government would be quite happy to see a full-scale uprising on the West Bank ahead of next month's Israeli elections.
And that raises another aspect of this story: that international actions against Israel often galvanise public opinion in favour of the government.
The UK-led actions this week come just as Netanyahu's standing with voters came under huge new pressures this week with revelations that he had been warned by the United Arab Emirates of the likelihood of a major Hamas attack in the days leading up to October 7, 2023, but failed to pass this intelligence on.
The man who has emerged as the greatest challenge to Netanyahu at next month's elections is Gadi Eisenkot.
While he supports maintaining established settlement blocs in the West Bank and opposes Palestinian statehood, he has also opposed unilateral annexation, criticised provocative outposts, settler violence and controversial construction plans like the E1 development, in part because of the diplomatic toll such moves impose on Israel's international standing.
In the Israeli landscape of 2026, that is quite a different position from that of the current government. But it's unclear whether it would be enough of a change to satisfy an increasingly frustrated international community.

Russian political prisoner Alexei Gorinov reports symptoms of possible poisoning, Moscow court refuses his request for medical help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:12:05 UTC
13:12:05 KST

During a hearing held on Sept. 8 via video link, Russian political prisoner Alexei Gorinov complained to the Moscow City Court of nausea and dizziness. His request for help obtaining medical care was refused, according to a report by the independent Russian outlet SOTAvision. Gorinov, 65, is currently incarcerated in Penal Colony No. 10 in Russia’s Altai Krai. He suffers from a chronic lung condition and was hospitalized in June 2025 with acute bronchitis after doctors found signs of tuberculosis during a prisoner transfer.
Gorinov’s support group said that after he was transferred to Penal Colony No. 10, officials confiscated his medication and forced him to spend the winter in an unheated cell-type facility — a stricter form of confinement inside the prison system. He said ice formed on the inside of the window frame and that he had to wear a sweater at all times to keep from freezing. Gorinov said he was hospitalized a total of three times with bronchitis and later asked to be admitted again. Prison officials refused and instead moved him to a warmer cell.
At Tuesday’s hearing, the Moscow City Court considered an appeal by Gorinov’s defense against prosecutors’ refusal to reopen an investigation into his case after a United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found Gorinov’s prosecution to be unlawful. His lawyer, Maria Tertukhina, said neither prosecutors nor Russian courts had addressed the UN experts’ findings, and in the end, the court upheld a March ruling by Moscow’s Tagansky District Court that found the prosecutors’ refusal lawful.
The Working Group adopted Opinion No. 78/2022 in November 2022. The document, reviewed by The Insider, identified violations of six articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and five provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights — 11 legal provisions in all.
The Working Group found Gorinov’s detention arbitrary under three categories: he was prosecuted for lawfully exercising his rights to freedom of expression and participation in public affairs; the proceedings against him involved serious violations of his right to a fair trial; and he was discriminated against due to his political views.
The panel called for Gorinov’s immediate release, said he should be entitled to compensation, and urged that an independent investigation into the circumstances of his prosecution be opened. Russian officials did not implement any of those recommendations.
A Working Group’s opinion does not have the authority to overturn a conviction in a Russian court. However, in 2021, the plenary session of Russia’s Supreme Court said information contained in such international findings can provide sufficient grounds for prosecutors to open proceedings based on new circumstances when the violations identified cannot otherwise be remedied. The Russian Supreme Court also instructed judges to determine whether prosecutors had examined all the circumstances raised by an applicant.
Tertukhina argued that the prosecutors in Gorinov’s case had not carried out such a review, as was clear from the rejection letter they issued. She asked the court to overturn the Tagansky District Court’s ruling and order prosecutors to review the application in accordance with the law.
Gorinov also said he had previously appealed to prosecutors but had received no response.
“I would like to understand why I, having taken no one’s life, maimed no one, killed no one, and poisoned no one with drugs, but merely spoken out about the need to end the war and stood up for children who had been killed, was sentenced to seven years — and effectively 10 years when the second sentence is taken into account?”
Gorinov was first Russian citizen to receive a prison sentence under a law criminalizing what the Kremlin calls “fake news” about Russia’s armed forces, adopted shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The case stemmed from a March 15, 2022, meeting of the municipal council in Moscow’s Krasnoselsky District. Gorinov proposed holding a minute of silence for those killed in Ukraine and questioned whether it was appropriate to organize a children’s drawing contest while children were dying in a neighboring country.
In July 2022, he was sentenced to seven years in a general-regime penal colony. The Moscow City Court later reduced the sentence by one month.
In 2023, Gorinov was hit with another criminal case, this time on charges of “justifying terrorism.” The accusation was based on conversations he had with other inmates in a prison hospital about the explosion on the Kerch Strait Bridge and Ukraine’s Azov and Kraken units. Gorinov said his cellmates had deliberately provoked him into discussing politics and that he had said nothing that justified terrorism.
In November 2024, a military court sentenced Gorinov to three additional years in a strict-regime penal colony over the new charges. Taking into account the unserved portion of his first sentence, the final punishment was set at five years in a strict-regime colony, extending his actual term of imprisonment by around one year.

Cluster munitions kill, wound over 1,000 globally in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:11:51 UTC
13:11:51 KST

Cluster munitions kill, wound over 1,000 globally in 2025
The 1,063 global casualties in 2025 one of the highest annual tolls on record, a report has found.
Cluster munitions have killed or injured at least 1,063 people in 2025, one of the highest annual tolls on record, according to a report produced by a global network of researchers.
Most casualties were civilians, including at least 34 children, the Cluster Munition Coalition’s annual report said on Tuesday. Deaths and injuries were recorded in Afghanistan, Cambodia, Iraq, Laos, Lebanon, Myanmar, Russia, Syria and Ukraine.
Ukraine had the highest number of recorded casualties for the fourth consecutive year in 2025, accounting for 87 percent of the global total.
The actual number is likely higher as many casualties go unreported, the report said. The highest toll was recorded in 2022, 1,172, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine that year.
Cluster munitions consist of small compartments that disperse small explosives indiscriminately, posing significant danger to civilian populations. Explosives can remain undetonated long after they are dispersed.
Adopted during the Oslo Process, the Convention on Cluster Munitions took effect in 2010 after Norway and several other countries aimed to create an international treaty to protect civilians from the controversial explosive weapons.
The convention prohibits the use, production, and collection of cluster munitions. The treaty has 112 states parties and 12 signatories. Lithuania is the first and only country to withdraw from the convention in March.
The Cluster Munition Coalition reported that cluster munitions were used by Iran, Myanmar, Russia, Thailand, Ukraine, and Mali, which is a party to the convention.
The report added that while it was not able to verify the claims, there were reports of use by Israel and the US in Iran, by Pakistan in Afghanistan, by Houthi forces in Israel, and by Israel in Lebanon.
Evidence of new production was found in China, India, Israel, Myanmar, North Korea, Poland, Romania, Russia, and South Korea. The report added that evidence suggests that the US plans new production of cluster munitions in the future.
The US and Russia voted against an annual resolution promoting the convention in the United Nations General Assembly in December, for the first time since it was introduced.
The report said the cuts in US foreign assistance last year disrupted clearance of cluster munition remnants, which resulted in the death and injury of at least 117 people in 2025.

Taiwan students rank fourth in science in latest PISA assessment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:11:43 UTC
13:11:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese students ranked fourth worldwide in science, third in reading, and fourth in mathematics in the latest Programme for International Student Assessment, maintaining their position among the world's strongest-performing educational systems.
The 2025 PISA results, released Tuesday by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development and Taiwan's Ministry of Education, showed Taiwan's 15-year-old students scoring 540 points in science, 508 in reading, and 546 in mathematics, per a press release.
Taiwan's science score was its highest ever in PISA and ranked fourth among the 91 participating countries and economies. Its reading ranking rose from fifth in 2022 to third, the country's highest-ever ranking, while its mathematics score slipped one point from 547 to 546 and its ranking fell from third to fourth.
The OECD averages in 2025 were 486 points for science, 466 for reading, and 469 for mathematics. All three were lower than in 2022, continuing a decline in student performance following the COVID-19 pandemic. Taiwan's scores changed much less, with science rising by two points from 2022, reading falling by seven points, and mathematics declining by one point.
Tsai Chin-chung (蔡今中), Taiwan's PISA project director and an honorary national chair professor at National Taiwan Normal University, said the results showed the resilience of Taiwan's education system, per LTN.
Science was the main subject assessed in PISA 2025. Taiwan's 540-point score was significantly higher than the OECD average and represented a new high for the country. About 20.1% of Taiwanese students reached Level 5 or above in science, compared with 15.4% in 2015. Meanwhile, 87.1% reached at least Level 2, the basic proficiency threshold, exceeding the OECD benchmark of 85%.
Taiwan's strong science performance placed it behind only China, Singapore, and Macao among participating countries and regions. The ranking should be interpreted with some caution, however, as China's PISA sample covers students in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang rather than the entire country, per CNA.
Taiwanese students scored 508 in reading, down seven points from 515 in 2022 but still ranking third internationally. The proportion of Taiwanese students reaching Level 5 or above was 13.4%, more than double the OECD average of 6.1%. Some 82.1% reached at least Level 2, compared with 70.5% across OECD countries.
Digital problem-solving
PISA 2025 also introduced a new assessment area, “Learning in the Digital World,” including computational problem-solving. Taiwanese students scored an average of 551 points in computational problem-solving, ranking fifth among participating countries and economies and above the OECD average of 500, per the press release.
Some 82.1% of Taiwanese students reached at least Level 3, compared with 64.1% across the OECD, while 46.2% reached Level 5 or above, compared with 26.1% in OECD countries.
The results also showed strong awareness of information verification. About 93% of Taiwanese students agreed that information should be checked against multiple reliable sources before being accepted, placing Taiwan third internationally and above the OECD average of 83.5%.
Tsai said the findings indicated that Taiwanese students had strong computational thinking, problem-solving, and information-verification skills. He cautioned, however, that using generative AI as a substitute for thinking could have the opposite effect, per LTN.
Students who used AI daily to support their learning tended to perform better, according to the analysis, while those who primarily used AI to summarize assigned reading or draft homework tended to perform worse.
The 2025 PISA assessment covered 91 countries and economies. Taiwan's participation involved 292 schools and about 7,300 students. PISA assesses the ability of 15-year-old students to apply knowledge and skills to problems in real-life situations rather than simply testing their recall of school material, per the Education Ministry.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Yageo Corp. reported its sixth consecutive monthly revenue record in August, supported by strong business from AI-related applications.
The passive component maker posted revenue of NT$16.33 billion (US$518.7 million) in August, up 51.8% from the same month a year earlier. Revenue for the first eight months of the year totaled NT$115.09 billion, an increase of 34.9% year-on-year, according to CTEE and LTN.
Yageo said strong sales of AI-related products and solid business in Asian markets offset the usual seasonal slowdown in Europe and the US during summer vacation. Revenue from its various product lines also continued to grow.
Yageo manufactures passive components, including resistors, capacitors and inductors, which are essential parts of electronic devices. Unlike active components, which process or amplify electrical signals, passive components regulate electricity flow and store energy, according to Gugu Fund and Business Weekly.
The company said it would continue to monitor market changes as AI adoption expands and the electronic components industry undergoes structural changes. Demand is shifting toward high-voltage and customized components, driven by growth in AI servers and automotive electronics.
AI servers require three to five times more multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) than traditional servers. Electric vehicles also use significantly more MLCCs than gasoline-powered vehicles.
Taiwanese suppliers of MLCCs, chip resistors, inductors, and aluminum capacitors have reported higher prices, stronger order activity, and longer delivery times for some products.

Tylenol use in pregnancy may be linked with uterus, ovary changes in daughters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:07:34 UTC
13:07:34 KST

Tylenol use in pregnancy may be linked with uterus, ovary changes in daughters
Sept 9 - Female reproductive organ development may be impacted by a mother's use of Tylenol during pregnancy, according to researchers who emphasize that their study does not prove the pain medicine is to blame and does not indicate any effect on the girls’ future fertility.
Whether the differences observed in the study of infants have implications for fertility later in life and age at menopause will require long-term follow-up, study leader Margit Bistrup Fischer of Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen said in a statement.
Women who during pregnancy have used Tylenol — also sold as acetaminophen, or paracetamol outside the U.S. — should not be alarmed by the findings, Fischer said.
Her team studied 302 three-month-old baby girls whose mothers' Tylenol use had been tracked during pregnancy.
Ninety-two of the infants were first exposed to Tylenol in utero before 17 weeks of pregnancy, 67 were first exposed after 17 weeks, and 143 were born to mothers who had not used the drug.
Tylenol exposure was assessed based on urine samples provided by the women at regular intervals. The mothers took relatively low amounts, and none exceeded the recommended daily maximum dose of 4,000 milligrams. Most took it for headaches or musculoskeletal pain.
On average, infants exposed in utero had smaller ovaries, fewer ovarian follicles, which are the structures that contain immature eggs, smaller uteruses and lower levels of reproductive hormones, researchers reported on Wednesday in Human Reproduction Open.
A woman’s reproductive function and window are established while she’s still in the womb, the researchers explained, and girls are born with all the eggs they will ever have.
Animal studies have suggested that fetal exposure to Tylenol, the most commonly used drug in pregnancy, might affect ovarian egg reserve and later reproductive function, but no one has reported similar findings in humans until now.
U.S. President Donald Trump has linked the use of Tylenol during pregnancy to autism, a claim that has been widely dismissed by the medical community and major health organizations as lacking scientific backing.
MEASURING IMPACT ON OVARIES AND UTERUS
The three-month-old girls in the study who were exposed to Tylenol in utero had, on average, a 40% smaller ovarian volume, a 13% smaller uterine volume and 23% fewer ovarian follicles, the researchers found.
Babies exposed early in pregnancy – before 17 weeks – also had lower levels of Anti-Müllerian hormone, an indicator of the amount and quality of eggs in the ovaries.
The researchers also looked at a separate group of 1,210 girls who were followed from infancy to adolescence and whose mothers had reported Tylenol use during pregnancy. In this group, fetal exposure was associated with smaller uteruses at puberty and smaller ovaries during adolescence.
The study cannot predict outcomes for any individual woman or child, Fischer said, noting that many women who used Tylenol during pregnancy had daughters whose ovarian measurements were similar to those of daughters born to women who did not use the drug.
Current guidelines continue to recommend Tylenol as safe for treating pain and fever during pregnancy. Untreated high fever or severe pain can themselves pose risks to the mother and the fetus, Fischer said.
In an accompanying commentary, Dr. Christian De Geyter, a reproductive medicine specialist at the University Hospital of Basel, Switzerland, said the researchers’ findings fit well with data from research in animals.
Follow-up of girls exposed to Tylenol in utero should extend into menopause, he said, adding that recommendations on its use during pregnancy should be reconsidered. REUTERS

Hong Kong will continue to serve as a gateway linking belt and road economies with mainland China and global markets, the chief executive has said, underscoring the city’s role in bringing together capital, talent and businesses to advance the national initiative.
Speaking at the opening of the annual Belt and Road Summit on Wednesday, John Lee Ka-chiu said more than 60 government and business agreements and memorandums of understanding (MOUs) would be signed during the event, with the total value of projects and deals exceeding US$3 billion.
“In a world struggling with unprecedented change and geopolitical fragmentation, connectivity, cooperation, and consensus are essential. That’s precisely what the Belt and Road Summit offers,” he said.
“The Belt and Road Initiative is not a map of the past, but a shared blueprint for the future. And Hong Kong is where we realise that future: where East meets West, where capital, talent, businesses and opportunities converge.”
Lee described Hong Kong as a “two-way springboard” for mainland enterprises seeking to expand overseas and international companies looking to access the mainland market.
He said the city would serve as a global gateway for belt and road businesses to raise capital, citing recent examples such as Kazakhstan’s national railway company applying to list on the city’s stock exchange.

Russia is raining death on Ukraine’s women and children. Our hands shake but we keep going for love | Alina Sarnatska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:01:00 UTC
13:01:00 KST

My grandma was as hard as nails. She had just turned 17 when the Nazis entered her village in the Kyiv region, near what is now the city of Bucha. She hid in the attic to avoid being taken for forced labour. They didn’t find her that time, but a few weeks later she was caught working in the fields. They put her in a cattle wagon and took her to Germany. She escaped and walked a couple of hundred kilometres back to her village. Grandma said that life was hard for everybody during the war, but she was lucky.
In the past month, two of my friends here in Kyiv happened to tell me that their hands have started shaking during Russian airstrikes. Everybody who knows that my hands shake during airstrikes tells me their stories. One day, during an airstrike in the Donetsk region, I had a meltdown and have never recovered. Today you could say I am an ambassador for people whose hands shake during airstrikes.
Those two friends said the same exact thing: their hands never used to shake before and now they do. Each one wrote: “I don’t understand what’s just happened to me.”
For nearly five years, the Russians have been targeting these women and their children with drones, rockets, jet-powered drones and missiles. They have threatened us with nuclear weapons. They have used an Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile in combat; carried out a siege; again threatened a nuclear strike; tried to freeze us by destroying Ukraine’s heat and power systems in the middle of winter; blown up a dam, flooding two city districts; used more drones and fired yet other types of long-range missiles at Ukrainian cities; organised terror attacks; and, once again, threatened to wipe us out with nuclear weapons.
In the early hours of 19 July, the general staff of the armed forces of Ukraine reported a massive combined Russian attack: 41 missiles and 125 drones, with Kyiv as the main target. Next morning, I got a message from my friend Valya. “Everything was fine, and then all of a sudden something happened,” she wrote. “Everyone but me is at home asleep. I’m the only one who’s so anxious.”
After every airstrike, the women I know “pull themselves together”, take their children to preschool, and go to work. Because children need to be fed – and if the state-run preschool doesn’t have a bomb shelter, the private one that does costs money. The women I know sleep beside their children in the corridors of their apartment buildings, in underground parking garages, in the metro or in pedestrian tunnels. “Everything’s fine,” say these women. After Russia fires dozens of missiles at Kyiv overnight, they say: “It was loud, but everything’s fine.” And they wonder why their hands shake and they even blame themselves for being weak.
My grandma’s name was Dina and she was as hard as nails. She would get very angry when I snuggled up to our relatives. Once, my grandma’s sister was over and I climbed on to her lap and wrapped my arms around her. Grandma Dina yelled at me: “Get down, what a disgrace, you’re a big girl now!” I was seven. My grandma was afraid I would be spoiled. Whenever I cried, she would say to my mother: “Look how you’ve spoiled her, how will she cope with life?”
Grandma Dina liked to feed stray cats. Grandpa protested, but she did it anyway. When she went out to feed them, for a few minutes she became a completely different person. First, she scolded them for being a nuisance, wearing her usual face. Then, as they ate, she would start to smile a bit and stroke their thin, fluffy backs. With one hand on her thigh, she would lean over and pet each cat once or twice, smiling. Then she would pick up the bowl, straighten up, and her expression would return to normal.
One morning, I found a large grey cat dead under a bush; a cat that my grandma had been feeding for 10 years, as long as I had been alive. He had probably died of old age or sickness. I burst into tears and ran to my grandma. She rolled up a towel and gave me a whack on the ribs. “Now stop that crying, you’re a big girl now!” When my mother came home from work in the evening, I said: “I think Grandma’s a robot.” To which mum replied: “Nonsense, now go finish your soup.”
There was nothing soft about Grandma Dina. If she were still alive today, she would be well prepared. She didn’t know much about getting along with people, but she did know how to pull herself together.
Now I understand that she could not cut herself any slack or allow herself any feelings of self-kindness and that’s why she also felt no compassion for others. Compassion was too risky for her.
And it’s true, we cannot let ourselves be as emotional or compassionate as we were before the war. We cannot live, let alone work, as we did before. On top of that, war reveals the sharp contrast between our reality and the cult of the self displayed on social media. Viral posts about “success, energy and choosing yourself” are irrelevant to anyone caring for a sick child when it is 5C inside your apartment.
Enduring daily death and the violence of Russia’s attacks has changed us irreversibly. The skin of Ukrainian women has thickened into armour. These women take part in combat, live under constant airstrikes, and keep working and caring for their families through it all.
But if it were up to me, I would keep my belly soft. I still want to hug people, hold them close, and feel the warmth of their hands. So what if Grandma Dina would say I’m not ready for life? I think that love is worth the risk.
We stay calm because our children are watching us, because they need to be taken to preschool in the morning, because there is still work to do. But when resilience becomes an obligation, every trembling hand starts to feel like a personal failure. I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards other people, or towards myself.
Translated from Ukrainian by Larissa Babij

  Alina Sarnatska is a Ukrainian writer, playwright and war veteran. She is the author of two books and nine plays, and her work has been staged and presented internationally

‘Miserable and impossible’: food scarce in Kyiv as Russia targets supply chains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:00:59 UTC
13:00:59 KST

Stocking up on cured sausages from the half-empty shelves in her local supermarket, Valentyna Sveshnikova is worried about money. The 68-year-old grandmother lives off her small pension and has already noticed the cost of several goods increase, including sausages. Russia wants “to make our life miserable and impossible. And they’re actually succeeding in it,” she says.
Russian strikes on food warehouses and logistics supply chains around several Ukrainian cities have left gaps on supermarket shelves and risk causing price increases.
Kyiv has faced a particularly intense barrage of attacks. A temporary truce that was in place between Moscow and Kyiv to ensure the safe passage of US negotiators over the weekend ended abruptly on Monday night when jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles pounded Ukraine’s capital, killing two people.
Many shelves at the Novus supermarket where Sveshnikova is shopping for groceries are empty. But customers, hardened by four years of war, are sanguine. “It’s scary, but I don’t plan to go anywhere,” says 40-year-old Dariya Malyukova.
The agrarian policy and food minister, Taras Vysotsky, has warned that food prices could increase by 2.5% because of the attacks on warehouse infrastructure.
But Dmytro Krymskiy, the co-founder of Bureau of Wine, which operates several high-end retail brands in Ukraine, including the supermarket chain Goodwine, says the impact could be as high as 15%.
One of Krymskiy’s warehouses near Kyiv was hit on 1 September, wiping out €4m (£3.4m) of stock. The attacks “seriously hurt our business”, he says.
Krymskiy says that prices will increase not because of a shortage of supplies, but because of the cost of reorganising supply chains to make them more resilient against strikes.
He is exploring several options, including moving his warehouses to a neighbouring country such as Poland, using underground storage facilities and splitting his stock across several smaller sites. “We understand that we cannot have only one big warehouse,” he said. Krymskiy thinks his prices could rise by about 5%.
The latest strike did not come as a complete surprise; it was the third time since the start of the full-scale invasion that his warehouses had been hit. The first, in 2022, destroyed €15m of supplies, while another attack in July this year annihilated €1.5m-worth of goods.
“It was really a matter of time,” he says. “The problem is, we had 3,000 pallets there, and you simply cannot move it,” he says. The recent onslaught of airborne attacks also meant that warehouse staff could only work for three to four hours per day, reducing the company’s ability to shift stock.
The raids come at a difficult time for Ukraine. Kyiv has been hit by a torrent of daily drone and missile strikes since late August, killing dozens of people and destroying key infrastructure. As well as the food warehouses, Russia has targeted e-commerce logistics hubs and stockpiles of medical supplies.
On Wednesday night, one of the World Health Organization’s main warehouses storing humanitarian aid on the outskirts of Kyiv was hit.
At the warehouse of Biokon, a pharmaceutical company, the air was thick with the smell of burnt fuel on Friday as firefighters picked through the wreckage of the building. The company said in a statement that three months of medicines had been destroyed and that it had suspended all operations.
Shopkeepers and customers say that most people are not panic-buying food in the way that they were in 2022.
“What’s the point?” says Iryna Mesyanzhynova, a 54-year-old woman shopping for groceries at ATB, a low-cost supermarket in Brovary, near some of the burnt-out warehouses. “I have a bit of extra products, like porridge oats, but for the rest – vegetables, fruits – why would I buy them? They will just rot.
“I’m trying to deal with today’s problem,” she says. “I try not to think about the future.”
In a statement to the Guardian, Vysotsky, the agrarian policy and food minister, said that the logistics hubs of all of Ukraine’s leading supermarket chains, including Novus, ATB, Silpo and Fora had been destroyed or significantly damaged in the recent strikes.
“This wave of strikes is the most massive since the beginning of the full-scale invasion,” Vysotsky said.
“If in 2022 the enemy attacked mainly export-agricultural infrastructure, and in the following years destroyed the energy sector, then the attacks of August-September 2026 are a systemic attack on the internal civilian life support system. The enemy is purposefully trying to destroy the logistics that provide Ukrainian cities with food.”
Aside from growing their own food, which many people already do, Ukrainians have few options other than trying to continue as normal. The attacks are “not our first of the war”, says Olena Zhuk, a 36-year-old travel manager shopping at a central Kyiv farmer’s market. “We will survive. We will not die from the hunger.”

Croatia on wheels: the great Adriatic motorhome route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:00:35 UTC
13:00:35 KST

On a 25-day road trip we travel along a coastline of striking contrasts, from Roman cities and Venetian towns to pebble beaches, islands and roads overlooking some of Europe's most spectacular scenery.
Travelling by motorhome lets you move at the pace of the landscape and stop in places that would probably never make it onto a conventional itinerary.
We set off from Rovinj, in the north of the Istrian peninsula, heading for Dubrovnik at the southernmost tip of the country. Along the way you pass a succession of historic towns, national parks, fishing villages, fortresses and islands, with the Adriatic as a constant backdrop.
But travelling Croatia on four wheels is not always straightforward. The coastal road is, in places, narrow and winding. And you cannot park the motorhome just anywhere: you have to rely on campsites and authorised areas, which are sometimes a long way from the historic centres and, on occasions, charge eye-watering prices.
In high season, especially in July and August, the problem only gets worse. That is why spring, early summer or autumn can be a better time to set off on this route.
Istria: Croatia's most Italian side
The journey begins in Rovinj, one of Istria's must-visit towns. Its historic centre of narrow, cobbled streets stands on what was once an island and is dominated by the church of St Euphemia. Colourful facades, the harbour and the small islands scattered just off the coast make the town one of the most recognisable sights on the Croatian Adriatic.
Further south lies Pula, at the southern tip of Istria. The city combines crystal-clear waters with one of Croatia's greatest Roman legacies. Pula Arena, built in the first century AD, is one of the six largest surviving Roman amphitheatres in the world. Today its stands host concerts, festivals and shows, weaving antiquity into contemporary cultural life.
A tour of Pula also takes in the Arch of the Sergii on the main street, the Gate of Hercules and the Kaštel fortress. This 17th-century Venetian castle stands on a hilltop and offers sweeping views over the harbour and the city's rooftops.
Istria stands apart from the rest of the Croatian coast. The heart-shaped peninsula is divided between Croatia, Slovenia and Italy and retains a strong Italian influence. Its green hills, vineyards, olive groves, forests and medieval hill towns have earned it the nickname 'the Tuscany of the Adriatic'. Inland, hilltop towns such as Motovun command the views. However, the lack of suitable facilities for motorhomes forced us to leave it off our itinerary.
From the elegance of Opatija to the lakes of Plitvice
After covering much of Istria, our next stop was Opatija, very different from the rest of the coast. Here grand villas, historic hotels and gardens dominate, all steeped in Austro-Hungarian elegance. For decades it was one of the favourite retreats of the Austro-Hungarian aristocracy, drawn by its spas and mild climate.
The Lungomare, a seafront promenade of around ten kilometres, runs along the coast past villas, small coves and crystal-clear waters. The best way to enjoy it is to stroll slowly and stop in the various little nooks for a swim. It is also worth continuing as far as Volosko, a charming old fishing village.
From Opatija you can continue south along the coastal road beneath the Velebit mountains, in one of the most spectacular stretches of the journey. In our case we chose the motorway to reach Nin, near Zadar. There the scenery changes once again.
The compact historic centre of Nin sits on a tiny island surrounded by lagoons. The town preserves some of the oldest traces of Croatian history and its 9th-century Church of the Holy Cross is one of its main landmarks. It is traditionally known as the smallest cathedral in the world. Nin is also known for its sandy beaches, therapeutic mud and salt pans.
In Zadar, motorhomes have a harder time finding somewhere to park, but the visit is well worth the effort. Amid Roman and medieval remains, the seafront concentrates two of its main attractions: the Sea Organ, which turns the movement of the waves into sound through pipes installed beneath the stone steps, and the Greeting to the Sun, a circle of solar panels that lights up at dusk.
Sunset is Zadar's calling card. The phrase attributed to Alfred Hitchcock, who described it as the most beautiful in the world, has become part of the city's tourist lore. From here we left the blue of the Adriatic behind for a day to plunge into the greenery of Plitvice Lakes National Park.
Its 16 lakes, arranged in tiers at different levels and linked by rivers and waterfalls, form one of Croatia's most breathtaking natural landscapes. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the park is the perfect counterpoint to the coast.
You explore it along footpaths and wooden boardwalks, with electric boats and internal vehicles used on some routes. The great waterfall, Veliki Slap, rises to about 78 metres and is the highest in Croatia. Although the turquoise water and the heat may tempt you in, swimming in the lakes is forbidden.
Šibenik, Trogir and the heart of Dalmatia
Back on the coast we reach Šibenik, a city of white stone, alleyways, staircases and small squares. St James's Cathedral, a World Heritage Site, was built entirely of stone and features an unusual frieze of 71 sculpted human heads, each one different. About 50 kilometres further on lies Trogir, a small island town that feels like Dalmatia in miniature.
The best thing to do is to lose yourself in its narrow stone streets before continuing to Split, the urban heart of the region. Split grew up around the vast palace of the Emperor Diocletian, built more than 1,700 years ago. Today its ancient walls, passageways and chambers form a living city centre where homes, shops, restaurants and cafe terraces all rub shoulders.
Its harbour is also one of the main gateways to the Adriatic islands, with ferries and catamarans to Brač, Hvar, Šolta and Vis. In high season passenger traffic is frantic and ticket prices can be steep. Croatia has more than 1,200 islands, although only around 60 are inhabited. On our trip we visited Korčula, Lopud and Lokrum, the latter just off Dubrovnik's old town and known for its small saltwater lake, the Dead Sea.
The Makarska Riviera and the Pelješac peninsula
Leaving Split, the road once again hugs the Adriatic and one of the most scenic sections of the journey begins: the Makarska Riviera. On one side lies the sea; on the other, the sheer Biokovo mountains. The distance between mountain and coast is minimal, and the bends offer some of the finest viewpoints on the road to Dubrovnik. Before reaching the walled city, we turn off towards the Pelješac peninsula.
Ston is one of its big surprises: a small town protected by a wall that climbs up the hillside, considered one of the most impressive defensive systems in Europe. Mali Ston Bay is famous for its oysters. Eating them freshly opened, raw and with a squeeze of lemon is one of the region's must-try food experiences.
After a stop at Prapratno beach, we continued to Orebić to board a boat to the island of Korčula. Its old town is laid out like a fishbone, a design intended to encourage air circulation and protect the streets from the winds. Korčula claims to be the birthplace of Marco Polo and his figure appears all over the town. Walls, towers and stone buildings recall centuries of Venetian rule.
Before leaving Pelješac, Žuljana offers a quieter reward: crystal-clear waters, mountains and coves with a distinctly Mediterranean feel. One useful tip for enjoying the sea: Croatian beaches are, with few exceptions, pebbly rather than sandy. It is worth bringing mats or airbeds, as locals do, and not forgetting water shoes.
Dubrovnik: The grand finale
The road to Dubrovnik marks the transition from a laid-back Croatia to its main tourist hotspot. After one last bend, the walled city comes into view, one of the most iconic sights on the Adriatic.
In high season thousands of visitors throng Stradun, the main thoroughfare, stopping at every corner to take photos. The city walls, cathedral and narrow lanes of the old town can be seen in a day, although spending three days lets you explore at a gentler pace and add a boat trip to one of the islands. A good option is to explore Dubrovnik at sunset, when many day-trippers have already left.
From Rovinj to Dubrovnik, Croatia changes face time and again. Istria brings its Italian heritage; Dalmatia, its stone-built cities and islands; Plitvice, its forests and waterfalls; and Dubrovnik, the great historical stage facing the sea. That variety, packed into a relatively compact coastline, explains why Croatia now competes with Europe's heavyweight tourist destinations and still offers far more than just sun and sea.

A European Central Bank rate hike is all but certain, the reasoning less so
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
04:00:01 UTC
13:00:01 KST

The European Central Bank is all but certain to raise interest rates on Thursday, with investors pricing the move at near-total probability, but the decision is more awkward than the numbers suggest as inflation is being driven almost entirely by energy with underlying pressures actually easing.
Frankfurt will almost certainly move on Thursday.
Market odds put a quarter-point hike at close to certainty, which would lift the European Central Bank's deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.5%.
What makes this a difficult call is not whether the ECB acts, but why, and whether the reasoning survives contact with the data.
The path here has been compressed as the ECB raised rates on 11 June for the first time in three years, lifting the deposit rate from 2% to 2.25% in response to the energy shock from the Iran war, and then held rates in July while Christine Lagarde pointed hawkishly towards September.
August's inflation figures removed any remaining doubt with eurozone inflation hitting 3.3%, up from 2.9% in July and the highest since September 2023, as energy inflation surged to 14.3% from 10.3%.
The inflation is not spreading
Look beneath the headline inflation and the picture inverts.
Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, actually fell to 2.4% from 2.5%. Services inflation, the component most closely tied to wages and domestic demand, dropped to 3% from 3.3%.
In other words, there is still little evidence that expensive energy is feeding through into everything else. That is what economists mean by "second-round effects", and their absence is the strongest argument against tightening.
The ECB's own research also supports the distinction.
In a paper published on Tuesday, ECB economists found that adverse energy supply factors, driven by geopolitical tensions, accounted for around 90% of the rise in energy inflation between January and May.
"This time the energy supply shock dominates, while demand and public policy stimulus have minor roles," the economists wrote, adding that "these differences are key to explaining why monetary policy responses differ."
The 2021-22 surge, by contrast, came from "a combination of large and unprecedented supply and demand-side factors," which is why the ECB then "raised interest rates forcefully and persistently" rather than gradually.
The national spread across the EU further underlines how uneven this is.
August inflation ran at 4.5% in Spain, 2.9% in Germany and 2.7% in France, three economies facing the same energy shock with very different results, all governed by one interest rate.
Economic growth is the other complication.
The eurozone has proved more resilient than expected, which ING attributes partly to luck, partly to Asian competitors suffering more from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and partly to fiscal stimulus. However, resilience does not mean the growth could not, or should not, accelerate.
ING characterises Thursday's expected move as "another insurance rate hike", or "a dovish rate hike," noting that even at 2.5% the deposit rate sits within the range the ECB itself considers neutral.
Going further would mean deciding restrictive policy is required, which would be a different judgement entirely.
Everyone is looking to hike at the same time
The ECB is not acting alone, and that matters for the euro.
The Federal Reserve meets on 15 and 16 September, with Chair Kevin Warsh having used his first Jackson Hole address to argue that financial conditions are not restrictive and underlying inflation has not improved.
Investors had put the odds of a US hike at roughly one in three before those remarks, but now price a 60% chance the Fed hikes the target range from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4%.
The Bank of Japan follows on 17 and 18 September, with markets pricing an 80% to 90% chance of a move to 1.25%.
On the other hand, the Bank of England is expected to hold rates at 3.75% on 17 September as it currently maintains a much higher interest rate than the rest.
If the Fed were to hike while the ECB held, the dollar would strengthen against the euro and that would cut both ways for Frankfurt.
A weaker euro makes European exports more competitive, but it also makes imports dearer, and since oil and gas are priced in dollars, it would push up precisely the energy costs driving the inflation problem in the first place.
Overall, we can assume a September rate hike is a done deal for the ECB but we can also project that it won't solve the central bank's current dilemma of raising borrowing costs against an inflation it cannot reach, while withdrawing support an economy could still use.
