First Overseas-Bound F-15EX Departs Boeing, Heading to Oregon First
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:08:04 UTC
06:08:04 KST

Editor’s Note: This article has been updated to include a comment from Boeing.
After months of delays from a factory strike, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to Portland, Ore.
“This is an important next step toward bringing the F-15EX home to Kadena,” Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, 18th Wing commander, said in a release. “Our team is ready to welcome the F-15EX, and this is another milestone that brings us closer to putting this capability in the hands of the Airmen who will fly, maintain and employ it from Japan.”
The F-15EX is the first Eagle II jet to feature the 18th Wing’s historic, distinctive “ZZ” tail flash and will actually arrive at Kadena sometime in fiscal 2027, which begins Oct. 1.
Spokespeople for Headquartes Air Force, the 18th Wing, and the Air National Guard did not immediately respond to queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine on Sept. 8.
Boeing spokesman Josh Roth told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the F-15EX-22 “was delivered with the baseline mission computing, communications, and sensor capabilities that provide the foundation for manned-unmanned teaming and future Collaborative Combat Aircraft integration.” He deferred additional questions to the Air Force.
This new jet is the first of 36 F-15EXs to be stationed at Kadena. The fighter, often described as halfway between fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft, will help usher in a new era in U.S. airpower within the first island chain surrounding China
The transition to the EX has been a long time coming for Kadena—the Air Force started retiring the base’s legacy F-15C/Ds in 2022 and confirmed plans to replace them with the F-15EX in 2024. The first jet was supposed to arrive in spring 2026, but a lengthy strike at the Boeing plant in St. Louis late last year slowed production until this Aug. 28 delivery.
The new F-15EX’s stopover in Oregon isn’t surprising—the Oregon Air National Guard was the first Air Force location with combat-coded F-15EXs at its Portland ANG Base. The base will conduct the final systems integration, add software updates, and other technical preparations before the aircraft can go to Okinawa.
In the interim, the Air Force has rotated F-16, F-15, F-22, and F-35 squadrons through Kadena to keep the tactical fighter presence steady at a key strategic base fewer than 400 miles from Taiwan.
Those rotational forces haven’t always matched the capabilities the F-15EX will bring. Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on the extended tour of aging F-16Cs out of the Colorado Air National Guard’s 120th Fighter Squadron, which ran from January through June. They brought a dozen fighters.
Both the squadron commander and the head of its parent wing, the 140th Wing, said in a call with the media on Sept. 3 that while the platform could keep up with fifth-gen fighters in the region, the pilots and maintenance crews were pushing the limits of the more than 30-year-old airframe
The permanent stationing of the F-15EX will “enhance Kadena’s ability to generate ready combat airpower while providing opportunities to train and integrate alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and other allies and partners,” according to the release.
The 18th Wing trains alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-15s at Naha Air Base in bilateral exercises and other training, according to the release.
Pacific Air Forces has been slowly phasing out its oldest fighters and introducing more modern jets in recent years. In addition to Kadena’s F-15s, the Air Force has also recently withdrawn the A-10s at Osan Air Base, South Korea.
The 35th Fighter Wing at Misawa Air Base, Japan, meanwhile, is slated to get 48 fifth-gen F-35 Lightning IIs, but only a trickle had arrived as of April. The wing transferred its F-16s to Osan last year.
The Air Force publicly confirmed delays in getting the F-15EX to Kadena in February.
The Eagle II is the first of its kind to include digital fly-by-wire flight controls, a large-area display glass cockpit with a touchscreen interface, an APG-82 Active Electronically Scanned Array radar, a Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System, and an Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System.
The jet flies faster and farther, carries a heavier payload than its F-15 predecessors, and has two additional weapons stations.

Hundreds of flights delayed, cancelled after UK air traffic control glitch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:07:33 UTC
06:07:33 KST

UK travellers face fresh chaos as more flights cancelled after glitch
Air traffic control provider NATS under scrutiny after technical fault disrupts UK air traffic.
UK travellers faced fresh travel chaos on Wednesday as more than 150 flights were scrapped nationwide, while air traffic control service scrambled to recover from a technical glitch at the National Air Traffic Services (NATS).
According to aircraft tracking platform FlightRadar24, at least 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday have been cancelled already, in addition to more than 1,300 flight cancellations to and from UK airports the previous day.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2UK air traffic issue fixed but flights remain affected
- list 2 of 2Hundreds of UK flights disrupted by air traffic control glitch
The IT malfunction on Tuesday happened three years after a flight-plan processing failure at NATS caused even more widespread disruption.
Nearly all the latest affected flights were at Britain’s busiest airport Heathrow in London, FlightRadar24 wrote on X.
NATS said it was still working to resolve disruption following a “system issue”.
“This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover,” it said in an X post late on Tuesday.
In an earlier post, NATS apologised to frustrated passengers in departure halls across the UK and said a problem with its flight data processing system had been fixed.
“Recovery from today’s system issue has taken longer than we had hoped. Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights,” it said.
Cancellations and delays
Airlines called for the resignation of Martin Rolfe, the CEO of NATS, questioned whether the UK’s air traffic control system was fit for purpose and urged the UK government to intervene.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been affected by delays of up to eight hours and that it had cancelled more than 50 flights.
In a video posted on X, Ryanair’s Chief Operations Officer Neal McMahon said “despite promises, reports and assurances that they would fix the systems, once again NATS, under Martin Rolfe’s leadership have failed UK travellers and have failed airlines which are trying to get their passengers to and from the UK”.
Aviation analyst John Strickland said the consequences of even a relatively short outage can be severe because delays quickly cascade through tightly scheduled airline networks.
“A few hours of outage may on the face of it sound limited but the impact is enormous when a substantial number of airports across the UK are affected,” Strickland said.
Britain’s aviation regulator said it would expect NATS to share a full report on Tuesday’s system failure.
The UK Civil Aviation Authority, the country’s independent aviation regulator, said it would then consider whether any reforms are needed to secure the reliability of the UK’s air traffic control system.

Santos chief calls for major changes to proposed national domestic gas reservation
Santos chief executive Kevin Gallagher used his address at the National Press Club to call for major changes to the proposed national domestic gas reservation plan.
Under the proposal, the federal government wants gas producers to supply the equivalent of 20 per cent of their exports to the local market every year.
Crucially, the government said exporters should be required to sell that amount of gas and not just simply offer it.
But Gallagher said forcing such a condition could backfire by oversupplying the market in the short term and scaring away investment in new supplies in the long term.
He says the government should instead follow the lead of Western Australia, where gas producers are only required to offer gas under that state's reservation policy.
"The practical solution here is to replace the must-sell provision with must-offer on commercial terms, the same as the Western Australian reservation," he said.
"If gas is not able to be sold on term contracts, then it should be made available on domestic spot hubs."
According to Gallagher, it was wrong to suggest Australia was facing gas shortages or a price crisis.
He said the country had "enormous" reserves under the ground but had simply failed in recent times to exploit them.
And while he said it was imperative the government avoid applying a reservation policy to existing long-term contracts with buyers overseas, it was a different story for new fields such as the Beetaloo Basin in the Northern Territory.
"Australians rightly expect their own needs to be met before we export gas overseas," he said.
"But it is not true that east coast gas supply issues were caused by Queensland's LNG export industry, nor that there is an imminent supply or price crisis.
"I have publicly supported domestic reservation as part of [the Beetaloo's] development since 2018.
"And the time to put a reservation policy in place is now before billions of dollars are invested."
Santos chief says he's living 'rent free' in the heads of his competitors
With the east coast gas export industry bracing itself for a federal reservation scheme, the boss of Santos has turned to mind games.
Kevin Gallagher used his address to the National Press Club today to taunt his rivals in the Queensland LNG industry.
Santos operates the Gladstone LNG (GLNG) project, one of three giant gas export plants built on Curtis Island, about 530km north of Brisbane.
Alongside GLNG are the Australian-Pacific LNG plant operated by Origin and ConocoPhillips, and Queensland Curtis LNG, run by Shell.
Long-running tensions between the competitors have spilled into the public domain in recent days amid frustration with Santos and GLNG.
At the heart of those frustrations are GLNG's historic and consistent depletion of domestic east coast gas supplies for export to customers in Asia.
Dan Clark, the head of Australian-Pacific LNG, this week took the extraordinary step of effectively blaming GLNG for driving up prices in the past.
In an opinion piece published in The Australian, Clark said it was no coincidence that domestic gas prices had "split" from the international market and fallen after "one LNG exporter chose to reduce" local purchases.
Gallagher hit back at those remarks today.
"It would appear that I'm living rent-free in a few of the heads of our competitors around Gladstone at this point in time," Gallagher said.
📷 Today's QT in pictures
Wong questioned on 'unintended consequences' of further Israel sanctions
The foreign minister has been questioned on the government's decision not to join the UK, France and Canada in imposing further sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank during Senate question time.
Yesterday Penny Wong confirmed to the Senate that Australia won't be joining the ban on imports from the settlements, which are considered illegal under international law, in part due to the risk of "unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis".
But she flagged that Australia is working on further action on the issue of illegal settlements alongside other countries.
Today independent senator Lidia Thorpe asked which unintended consequences the government was concerned about.
"We've been clear that the Netanyahu government's actions in the West Bank, the rapid expansion of settlements, the proposed E1 settler development and flagrant settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two state solution," Wong said.
"And that remains the only path to enduring peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians. And that is why with international partners we recognised the state of Palestine, it is why we are strengthening the institutional foundations of the state.
"Yesterday I announced we are continuing to pursue further targeted measures in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence."
And that's the end of Question Time!
Nationals frontbencher Michael McCormack has stepped up to ask a question just as the PM moves to wind down Question Time.
"If it is about Grayndler, they'll get an extra one, but I'm told it's not. I'm quite happy to tell my electorate what a good local member they have, Mr Speaker," Albanese says.
A little argy-bargy ensues before the PM finally moves to bring questions without notice to an end for today, until tomorrow afternoon.
Time to get on with the rest of the day!
Chaney questions A-G on government automated decision-making
Independent MP Kate Chaney is up next and has asked the attorney-general when Labor will legislate a framework around automation in government.
"When will you introduce a legislative framework for automated decision-making that includes safeguards, human override and transparency?" Chaney asks.
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland says Labor is developing a whole-of-government framework for automated decision-making that will implement recommendations of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme.
"I can assure the member and the House that the government is taking a careful and methodical approach to the development of the ADM [automated decision-making] framework," Rowland says.
"The Albanese government's approach is focused on delivery in the future, enabling Australians to adopt new technologies responsibly, deliver high quality services more efficiently, and prevent the systemic failures identified in the Robodebt royal commission."
Coalition 'led by the nose' by One Nation on tobacco, Butler says
Liberal MP Mary Aldred asks if the prime minister will cut the tobacco excise, noting Anthony Albanese has so far declined to do so.
Health Minister Mark Butler takes this one instead. He claims that under the Coalition, the excise was raised by 215 per cent and that not a cent was spent on compliance or public health campaigns.
The Labor frontbencher repeats much of the same lines as the government has all week: this is a compliance and law enforcement issue.
"Of course we are open to other sensible ideas about how we can fight organised crime while not prejudicing our most important public health campaign," he says.
"But this is the problem I have with the announcements that One Nation first made and then, sure enough led by the nose, the Coalition followed."
Housing minister asks Treasury to draw up definitions of affordable housing
Independent MP Nicolette Boele has asked the treasurer whether Labor will back a definition of affordable housing to make sure new homes go to people who need them.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the housing minister has asked Treasury to do work on affordable housing definitions.
He says that will include looking at the different definitions and frameworks that currently operate across Australia.
"We do think that's an important objective. Minister [Clare] O'Neil is doing that work with state housing ministers and I undertake to keep the honourable member informed of our progress as that work continues," Chalmers says.
"We're coming at this housing challenge from every single responsible angle."
Coalition continues pressure on Albanese over golf club grant
Nationals deputy Darren Chester notes that a full membership to the golf club Anthony Albanese is an honorary member of would set someone back $1,100.
"Now, given the value of his honorary membership exceeds the gift declaration threshold, will he correct the record and update his register of interests today?" he asks.
Albanese repeats he was given the membership back in 2012 and it was a social club membership. He says that costs $5 for two years.
"I don't play golf ... I leave that to my deputy prime minister [Richard Marles] who is a very good golfer," he says.
Albanese says he used to walk his dog at the club and he attended a birthday party there for Louis the Cavoodle and dogs on the fairway.
Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan tries to raise a point of relevance, asking for Albanese to address whether he'll update his register of interests.
Albanese again says he wasn't aware of the membership.
"If you're a good local member a whole lot of people will give you honorary memberships of things," he says.
Chris Bowen calls allegation of fraud in cheaper home batter scheme a 'lie'
Nationals MP Alison Penfold has asked on what date the minister was made aware of alleged fraud impacting the federal government's cheaper home battery program.
Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen hasn't initially answered the question, saying he created a committee that informed him of the scheme's progress and "all issues".
"Complaints per thousand installations have halved since this came in," Bowen says.
Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan has stepped up on a point of order, asking what date the minister was made aware of the allegations.
Speaker Milton Dick agrees with Tehan's point and asks the minister to remain directly relevant to the question.
Bowen says he started receiving updates on the implementation of the program on July 1, 2025, and that allegations of fraud are a "lie".
"I started receiving updates on the implement aches of the program on 1 July 2025 and have received them regularly. Those updates have shown the the manager of opposition's claims of systemic fraud are not true, are a lie," Bowen says.
Bowen asked if he can guarantee safety in home battery installations
Liberal frontbencher Dan Tehan is up next, asking the energy minister if he can guarantee all the batteries installed under the Cheaper Home Batteries program have been installed safely.
Chris Bowen says the scheme has "one of the most rigorous schemes for compliance which has been operating under governments of both persuasions".
"[It] has ensured the safe rollout of more than four million rooftop solar installations or more than half a million cheaper home battery installations," he says.
Tehan tries to raise a point of order but is promptly shut down by Speaker Milton Dick.
Bowen continues:
"I think every Australian ... knows that every electrical instrument, every electrical application comes with risk," he says.
He says that while it's a government scheme, the private sector, some 12,000 installers, are the ones doing the work.
"I've got to say these are highly credentialled, well qualified, hardworking Australians."

Cuba says it will never be colony after Trump posts map with island under US colors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:05:23 UTC
06:05:23 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel said Tuesday that the island nation "will never again" be a colony of any "empire" after US President Donald Trump published a map depicting it and other territories under the US flag.
"Cuba knows well the meaning of having been a colony and neocolony of two empires," Diaz-Canel wrote on US social media company X, without explicitly referring to Trump's publication.
"The blood that has been shed for our independence, sovereignty and self-determination will not have been in vain, and we will defend them to the last consequences," he added.
Trump published the map Monday on his Truth Social platform. The image shows the colors of the US flag covering Mexico, Canada, Cuba, Greenland, Iceland and parts of the Caribbean and Central America.
Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez referred to the publication, responding sarcastically that the US government would leave its citizens "geographically disoriented."
"Soon they will not know in which gulf, lake, building, country, continent or planet they are," Rodriguez wrote in a social media post.
The Cuban statements come as relations between Havana and Washington face their highest tensions in decades.
The Trump administration has pursued a policy of "maximum pressure" against Cuba since the beginning of 2026, including an oil blockade and secondary sanctions introduced in May that have deterred foreign companies from operating on the island.
Washington has also maintained the possibility of military intervention as a source of concern for the Cuban government.
Rodriguez said Monday that the US economic embargo cost Cuba $8.08 billion between March 2025 and February 2026, the highest recorded for 12 months, and 7% more than the previous year.
He described Washington's measures as a "cruel collective punishment" against the Cuban population.
Cuba's economy has also been severely affected by an energy crisis. The country's economy contracted 15% between 2020 and 2025, while independent forecasts project an additional contraction of up to 10.3% this year.

Accelerating diversification: Canada seeks economic sovereignty amid Trump's 'nonsensical' posturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
21:02:16 UTC
06:02:16 KST

Accelerating diversification: Canada seeks economic sovereignty amid Trump's 'nonsensical' posturing
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Jean Simard, President and CEO of the Aluminum Association of Canada. According to Simard, the US-Canada aluminum dispute is not your conventional disagreement over trade, but rather a 'Trump posture that makes no sense". As American industrial demand substantially exceeds domestic production capacity, tariffs will do nothing to reduce Canadian aluminum from the US market. Protectionism does not eliminate interdependence, explains Simard, it makes that interdependence considerably more expensive.
More significantly, however, he interprets the conflict as an accelerator of structural change within Canada. External pressure from Washington is, in his account, encouraging Canada to reduce internal trade barriers, diversify export relationships, protect strategically important industries and research capacity, and deepen its relationship with Europe. And this now rises to the level of economic sovereignty and geopolitical realignment.
Rather than forcing Canada to submit to US demands, sustained economic pressure may now be strengthening domestic support for full-on resistance and diversifying away from US dependence. His striking assertion that Canada is “making a new country out of our country” captures this broader thesis: the trade war is damaging and disruptive, but he sees it simultaneously as an opportunity to reconstruct Canada’s economic model and embrace new partnerships in other corners of the globe .
Europe occupies a particularly important place in this transformation and has the potential to move “from being a bystander to being a full actor”. Simard highlights the dispute as part of a larger contest over whether US allies will respond individually to American economic coercion or develop greater collective strategic autonomy.

Ukraine contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles from allies, defence chief says
KYIV - Ukraine is contracting a supply of around 1,000 missiles for US-designed Patriot air-defence systems with the help of allies and through a European Union loan, Kyiv’s defence minister said on Sept 8.
Speaking at a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, Yevhenii Khmara also said that the majority of the missiles would only be shipped in the coming years, and called for more urgent aid.
In comments posted later by the Defence Ministry, Khmara said Ukraine was asking its Western partners to provide more air defence missiles from their stocks in exchange for improvements in missile performance under contracts signed with Kyiv.
He said Ukraine was being hindered by a shortfall of US$27 billion (S$34 billion) in financing for drone supplies.
The ministry’s summary of the meeting said Khmara had presented a plan for Ukraine’s conduct of the war that was already being implemented along with a list of what Kyiv considered to be the biggest threats posed by Moscow.
Khmara said Russia was making no strategic gains along the 1,200km front line, but Moscow was making up for its battlefield failures with “terror against Ukrainians”.
Russia resumed its near-constant drone and missile attacks on Kyiv on Sept 8 after a brief halt for the visit of US peace negotiators.
Officials said five people were killed in the capital along with others in various regions.
NATO secretary-general Mark Rutte told the meeting that Ukraine’s allies had no choice but to boost their support to enable Kyiv “to seize the opportunities it is creating now across all fronts and to defend itself in the skies”. REUTERS

Kallas stated that the threat to the Baltic countries has &quot;completely changed&quot; following the revision of NATO plans
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Kallas stated that the threat to the Baltic countries has "completely changed" following the revision of NATO plans
Kyiv • UNN
Kaja Kallas said that NATO had abandoned plans for the temporary loss of Baltic territory and strengthened the region's defense. She also warned about Russia's shadow war.
The security situation of the Baltic countries has changed significantly compared with 2022, when NATO’s defense plans at the time envisaged the possibility of temporarily losing territory in the event of an attack. The Alliance abandoned this approach and strengthened the region’s defense, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas said in an interview with LRT, reports UNN.
Details
Kallas recalled that before the 2022 NATO summit, there was a concept according to which, if territories were seized, the allies would liberate them later. According to her, Ukraine’s experience demonstrated the unacceptability of such a scenario.
This has completely changed. At that time, before the 2022 NATO summit, there was a plan based on a remote concept: if territories were seized, they would only be liberated later. Using Ukraine as an example, we saw that such a plan cannot exist
NATO changed its approach to the defense of the Baltic region
According to Kallas, since then the Alliance has reviewed its defense plans, and its members have significantly increased investments in military capabilities. This has made the Baltic region much better prepared for possible aggression, although work to strengthen its defense has not yet been completed.
She also said that there are currently no signs of a possible withdrawal of U.S. troops from the region. According to Kallas, their presence remains an important deterrent to Russia. At the same time, European states must continue strengthening their own contribution to NATO.
Kallas separately warned that Russia is already waging a "shadow war" against Europe, which she said includes sabotage, cyberattacks, and attempts to destabilize European societies.
Speaking about negotiations concerning Ukraine, Kallas said that she currently sees no signs of Moscow’s serious readiness for peace. In her view, the first such signal should be the cessation of Russian attacks on civilians.

Turkish Airlines carried 64 million passengers in the first eight months of 2026, up 5.4% from the same period last year, according to date released on Tuesday.
The flag carrier said in a filing with Türkiye’s Public Disclosure Platform (KAP) that the number of international passengers increased 6.1% year-on-year to 41.8 million, while domestic passenger traffic rose 4.3% to 22.2 million.

International passenger numbers rose 5% to 6.4 million, while domestic passenger traffic increased 6.8% to 3.6 million.
The carrier’s passenger load factor reached 88% in August, up from 86.6% a year earlier.
The international load factor was 87.6%, while the domestic load factor stood at 91.3%.

ChatGPT 6 claims to have solved one of the millennium’s major mathematical mysteries
Kyiv • UNN
OpenAI said that 10,000 AI agents created a proof of the Navier–Stokes problem in 88 hours. Mathematicians have not yet verified it.
OpenAI stated that its new ChatGPT 6 Astra model had found a solution to the Navier–Stokes problem—one of the 7 famous "Millennium Problems." The proposed proof has not yet been confirmed by the mathematical community, Yle reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the company, around 10,000 AI agents worked on the problem simultaneously. They needed 88 hours to formulate the proposed mathematical proof.
The issue concerns the existence and smoothness of solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations, which describe the motion of liquids and gases—in particular, water and air. It remains one of the most famous unsolved problems in modern mathematics.
A $1 million prize is offered for a correct solution
The Navier–Stokes problem is included among the 7 "Millennium Problems" compiled by the Clay Mathematics Institute in the early 2000s. A $1 million prize is offered for solving each of them.
ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok simultaneously experienced a major outage03.09.26, 18:15 • 5166 views
At present, only one of the 7 problems has officially been recognized as solved. Therefore, if OpenAI's proposed proof passes independent verification and is accepted by the mathematical community, it will constitute the solution of another "Millennium Problem."
At the same time, the Clay Institute has not yet recognized the proposed AI proof. Thus, OpenAI's statement currently remains the company's own claim, and the final conclusion will depend on mathematicians' review.

Brazil Supreme Court rift deepens as justice suspends federal police chief
Allegations of misconduct between two justices threaten to pull court into political battles ahead of upcoming election.
Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca has ordered the suspension of federal police chief Andrei Rodrigues and the force’s intelligence chief Leandro Almada amid growing divisions that have tested the credibility of the country’s highest court.
The suspensions were announced on Tuesday. Mendonca, appointed by former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, has accused Rodrigues and Almada of producing six illegal reports on the activities of justices.

The move was backed by a majority on one of the high court’s five-member panels.
But it is likely to be challenged by the government, possibly pulling the administration of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva into a political battle ahead of October’s presidential election.
“Investigating possible evidence of crimes is correct,” Institutional Relations Minister Jose Guimaraes, a top aide to Lula, said in response to the decision on social media. “But this measure smells electoral to me. That cannot happen.”
Polls show Lula and Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, in a tight race ahead of the first round of voting on October 4.
The Supreme Court has been roiled by mutual accusations of wrongdoing between Justice Alexandre de Moraes, appointed under centre-right President Michel Temer, and Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee.
De Moraes has become a prominent target of right-wing criticism, particularly after he oversaw the case against Jair Bolsonaro for plotting a coup after the 2022 election.

The Vorcaro corruption scandal has widened to include powerful political figures on both the left and right.
Vorcaro was arrested in 2025 for allegedly overseeing one of the largest bank fraud schemes in the history of Brazil, leaving billions in owed money.
Flavio Bolsonaro has also faced scrutiny for his ties with Vorcaro, after he approached the banker for assistance in funding a film about his father. Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence.
The right-wing senator used Tuesday’s suspension to push his claim that the prosecution of his father was a political “witch-hunt”. The Federal Police had recommended charges be brought against the elder Bolsonaro in November 2024.
“Lula’s special group in the Federal Police officially unmasked,” Senator Bolsonaro wrote in a social media post. “May the honourable and glorious Federal Police regain its autonomy to go after criminals, and not Lula’s political adversaries.”
William Marcel Murad, the federal police’s executive director, released a statement saying that Rodrigues has the agency’s “full confidence” and that agents “will not be shaken by attacks”.

What we know about the UK's fresh Israel sanctions, and why Australia won't follow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:40:25 UTC
05:40:25 KST

IN BRIEF
- The UK, France and Canada have announced trade restrictions with Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
- The settlements are widely considered illegal under international law, which Israel disputes.
Israel will close the British consulate in East Jerusalem after the United Kingdom, France and Canada announced plans to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank — something Australia has ruled out.
Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa'ar said the UK will no longer participate in a US-led coordination mission for Gaza while some British officials and nationals — including former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn — would be banned from entering the country.
"The British move is morally distorted, and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process," he said.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has ruled out Australian support for a similar blanket ban, saying it may have unintended consequences, but has flagged a raft of new sanctions against Israel is in the works.
Sa'ar said Israel's response had been coordinated with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The multilateral trade action is the latest to target Israel's settlement policy and underscores the country's growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies.
The UK, Canada, and France were joined by 10 other foreign ministers from countries including Denmark, Norway, Poland, Spain and Sweden in a statement reaffirming support for a negotiated two-state settlement — a Palestinian state co-existing peacefully alongside Israel.
International concern is mounting over the recent rise in settlement expansion and violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, territory traditionally inhabited by Arab communities.
"Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace," the statement read.
Australia plans new sanctions
Wong has warned that Netanyahu is at risk of "extinguishing the possibility" of a two-state solution as her government plans its own sanctions package.
"I can announce Australia is pursuing further targeted measures in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence," Wong said during a speech in the Senate on Tuesday.
"Australia is not, at this time, pursuing a blanket-style import ban. We have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis, and we will continue to work with partners to protect the prospects of a two-state solution."
She noted that Australia "continues to call on Israel to take urgent steps to address the situation on the ground", which includes stopping settlers "destroying properties, displacing families and beating, torturing, sexually assaulting and killing Palestinians".
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also said that Australia's position on the Middle East remains the same.
"I have made clear on a number of occasions — we support a two-state solution in the Middle East. We think that is important for both Israelis and Palestinians to be able to live in peace and security," he said.
Why did the UK issue an import ban?
UK foreign minister Ed Miliband said the UK could no longer simply "call out" injustice and suffering, but had to act to oppose the expansion of settlements, which he said threatened the viability of a Palestinian state.
The former Labour leader, who was appointed to the role in July, added that the UK believes the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians is happening in areas of the West Bank.
"Today we refuse to be bystanders to further suffering and to the destruction of the two-state solution," Miliband said.
Sa'ar described the comments about ethnic cleansing as "outrageous lies" while Israeli President Isaac Herzog accused the UK of interfering in Israel's upcoming elections, due in late October.
Canadian foreign minister Anita Anand voiced her country's long-held support for a two-state solution in announcing the ban on West Bank imports.
"A two-state solution is the way forward for long-term peace that also addresses Israel's legitimate security concerns," she said. "Illegal settlements in the West Bank significantly undermine these objectives."
The United Nations, Palestinians and most countries regard settlements as illegal under international law. Israel disputes this.
The Reuters news agency published a report on Tuesday showing Israel's government is financing some of the West Bank's most radical settlers, who use illegal outpost farms to displace Palestinians.
In introducing its ban, France cited the "frenzied expansion" of settlements there and a "flare-up of violence" as the reasons for taking action.
However, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the sanctions could destabilise the West Bank and that Washington would not support a block on imports.
What products come from the West Bank?
Direct exports from Palestinian territories — comprising the West Bank and Gaza — to Australia are minimal, with economic analytics firm ISI Markets valuing Palestinian trade to the Oceania region at less than $415,000 per year in 2017.
Most commercial goods originating in the West Bank are routed through Israeli infrastructure and customs, making precise sourcing difficult.
West Bank settlements mainly produce agricultural products, including dates, citrus fruits, herbs and wine, which make up a small fraction of Israel's total exports.
Israel was Australia's 49th largest two-way economic partner in 2023, with goods valued at approximately $1.4 billion traded between them. Industrial machinery, plastics, medical and electronic devices are Australia's main imports.
Given the small volume of exports from the settlements, the trade bans are largely symbolic and will not dent larger bilateral trade flows.
Still, they are part of wider efforts to reinforce support for the two-state solution — announced as Israel revealed plans for 1,000 new West Bank homes on Tuesday.

Hungary Blocks Ukraine's EU Accession Clusters for Fourth Time, Withholds Its Demands

Hungary has blocked the opening of the EU accession negotiating clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine, marking the fourth such refusal, as Kyiv said Budapest has yet to specify its demands in exchange for lifting its objection.
The Council of the EU’s Working Party on Enlargement (COELA) failed to approve the screening results for Ukraine on Tuesday, Sept. 8. Citing its own sources, Ukrainska Pravda reported that EU diplomats were unable to persuade Hungary to change its position.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are practically negotiating with our Hungarian partners with the EU every day to avoid artificial delays in the negotiation process,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told European Pravda, speaking separately at a Foreign Ministry briefing earlier Tuesday.
Moldova’s accession caught in the same dispute
The move follows a previous refusal on Sept. 1, when Hungary offered to lift its objection only if Kyiv demonstrated progress in protecting the rights of the country’s Hungarian minority in the Transcarpathia region.
However, the legislative steps Ukraine is expected to take remain unspecified.
The blockage also affects Moldova, as the two countries’ processes are directly intertwined.
In July, Hungary indicated that it was prepared to approve the screening results for Moldova’s cluster 3, but other EU member states, including Ireland – which holds the Council presidency – opposed separating Moldova’s accession path from Ukraine’s, meaning no decision was reached for either country, as all decisions require unanimity from all 27 EU member states.
Russian Strikes Kill 2 in Dnipropetrovsk, Wound Over a Dozen Across Kharkiv, Chernihiv Regions
Ministry cites influence of former Hungarian government
According to Tykhyi, Hungary’s previous government, led by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, played a role in creating recent obstacles to Kyiv’s EU accession.
“For 17 months, the government of Viktor Orbán blocked the opening of clusters, although Ukraine has fulfilled all the conditions for this,” Tykhyi said.
“But even having lost power, Orbán’s team continues to disrupt the normalization of Hungary’s relations with Ukraine,” he continued.
Though Hungary previously also blocked technical work on clusters 2 through 6 for Ukraine, it later lifted its objection to Cluster 6, covering foreign and security policy, trade policy, and relations with third countries.
Cluster 2 covers the EU internal market, while Cluster 3 covers competitiveness and inclusive growth.
After the EU opened the first negotiating Cluster 1 – Fundamentals – for Ukraine and Moldova on June 15, Budapest delayed a joint EU letter concerning the two countries’ accession bids, blocking a key procedural step by opposing a joint letter to EU institutions that requires unanimous approval.
During his tenure, Orbán repeatedly cited concerns over the rights of the Hungarian minority as a reason Hungary had delayed opening the first negotiation cluster.
Current Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar appeared to take a detour from Orbán’s approach, ultimately sealing what he called a “historic agreement” with Ukraine earlier in June, formally securing the educational, cultural, linguistic and political rights of ethnic Hungarian communities in the Transcarpathia region.
“In just a few weeks, we have succeeded in resolving an issue that the Orbán government was unable to address in ten years,” Magyar said.
However, despite Magyar’s agreement with Kyiv on minority rights, that deal has not proven sufficient, as Hungary continues blocking Ukraine’s EU accession bid.

how do california architects design a house to live with wildfire?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:35:41 UTC
05:35:41 KST

learning to live with fire
In the days after the Palisades and Eaton fires swept through Los Angeles in January 2025, some of the strangest photographs were of the houses still standing. A home built by Chansen Architecture in 2024 sat almost untouched beside burned lots in Pacific Palisades. In Malibu, a concrete beachfront house remained above a field of debris.
Together, the two fires destroyed more than 16,000 structures, which made these isolated survivors look almost impossible. They were quickly treated as examples of architecture beating fire, though their survival came down to a far messier combination of design, wind direction and firefighting.
Still, look closely at the houses that survived and certain details begin to repeat. Metal roofs replace shingles, and roof edges become simpler. Concrete or plaster appears where timber siding might once have been, and vegetation pulls away from the facade. For architects working across California, these choices are becoming part of the house from the first sketch. This means that wildfire is entering the brief as something the building may actually encounter.
image via @ChasenGreg
wildfire usually arrives as something very small
Although the image of a wildfire approaching a house tends to involve a wall of flame, buildings often ignite in a much subtler way. Wind carries burning embers far ahead of the fire front, where they can collect against a wall or slip through a vent and begin burning the house from within. The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety estimates that embers are responsible for up to 90 percent of home ignitions during wildfires. NIST similarly identifies embers as the source of the majority of structural losses in wildland-urban fires.
That changes the scale of the architectural problem. A massive concrete wall can withstand heat, yet a small opening nearby may leave the building vulnerable. Roof geometries suddenly have consequences beyond their appearance. The same goes for the edge where a deck meets the house or the strip of planting immediately outside a window.
CAL FIRE now advises homeowners to close gaps at eaves and use ember-resistant vents, among other forms of home hardening. California has also consolidated its wildfire construction requirements into a dedicated Wildland-Urban Interface Code, which went into effect at the beginning of 2026. The house designed for wildfire starts to look slightly different because its weakest points are being drawn differently.
Pine Flat Residence, Faulkner Architects, Healdsburg, California, 2025 | image ©Joe Fletcher
a timber house with concrete underneath
Mork-Ulnes Architects‘ Frame House in Sonoma makes the idea unusually easy to see. The studio had already built three small concrete guesthouses on the property when the Nuns Fire tore through the area in 2017. The family’s main residence was badly damaged while the concrete structures survived. When the owners returned to Mork-Ulnes for a replacement house, fire resistance was already written into the project by experience.
The new home is organized around an exposed concrete structure with metal-clad windows and noncombustible roofing. Yet the architects resisted turning it into a concrete bunker. Western red cedar panels sit over parts of the shell to give the house the warmth of the timber buildings common across Northern California. Casper Mork-Ulnes describes the cedar as a ‘sacrificial layer of wood.’ In a fire, that outer skin can be lost while the concrete structure behind it offers another line of defense.
It is a compelling way to think about a house. Some pieces are permanent, while other cosmetic layers are allowed to be vulnerable. Fire resistance here comes from accepting that a building may have to lose part of itself.
Frame House, Mork Ulnes Architects, Sonoma, California, 2022 | image © Bruce Damonte
a roof becomes a fire blanket
Further south in Topanga, 4/Way House by Deegan-Day Design & Architecture turns the same concern into a much more expressive form. The site sits along Skyhawk Lane in the Santa Monica Mountains, an area hit by the devastating Old Topanga Fire in 1993. Architect Joe Day and Nina Hachigian bought the land later that decade, and over the long process of designing and constructing the house, fire eventually became central to how they understood the site.
A web of steel trusses supports a faceted standing-seam zinc surface that folds across the roof and down parts of the building. Day calls it a ‘fire blanket.’ Around the house, terraces create outdoor rooms while doubling as buffers between the building and surrounding vegetation. A concrete retaining structure brings another durable layer underneath.
Deegan-Day also considered what would happen beyond the property itself. Because the house sits below other homes on the ridge, its design asked how the site could give firefighters somewhere to work and potentially help protect structures uphill. The wildfire house begins to operate at the scale of the street.
4/Way House, Deegan-Day Design & Architecture, Topanga, California, 2018 | image courtesy the architects
the california glass house turns inward
Fire can also change something as basic as where a house chooses to look. At CAMPout, Faulkner Architects’ residence near Lake Tahoe, the surrounding pine forest is at once the reason to be there and a source of combustible material.
The architects limit glazing where the house meets the forest and concentrate larger openings around an internal courtyard. Double concrete walls and steel-sash tempered glazing establish a fire-resistant perimeter, and native cedar lines much of the interior. Thus, the interiors are warm and woody, while from the outside, the building meets the landscape with resilient concrete and steel.
There is an interesting reversal here. California residential architecture spent decades perfecting the idea of dissolving the wall between house and landscape. CAMPout keeps that relationship, but edits where it happens. The widest connection to the forest occurs through the courtyard, where the edge can be controlled.
CAMPout, Faulkner Architects, Lake Tahoe, California, 2023 | image © Joe Fletcher
rebuilding on the same ground
Near Healdsburg, just north of San Francisco, Faulkner Architects designed another dwelling: the Pine Flat Residence. had an even more direct encounter with wildfire. The clients’ earlier off-grid house was destroyed by the 2019 Kincade Fire, leaving its concrete foundation behind in the Mayacamas Mountains. The new residence sits within that footprint, incorporating around 90 percent of the existing concrete instead of starting over with a freshly excavated site.
Above it, a long Corten steel shell wraps the house from wall to roof. Sliding screens can cover openings against embers, while sprinklers sit above the exterior decks. Water infrastructure becomes part of the defensive system too, with a dedicated tank supplying the fire hydrant and sprinklers.
Here, wildfire resilience has a physical history beneath it. The old house determines where the next house stands. Concrete that survived one fire becomes part of the architecture built for the next.
Pine Flat Residence, Faulkner Architects, Healdsburg, California, 2025 | image © Joe Fletcher
the first five feet around the house are becoming architecture
Perhaps the biggest change is happening outside the walls altogether. In August 2026, California’s Board of Forestry and Fire Protection approved statewide Zone 0 regulations aimed at creating an ember-resistant area within the first five feet around structures in designated fire-hazard areas. The rules were filed with the Office of Administrative Law on August 28 and, as of September 8, remain under review before taking effect statewide.
A plant burning against the facade can ignite the building. So can a combustible fence that physically meets it. The territory which was once treated as landscaping starts behaving like part of a vulnerable wall assembly.
This may eventually produce one of the clearest visual signatures of the wildfire-adapted house. The building sits within a small mineral or paved perimeter before vegetation begins, almost as though the architecture has been given a little breathing room. Beyond that zone, planting can return with greater spacing and management.
Amnesia House, Edmonds + Lee Architects, Napa Valley, California, 2025 | image © Joe Fletcher
No house becomes invulnerable through these moves. Studies of previous California fires have found cases where structures ignited one another, and wildfire researchers repeatedly warn against reading lone surviving houses as simple proof that one material or detail works every time. Wind can change. Firefighters can arrive at one block and be overwhelmed elsewhere. A neighboring structure can become a powerful source of heat.
The strongest examples therefore avoid the fantasy of a sealed fortress. They still use timber and open toward views. They keep courtyards and terraces. What changes is the threshold between domestic space and the landscape around it.
For centuries, the house has been designed to keep rain outside and control heat moving through its walls. In fire country, another environmental force is entering that equation. Wildfire is becoming something the roof anticipates, something the facade filters and something the garden leaves room for. The fire may never arrive. The architecture increasingly assumes that it could.
CAMPout, Faulkner Architects, Lake Tahoe, California, 2023 | image © Joe Fletcher

Crimea Tourism Losses Surge 96% as Ukrainian Strikes Hit Travel Industry
The travel sector in temporarily occupied Crimea incurred over 4 billion rubles ($46 million) in losses during the first six months of 2026.
This figure marks a 95.7% increase compared to the same period last year, based on Russian state statistics data reviewed by the media outlet Verstka.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Financial losses peaked in May at 850 million rubles ($9.8 million), coinciding with increased strikes by the Armed Forces of Ukraine against power facilities and supply routes on the peninsula.
Industry profits dropped by 60% over the same period. Local travel companies earned roughly 530 million rubles ($6.1 million) between January and June, down from nearly 1.3 billion rubles ($15 million) the previous year.
In July, the volume of paid tour operator services in Crimea fell by nearly 55% compared to last year, while Sevastopol recorded a drop of about 73%. Hotel revenues dropped by 74% and 10% in these respective areas.
Disturbances in electricity and water supply, alongside shortages of fuel and specific goods, have impacted the peninsula since May due to Ukrainian attacks. A regional state of emergency has been active since June 26. According to the Association of Tour Operators of Russia, roughly 1 million trips to Crimea and Sevastopol were canceled by the end of July.
The organization estimated total canceled bookings at 20 to 25 billion rubles ($230 million to $288 million), with 5 to 7 billion rubles ($58 million to $81 million) of that total directly affecting tour operators.
In July, the Russian cabinet allocated over 4.3 billion rubles ($49.6 million) to support the sector. Out of this funding, 3.7 billion rubles ($42.7 million) were directed to Crimea and 584.5 million rubles ($6.7 million) to Sevastopol. The payouts were intended to reach employees across more than 4,600 travel enterprises.
By late August, local businesses operating in tourism and other sectors received deferrals on insurance contributions, along with extensions on debt collection deadlines. On-site tax audits for these businesses were also suspended.
In September, regional authorities announced plans to submit a bill to the State Duma seeking nationwide support for the local hospitality industry. The regional minister of resorts and tourism, Sergey Ganziy, noted that the measures introduced by the federal government remain insufficient, pointing to tourist refunds for pre-booked trips as one of the most critical challenges.
Earlier, Russia’s State Duma backed a proposal to introduce a special fee on citizens traveling abroad.
Lawmaker Sangadzhi Tarbayev said the measure is intended to redirect spending into the domestic tourism sector, arguing that money spent overseas could instead support the local economy and create jobs.

The US military on Tuesday said it had “destroyed” several Iranian tankers after Iran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles, as violence once again surged across the region, pushing the price of oil past $100 a barrel.
American forces struck the tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg Island, US central command (Centcom) said in a statement, adding that American forces “directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck”.
Centom said the strikes came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. “The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement.
The IRGC said they had struck a US military base in Jordan in retaliation. Air-defence systems destroyed 18 of the 20 ballistic missiles originating from Iranian territory, Jordan’s state news agency reported, citing the armed forces, adding that two missiles fell in unpopulated areas and there were no casualties.
The IRGC also said they attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Gulf, after warning crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels.
After a month of relative calm in August, Iran and the US have resumed exchanges of fire, sending global oil prices back up to levels last seen in July. On Wednesday, oil prices rose above $100 a barrel in early Asia trading.
On Tuesday, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war.

In a statement, the IRGC said images of the vessel would be released shortly.
In a statement, US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a United States Centcom spokesperson, said the submersible was “defective” and an older model “that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”. Operations in the area continue, he said.
Iran has maintained a blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of the global oil and gas shipments, since the outbreak of the war more than six months ago, while the US has imposed its own blockade of Iranian ports.
In Paris, South Korean president Lee Jae Myung and French president Emmanuel Macron discussed cooperation on security and freedom of navigation in the strait of Hormuz.
South Korea’s defence ministry said it had sent an inspection team to the United Arab Emirates to assess security conditions in the region, but stressed that the mission was intended to gather information and did not presuppose a troop deployment.
A South Korean official said Iran had expressed interest and sought explanations through diplomatic channels after media reports about a possible South Korean role in Hormuz security efforts.
South Korea’s presidential office separately said reports that the US had set a deadline for Seoul to send assets to Hormuz were untrue.
Seoul said last week it was reviewing various options, including military measures, to contribute to freedom of navigation in Hormuz, but denied reports that the US had set a deadline for Seoul to dispatch assets to the strait.
Trump has struggled to end the unpopular war, which has claimed the lives of 18 US service members.
Iranian authorities have previously put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures that outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated.

The world is facing a diesel shortage this winter due to the wars in Ukraine and Iran – Reuters

The world is facing a diesel shortage this winter due to the wars in Ukraine and Iran – Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
The market is short about 4 million barrels of oil products per day due to the wars and constrained refining capacity. Diesel in the US has risen to a record high.
Global diesel supplies will remain constrained throughout the winter due to a lack of available refining capacity, reduced supplies from Russia and the Middle East, and a seasonal increase in demand. Overall, the market is short approximately 4 million barrels of petroleum products per day, Reuters reports, citing executives at energy companies, according to UNN.
Details
Vitol CEO Russell Hardy said that the global market had lost approximately 2 million barrels per day due to the situation in Russia. Nearly another 2 million barrels per day had been removed from supplies from the Middle East amid the U.S. war with Iran and damage to oil-refining infrastructure.
There is actually a shortage of petroleum products because we are missing 2 million barrels per day from Russia and nearly 2 million barrels per day from the Middle East
Global fuel inventories have approached record lows
According to the head of Vitol, there is currently more crude oil than refined petroleum products on the global market. The main problem has been the insufficient amount of available refining capacity, which is forcing countries to continue drawing down accumulated fuel inventories.
We continue to consume the surplus that exists in the world, and we have practically reached the bottom of our inventories
Phillips 66 Senior Vice President Mark Senn added that most U.S. refineries are already operating at maximum capacity. With the winter demand peak approaching and diesel inventories low, the strained market situation may persist over the coming months.
The fuel shortage has already affected prices: last week, diesel in the United States rose to a record level, while the refining margin for diesel reached a record $108.02 per barrel during trading.
Vitol expects that high prices and limited fuel availability could reduce global oil demand by approximately 1.5 million barrels per day in 2026 compared with 2025.

Why the U.K., Canada, and France Are Banning Trade With Israeli Settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:32:53 UTC
05:32:53 KST

Israel ordered the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem after the United Kingdom led a coordinated effort by 12 governments to restrict trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the import ban on all goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday.
“The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists,” he said during remarks at the House of Commons, referring to growing incidents of violence against Palestinians living in the West Bank.
Eighty attacks carried out by Israeli settlers resulted in casualties or property damage between Aug. 11 and Aug. 24, according to the United Nations High Commission for Human Rights.
More than 1,040 Palestinians have been injured in such incidents across 2026, it reports, and 79 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed by either Israeli military personnel or settlers so far this year.
That adds to the escalating violence against Palestinians in the West Bank since the terror attacks led by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed around 1,200 people and took more than 200 hostage. Since then, another 1,100 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank.
Miliband said that the Israeli government had too often “turned a blind eye.”
Following the U.K.’s lead, Canada and France announced similar trade bans Tuesday. Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden also joined those three countries in backing national or European restrictions, although their individual commitments vary.
In a joint statement, the 12 governments said Israel’s actions were undermining the prospect of a two-state solution. The statement calls for a halt on settlement expansions and accountability for settler violence.
What the Israeli settlement trade bans cover
The planned sanctions will ban the import of any goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, but will not impact any goods from Israel.
Annual trade between the U.K. and Israel totaled around £6 billion ($8.1 billion) in the four quarters leading to Q2 2025, with goods imported by the U.K. from Israel valued at £1.2 billion ($1.6 billion). It is unclear how much of this trade originates from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
Chris Doyle, director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding, says that the settler economy produces mainly produce.
“You see a lot of exports of agricultural goods like dates and avocados to Europe. You also see a lot of export of herbs, so this is in part the basis of the economy,” he says.
A report published by Global Echo in June found that over 17% of the agricultural shipments to Europe that it analyzed contained settlement products.
Doyle also says some settlements have been expanding industrial zones which “contribute to the production of many different types of Israeli exports.”
And while the sanctions will not target goods from Israel, Doyle says that some products originating from settlements are instead labeled as originating from Israel.
European policy has previously sought clarity on the exact origin of Israeli products and whether goods have come from West Bank settlements.
“It's incumbent, therefore, on Israel to stop this, to bring itself in line with international law, and not export these products,” said Doyle in light of Tuesday’s sanctions.
But Hirschhorn argues that given how intertwined the economies of settlements and Israel are, it is difficult and unrealistic to separate the two.
“The lid to the container of hummus that's made in the settlement of Ariel is filled by hummus itself that was pumped out of a tube in the city of Ashkelon,” she suggests as an example.
“There's no real way necessarily to separate the goods here from the goods there,” she tells TIME, arguing that Tuesday’s sanctions will ultimately impact Israeli businesses beyond the initial scope of the ban.
“I’m not sure how an economic boycott of settler goods, no matter how specific or how tailored, would really achieve the policy goals that ultimately are desired here, which is the two-state solution,” she says. 
Despite the potential unintended impact sanctions could have, Doyle argues that this is down to the Israeli government to resolve.
“It’s up to the state of Israel to uncouple its economy from the settlement economy,” he says. “Settlements do not lie within the sovereign borders of the territory of the State of Israel.”
Why West Bank settlements are illegal under international law
Under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, the individual or mass forcible transfers, as well as deportations of protected persons from occupied territory, are illegal. It is also illegal for an occupying power to deport or transfer parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies.
In light of Article 49, and in line with its view that Israel occupies the West Bank, the U.N. deems settlements in the West Bank illegal. Miliband reaffirmed Tuesday that the U.K. observes this position on the matter, as well.
“To those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements, let me say this: You will face the full force of U.K. sanctions,” said the Foreign Secretary, outlining that action will be taken against those who provide construction or financial support for expansions.
There are an estimated 620,000 Israeli settlers living across the West Bank, as well as in East Jerusalem, according to B’Tselem, the Israeli Information Center for Human Rights in the Occupied Territories.
Settlers “live on occupied territory, using resources, particularly water, which is so crucial that they're not entitled to, and they do that with the blessing, encouragement, and active support of the Israeli government,” says Doyle.
The Israeli government has also been enabling and in some instances supporting the expansion of settlements across the West Bank. Last month, it opened bidding for more than 1,200 homes in E1, a largely undeveloped area between East Jerusalem and the existing Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim.
The broader plan for roughly 3,400 homes was approved last year and championed by far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has previously been sanctioned by the British government and others.
Critics say that construction would connect Ma’ale Adumim more closely with Jerusalem while disrupting Palestinian territorial continuity between East Jerusalem and the northern and southern West Bank—further undermining the prospects for a viable two-state solution.
Arguments for and against the sanctions
Supporters say that the sanctions are significant because they turn longstanding international condemnation of Israeli settlements into economic action.
“There is a line drawn here that many actors in the international community are now prepared to say, ‘We're going to back up the criticism with action,’ and that ‘Israel, you have to stop massive expansion of settlers,’” Doyle says.
Others question whether broad restrictions on settlement trade effectively address the violence used to justify them.
“The sanctions first and foremost don't target the perpetrators of settler violence specifically,” says Sara Yael Hirschhorn, a professor of history and American Jewish studies at the University of Haifa, suggesting that only a small number of settlers actually carry out such violence.
Hirschhorn also notes that the timing of the measures, weeks before Israeli elections, could embolden far-right parties and hinder discussions around settler violence.
“All it does is stir the pot in the midst of an election campaign, and strengthens the Israeli right, rather than approaching these issues with more subtlety when a new Israeli government had been elected,” she says.
How Israel and the U.S. have responded
Israeli President Isaac Herzog warned that British sanctions on Israeli settlements “will prove to be a grave miscalculation.”
“Sanctions are not a solution—dialogue is,” said Herzog. “Step away from the dead-end of sanctions and boycotts, and turn toward constructive dialogue and toward cooperation.”
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also called on the British consulate in East Jerusalem, that works with the Palestinian Authority, to be closed.
“This must be Israel's resolute response to British audacity,” he said.
Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, said he did not know what “sanctions, repercussions or retaliations” might follow from Washington in response to the U.K.
“I don’t know if they’re really aware of the implications and how it’s going to affect Brits,” he said, pointing toward legislation in 38 states that restricts government contracts or investments involving companies that boycott Israel.
Asked about the sanctions, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters: “Obviously we're not gonna do what the U.K. did.”
“We don’t want to see anything destabilizing going on in the West Bank with so much going on in the region, we think it has implications on our ability to make progress with regards to Gaza,” Rubio continued.
President Donald Trump is yet to publicly address the sanctions. When asked for comment on the matter, the White House directed TIME to Rubio's remarks.
Alongside the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar confirmed the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center, which coordinates relief efforts.
Israel has also suspended the British training of Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank and it has barred an NGO director and 11 elected representatives in the U.K. from entering Israel.
Among those denied entry is Labour lawmaker Richard Burgon, who has backed accusations of genocide put against Israel for its conduct in Gaza.
“The decision by the Israeli government to sanction me today will not intimidate me into silence,” said Burgon in response to the move. “I will continue to do what is right, speak out in defense of international law and stand up for justice for the Palestinian people.”

Head of Smithsonian museums announces he will be stepping down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

05:32:52 KST

Head of Smithsonian museums announces he will be stepping down
The US institution is under pressure from the Trump administration to change how it portrays the country’s history.
The head of the Smithsonian Institution will be stepping down from his position by the end of the year, following pressure from the administration of United States President Donald Trump.
In a statement on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch announced he was leaving the institution, an organisation that oversees one of the world’s largest collections of museums and educational and research centres.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump admin orders Smithsonian museums to be reviewed for ‘Americanism’
- list 2 of 3Trump says Smithsonian museums only cover ‘how bad Slavery was’ in US
- list 3 of 3Why is Trump going after the Smithsonian museums?
“I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward,” Bunch said.
“It is time for my next chapter, a chapter that will allow me to continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and celebrates the complex story of our nation.”
Many of the Smithsonian’s museums occupy a place of pride on the National Mall in Washington, DC.
But since the start of Trump’s second term as US president, the institution has come under increasing fire from conservatives who object to its depictions of racism, colonialism and other aspects of US history.
While the Smithsonian does not fall under the president’s direct authority, a large part of its budget comes from the federal government, and the Trump administration has threatened to sever that funding stream over the institution’s alleged “anti-American ideology”.
In July, Trump had ordered the US Department of the Interior to erect “warning signs” near the entrance to the National Museum of American History to inform visitors about the museum’s alleged bias.
In August, the Interior Department also sent a letter to the Smithsonian detailing its criticism if the institution did not address its concerns by changing its top leadership.
“Because these concerns arise from executive leadership and institutional ideology at the Smithsonian, the appropriate response must likewise address executive leadership and institutional ideology,” the letter said.
‘American exceptionalism’
The Smithsonian museums are free for the public to visit, and they draw millions of people each year.
They include the National Air and Space Museum, National Museum of American History, National Museum of the American Indian, National Museum of Natural History and National Portrait Gallery.
Bunch was appointed as the secretary of the Smithsonian in 2019, becoming the first African American to serve at the helm of the 180-year-old institution.
He previously served as director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which opened in 2016 after a years-long effort.
But the Trump administration has sought to crack down on institutions it accuses of promoting left-wing “woke” ideology and movements like diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), a social justice initiative to encourage the participation of marginalised groups.
As part of that effort, Trump has sought to exert greater control over programming at cultural institutions like the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, one of the US capital’s most prominent theatre venues.
He has also ordered probes of other entities, from schools and universities to the military and national parks, in an effort to rid federally supported institutions of what he called “discriminatory” DEI practices.
The Smithsonian, however, was an early target of the Trump administration’s anti-DEI campaign.
Within months of taking office in 2025, Trump issued an executive order titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History”, which called for changes to ensure the Smithsonian returned to its “rightful place as a symbol of inspiration and American greatness”.
The White House, at the time, accused the Smithsonian’s American Art Museum and National Museum of African American History and Culture of promoting narratives that portrayed US values as harmful and oppressive.
In May 2025, Trump also said he had fired Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, a Smithsonian museum, after he accused her of being a “highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI, which is totally inappropriate for her position”.
Critics, however, argued that Trump did not have the authority to fire Sajet, who resigned under pressure in June of that year.
Further controversies erupted when the Smithsonian removed references to Trump’s two first-term impeachments from exhibits, before reversing course amid public outcry.
Soon after, in August 2025, the White House wrote to Bunch’s office saying it would conduct a review of the museum’s content, including its exhibits and social media content, to ensure the narratives shared would “celebrate American exceptionalism”.
Bunch has remained under pressure since that time, facing the prospect of balancing the institution’s funding requirements with the need to shield itself from political interference.
In the wake of his resignation on Tuesday, historians and artists like director Ken Burns voiced their support for the outgoing Smithsonian head.
“Lonnie Bunch is a great historian, public servant and a dear friend,” Burns wrote on social media.
“He has devoted his career to helping us understand the full American story in all its complexity. Our country is better for his work, and I am deeply grateful for it.”
