Bosnia and Herzegovina expels two Serbian diplomats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:46:27 UTC
03:46:27 KST

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic has announced that two members of the Serbian Embassy’s diplomatic staff in Sarajevo have been declared persona non grata while Sarajevo plans to withdraw support for a regional cooperation declaration.
Speaking at a news conference on Tuesday, Konakovic said he declared Serbian Embassy military attaché Milan Dulanovic and adviser to a representative of Serbia’s Security Information Agency (BIA) Darko Maksimovic persona non grata.
"These two individuals have 48 hours to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina,” said Konakovic, adding that their diplomatic identification cards would be revoked.
He urged members of the diplomatic corps in Bosnia and Herzegovina to stop communicating with Dulanovic and Maksimovic.
Konakovic cited the response of Serbian officials to the late convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic following his burial in Belgrade, describing recent developments as crossing “all red lines,” for the decision.
Konakovic said Bosnia and Herzegovina would not allow the glorification of individuals convicted of genocide and other international crimes to be portrayed merely as the views of individuals.
“Nothing else is more important. No economic, commercial, social or administrative process is more important than what Serbia is currently doing in Bosnia and Herzegovina,” he noted.
Konakovic also announced that Sarajevo had withdrawn its consent to the joint declaration on good-neighbourly relations and regional cooperation scheduled to be signed October 1 in Montenegro.
He stressed that Bosnia and Herzegovina would not sign the document until the situation in Serbia changes.
“We will not sign such declarations, empty pieces of paper, while we are seeing the Serbia we have witnessed in recent days — the Serbia of the 1990s, which truly warns us that things are not normal,” he underscored.
Konakovic reaffirmed that Montenegro had been informed of the decision, stressing that Bosnia and Herzegovina had no objection to the document but rather to Serbia’s current actions and approach.
He also announced a review of the staffing structure of the Serbian Embassy in Sarajevo, including the number of diplomatic personnel required for operations.
The foreign ministry will also consider changes to the consular jurisdiction and a gradual reduction in the number of employees at Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Embassy in Belgrade, in accordance with domestic procedures.
“Until normal politicians emerge who are ready for compromise and agreement — we do not have to agree on everything in history — you will never again insult and humiliate us,” said Konakovic.
Mladic, known as the "Butcher of Bosnia," was found guilty by a UN tribunal of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity, including his role in the 1995 Srebrenica genocide. He died Aug. 27 while serving a life sentence in prison in The Hague.

Ikea wins right to launch legal action against Belgian far-right party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:45:49 UTC
03:45:49 KST

Ikea has won the right to take legal action against a Belgian far-right political party that parodied the Swedish flatpack furniture firm’s branding in its anti-immigration campaign.
In a ruling on Tuesday, Europe’s highest court said that Ikea had the right to oppose the use of its trademarks and distinctive graphics by Vlaams Belang, a rightwing Eurosceptic political party that advocates for an independent Flemish state.
The court found that Vlaams Belang’s use of Ikea’s trademarks to illustrate its policy on asylum and immigration could “cause significant detriment to the repute” of the company.
The party, which has called for a near total stop to immigration and limitations on the building of mosques, had used Ikea’s branding in political material published in 2022.
One image featured characters modelled on the cartoon people used in Ikea instructions, one carrying a flag featuring a lion – the symbol of Flanders – and another holding a shield in Ikea’s distinctive blue and yellow livery.
The image was titled “Ikea plan” with the subtitle “Immigration really can be different.”
After Ikea issued proceedings against Vlaams Belang, the party argued that its freedom of expression should override the Swedish company’s rights over its brand.
But the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the European Union ruled on Tuesday that Ikea could proceed with legal action against Vrijheidsfonds, the association behind the party.
In a statement, the court said “it does not appear that the use of the Ikea trademarks for the sole purpose of taking advantage of their reputation to reinforce a political message and increase its dissemination, takes precedence over the rights and interests of the proprietor of those trademarks.”
However, it said a final decision on the dispute could only be made in subsequent legal proceedings in a Belgian court.
Pauline Piernez, a trademark and design associate at Marks & Clerk, an intellectual property law firm, said: “While the CJEU rightly confirms that political parody is not prohibited, it also makes clear that freedom of expression is not a blank cheque to appropriate the identity of a famous brand simply to amplify a message.
“In this case, the court found that the use of the Ikea trademarks was liable to damage their reputation and was primarily intended to take advantage of their notoriety in order to increase the reach of a political message entirely unrelated to Ikea itself.
“The decision should be welcomed as an important safeguard for the system of protection afforded to reputed trademarks.|
“Inter Ikea fully believes in – and deeply respects – freedom of expression,” the company said in a statement. “At the same time, it cannot accept the use of the Ikea trademarks in ways that damage their reputation or distinctive character, particularly when such use serves no other purpose than to free-ride on the reputation of the Ikea brand.”
Vlaams Belang said its campaign association had taken note of the judgment and that it “will thoroughly study its scope in the context of the further legal proceedings”.

Student visa refusals hit 10-year high, shattering dreams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:44:51 UTC
03:44:51 KST

Australian student visa refusal rate hits 10-year high amid government crackdown
Read the story in bahasa Indonesia
Angelica Felincia has dreamed of studying in Australia since her first year of high school.
"I wanted to experience life outside of Indonesia and see different cultures," she said.
"Australia has many beautiful places, and I feel that I connect with the culture there."
Ms Felincia, who said she enjoyed being around children, found that early childhood education was a "well-regarded and popular field in Australia".
She said her desire to study in Australia had made her give up a place at an Indonesian university.
However, her visa application, which included a 27-page statement on why she wanted to study in Australia, was rejected within a day.
The case officer questioned why she could not pursue her studies in her home country.
"I was extremely disappointed,"
"The letter said that my Genuine Student statement did not provide a strong enough reason for studying in Australia."
Department of Home Affairs (DOHA) data shows refusal of student visa applications has hit a decade high, with the rate climbing from 7.9 per cent in June 2016 to 24.2 per cent in June this year.
More than 51 per cent of all student visa applications from Nepal were rejected in 2025-2026, while India saw more than 40 per cent knocked back.
China recorded a rejection rate of 5.8 per cent for the same period.
Nepali applicant Asif Rahim lodged his application in March to study an accounting master's degree in Melbourne but was rejected in April.
He said he witnessed "a massive rejection" among his Nepali friends who also applied at the same time.
Mr Rahim said the department was not satisfied with his study proposal.
"I'm very disappointed with the rejection because I've invested 15 to 16 months preparing everything," he said.
"I'm emotionally so broke."
A DOHA spokesperson said the department did not assess applications based on nationality.
Refusals 'copy-paste'
The refusals were recorded as international students became the centre of discussions around migration cuts in Australia.
Last week, the government shut down a Vocational Education and Training course amid concerns students were using it to maintain their visas rather than for genuine study.
To obtain a student visa, the DOHA website states applicants have to provide a "Genuine Student (GS) requirement", which details a "student's intention to genuinely study in Australia".
But several migration agents questioned how case officers assessed the applications under the GS criteria.
Umar Ashraf, a migration agent at Magpie Consultants, said he understood that the government would refuse a visa when there was a time gap in studies, misalignment of career pathway, or an intention to stay longer than necessary in Australia with the student visa.
But he was confused by many of the offshore application refusals he had seen.
"About 60 to 70 per cent of those refusals, I feel, the department is just throwing it back," he said.
"There are genuine people who are getting refusals, but we can't do much."
Phu Vu Minh, a migration agent at VisaEnvoy, said the department gave "unreasonable" reasons in their refusal letters, which she said were often "vague".
"It's like copy-paste from one to the other," she said.
"It doesn't … show that the case officer has carefully assessed all the evidence submitted together with the application."
The ABC has reviewed some refusal letters from the department, finding almost identical paragraphs, minor wording changes, and similar paraphrased sentences used to outline why the assessment points in the applicant's documents were not accepted.
"The use of standardised language in decision letters helps ensure our decisions are consistent, legally robust, and explain the reasons for a decision in accordance with legislative requirements across a large-volume visa program," a DOHA spokesperson said.
Ms Minh said despite applicants submitting up to 15 pages to address the required points, the GS assessment was "highly subjective to the case officer".
"You may get approval from one case officer, but with the same case [or application] you may get refused by another case officer," she said.
Work Visa Lawyers' Chris Johnston said he had seen a fivefold increase in the number of appeals launched by onshore applicants against refusals in recent months.
He said the "very common patterns" in refusal letters for offshore applicants, who could not appeal, were "concerning".
"When someone pays the money and gets everything ready … the evidence should be considered on its merits," he said, adding applicants had to pay up to $2,500 to apply.
"That's not fair if they [the government] are just refusing because they don't want people to come to Australia."
The DOHA said a range of measures had been implemented to "strengthen the integrity and quality of the international education sector and student visa program".
A spokesperson said the action had resulted in "greater scrutiny of applications and higher refusal rates for applications that do not meet visa requirements".
"Student visa applications are assessed on their individual merits against the requirements of Australia's migration legislation," the spokesperson said.
'An easy target'
Ly Tran, an education professor at Deakin University, said there was "a legitimate need to address poor-quality providers, course-hopping, and the misuse of student visas in Australia".
But she said she "would be cautious about a broad "crackdown' approach".
"We need to distinguish between problematic providers, problematic courses, and individual students,"
"There is also a risk that repeated restrictive measures create the impression internationally that Australia is becoming much less welcoming to international students."
She said international students had become "an easy target", with their cohort being one of the largest components of temporary migration.
"My bigger concern is that international students are increasingly being treated as political objects rather than primarily as students and members of our education community," she said.
Luke Sheehy, CEO of Universities Australia, said current student visa processing was having a "detrimental effect" on universities.
"[It's] devastating, particularly for our regional universities and some of our universities in the growth corridor areas of our country," he said.
"It takes years … to engage with the student, go to their country, talk to them … so they can come to Australia and study at our world-class institutions."
The DOHA said "a strong and trusted student visa program supports students, education providers and communities across Australia, including regional areas".
"And helps preserve Australia's reputation as a world-class education destination."

China and Qatar are strengthening bilateral ties: What that really means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

03:44:39 KST

China and Qatar are strengthening bilateral ties: What that really means
Beijing says it will increase coordination with Doha to help de-escalate regional tensions amid the ongoing war on Iran.
Beijing, China – Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani has completed a two-day visit to China, with officials describing the relationship as entering a new “golden decade”.
China has called Qatar an “important strategic partner” in the Middle East and the Gulf, and the two sides have agreed to expand cooperation in energy, investment and advanced technologies.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran and Ukraine wars: Why ship fuel is running short, and why it matters
- list 2 of 4Oil prices surge as US-Iran strikes intensify in Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4IAEA warns over Iran nuclear access as Western powers push UN referral
- list 4 of 4Qatar says reopening Strait of Hormuz ‘unconditionally’ is a priority
But it’s clear the continuing US-Israeli war on Iran, and ongoing Qatari efforts to mediate between Tehran and Washington, were central to discussions.
“It’s not acceptable at all to have this state of no war and no peace. This is not beneficial to the region, the countries of the region, and the people,” Ibrahim bin Sultan al-Hashmi, director of the Department of Media and Communications at Qatar’s Foreign Ministry, told reporters in Doha on Tuesday following the meetings. “Qatar is working hard with its partners, including China. Diplomatic efforts are being exerted and new ideas are being discussed.”
Beijing pledged to increase communication and coordination with Doha to help restore regional peace and stability. Qatar has told China it would prioritise its energy supply despite the difficulties.
Raised stakes
The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has raised the stakes for both sides.
Qatar is one of the world’s biggest exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG), while China is the world’s largest importer of crude oil. Both have a significant interest in restoring stability to the strait, through which around one-fifth of global oil and LNG normally passes.
Energy is also the backbone of the relationship. China is Qatar’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade worth $23.8bn last year. Qatar is China’s second-largest source of LNG, supplying 19.4 million tonnes in 2025. QatarEnergy has signed 27-year LNG supply agreements with Chinese state-owned energy giants CNPC and Sinopec, which have also taken stakes in Qatar’s massive North Field gas expansion.
Overlapping interests, different approaches
But despite these shared interests, Doha and Beijing have different ways of dealing with Tehran.
China has repeatedly voiced support for Qatar’s mediation efforts but has largely refrained from direct criticism of Tehran’s attacks or its disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. It’s also consistently placed primary blame for the conflict on the US and Israel, a conflict Chinese officials say “never should have happened”.
Beijing is arguably Tehran’s most important economic and diplomatic partner. China has for years been the largest buyer of its oil and continues to oppose unilateral sanctions against it.
During talks with Al Thani, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi repeated calls for a diplomatic solution, saying “pressure exerted through military means is not a solution; dialogue and negotiations are the only viable path”.
For its part, Qatar has publicly condemned Tehran for attacks on its own territory and on neighbouring Gulf states. It has grown increasingly frustrated with failed or stalled attempts to resolve the crisis, while continuing to facilitate dialogue.
From Doha’s perspective, closer coordination with Beijing potentially brings another influential player into its efforts to end the conflict, one with unusually strong economic and political ties to Tehran.
Balancing act
China is also aware of Qatar’s longstanding security and military partnership with Washington, Beijing’s biggest strategic rival.
Qatar hosts Al Udeid, the largest US military base in the Middle East. On March 3, Iran fired two ballistic missiles at Qatar. One was intercepted while the other struck Al Udeid, causing no casualties. This prompted Doha to call for even stronger security ties with Washington.
Still, China has no interest in replacing the US as a security guarantor, says Zoon Ahmed Khan, a research fellow at the Center for China and Globalization in Beijing. “What we are seeing is Beijing positioning itself as a relevant political and economic actor at a moment when several states in the region are looking for additional options,” Khan said.
The question is how much of its own influence Beijing is prepared to use when it comes to Iran. China has so far shown little appetite for using its leverage to exert significant pressure on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Broader horizons
The Qatari prime minister’s two-day visit was, of course, about more than Iran. If anything, the conflict has increased the incentive for Doha and Beijing to expand their relationship towards what Qatar has described as “broader horizons”. China’s Premier Li Qiang called for deeper cooperation in traditional and renewable energy, infrastructure, artificial intelligence and finance, while Al Thani singled out high technology and advanced manufacturing.
Invest Qatar reports that 520 Chinese companies operate in the country, with Chinese investment projects generating more than $3bn and creating more than 3,200 jobs this past decade.
The visit underlines a partnership that is becoming broader economically, and potentially more important diplomatically, as the Iran war tests both countries’ ability to protect the interests that bind them together.

Lior Raz, one of the show's creators, told Netflix's Tudum site that he hoped viewers would understand "how peace is important, and how we need to think differently and how war is ruining the universe."
Israeli TV show Fauda returned to Netflix on Tuesday with its fifth season.
In its early seasons, the series sought to portray human stories on both sides of the Israel-Palestine conflict.
The show's newest iteration, created by Avi Issacharoff and Lior Raz, takes place two years after the 7 October 2023 attacks by militant group Hamas on southern Israel.
It follows the story of Doron Kavillio, a commander of an undercover Israeli military unit hunting down a Hamas operative he thought he had killed.
Doron also heads to France's Marseille after discovering that an old friend has gone rogue on an unsanctioned revenge mission.
Raz, who plays Doron, told Netflix's official companion site Tudum that season 5 was “not about trying to show what happened."
“It was about trying to tell a story, to see how we can implant our characters inside those situations and in that story that really happened," Raz said.
"So for us, it was important to be very accurate to what happened in real life, but also to put our characters into this unpredictable situation".
Raz added that he hoped viewers would understand "how peace is important, and how we need to think differently and how war is ruining the universe."
"It’s ruining our region, it’s ruining our country, and their countries, for sure. We know that people see this show all over the world — in the Arab world, in Israel — [and they’ll see] that the price of the war is hard, and we need to have hope to solve this situation," he said.

Village head's appeal drove Ladakh LG's initiative to tap 90 million litres of glacial water for irrigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:41:49 UTC
03:41:49 KST

Village head’s appeal drove Ladakh LG’s initiative to tap 90 million litres of glacial water for irrigation
SRINAGAR: Nearly 90 million litres of glacial water have started irrigating more than 1,000 acres of parched farmlands across 12 villages in Ladakh every day, thanks to a pioneering initiative by lieutenant governor (LG) V K Saxena last month.The massive volume of glacier-melt, previously flowing untapped into the River Indus, is now being channelised from Stok village nallah in Leh into the Igoo-Phey Irrigation Canal using simple earthwork that incurred little capital expenditure.
It was an appeal from a village chief that drove the LG to brainstorm on harnessing glaciers and snowmelt for productive use. According to officials, Saxena was on a visit to Chuchot village in Leh where the ‘goba’ (or nambardar, the traditional village head), Mirza Hussain, sought his intervention to address the acute water shortage in the village.The plea prompted the LG to spearhead a comprehensive and systematic campaign to identify locations where large volumes of glacial water were flowing down unused, draining straight into the Indus, even as surrounding farmlands remained dry, officials said.The govt first identified Stok village nallah, fed by the Stok Kangri Glacier, as one such place where glacier water could be diverted into the existing canal.
Officials said the discharge from Stok nallah was assessed at 36 cusecs, or approximately 90 million litres of water in 24 hours.Two channels were then created to divert nearly 80 million litres of water into the Igoo-Phey Canal — 62 million litres toward Igoo village upstream and approximately 18 million litres toward Phey village downstream.This daily flow has substantially augmented the total water flow in the Igoo-Phey Canal — from 50 cusecs to nearly 90 cusecs. As a result, water supply will be guaranteed daily to the 12 villages fed by the canal. Previously, water from the 43-km-long Igoo-Phey Canal was distributed to villages on a restrictive roster basis due to limited availability.Having successfully channelised 80 million litres of water into the Igoo-Phey Canal, the remaining 10 million litres were diverted into another dry canal at Chuchot, and will help irrigate farmland in and around the village, officials said.
“The entire 90 million litres of water was tapped and the discharge from Stok Kangri glacier into the Indus River was reduced to zero in just two days at no cost,” said an official, adding that the success of the initiative serves as a blueprint for water management across the Union Territory.

'Battery cowboys' accused of gaming taxpayer-funded scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:40:34 UTC
03:40:34 KST

Whistleblowers accuse solar battery installers of fraud, misconduct in federal rebate scheme
In short:
Allegations of fraud and misconduct have been revealed in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Cheaper Home Batteries Program.
The untested claims were obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information request.
What's next?
Shadow Minister for Energy Dan Tehan is calling for an independent Senate inquiry into the revelations.
There are fresh claims a multi-billion-dollar taxpayer-funded program to encourage households to install solar batteries is being rorted by unscrupulous operators.
They are accused of mocking up installs, forging signatures, using unlicensed tradies for cash jobs and leaving customers with unsafe or broken systems.
The allegations of fraud and misconduct were contained in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Albanese government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program.
These untested claims were obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, which did not detail any regulatory action that may be underway.
The Cheaper Home Batteries Program offers a generous subsidy for households — up to 30 per cent of the cost of solar battery systems.
Australians have rushed to sign up, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025.
The program is estimated to cost more than $7.2 billion over four years — about $5 billion more than originally announced.
Solar and consumer advocates have labelled the accusations "absolutely shocking".
The federal opposition will push for a Senate inquiry to probe the allegations while advocates want an urgent increase to safeguards, including more inspections and better consumer protections.
'Battery cowboys' targeted scheme
The FOI documents included 95 tip-offs detailed over hundreds of pages and sent between March and June to the Clean Energy Regulator (CER).
The tips were primarily about the Cheaper Home Batteries Program.
The names of installers, retailers and individuals have been removed, and no responses from accused parties were included.
Finn Peacock, founder of the comparison website Solar Quotes, is a supporter of the Cheaper Home Batteries Program.
However, he said the original design of the program, which saw companies paid through tradeable certificates known as STCs, created strong incentives for larger battery installations and attracted what he dubbed "battery cowboys".
In a bid to clamp down on over-selling, changes to the scheme were announced in December last year to reduce the subsidies from May 1.
"There was a massive temptation to get as many of those jobs installed as possible before the deadline," he said.
'Staged' photos of installations, tips claimed
The CER has strict requirements for installers when putting in solar batteries.
However, whistleblowers alleged some operators manipulated the photo requirements, including pictures being time-stamped with the location, to claim rebates for incomplete jobs.
One tipster claimed a Queensland solar installer was fraudulently putting in claims for battery installations that were "staged" and the behaviour appeared to be "systematic".
Extra batteries were positioned temporarily, "then removed after [STC] claims have been submitted", with the customers unaware.
In one case, equipment was "staged in front of a roller door without visible cable connections", they wrote.
A similar tip came from another installer.
It was allegedly done by "unpacking the battery boxes … stacking the batteries and just taking enough photos to show on their STC Trading Application".
"This is illegal and whoever is behind this must be held accountable," they wrote.
In one extreme case, a customer alleged an installer turned up at night to remove their fully paid-for batteries two months after the installation.
The man and his wife felt threatened and called the police.
Mr Peacock said he was shocked by the allegations of "outright theft" from staged jobs.
"That blew me away…the brazenness of that,"
Stephanie Tonkin, the CEO of the Consumer Action Law Centre, said if the claims of rorting were proven it would undermine the "policy goals and the trust in that system".
Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan said the federal opposition would seek support across the parliament for a Senate inquiry.
"Given the seriousness of the revelations as a result of the unearthing of these FOI documents, we need an independent inquiry," Mr Tehan said.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was asked on ABC News Breakfast about whether he would support an inquiry, but would not commit.
"This has been a fantastically successful program," Mr Albanese said.
Cash jobs for unlicensed tradies, tips claim
Installers must be accredited by Solar Accreditation Australia to install batteries under the federal scheme.
But industry tip-offs alleged some operators used unlicensed workers, falsified paperwork and claimed rebates before installations were complete.
One whistleblower said they were offered cash to sign off on jobs completed by unlicensed foreign workers and raised concerns about manipulated site photos, while another similar claim involved "systematic" non-compliance at a company.
Mr Peacock said unscrupulous operators could cut worker costs by using unlicensed crews instead of paying qualified solar electricians, but they risked getting caught.
It also came with serious risks including battery fires, injuries, or poor system performance.
The CER has inspected more than 3,600 batteries out of the more than half a million already installed and shared results with state and territory regulators and Solar Accreditation Australia.
Financial losses caused by missed rebate deadline
Multiple consumers feared installers had claimed the government rebate even though their system was not working.
Others said they were thousands of dollars worse off after companies failed to put in the system before the rebate deadline.
The CER declined an interview.
In a statement, a spokesperson said it had "an active compliance program", and confirmed allegations were currently under investigation.
The regulator has the power to suspend companies from the scheme or take civil or criminal action.
"Where matters relate to sales practices, contracts, refunds or consumer guarantees, responsibility sits primarily with state and territory consumer protection agencies and the ACCC."
In 2025–26 it received 315 formal referrals about the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme, which included installer conduct under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program with 17 referred for formal investigation and 106 referred to external agencies.
Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen was unavailable for an interview.
In a statement, a spokesperson said: "The government has zero tolerance for poor behaviour from installers.
"The Cheaper Home Batteries program utilises the tried-and-tested Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) framework, which includes built-in product, installer and electrical safety requirements, including compliance with state and territory electrical safety and consumer regulation, which has operated since 2011, under consecutive governments."
Mr Bowen also said a new National Technical Regulator would soon be created to ensure household solar and batteries met requirements, including that they were properly installed and commissioned.
The peak renewables body, the Smart Energy Council, said anyone flouting electrical licensing and battery accreditation laws "should be named, shamed and punished".
However, it said the regulator's statistics showed few were doing so.
"Of the 530,000 batteries installed in Australia in just over a year — more than the entirety of the United States — just 17 are being formally investigated for legal compliance by the Clean Energy Regulator."

'I made mistakes but I am not a killer': Strobel boyfriend breaks silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:37:51 UTC
03:37:51 KST

Simone Strobel boyfriend accuses police of 'tunnel vision' in cold case investigation
A Perth man police long suspected of killing his backpacker girlfriend Simone Strobel has protested his innocence and accused investigators of "tunnel vision" in his first media interview since her death in 2005.
For almost 20 years, New South Wales Police regarded Tobias Moran as the main suspect in the murder of his 25-year-old German girlfriend.
Following a 2024 inquest that disagreed with key aspects of the police theory, Mr Moran, previously known as Tobias Suckfuell, has spoken to the ABC's Unravel: Lies In Lismore podcast to claim he was not involved.
"I made mistakes and I'm here to sort of own them, but I'm not a murderer,'' he said.
"I did not kill Simone."
Ms Strobel disappeared from a caravan park in Lismore late at night after the pair had an argument in February, 2005.
Her naked body, which had been covered by palm fronds, was found less than 100 metres away from the couple's campsite six days later.
Mr Moran, who was 24 at the time, became an early suspect after he lied to police about arguing with Ms Strobel the night she disappeared, and about how much they had to drink.
He also lied about not smoking marijuana and encouraged two other German travellers, Mr Moran's sister and a friend, to tell the same lies.
In 2022, Mr Moran was charged with murder and intending to pervert the course of justice.
The lies he told were a central part of the case against Mr Moran, but the charges were dropped the following year.
A NSW Local Court later found he was charged without reasonable grounds.
Mr Moran told Unravel he lied because he believed police were not taking her disappearance seriously.
He claimed police were reassuring him that Ms Strobel was probably OK and had likely hitchhiked to another town.
"I was not lying for any other reason than to get these guys to take Simone serious," he said.
"I knew … that she was not on a bender in Nimbin or having a great time in Byron Bay."
NSW Police did not respond to specific questions about Mr Moran's criticisms about the early investigation.
Investigators accused of 'tunnel vision'
Last year, NSW State Coroner Teresa O'Sullivan rejected a finding from an earlier inquest that said there was a "very strong suspicion" Mr Moran was involved.
The more recent inquest finding cast doubt over key aspects of the police theory as to how Mr Moran allegedly killed Simone.
Police had long alleged Mr Moran killed Ms Strobel by suffocating her in their campervan and then moving her over a road with the help of one or both of his fellow German travellers.
Neither of those people have ever been charged and both have denied any involvement.
The coroner found both of the fellow travellers were "unlikely" to have been involved and that Mr Moran was "unlikely" to have acted alone.
Judge O'Sullivan stopped short of finding it was "very unlikely" that Mr Moran was involved and recommended the case be transferred from Lismore detectives to the Unsolved Homicide Unit.
She also recommended a review of forensic exhibits, including DNA profiles.
In his interview with Unravel, Mr Moran claimed he had been unfairly targeted by police due to what he called "tunnel vision".
"This entire case has been based on a theory, on a hypothesis, and crucial evidence has not been considered," Mr Moran said, adding that he believed the killer was still at large in Lismore.
"It's time for someone from the New South Wales Police to step forward and go, 'Sorry, we are really sorry' … they should apologise to my wife and my kids for locking me up."
NSW Police declined to answer detailed questions from the ABC, instead issuing this statement:
"The matter is currently being assessed by the Unsolved Homicide Unit and a forensic review is being conducted in line with the coroner's recommendations," it said.
"No further information is available at this time."
Ms Strobel's parents, Gabi and Gustav, still regard Mr Moran's lies as suspicious and believe he is yet to tell them the full truth of what happened to their daughter on the night she died.
"We have always been confounded by the multiple and conflicting versions Tobias gave to the Australian and German police about important events surrounding her death," they said in 2023 after the charges against Mr Moran were dropped.
The Strobels told the ABC that they were disappointed with the result of the more recent inquest.
Lies in Lismore, the latest season of the ABC's true crime podcast Unravel, is out now. Find Unravel on ABC listen or wherever you get your podcasts.

Sara Netanyahu’s remarks suggesting that Yair Golan knew about the October 7 attack are not merely a brazen lie aimed at a political rival ahead of crucial elections. They are also an irresponsible legitimization of conspiracy theories targeting Israel and Jews at a time of an explosion in radical anti-Zionism and antisemitism.
Speaking on Israeli television, Sara implied that Golan, leader of the opposition party The Democrats, who behaved with exceptional bravery that day, had known about the October 7 attack in advance.
This defense was primarily intended to exonerate her husband while accusing the country’s security services of failing to inform him in time, either to put him in difficulty or because they did not trust him.
It is also symptomatic that this attack came at exactly the same time as the prime minister himself was declaring that the security services – headed by IDF Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ronen Bar, and former head of the IDF Intelligence Directorate Aharon Haliva – had not deemed it necessary to wake him even as warning signs multiplied, because they anticipated a strong and determined response from him, which they wanted to avoid for fear of escalation.
This genuine revisionism would be pathetic and ridiculous if it did not once again highlight Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s absolute inability to accept even the slightest share of responsibility, instead shifting the blame onto others – the security services, members of the “elites” and the “deep state” against whom he has fought throughout his political career in the name of the Israeli people, according to his own mythical and mendacious narrative.
Golan, a former deputy chief of staff, is the archetype of this despised and supposedly untrustworthy army. By insinuating that Golan “knew,” Sara Netanyahu merely reinforced her husband’s narrative of deflection with the conspiratorial overtones that have proliferated in Israel and elsewhere since October 7.
That is precisely what makes her statement not only disgraceful, but irresponsible.
Antisemitism and radical anti-Zionism have exploded since October 7, with a particularly painful summer of 2026. They feed on clichés, simplifications, false and reductive accusations, and also conspiracy theories, which have always accompanied waves of antisemitism throughout history.
As New York prepares to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attack on the Twin Towers, the theory that Jews did not go to work at the World Trade Center and that the Mossad was behind the operation continues to thrive.
In the hours following the October 7 attack, theories began circulating that the Israeli army had known about it, that the people killed had been killed by the IDF, and that the army had allowed the incursion to unfold so that it could better justify the attack on Gaza and subsequently the “genocide” of Palestinians.
These theories gained even more traction because the image of an invincible, technologically advanced army was incompatible with the picture of a major defeat at the hands of Hamas, which was able to massacre 1,200 people within hours and take more than 250 hostages back to Gaza.
Adding fuel to the fire
In Israel, some of these theories circulated very early on in another form, particularly among Netanyahu supporters seeking to exonerate him, as his wife has done this week, by blaming the army, which supposedly concealed crucial information from him to make him bear responsibility for the failure surrounding this catastrophe, force him to resign, and thereby take revenge for the judicial reform he had initiated, which had brought hundreds of thousands of Israelis into the streets to oppose it.
Sara Netanyahu has therefore just added fuel to this infernal machine of lies with her latest remarks. Politically, they were undoubtedly foolish, because they resulted in television screens being flooded with images of Golan in uniform heading to the Nova festival to save young people.
But above all, they are a gift from heaven to all the antisemitic conspiracy theorists who can now bolster their lies with the words of the Israeli prime minister’s own wife.
The accusations of “genocide” can now be reinforced by claims of “premeditation by a murderous Zionist regime” that knew what was coming but allowed it to happen in order to indulge its “genocidal passion,” thanks to an irresponsible first lady who will undoubtedly be portrayed as a courageous whistleblower by antisemites such as Candace Owens, Nick Fuentes, or Tucker Carlson.
Congratulations, Mrs. Netanyahu.

Miliband announced that Britain would ban imports from Israeli settlements, prohibit advertising for settlement property in the UK and impose sanctions on companies and individuals involved in financing, construction, infrastructure and other activity supporting settlement expansion. The legislation is expected to take effect within six to nine months.
He stressed that the measures targeted settlements rather than Israel within the Green Line and said Britain would continue what he described as important trade with Israel. He also said he opposed the broader Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement.
Turning to Gaza, Miliband said there was growing evidence that war crimes may have been committed and backed international legal proceedings examining Israeli conduct. He stopped short of determining that genocide had occurred, saying Britain would await the conclusions of competent courts.

German economy frets about Saxony-Anhalt election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:35:00 UTC
03:35:00 KST

German economy frets about Saxony-Anhalt election results
September 8, 2026
The results came in as predicted: The AfD, which is considered far-right extremist in parts, won the election in Saxony-Anhalt and could now put forward the state’s minister-president and take over the state government.
What hardly anyone expected, however, was this: The governing CDU is now barely half as strong as it was, while the other parties have been left far behind. Calling it a landslide victory for the AfD is no exaggeration. And many commentators go so far as to call it a turning point in Germany’s postwar history.
Keep calm and carry on?
"A state government led by the AfD would certainly be seen by many as a turning point and would further fuel the debate over how best to deal with the party," Commerzbank economist Ralph Solveen told Reuters.
At the same time, he advises waiting to see what happens, saying that things are rarely as bad as they seem.
"Many of these decisions are unlikely to affect the economy until the medium to long term," he said. "Decisions on most taxes, the structure of the labor market and social security systems are made at the federal level. That is why the AfD, in many of its pledges, only promises to advocate for something in the Bundesrat, which is unlikely to succeed given the foreseeable isolation of an AfD-led government."
Local political pragmatism?
Many business community concerns had already been raised before the election. It also became clear that there are differing views within the AfD, which could lead to unpredictable policies.
For example, DW reported two months ago that Hannes Loth, a member of the AfD and the mayor in Raguhn-Jessnitz, Saxony-Anhalt, sought to have six new wind turbines installed. This pledge puts him at odds with the official stance of his own party.
Whether this is a sign of internal party pluralism or simply local political pragmatism will become clear during the coming legislative term, especially if the AfD ends up in the state government. It is not, however, serving to reassure business leaders.
Consequences of xenophobia
One issue the AfD campaigned on was a promise to limit the number of foreigners. But will the party actually be able to implement its goal? On this point, Michael Berlemann, director of the Hamburg Institute of International Economics (HWWI), remains skeptical.
"A large part of the measures it has promised cannot be implemented at the state level because the federal government is responsible for them," he said. "Another part would be illegal and would be overturned by the courts after some delay: The AfD cannot restrict the immigration of foreign skilled workers in Saxony-Anhalt."
ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski pointed to the national shortage of skilled workers: "Forced deportations in Saxony-Anhalt would probably be limited. However, the symbolic effect cannot be underestimated. As with Trump, such headlines would act as a deterrent for foreign skilled workers."
Wido Geis-Thöne, an economist at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, sees it the same way.
He told DW that the AfD would "do everything in its power to pursue its migration policy goals." However, it could only "do things that actually fall under the responsibility of the state rather than the federal government."
Economic fallout for Saxony-Anhalt
Geis-Thöne said the state itself would be the main victim of such a policy: "With an anti-immigration state government, Saxony-Anhalt will become significantly less attractive a destination for foreign skilled workers, regardless of whether anything actually changes for them from a legal perspective."
For HWWI Director Berlemann, the indirect impacts of the AfD's plans are particularly problematic. The measures announced would mean "that many skilled workers who are particularly needed in health care and nursing, hospitality and tourism, the food industry and agriculture and in construction and logistics will avoid the state in the future."
This would exacerbate the shortage of skilled workers and widen the state's economic gap.
Openness and diversity are key
Saxony-Anhalt must remain a state where people from around the world want to live and work and where companies want to invest and new technologies can emerge, Bitkom President Ralf Wintergerst warned.
He told the Catholic News Agency KNA: "The digital economy thrives on openness, diversity and international cooperation. Companies invest where they find good conditions and where skilled workers from Germany and abroad are welcomed."
Regarding foreign investment, ING Chief Economist Carsten Brzeski told Reuters: "Sure, there could be a symbolic effect on foreign investors. But let's not forget: Saxony-Anhalt is not the entire German economy."
How should Berlin react
DIW President Marcel Fratzscher painted a bleak picture of the economic future after the Saxony-Anhalt election.
"Regardless of the makeup of the next state government, a controversial or weak government and the polarization during the election campaign are likely to accelerate the departure of people and companies from Saxony-Anhalt, thereby significantly worsening conditions in the state," he said.
He told Reuters that the election result was "above all a vote of no confidence in the federal government." The consequence, he added, must be "that the federal government changes course and implements far-reaching structural reforms involving subsidies, bureaucracy, taxes, the social security system and Europe."
Tanja Gönner, managing director of the Federation of German Industries (BDI), took a similar perspective. Following the state election, she called on the federal government to be single-minded in pursuing a reform agenda.
"The response to this state election result must not be political paralysis at the federal level," she said.
The federal government must now consistently implement and expand reforms to boost investment, innovation and growth, she told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland, adding that "the positions of radical parties are not suitable for this."
The political center must now show that it is capable of taking action, BDI's managing director said, adding that what is needed is a policy focused on competitiveness and growth at both the state and federal levels. A single state election result must not distract from that goal, she concluded.
This article was originally published in German.

Ed Miliband has overturned decades of Foreign Office inertia on illegal Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:34:03 UTC
03:34:03 KST

The indefatigable ability of UK Foreign Office ministers over decades to issue boilerplate statements of concern about the extension of illegal settlements in Israel has long been a matter of ridicule.
Even some of the Conservative ministers who issued them, notably Alan Duncan and Alistair Burt, have agreed. Duncan described the UK stance towards settlements as weak and naive, while Burt wondered at the ability of the Foreign Office to find new forms of diplomatic condemnation that never amounted to any specific action. Margaret Thatcher, often torn as prime minister between her natural sympathy for Israel and her fear of the Gulf states falling under the sway of the Soviet Union, similarly expressed her anger at the settlements.
But in the face of the Israeli disillusionment with a two-state solution – to which the UK had been committed at the UN since 1946, if not before – the UK produced little practical policy to prevent the spread of Israel’s illegal settlements.
The UK-Israel trade agreement prevented preferential tariffs applying to goods coming from territories brought under Israeli administration after June 1967. The business department also advised companies not to trade with the settlements – but many simply ignored the advice or, to secure the preferential tariff, relabelled their goods as from Israel. The then trade minister Chris Bryant told the business select committee in June it was very difficult to be certain of the origin of goods.
At the same time, the legal advice was that the UK regime could place sanctions on entities only if they were linked to settler violence, but could not put a contractor under sanctions simply for working on settlements.
It was this unhappy moral and legal mess that Ed Miliband inherited. As soon as he took office as foreign secretary, he said he refused to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution that settlement expansion represented. In this he had the support of the prime minister, Andy Burnham.
Above all, Miliband felt that the UK could not feign powerlessness, and to do so, or pay lip service to action, would prove disastrous to Israel’s own future. He was perhaps the only front-rank Labour politician who could push this argument through at such pace, overturning the inertia and caution built into Foreign Office legal advice.
His Jewish heritage – his mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – his life growing up with the Palestinian question and empathy for those subjected to antisemitism put him in a near unimpeachable position to adopt the role of Israel’s critical friend.
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, might this week say the Labour government is gripped by Jew-hatred, a charge he laid at Miliband’s door knowing he is Jewish, but Miliband’s riposte is simple. The best route to Israel’s security lay in Palestinian self-determination and the introduction of the two-state solution in its fullest form. To equate Israel only with the current Likud-led government as too many Conservatives have been prone to do, was a category error, he said: “Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, plain and simple.”
He is thus the first UK foreign secretary to describe what is happening in the West Bank as ethnic cleansing, and in so doing to in effect to accuse Israel of turning a blind eye to acts that amount to war crimes.
Miliband also ended the two years of delay in responding to the international court of justice advisory opinion in June 2024 that the occupation is unlawful. In what he admitted was an overdue statement of reality, he accepted the ICJ opinion that the occupation, and not just the settlements, were so designated. Accepting the ICJ opinion arguably places stronger obligations on the UK government to not assist the occupation. It may help to explain why the trade ban extends into services such as providing insurance for illegal settlements.
The biggest diplomatic rabbit Miliband pulled from the hat was the agreement of France and Canada to impose similar trade bans. France took the lead last year on recognition of Palestine; this year, it is the turn of the UK to lead on following through on the consequences of that recognition.
Paris appears to have been persuaded by the UK to stop waiting for the EU to reach an agreement on collective action, since it seemed unlikely the opposition in Germany and indifference in parts of the European Commission would end. A group of countries imposing the trade ban together of course makes Israeli reprisals harder, and serves to underline Israel’s isolation.
The perceived weaknesses are obvious.
Miliband still left it to the international courts to determine whether a genocide occurred in Gaza, something that might not be adjudicated for at least five years. There was mounting evidence of ethnic cleansing in Gaza, he said, but again it was for the courts to determine if that was so.
There is no pledge to protect the international court of justice or the international criminal court from the US drive to render them inoperable. As to a UK arms sales ban, an exemption continues for the sale of parts for F35 jet planes to the main US spares pool – all on the basis the F-35 jets “do not materially support the occupation” – the criteria the foreign secretary has set.
Miliband specifically condemned the Boycott, Disinvestment and Sanctions movement because it targets the whole Israeli economy and not just the occupied territories. The secondary legislation required to make sanctions as wide as envisaged may take as long as nine months, contrasting with the speed with which sanctions were enforced against Russia over the annexation of Crimea.
But to focus solely on what is absent is to miss the moment. Duncan, for instance, said: “At last, in the face of state-backed terrorism by illegal settlers, the British government has shown unprecedented moral courage.”
There is a risk of a cascading backlash from the White House – but Trump, trapped in a political labyrinth after he was persuaded to attack Iran, has little reason to come to Benjamin Netanyahu’s aid. Miliband has taken a risk, but after more than 70,000 deaths in Gaza, and the two-state solution on life support, it may be time to dare.

Trump, Putin hold ‘frank’ phone call as US revives Ukraine peace efforts
The phone call comes after US special envoys travelled to Russia and Ukraine to discuss ‘a proposal to end the war’.
United States President Donald Trump has spoken by phone with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin as the White House ramps up efforts to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
On Tuesday, Yury Ushakov, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser, described the two leaders as having a “constructive and quite frank” hour-long conversation.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Witkoff and Kushner will travel to ‘end’ Russia’s war in Ukraine: Trump
- list 2 of 3Witkoff says peace talks have been ‘very meaningful’ in Ukraine
- list 3 of 3At least five people killed in Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s Kyiv
According to Ushakov, Putin talked with Trump about the ongoing war in Ukraine and Russia’s plans to advance its military goals on the battlefield.
“An objective and thorough analysis of the ongoing special military operation and generally our view of prospective battlefield advances and the achievement of the special military operation’s goals and tasks was given,” Ushakov said.
The adviser added that Putin pushed back against rising concern that Russia could launch future attacks in Europe, including on NATO members.
“It was underlined that we don’t have any aggressive plans regarding Europe,” Ushakov said.
The White House did not return Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the reported call.
The phone call comes just days after US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss what Trump has described as “a proposal to end the war”, Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
Ushakov told reporters Putin and Trump “exchanged views on the outcome of the visits”, saying some “very good, worthwhile ideas” were presented.
After his Sunday meeting with the US envoys concluded, Zelenskyy thanked Trump for “allowing them to come” to Ukraine, despite the ongoing fighting, which was briefly paused for the negotiations.
“It is very important that the delegation has arrived to see us. We have been waiting a long time for Steve and Jared, Witkoff and Kushner,” Zelenskyy said.
“To us, it is very important to do everything so that this war ends,” he added.
The meetings, despite being lauded by all sides, appeared to produce no breakthrough on ending the fighting. After the brief weekend truce, both countries resumed strikes.
Officials in Ukraine said Russian attacks on Tuesday morning killed at least five civilians and wounded 25 others in Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Russian officials reported three people killed in the Bryansk and Kursk regions, with 13 others wounded. Ukrainian attacks on Russian-annexed Crimea also killed approximately five people, according to local authorities.
The war began in February 2022, after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, considered the breadbasket of Europe.
Trump has made ending the war a priority of his second administration, pledging on the campaign trail that he could achieve a settlement within 24 hours.
He later backtracked on that claim, calling it an exaggeration. Faced with reports that certain US munitions stocks are dwindling, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukraine for putting a drain on the country’s missile supplies and finances — though critics point to US actions against Iran as a major factor.
While Trump has had a rocky relationship with Ukraine and its president, he has cultivated a close relationship with Putin, saying they went through “a hell of a lot” together.
Last year, Trump invited him to Alaska for his first visit on US soil since 2015.
The Trump administration has faced criticism for seeking to end the war in Ukraine without fully involving Ukrainian and European officials. Trump and Zelenskyy are expected to meet later in the month, according to Ukrainian officials.

Singapore man Malone Lam pleads guilty after massive US bitcoin heist and spending spree
The 22-year-old helped launder the stolen funds, then used the money to buy sports cars, rent mansions and spend millions at nightclubs
A 22-year-old man pleaded guilty on Tuesday to teaming up with friends to steal nearly a quarter-billion dollars in bitcoin from a Washington resident – one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts in US history – and then embarking on a wild spending spree with the laundered proceeds.
Malone Lam, an eighth-grade dropout who came to the US from Singapore, faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years after pleading guilty to a federal racketeering conspiracy charge. US District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly did not immediately schedule Lam’s sentencing hearing in Washington.
Lam was an organiser for a network of young men who carried out a string of cryptocurrency scams starting in 2023, prosecutors said.
He is one of 18 defendants charged in the case and is the 11th to plead guilty, but his conviction marks a breakthrough for the Justice Department’s investigation.
In August 2024, Lam and others used “social engineering” techniques to dupe the Washington man out of bitcoin worth over US$245 million.
Two of Lam’s alleged co-conspirators posed as representatives of Google and the Gemini cryptocurrency exchange to manipulate the man into giving them access to his Google Drive and revealing security codes that allowed Lam to siphon off over 4,100 bitcoin, according to prosecutors.

Colin from Accounts star leads new thriller set in bushranger country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Patrick Brammall and Brendan Cowell star in Aussie child abduction thriller Last Seen
Patrick Brammall wasn't sure he was the right fit for the new thriller TV show Last Seen.
"When I was cast, I was like, fantastic, amazing, what a role'," Brammall tells ABC Radio National's The Screen Show. "But 5 per cent of me was going, 'I think they made a mistake'."
It's not an unusual feeling for the actor, who is perhaps best known for his roles in Offspring and ABC TV supernatural drama Glitch, and as the co-creator and star, with his wife Harriet Dyer, of the internationally lauded comedy Colin from Accounts.
"It's important that doubt is there because you're required to put it all on the line every time you embody a character — especially so for me with this role, which is really vulnerable," he says.
In Last Seen, Brammall plays Ian, an alcoholic emergency dispatcher and former police officer trapped by grief at the disappearance of his daughter, Maggie, 11 years ago.
When the remains of a girl are discovered near where he lives on the Victorian coast, Ian seems to finally be about to find closure.
Instead, the discovery pits Ian in opposition to the reclusive fundamentalist Henry (Brendan Cowell), who has a 14-year-old daughter of his own.
It's a return for Brammall to a more dramatic mode after a year that has seen him play Anne Hathaway's love interest in the Devil Wears Prada sequel and wrap up the final season of Colin from Accounts.
Brammall and Dyer were even writing the season, its third, while he was filming Last Seen in regional Victoria in early 2025.
"It was a great relief to inhabit that world as opposed to this world," he says.
"[But] I don't approach comedy any differently than I approach drama. It's not like, here's a different style.
"The tone is all embedded in the writing. If it's written well, it unlocks those things in you."
Laughs on set
The darkness of Last Seen — with its story of grief in the wake of child abduction, paired with high-intensity car chases and shoot-outs — might have made for a difficult experience on set.
But Brammall describes the shoot as joyful.
"We had the space and the grace to have these emotional and highly charged moments, but to let off steam there was a lot of laughter on set," he says.
Brendan Cowell, whose character Henry is devoted to protecting his feeble wife (English actor Maxine Peake) and sheltered daughter Sarah (newcomer Chloe Jean Lourdes), describes the atmosphere on set as reliant on mutual respect.
"I tend to have more fun on the darker [shows] because you need the humour and you need each other," he says. "We formed this kind of feral gang in a lot of ways."
Working with dark material is a "strange occupational hazard", he says.
"We have to live on the edge of our own emotions and experiences to access them. Our pain and our history and our experiences are our instruments.
"Every now and again, you dig into some father stuff or you find some rage that's kind of distressing, and you've just got to walk that off or let it pass."
Still, for Cowell, the grittiness of Henry isn't too far from other recent roles, which include the ruthless whale hunter Captain Scoresby in two Avatar movies and the titular down-and-out ex-rugby player in Plum, the TV series he adapted from his own novel.
"I was reading [the script for Last Seen] and I thought, 'I never get offered that role of the cop or the guy in the suit, the guy that has a proper job'," he says.
"But when I started reading Henry, I was like, 'No, I'm happy here'.
"I like trying to allow audiences some access into how these kinds of characters operate and I try to make them likeable and understood."
Finding an international audience
The series reunited Brammall and Cowell with Australian screenwriter Kris Mrksa, who adapted the series from American author Ryan David Jahn's book The Dispatcher.
Mrksa was a writer on Glitch, and he and Cowell were both writers on the TV adaptation of Christos Tsiolkas's much-loved family epic The Slap.
Cowell credits the writer with coming up with the idea of transplanting the story from the American Midwest to regional Australia.
That makes it the first Apple TV show to be both made and entirely shot in Australia.
"I think it was [Mrksa] who said, 'Why not Australia?'" Cowell says. "We keep the scale, but it's in bushranger territory, with Aussie talent."
Thus, the show leans into Australian humour and "menace", he adds, but not so much as to isolate international viewers.
"For overseas projects, I've been asked to do my Australian accent, but 'well-read Australian, so we can understand what the hell you're saying'," Cowell says.
"I feel like we lent into [the Australianness] because it offers so much in a thriller."
Brammall understands Cowell's experience all too well, after three seasons of Colin from Accounts. He and Dyer resisted suggestions to change Australian slang — like saying "arvo" instead of afternoon — and just let the show "be what it is".
"I grew up exposed to American and British stuff and there's a lot of references I didn't get, but it didn't stop my enjoyment of those shows," he says.
"I think the more specific you can be, then potentially the more universal the appeal."
That theory is reflected in the growing international appetite for Australian-led stories, seen in the success of My Brilliant Career — which reached number two on Netflix's English-language TV chart last month — and homegrown comedies like Fisk and Colin from Accounts.
Brammall reckons Australian productions consistently hit the "quality of storytelling" needed to find a global audience but "it takes some help to expose it to the rest of the world".
"We don't all have to do a remake for the American market. We don't have to put subtitles on so much. We'll watch something from Ireland or Korea.
"But you do need to have the support."
Last Seen is streaming on Apple TV.

Iran seizes US autonomous underwater vehicle in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:29:38 UTC
03:29:38 KST

Iran seizes US autonomous underwater vehicle in Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN- Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Tuesday that it had seized an advanced US unmanned underwater vehicle at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the IRGC said its naval forces had captured one of the most advanced autonomous and “smart” underwater systems in the US fleet. Tehran said the vehicle had entered service with the US military in 2025 and that images of the captured platform would be released.
The reported seizure would represent a significant development in the increasingly contested undersea domain around the Strait of Hormuz, where autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly relevant to intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), seabed mapping, mine-countermeasure operations and monitoring of critical maritime infrastructure.
Iranian media identified the vehicle as Anduril’s Dive-LD, a large-displacement autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-endurance operations. Anduril’s published specifications describe the platform as approximately 5.8 meters long and capable of operating autonomously for up to 10 days and reaching depths of about 6,000 meters. The system has a modular payload architecture, allowing it to be configured for different mission sets and sensor packages.
The Dive-LD is designed for missions including hydrographic surveying, intelligence collection, mine warfare, seabed reconnaissance, and inspection of subsea infrastructure such as pipelines and communications cables. Its deep-diving capability and modular architecture are intended to provide persistent undersea access without exposing a crewed platform to the operational risks associated with contested waters.
The US Navy received its first Dive-LD in April 2025 for Unmanned Undersea Vehicle Squadron 1, which develops and operates autonomous underwater systems for ISR and other naval missions.
The reported capture comes amid heightened military tensions in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime chokepoint through which a substantial share of global energy supplies normally passes.
The incident could offer Iran access to sensitive information on an advanced US autonomous undersea platform, including its sensors, navigation architecture, communications systems, and mission-planning capabilities—making the reported seizure potentially significant beyond the immediate tactical episode.

OpenAI says AI model solved one of mathematics' Millennium Prize Problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:29:25 UTC
03:29:25 KST

Seyit Kurt
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
OpenAI said on Tuesday that an unreleased artificial intelligence model has solved the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of mathematics' seven famed Millennium Prize Problems.
The company said the model took 88 hours to produce the solution, deploying as many as 10,000 AI agents working in parallel, in what could mark one of the most significant demonstrations yet of AI's growing ability to tackle advanced mathematical research.
The Navier-Stokes problem concerns equations used to describe the motion of fluids such as water and air, and asks, broadly, whether their solutions always remain well-behaved or can develop singularities under certain conditions.
OpenAI's proof claims to demonstrate such a breakdown, or "blowup," providing an answer to a problem that has remained unresolved for decades.
The problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems designated by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, with a $1 million prize offered for a correct solution to each. Only one of the seven had previously been solved.
OpenAI also released a paper detailing its proposed solution, including a proof written in Lean, a programming language and theorem-proving system used to formally verify mathematical arguments.
The claim, however, will require scrutiny by the wider mathematical community before the problem can be considered definitively settled.
The announcement comes amid a dispute about parallel research by New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpoge, a mathematician working at rival AI company Anthropic. OpenAI acknowledged that it intensified its work on the problem after learning that other mathematicians were pursuing a similar direction, but said it had not seen their work.
The development highlights the rapidly expanding role of AI in higher mathematics, after AI systems in the last year solved several longstanding problems that had resisted mathematicians for years or decades.

Belgian students continue to struggle with basic skills, PISA results show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:26:55 UTC
03:26:55 KST

Melike Pala
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Belgian students continue to struggle with basic skills in reading, mathematics and science, according to the latest results of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) released Tuesday.
The assessment shows a continued decline in student performance, particularly in reading and mathematics, with significant differences between Belgium's language communities and students from different socioeconomic backgrounds.
Until 2013, the Flanders region had more top-performing students in mathematics than low-performing students.
The balance has since been reversed, with roughly one in four students now failing to reach the basic level.
In Flanders, 29.4% failed to reach the basic proficiency level in reading comprehension. The figure stood at 25.6% in mathematics, and 22.6% in science.
The results also highlighted a persistent socioeconomic divide.
Around one in three Flemish students from a disadvantaged socioeconomic background was classified as a low achiever, compared with one in 10 students from a more privileged background.
Students in the French-speaking community performed around the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development average in reading, mathematics and science.
Their results, however, remain considerably below those recorded in Flanders.
Flanders and the French-speaking community have experienced a decline in performance in the last 15 years.
While Flanders remains among the top 20 countries, the French-speaking community ranks approximately 10 places lower.

UK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:25:01 UTC
03:25:01 KST

Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.
The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.
Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.
Talks with Google and Apple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday.
Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required.
“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation.
Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.”
Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side.
Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves.
However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”.
Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.”
Last year the IWF said a quarter of the images or videos of CSAM it recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period.
One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime minister was to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market.
The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent.
“Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.”
Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”.
Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”.
An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos.
“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”
