Australia proposes ‘opt out’ legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

Australia has proposed legislation that would allow social media users to opt out of platforms’ algorithms, a potentially far-reaching step that deepens regulatory efforts worldwide to rein in Big Tech and limit online harm.
Under the Labor government’s draft Digital Duty of Care bill released yesterday, social media users would be able to block content suggested by algorithms, and instead choose the material they want in their feeds.
The proposal opens up a new domestic battleground with Instagram and Facebook-owner Meta Platforms Inc, TikTok and other platform operators. The country’s world-first social media ban for under-16s — which went into effect late last year — was quickly followed by governments around the world adopting similar restrictions.
Photo: EPA
Meta declined to comment on Australia’s proposal, while representatives for TikTok and Snap Inc did not immediately reply to e-mails.
Regulators are increasingly targeting what they perceive as the addictive design of the platforms. Last month, Meta agreed to pay up to US$18 billion in landmark settlements to resolve social media claims from US states.
Key parts of that deal require the company to put new guardrails on its platforms, including restricting how much time young people can scroll and preventing them from switching off certain safety settings without parental consent.
“There’s been some seismic cases in the past few weeks,” Australian Minister for Communications Anika Wells said at a press conference yesterday.
“This is our contribution,” she said.
The duty-of-care approach aims to force technology companies to make their products safe by design, imposing fresh burdens on the operating models of major platforms. Breaches of Australia’s proposed law could be penalized by up to A$109.2 million (US$79 million), the government said.
The EU has been investigating claims that Meta’s products are addictive to children, as the bloc increases regulatory pressure on the US social media company.
While details on implementation are still unclear and will be critical in assessing the potential impact, Australia’s move appears to be “a continuation of a trend rather than a completely novel innovation,” said Ewan Lusty, a Singapore-based partner at political and regulatory consultancy Flint Global.
“There is a global shift toward governments seeking to empower users and provide them with more control over how they interact with digital services, including the option to restrict personalization elements,” he said. “Digital services are also taking important steps and providing users with more granular controls over their experience.”
Australia’s draft legislation requires platform owners to send a notification to new and existing users offering them a choice over their default feed.
Other features of the Digital Duty of Care include: Digital services like online games, apps and AI chatbots would be required to protect under-18s from design features that have negative behavioral impacts, such as addictive features or those that can have an effect on a young person’s self-esteem
Such services will also be required to protect under-18s from: content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; content that promotes hostile ideas about women and gender equality; pornography; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental distress, including abuse and bullying

Too many options obscuring languages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

As the new school year begins, the number of students choosing Taiwan Sign Language (TSL) for their local-language classes has continued to rise. In some schools, more than 40 percent of students have reportedly chosen TSL. In elementary schools, students can choose to study other languages such as Vietnamese and Indonesian. The overall proportion of students choosing these languages remains low, but the growing number of options might risk obscuring the purpose of local-language education all in the name of respecting diversity.
Local-language classes are distinct from general language courses; they are intended to revitalize the languages of Taiwan that declined as a result of the Mandarin-only language policy implemented by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) regime. The current system seems to have lost sight of that goal.
Taiwan is linguistically diverse, but its languages have different roles and functions. Taiwanese served as a lingua franca across ethnic groups and regions, while Hakka and indigenous languages are associated with particular communities and geographic areas. They should not all be treated under the same system.
Today, sign language and the heritage languages of immigrant families have been placed in the same pool of language electives as local languages, from which students can choose. Does this really serve the revitalization of Taiwan’s local languages, or is it just creating a language buffet under the thinking that more options equals more progress?
Sign language and the languages spoken at home for children from immigrant families should be protected, but this should be planned independently and according to their respective communication needs and educational objectives.
More students are choosing to study sign language not out of a practical need, which is not the point of local language revitalization. The Southeast Asian languages offered as options are already official languages of their respective countries; they are not endangered, nor are they languages of Taiwan.
The need to offer them should be assessed in light of Taiwan’s broader needs and they should be incorporated as part of a foreign-language education distinct from local-language classes.
Local-language education originally sought to restore Taiwan’s multilingual environment, but the dominance of Mandarin remains unchanged. Those languages whose place in the education system is being “diversified” are precisely those that are most vulnerable.
Given that these languages are the only ones designated as “local,” would the Ministry of Education be willing to acknowledge Mandarin Chinese to be a foreign language? Or to answer why a foreign language enjoys such an advantage in teaching hours and assessment?
Taiwan’s language education system is in need of a comprehensive review.
Languages should be classified according to their status, geographic use and revitalization needs as common languages, regional languages, foreign languages or second foreign languages, with curricula then designed accordingly.
Otherwise, we might end up with an increasingly rich list of language choices, but with the Taiwanese languages in genuine need of being passed on disappearing even more rapidly under a system of “diversification.”
Khoo Hui-lu is a professor of the Department of Taiwan Culture, Languages and Literature at National Taiwan Normal University.

Ukraine’s new Hryfon Zakhid runs the whole drone chain on one screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

Ukraine's Operational Command West has built an app that lets a single operator route drone strikes from a phone or tablet, in real time and without radio. The system, called Hryfon Zakhid, speeds the flow of tasks to drone crews and helps hide their positions from Russian reconnaissance, soldiers at the command's training center told Suspilne Rivne.
Drone war is won on the speed of the kill chain — the minutes between spotting a target and hitting it. The system compresses the decision and covers Ukrainian troops from Russian electronic reconnaissance. Hryfon Zakhid is a regional take on the digitization that Ukraine has pushed nationally with systems like DELTA, which has shortened the path from detection to strike from roughly 20 minutes to a few.
One operator runs the whole chain
The app replaces the manual scramble of calling crews up one by one.
"It is a very mobile program, and it speeds up decision-making," said Volodymyr Shvediuk, commander of the Operational Command West troops.
The military can share it with everyone who wants it — air-assault troops, marines, and army corps.
"You do not have to tell anyone, 'Petro, Vasyl, get ready.' One operator controls everything," he explained.
The program runs on a smartphone, tablet, or computer, and works in real time without radio, according to a training-platoon commander with the callsign Vegas.
The board turns recon into strikes
A soldier with the callsign Wolf described the system's workflow.
"A task comes to me from reconnaissance, and we send it to the striker's board. A target appears, and I choose the crew in the zone to work it," he said.
Then he chose which drone would carry out the strike and sent it.
"The board shows everything — where to fly, what to hit, and it even adds photos if we do not know which window to fly into," the Wolf adds.

Leaked docs allege a wide pattern of Chinese bribery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:40 UTC
01:41:40 KST

A national security official yesterday said that allegedly leaked Chinese documents indicated Beijing put a price on efforts to block Taiwan from the World Health Assembly (WHA).
National Security Council adviser Alex Huang (黃重諺) made the remarks in an interview with the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) when asked about suspected Chinese diplomatic documents leaked online that allegedly shows Beijing offered Micronesia 1 million yuan (US$149,002) to cover the cost of purchasing a vehicle in exchange for the Pacific island nation blocking Taiwan’s participation in the WHA.
The leaked documents allege to show a diplomatic note from the Chinese embassy in Micronesia in March asking the island nation to sign a letter supporting Beijing’s stance on Taiwan at the WHA.
Photo: Reuters
On April 8, Micronesia reportedly wrote to WHO Secretary-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, asking that Taiwan-related issues not be discussed.
The WHA subsequently rejected Taiwan’s proposal in May.
On June 10, China sent a 1 million yuan “grant” to Micronesia for the ostensible use of purchasing a vehicle for official receptions, and Micronesia replied on June 23 accepting the funding.
The documents also show the African Union accepted a 200 million yuan “renovation grant” from China in April, then sought an additional US$50 million to build a new headquarters and recreation center.
Following Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi’s (王毅) visit to Africa earlier this year, Taiwan faced a number of complications, including the withdrawal of flight clearance for President William Lai’s (賴清德) chartered aircraft in April, Kenya blocking of Taiwan’s participation in a UN ocean conference in June, Morocco suspending visa issuance in July and Uganda withholding passports last month.
Huang said in the interview that the allegedly leaked documents closely match intelligence held by Taiwan in terms of the officials’ titles, narrative and timeline, adding that they could “to some extent be considered highly credible.”
He said the documents focus on two major sets of activities. One involves Beijing’s efforts to rally Pacific island nations to sign a joint letter to the WHO calling for Taiwan to be excluded and for Taiwan-related issues not to be discussed.
The arrangements appear to be “almost something that can be priced,” Huang said, with the number of signatories on the letter roughly corresponding to how much money would need to be spent.
The other set of allegedly leaked documents focuses on the African Union.
Huang said that “some of what we saw came as a shock.”
Lai was scheduled to visit Taiwan’s diplomatic ally Eswatini on April 22, but the trip was canceled after three African Union member states along the planned flight route withdrew overflight clearance.
On the same day the Presidential Office announced the cancelation, the African Union wrote to China requesting another round of funding.
Huang said the strikingly coincidental timing reveals the pattern of Beijing’s operations.
China’s efforts to pressure Taiwan have never stopped, with Beijing constantly adopting new tactics, Huang said.
Stressing that friendships bought with money would not stand the test of time, Huang said that once recipient countries fall into Beijing’s trap and their overall national strength comes under its influence, China gains greater control over international resources that can be used to pressure other countries.
Huang said that China does not have unlimited resources to sustain an endless campaign of dollar diplomacy.
Moreover, if Beijing no longer respects the international order, he asked: “How can other countries expect [China] to honor its commitments to them?”

16:41:39 UTC
01:41:39 KST

Refits to Chinese nuclear submarines to carry JL-3 intercontinental ballistic missiles would put much of the US in striking distance, Taiwanese defense analysts said in a report commissioned by the Mainland Affairs Council.
Researchers from National Defense University’s Graduate Institute of China Military Affairs Studies said that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) in July test-fired a missile with a training warhead.
Chinese state media reported without elaborating that a PLAN nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN) launched a missile with a training warhead, which accurately hit the designated target area in the Pacific, the report said.
Photo: AFP
The launch was a rare display of the PLAN’s nuclear might, despite the taciturn announcement from Beijing, it said.
Taiwan and the US tracked the ballistic missile’s trajectory during its descent and concluded that the weapon, a JL-2 intercontinental ballistic missile, splashed down in international waters near Nauru in the southern Pacific, the report said.
Several Pacific nations have protested China’s missile test, as the warhead fell close to their exclusive economic zones, it said.
Citing Ministry of National Defense officials and military officers’ remarks at a Legislative Yuan meeting, the report said Taiwan was able to confirm that the Chinese SSBN launched the missile from the surface and not underwater.
The launch, which was tracked jointly by the Taiwanese and US intelligence organs, took place in the waters off southern Guangdong, they added.
The JL-2, a sub-launched missile with an effective range of about 6,000km to 7,000km, is widely used in the PLAN’s SSBN fleet, the report said.
Chinese state-affiliated media withheld almost all technical information about the launch, declining to identify the submarine or missile involved, its location at the time of launch, or the coordinates of the target, it said.
The vagueness of Beijing’s release about the live-fire test was intended to strengthen its deterrence posture without giving away information about its capabilities, it said.
The report said that the PLAN is refitting its Type-094 SSBNs to carry the newer JL-3 ballistic missiles.
US Strategic Command former commander Anthony Cotton testified in the US Congress that Beijing is treating the JL-3 retrofit, with the missile’s 10,000km range, as a top priority, the report said.
A PLAN SSBN equipped with JL-3s would be able to launch nuclear strikes at most of the continental US from the relative safety of China’s littoral waters, it said, a feat the JL-2 cannot replicate.
Taiwanese intelligence analysis indicated that the launch’s purpose was to certify the submarine’s capability to deploy the JL-2, not to unveil a new capability to the world, it said.
This could indicate that the PLAN has not yet fully certified the use of JL-3, suggesting that it is not deemed a fully operational weapon, the report said.
The PLAN continues improvement of the seaborne leg of its nuclear triad, including construction of next-generation vessels, developing improved missiles and holding its established patrol perimeters, it said.
The Chinese SSBN fired the test missile from the northern part of the South China Sea, which is consistent with the PLAN’s established pattern of deploying SSBN patrols out of the Hainan naval base.
The PLAN test launch has ramifications for regional security, highlighting inadequacy in US-China communication mechanisms regarding nuclear weapon tests, it said.
Washington and its NATO allies have formally acknowledged that the lack of communication channels are a risk that could lead to dangerous misunderstandings, the report said.
In addition, Pacific nations and neighbors were alarmed by the southern drift of the PLAN’s missile tests, which crossed the boundaries of the region’s nuclear-test free area, it said.
Taipei should carefully monitor the changes in Beijing’s relationship with Pacific nations, the report said.

Taisun files suit over cooking oil case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:39 UTC
01:41:39 KST

Taisun Enterprise Co (泰山企業) yesterday filed a lawsuit against Central Union Oil Corp (中聯油脂) and three other companies, seeking NT$1 billion (US$31.71 million) in joint compensation over a food safety scandal involving Central Union-produced oil with excessive levels of the carcinogen benzo[a]pyrene (BaP).
The Taichung District Prosecutors’ Office on Aug. 18 indicted Central Union Oil, Taisun, Fwusow Industry Co (福壽實業) and Formosa Oilseed Processing Co (福懋油脂), as well as individuals, with the charges ranging from contraventions of the Act Governing Food Safety and Sanitation (食品安全衛生管理法) to forgery and fraud related to alleged distribution of tainted cooking oil.
The key issue to determine responsibility is when the information about abnormal BaP levels emerged and whether it was promptly passed on, Taisun lawyer Chen Cheng-hsi (陳政熙) said.
Photo courtesy of Taisun Enterprise Co
Namchow Oil and Fat Co (南僑油脂事業股份) received three test reports on May 13, May 22 and June 4 showing excessive BaP levels, but only privately notified Fwusow, Chen said, adding that neither company fulfilled its obligation to promptly report the findings to authorities.
Fwusow also failed to promptly notify authorities after learning of abnormal test results on May 18, he added.
Comparing the information in the indictment with Namchow’s public statements shows significant differences in when the companies obtained information, how much they knew and how they responded, he said.
The firms’ failure to report the problem meant the tainted oil was not identified and taken off shelves for two months, the lawyer said.
Companies, including Taisun, continued to use the oil without knowing there was a problem, later leading to major losses from product recalls, inventory disposal, consumer compensation, reduced profits and damage to their reputations, he said, adding that Taisun’s losses were about NT$1 billion.
Taisun initially believed that as long as a product bearing its name was on the market, it had a responsibility to consumers, Taisun marketing vice president Niu An-tse (鈕安澤) said.
However, while handling consumer complaints and during the confidential investigation, the firm did not know when other companies had discovered problems in their supply chains, Niu said.
After the indictment was released, Taisun compared it with statements from Fwusow and other companies and news reports, as well as its own test results from April and May, and filed a lawsuit against the companies to clarify responsibility, she said.
Taisun received the same Central Union Oil soybean oil as Namchow on April 8 and 9, had its own products tested by Switzerland-based SGS on April 10 and received passing results on April 21, giving it no reason to believe its products were unsafe, the company said.
If Namchow had disclosed the abnormal test results when they were first detected in the middle of May, Central Union Oil and other companies in the supply chain could have begun tracing the source, conducting additional tests and managing the risks, it said.
Mid-May to mid-June was a crucial period for containing the problem, but the delayed sharing of information postponed supply-chain tracing and risk controls, worsening the company’s loses, Taisun added.
The courts should determine the responsibility of Central Union Oil, Fwusow, Namchow and Formosa Oilseed based on when they learned of the problem and how promptly they reported it, Taisun said.
Additional reporting by CNA

Saudi Arabia vows response as Houthis hit oil sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:36 UTC
01:41:36 KST

Saudi Arabia yesterday threatened to hit back after a wave of missiles from Yemen’s Houthis set oil facilities ablaze and wounded dozens, the Iran-backed rebels’ heaviest attack in years.
The overnight attacks caused “temporary” shutdowns at oil sites and left 73 injured, Saudi authorities said, a reminder of the danger posed by the group across the southern Saudi border.
Fighting between the Tehran-supported Houthis and Saudi forces has reignited after a four-year truce collapsed in July, months into the Middle East war between the US and Iran.
Photo: EPA
Hundreds have died over the past few days in clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the mouth of the vital Red Sea shipping route.
The Houthi attacks on energy facilities are likely to increase upward pressure on oil prices, which have spiked since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, slowing Gulf shipments to a trickle.
Saudi Arabia would “take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty,” a foreign ministry statement said, demanding a halt to the Houthi strikes and their attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis fired dozens of ballistic missiles, their military spokesman said.
They hit Abha International Airport, King Khalid air base and facilities belonging to state oil giant Aramco in Abha and Jizan, the rebels’ official media said.
Jizan, on the Red Sea coast just north of Saudi’s Yemen border, has one of the country’s biggest oil refineries with a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day.
According to maritime tracking company Kpler, it was out of action for several weeks until at least Aug. 20 following Houthi attacks.
The latest attacks came after the rebels accused Riyadh on Monday of a prison attack that killed 11 people and left 20 inmates missing, the rebels’ al-Masirah TV channel said.
Grim images from the scene showed rescuers digging in the rubble with their bare hands and carrying bodies wrapped in blankets.
The Houthis triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen’s civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
They have also been attacking Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, a vital export route since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz as part of its war with the US.
The Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting the Houthis on the government’s behalf since 2015, also said it would respond to the latest attacks.
The coalition’s Joint Forces Command will “take all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat and neutralize its danger,” a statement said.

Taiwan bags seven medals at International AI Olympiad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:35 UTC
01:41:35 KST

Taiwanese senior high school students won three silver and four bronze medals at the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI), according to National Central University (NCU), which organized Team Taiwan.
The third edition of the competition was held in Astana, Kazakhstan, from Aug. 2 to 8, attracting 466 students from 108 countries and regions, NCU said in a news release yesterday.
The university’s Department of Computer Science and Information Engineering selected and trained eight students to represent Taiwan at the competition with subsidies from the K-12 Education Administration under the Ministry of Education.
Photo courtesy of National Central University
Contestants in the individual contest were required to complete up to six tasks that tested their ability to apply AI tools and machine learning to solve real-world problems, the IOAI program booklet said.
Gold medals were awarded to the top 37 contestants in the individual contest. Silver medals went to the next 72 participants, while bronze medals were awarded to the next 110 contestants.
The three silver medalists from Taiwan were Hung Chun-jui (洪鈞睿), a student at Taichung Municipal Taichung First Senior High School, who placed 44th overall; Wen En-han (溫恩翰), from Taipei Municipal Zhonglun High School, who placed 47th; and Wang Hung-min (王泓閔), from Tainan First Senior High School, who placed 97th.
The four bronze medals were won by Yen Kang-yu (顏康宇), a student at Kaohsiung Municipal Kaohsiung Senior High School, who placed 113th overall; Huang Pin-hsun (黃品薰), from Kaohsiung Municipal Kaohsiung Girls’ Senior High School, who placed 125th; Hsieh Meng-shan (謝孟杉), from Taipei’s non-school-based experimental education program, who placed 156th; and Chiu Yen-sung (邱彥淞) from Taipei Chingshin Academy High School, who placed 162nd.
NCU said this year’s IOAI was the second-largest international science Olympiad competition in terms of participants, after the International Mathematical Olympiad, with students from 108 countries and regions taking part.
The university said it plans to continue selecting and training promising AI talent to participate in international competitions.

Medical visits top 110,000 as flu epidemic spreads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:34 UTC
01:41:34 KST

The seasonal flu has entered an epidemic period, with more than 110,000 medical visits, 19 deaths and 105 severe cases reported last week, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
The centers also reported the youngest severe COVID-19 case on record in Taiwan and two new cases of acute hepatitis C linked to a cluster in New Taipei City.
Influenza and COVID-19 viruses were the most common respiratory pathogen spreading locally in the past four weeks, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Director Guo Hung-wei (郭宏偉) said, adding that influenza A(H1N1) was the dominant flu strain detected.
Photo: CNA
There were 115,136 medical visits for flu-like illnesses from Aug. 30 to Saturday last week, 11.2 percent of which were emergency cases, surpassing the epidemic threshold of 11 percent, he said.
“We have entered the flu epidemic period,” he said.
A total of 105 severe flu cases and 19 flu-related deaths were confirmed between Tuesday last week and Monday, and more than 80 percent of them have or had chronic underlying conditions, he said.
As for COVID-19, there were 20,199 medical visits from Aug. 30 to Saturday last week, slightly lower than the week before, but still at a relatively high level, he said, adding that 73 severe cases and 15 deaths were confirmed between Tuesday last week and Monday.
Among the severe COVID-19 cases was a less than month-old baby who does not have underlying health conditions, and is not eligible for vaccination, making it the youngest severe case on record, CDC physician Lin Yung-ching (林詠青) said.
The boy had a mild fever and nose congestion late last month and was taken to see a doctor the next day, but as his symptoms persisted, he was hospitalized this month and later transferred to an intensive care unit when he experienced difficulty breathing and respiratory distress, and was confirmed to have pneumonia, he said.
Contact tracing found that the boy had been exposed to a person who has COVID-19, Lin added.
CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said that medical visits for flu-like illness last week was the highest of the same week in a decade, and is expected to continue increasing in the next four weeks.
While COVID-19 cases have dropped, severe cases and the number of deaths remain high, he added.
The CDC also provided an update on a cluster of confirmed acute viral hepatitis C cases traced to a clinic in New Taipei City, with two more cases identified through expanded testing, Lin Min-cheng said.
The CDC last week reported 11 confirmed cases who all received injections at the Antai Songhe Clinic (安泰淞鶴診所).
With the onset of symptoms occurring between Jan. 29 and Aug. 18, 1,118 people who received an injection at the clinic between July 1 last year and Aug. 27 are urged to get a blood test, it said.
As of Monday, 1,096 people have been notified and 353 have ben tested, Lin Min-cheng said.
Two were confirmed to have acute viral hepatitis C — a woman in her 60s who is asymptomatic and a man in his 50s who has symptoms including loss of appetite, dark urine and general fatigue, and has been hospitalized for treatment, he said.
Experts had estimated that the positivity rate would be about 5 percent, but so far only two had been confirmed among the 353 tested, which is an encouraging sign, he said, adding that testing and follow-ups were ongoing.
Symptoms of acute viral hepatitis C may vary, so the absence of symptoms does not necessarily mean no infection, he said, urging those who have been notified to get tested as soon as possible.

Taoyuan airport expects busy long weekend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:34 UTC
01:41:34 KST

Passenger traffic at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport could exceed 930,000 people over the Mid-Autumn Festival and Teacher’s Day travel period, the airport’s operator said yesterday.
Taoyuan International Airport Corp (TIAC) expects the peak holiday travel period to run from Sept. 24, the day before Mid-Autumn Festival, to Sept. 29, the day after Teachers’ Day, company senior vice president Tony Yu (余崇立) said.
“We estimate that more than 930,000 passengers would pass through Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport during the six-day period, with an average of approximately 155,000 passengers per day,” Yu said.
Photo: Chu Pei-hsiung, Taipei Times
Peak outbound passenger traffic is expected on Sept. 24 and 25, with an average of about 84,000 outbound of 160,000 total passengers per day, while inbound traffic was projected to peak on Sept. 28, when an estimated 85,000 inbound of 158,000 total passengers, he said.
Passenger volume in July and last month was 8.6 million, with a daily average of about 138,000 passengers, he said.
Daily average passenger volume in July and August last year exceeded 132,000 and 137,000 in 2019, he said.
This year’s single-day high for passenger traffic was 169,000 on Feb. 14, the first day of the Lunar New Year holiday, he said.
Passenger traffic at Taoyuan airport this year was more than 30 million as of July 31, Yu said, adding that it could reach 50 million by the end of this year.

How Taiwanese claimed its space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:32 UTC
01:41:32 KST

When the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary cataloged “Taiwanese,” it dated the word’s entry into written English to the mid-20th century, recording five distinct meanings: a native or inhabitant of Taiwan, the primary local language and the adjectives describing the place, its people and its speech. Equivalent multilayered entries appear in Random House Webster’s Unabridged Dictionary, The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language and Wiktionary. Yet behind these orderly lexicographical entries lies a broader linguistic evolution — one in which the precise boundary between a “dialect” and a “language” reflects changing global perspectives on identity and regional culture.
While dictionary entries aim for succinct clarity, their choices mirror shifting academic and geopolitical frameworks over time. Oxford defines Taiwanese as “the Chinese dialect of Taiwan.” Random House adds descriptive precision, recognizing it as “the Chinese dialect of Taiwan, a member of the Min group.” American Heritage states it is “the variety of Chinese spoken on Taiwan.” Wiktionary, drawing on crowdsourced academic contributions, offers the sharpest linguistic nuance, defining it as “the variant of Hokkien spoken in Taiwan, the native language of the Hoklo.”
[ Editor’s note: The Oxford entry also includes an adjective definition reading “of or pertaining to Taiwan, the Taiwanese or their dialect,” while American Heritage includes an adjective entry “of or relating to Taiwan or its peoples, languages or cultures. ”]
For a speech community seeking recognition, standard inclusion in major English reference works represents an important milestone. Dictionaries, by their nature, cannot offer encyclopedic coverage; they must extract core linguistic features and present them concisely. The recognition of “Taiwanese” as an ethnic and linguistic designation in the English-speaking world reflects a growing global acknowledgement of the nation’s unique linguistic reality.
Under traditional Chinese dialectology, Taiwanese was long categorized as a regional fangyan (方言, “dialect”), placing it in a subordinate relationship to standard Mandarin. Yet through the lens of modern Western linguistics, mutual intelligibility serves as the primary benchmark for distinguishing separate languages rather than mere dialects.
A monolingual Mandarin speaker cannot inherently understand a conversation in Taiwanese, just as a Spanish speaker cannot automatically follow German. By this structural criterion, Taiwanese, Mandarin and Hakka stand on equal footing as distinct, coordinate languages within the broader Sinitic family — a distinction increasingly recognized by international standards such as ISO language codes.
The English term “Taiwanese” neatly parallels the local phrase Tai-oan-ua (literally “Taiwan speech”), where the suffix “-ese” denotes the language of a specific people and geographical region. Naturally, the term exists alongside several related designations in the international lexicon. “Hokkien,” widely used across Southeast Asia and derived from the Southern Min pronunciation of Fujian, refers broadly to the speech of early diaspora communities.
Academics often prefer the broader academic term “Southern Min” (Minnan), while “Taiwanese Hokkien” specifies the localized linguistic branch that evolved on Taiwan over centuries of regional contact and cultural synthesis.
In the past few years, a new term has rapidly gained ground in domestic and international discourse: “Taigi,” the direct transliteration of the language’s native name Tai-gi Its increasing usage across digital platforms, arts and contemporary youth culture signals a conscious effort to name the language on its own terms. Rather than relying on foreign Anglicization or externally imposed regional labels, “Taigi” represents a shift toward self-defined linguistic identity.
Language is never static; it continuously records the social realities of those who speak it. As global reference works update their entries to reflect modern usage, the institutional evolution of terms like “Taiwanese” and “Taigi” highlights a fundamental truth: naming a language is ultimately an act of self-definition.
Hugo Tseng has a doctorate in linguistics, and is a lexicographer and former chair of the Soochow University English Department.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:29 UTC
01:41:29 KST

“OK.” You say it dozens of times a day without giving it a second thought. It slips effortlessly into text messages, office meetings and casual chats alike. Yet behind this surprisingly simple expression lies one of the most entertaining origin stories in the history of language.
The story begins in 1839, when a craze for creative abbreviations had swept through New England’s educated classes. Editors at the Boston Morning Post led the trend, though nearly all their inventions faded within months. One, however, proved far more enduring. On March 23, editor Charles Gordon Greene coined “OK” as a humorous abbreviation for “oll korrect” — a playful misspelling of “all correct” evidently intended to amuse.
What truly elevated “OK” to everyday usage, though, was a presidential election. In 1840, supporters of Martin Van Buren—nicknamed “Old Kinderhook” after his New York hometown — seized on “Vote for OK” as a campaign slogan, set up OK Clubs nationwide and popularized the accompanying hand gesture. Van Buren lost, but “OK” did not. Telegraph operators subsequently adopted it as a quick confirmation signal, circulating it across the continent.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
Part of OK’s lasting appeal lies in its remarkable neutrality. Imagine a friend says, “I signed us up for a 6am run tomorrow.” Reply with “Fantastic!” and you sound enthusiastic. Say “I suppose so,” and you sound reluctant. But a simple “OK” discloses nothing beyond consent. No other word in English manages the same trick.
From there, “OK” spread far beyond American borders, taking root in hundreds of languages. When astronaut Buzz Aldrin touched down on the Moon in 1969, among his first words were “OK, engine stop.” A humble editorial joke from a Boston newsroom had literally reached another world.
「OK。」你每天不假思索地說上數十次。它輕鬆地出現在簡訊、辦公會議和閒聊中。然而，在這個看似簡單的表達背後，卻藏著語言史上最有趣的起源故事之一。
這個故事始於1839年，當時一股創意縮寫詞的熱潮席捲了新英格蘭的知識階層。《波士頓早報》的編輯們引領了這股潮流，不過他們創造的大多數縮寫都在幾個月內消失了。然而，其中有一個特別歷久不衰。3月23日，編輯查爾斯．戈登．格林創造了「OK」這個幽默的縮寫，代表「oll korrect」──也就是故意把「all correct」拼錯，顯然是為了逗人發笑。
不過，真正讓「OK」進入日常用語的，是一場總統選舉。1840年，馬丁．范布倫——因其紐約故鄉而獲綽號「老金德霍克(Old Kinderhook)」——其支持者利用「投票給OK」作為競選口號，在全國成立OK俱樂部，並推廣與之搭配的手勢。雖然范布倫落選了，但「OK」沒有消失。後來，電報員採用它作為快速確認的訊號，使它傳遍整個美洲大陸。
OK能夠維持長久吸引力的部分原因，在於它驚人的中立性。想像一下，朋友說：「我幫我們報名了明天早上六點的跑步活動。」如果你回答「太棒了！」，聽起來會充滿熱情；如果你說「我想應該可以吧」，聽起來又有些不情願。但只要簡單說一句「OK」，除了表示同意之外，什麼情緒也不會洩露。英文裡沒有其他字能同樣做到這一點。
從那之後，「OK」傳播到美國以外的許多地方，並在數百種語言中扎根。1969年，當太空人巴茲．艾德林登陸月球時，他最早說出的話之一就是：「OK，引擎熄火。」波士頓新聞編輯室裡一個不起眼的玩笑，竟然真的抵達了另一個世界。
MORE INFORMATION
craze n. 狂熱；風潮
abbreviation n. 縮寫；簡稱
misspelling n. 拼字錯誤；拼錯的字
popularize v. 普及；推廣
confirmation n. 確認；證實
neutrality n. 中立；中性
astronaut n. 太空人
editorial adj. 編輯的；社論的
newsroom n. 新聞編輯室；報社編輯部
KEY VOCABULARY
1. entertaining adj. 有趣的；娛樂性的
The movie was so entertaining that the whole class stayed awake until the end.
那部電影非常有趣，所以全班一直清醒地看到最後。
2. invention n. 發明；創造
The invention of the washing machine changed life for many families.
洗衣機的發明改變了許多家庭的生活。
3. intend v. 打算；想要
Amy intends to join the art club after school and practice drawing every Tuesday.
艾美打算放學後加入美術社，並在每週二練習畫畫。
4. amuse v. 逗樂；使發笑
The clown used funny tricks to amuse the children during the school festival.
小丑在校慶時用有趣的把戲逗孩子們開心。
5. slogan n. 口號；標語
The team created a simple slogan to show school spirit during the sports event.
隊伍想出了一個簡單的口號，在運動會中展現學校精神。
6. telegraph n. 電報；電報機
Before phones were common, the telegraph helped people send important news across long distances.
在電話尚未普及前，電報幫助人們跨越長距離傳送重要消息。
7. circulate v. 傳播；流通
Fresh air must circulate in the room to keep the space comfortable and healthy.
新鮮空氣需要在房間裡流通，才能讓空間保持舒適與健康。
8. consent n. 同意；准許
The doctor needed the patient’s consent before starting the medical treatment.
醫生在開始治療前需要取得病人的同意。
9. literally adv. 真正地；確實地
Tom was so tired that he literally fell asleep while reading at the desk.
湯姆累到真的在書桌前看書時睡著了。

Several European cities are replacing traditional white streetlights with red lighting to reduce light pollution and protect wildlife. In Copenhagen’s suburb of Gladsaxe, red LED lights have been installed along roads and cycle paths near bat habitats. The lights are placed at intervals that create darker gaps, allowing light-sensitive animals to cross safely without being exposed to predators and still providing enough visibility for people. Studies have shown that white and green light can reduce bat activity, whereas red light has little to no effect. Studies conducted in the Netherlands found that light-sensitive bats remain active under red lighting.

16:41:29 UTC
01:41:29 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) yesterday said it received a report about three Taiwanese who have been arrested and indicted in Myanmar for alleged involvement in online fraud.
As part of efforts to crack down on telecom fraud, Myanmar on July 31 enacted the Anti-Online Scam Law, which is the government’s first major legislation imposing heavy penalties for perpetrators of online fraud, severe abuse in scam centers and cryptocurrency crimes, MOFA spokesman Hsiao Kuang-wei (蕭光偉) said.
“The law applies to foreign offenders, and violators face penalties that may include the death sentence,” he said.
Photo: screen grab from a MOFA livestream
The law states, people involved in telecom fraud would face severe criminal liability, rather than being prosecuted under lighter immigration laws or simply deported, Hsiao said.
Meanwhile, Thailand has enacted stricter entry, exit and immigration controls, such as the Prime Minister’s Office Regulation on Deportation, which went into effect on Aug. 28, he said.
Under the regulations, foreigners convicted of offenses carrying a prison sentence of five years or more, or who are convicted of illegal entry, overstaying their visa, working without a permit, operating illegal businesses or government document forgery would be deported upon completing their imprisonment and might be banned from re-entry, he said.
Thailand last week announced that it would reduce visa-free travel for nationals of 60 countries, including Taiwan, to 30 days from 60, Hsiao said, adding that the change takes effect on Tuesday next week.
The ministry reminded Taiwanese traveling to Thailand to stay informed of the latest entry regulations prior to departure and not to exploit visa-free privileges by engaging in illegal activities, he said.
The travel advisories are updated on the Bureau of Consular Affairs’ Web site, he added.
As combating overseas telecom fraud has become a regional consensus, some Southeast Asian countries have stepped up their efforts to crack down on transnational crime, he said.
The ministry urges people not to fall for promises of high payment, free airfare or free accommodation to engage in illegal activities overseas, which could result in judicial prosecution, Hsiao said.
“Taiwanese are obligated to abide by local laws of any country they visit,” he said.
People should cherish the hard-earned visa-free treatment Taiwan has with many countries and safeguard the nation’s international reputation.

President welcomes Quebecois parliamentary group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:26 UTC
01:41:26 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday welcomed the first Bloc Quebecois delegation to Taiwan and called for closer cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors and supply chain security.
The delegation, led by Yves-Francois Blanchet, a member of parliament and leader of Canada’s Bloc Quebecois, is the bloc’s first official delegation to Taiwan since the party’s founding in 1991, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
During the meeting with the delegation at the Presidential Office, Lai said that in November 2024, the Bloc Quebecois became the first party in the Canadian Parliament to introduce a motion countering China’s attempts to distort UN General Assembly Resolution 2758.
Photo: Screen grab from the Presidential Office’s Flickr page
In February, Blanchet called on the Canadian government to sign a Taiwan-Canada trade cooperation framework agreement.
Bloc MP Alexis Brunelle-Duceppe called on the government from the House Foreign Affairs Committee to ensure Canadian warships continue to transit the Taiwan Strait.
Lai expressed gratitude for the lawmakers’ repeated actions in parliament, which he said have shown the world that peace in the Taiwan Strait and Taiwan’s international participation are issues of concern to the international community.
Quebec is an important global hub for the aerospace industry, while Montreal is a major center for AI research, he said.
Lai said he looks forward to Taiwan and Quebec building closer partnerships in AI, semiconductors, aerospace, critical minerals, renewable energy and supply chain security.
Blanchet said the visit is historic, as it is the first time a delegation made up entirely of Quebec-based members of the House of Commons has visited Taiwan.
There are many areas in which Taiwan and Quebec can deepen exchanges and cooperation, he added.
He said the Bloc Quebecois would continue to speak up for the people of Taiwan in the Canadian parliament until all governments in the free world can act according to their conscience without being intimidated by China.
This would give Taiwan the opportunity to participate in multilateral mechanisms, showcase its strong economic capabilities and outstanding talent, and enjoy equal rights to freedom and security, he said.

Thieves steal ‘four’ works of art from Renoir museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:22 UTC
01:41:22 KST

Two thieves yesterday broke into a museum dedicated to French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir in southern France, stealing “four works of art,” one of which they dropped as they fled, a mayor said.
“This morning, two individuals broke into the Musee Renoir and stole four works of art,” Cagnes-sur-Mer Mayor Bryan Masson said.
“Spotted thanks to the town’s video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran,” he said, adding that his office estimated the value of the stolen works at 9 million euros (US$10.45 million).
Photo: AFP
The Musee Renoir opened in 1960 in the painter’s last home before his death in 1919.
Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes and nudes painted by the artist.
The mayor said it took just five minutes for the authorities to respond.
“The museum alarm went off at 5:48am. At 5:53am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene,” he said.
The theft comes less than a year after eight items valued at about US$100 million were stolen during a daylight robbery from the Louvre in Paris.
The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items have still not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond.

Eiffel Tower reopens after female staff row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:20 UTC
01:41:20 KST

The Eiffel Tower reopened yesterday after staff walked out over the removal of female colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group which later apologized.
SETE, the operating company that runs the Paris landmark, acknowledged that the Hindu delegation had requested the visit on Saturday be organized so as to limit “interactions with women” and said that “these conditions should not have been accepted.”
The Eiffel Tower, which says it receives nearly 7 million people a year, reopened yesterday morning, with visitors making their way through security checkpoints at the base.
Photo: AFP
The monument was closed on Monday, when SETE said it held a meeting between staff and management.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement apologized for “any pain or inconvenience caused” by the incident.
“To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower,” the organization wrote on X.
“Due to the size of our delegation, the visit was arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal operating hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others,” it said.
Eiffel Tower staff condemned “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit by the delegation.
“Instructions were given to female employees of the Eiffel Tower and to female employees of contractors to make themselves invisible in order to welcome this delegation,” the staff said in a statement, adding that they were shocked to have been put in such a situation.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present,” they said.
BAPS, which is close to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling conservative Hindu nationalist party, opened its first major temple in France on Sunday, near Paris.
BAPS spiritual leader Mahant Swami Maharaj, 93, consecrated it himself.
The BAPS claims a worldwide network of more than 1,300 temples, some of which have been inaugurated by Modi himself.
French Minister Delegate for Equality between Women and Men and for the Fight against Discriminations Aurore Berge voiced indignation after the Eiffel Tower incident.
“In France, we do not ask women to erase themselves,” she said.
Candidates in next year’s presidential election also weighed in.
Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen also criticized the incident, saying France would “never accept that women’s presence be ‘limited’.”
Gabriel Attal, a centrist rival to become head of state, said: “In France, no culture, no belief, no religion, nothing and no one can come and dictate to women what their place should be.”

EDITORIAL: Taiwan draws tech leaders closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:20 UTC
01:41:20 KST

Taiwan’s artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain is evolving from an original equipment manufacturing role into technology integration, driven by global technology giants stationing top-tier executives in Taiwan to accelerate technology development.
As AI technology advances, collaboration across diverse ecosystems is crucial because the complexity and societal impact of modern AI exceed what any individual enterprise, academic institution or single discipline can achieve.
“Collaboration” dominated the discourse at technology forums during the Semicon Taiwan trade show in Taipei last week. The consensus among many keynote speakers and senior technology executives is clear: The future of AI hinges not on isolated breakthroughs, but on radical collaboration.
While Silicon Valley tech giants such as Nvidia Corp craft the digital blueprints of AI, Taiwan turns these visions into reality through its world-class hardware manufacturing. With the acceleration of AI, cross-industry collaboration has become essential to mitigate risks early in the development process, where a single mistake can be financially devastating. Such localization could help shrink time to market.
To that end, Google plans to expand its Taiwan office space by 60 percent as local partners take on a growing role in developing the company’s AI infrastructure, Google senior vice president and chief technologist for AI and infrastructure Amin Vahdat, said last week.
Taiwanese chip designer MediaTek Inc helps design Google’s tensor processing unit, a custom application-specific integrated circuit to accelerate AI machine learning workloads, as the US technology giant seeks to reduce its dependence on Nvidia for AI chip supply and to cut the cost of ownership.
Carl Zeiss AG last week said it is expanding its local engineering team and assigning more technology and application engineers to Taiwan to promote “knowledge exchange.” The German company is ASML’s sole supplier of its extreme ultraviolet lithography optical systems, a critical component in chipmaking. It is a key technology used to make the world’s most advanced semiconductor chips, such as 2-nanometer chips.
Zeiss is developing an advanced inspection tool for next-generation copackaged optics technology, which is crucial to overcoming bandwidth and thermal issues in AI data centers. Zeiss is considering bringing this new optical inspection tool to Taiwan for on-site testing.
The company is also planning to build a semiconductor innovation center in Taiwan, which would minimize the company’s research-and-development team’s international travel, it said.
Merck Group, one of the world’s largest semiconductor material suppliers, is replicating this strategy to improve customer proximity and minimize service latency. Bing Han (韓冰), executive vice president of its global thin films business, is moving from California to Taiwan next month, highlighting the company’s decision to move senior technical and decisionmaking talent forward to Asia. The arrangement is designed to shorten the distance between technology development, customer validation and decisionmaking, Merck said, adding that Taiwan’s innovation and research investment would only grow. Han said he has visited Taiwan more than 50 times in the past few years.
As the number of companies globally capable of manufacturing the most advanced semiconductors is limited, and materials suppliers seeking to participate in cutting-edge process development cannot simply deliver products after receiving specifications — they must engage with customers earlier to jointly solve process challenges, Merck said, adding that speed, customer-centricity and enhanced internal collaboration are the key elements in the company’s latest restructuring drives.
These technology giants’ latest movies indicate that Taiwan is increasingly shifting toward a “heterogeneous” integration of AI technology, rather than simply being a manufacturing hub of AI hardware. As US AI chip supplier Nvidia and memory chipmaker Micron Technology Inc have built their presence in Taiwan and deepened on-site collaboration to integrate wafers, memory chips and cooling systems directly within local facilities for assembly and testing, it triggers a new shift of “anchoring localization” in Taiwan. Such on-site collaboration could be the optimal solution for the AI ecosystems to catch up with rapid AI chip migration and explosive growth of new AI models.
Taiwan is home to thousands of foreign residents who build careers, families and lives here. However, what happens when one of those residents loses the ability to prove his identity — not because he has broken Taiwan’s laws, but because his own government refuses to renew his passport? That is the situation my husband, Matteo (not his real name), a Nicaraguan national, has found himself in. After about three years of attempts to renew his passport, our future in Taiwan remains uncertain. It all comes back to Taiwan’s giant geopolitical issue: the multitude of countries cutting diplomatic ties with Taiwan
Well, sort of. Tomorrow is the seventy-fifth anniversary of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, signed by forty-nine nations on September 8, 1951. The Republic of China wasn’t one of them. Article 2(b) of the Treaty reads: “Japan renounces all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores.” So, tomorrow would be the Diamond Jubilee of Formosa’s freedom from Japanese sovereignty. As my good friend and former Examination Yuan President Yao Chia-wen (姚嘉文) voiced in these pages last year (“San Francisco treaty should be taught: adviser”, Sept. 7, 2025), the Japan peace treaty should be taught in all Taiwan schools to

For this reason, many were published on this page. Several months ago, this person contacted the Taipei Times and requested that the articles be unpublished. Unknown

01:41:17 KST

The most ambitious NFL season in history kicks off today with a Super Bowl rematch, an unprecedented global schedule and a clutch of contenders plotting to dethrone the Seattle Seahawks.
Seven months after Seattle defeated the New England Patriots to win their second Super Bowl crown, the two teams meet again to launch a sprawling campaign that would play out across seven countries in four continents. The Seahawks’ bid to retain their title will be tested by a crowded field of contenders that includes their NFC West divisional rivals, the Los Angeles Rams.
The Rams are chasing a repeat of their 2022 Super Bowl triumph in front of their home fans in Los Angeles, with the climactic game of the season returning to the SoFi Stadium in February next year.
Photo: AFP
Los Angeles have rolled the dice assembling a star-studded roster, adding Myles Garrett to an already fearsome defense while luring defensive great Aaron Donald out of retirement.
Yet the Rams are just one of a clutch of teams with realistic title ambitions.
The Denver Broncos look well placed to build on their promising last year’s campaign, when the team finished with a 14-3 record, but saw their playoff hopes derailed by an injury to quarterback Bo Nix.

One of the sub-plots of the season would see the NFL expand its global footprint as never before.

The NFL’s international roadshow will then roll into Rio de Janeiro on Sept. 27, when the Baltimore Ravens face the Dallas Cowboys at the iconic Maracana Stadium.
The now traditional slate of fixtures in London will be followed by the first ever NFL regular season game in France on Oct. 25, when the Pittsburgh Steelers face the New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France in Saint-Dennis, near Paris.
Other international games are scheduled to take place in Munich, Madrid and Mexico City.
The NFL’s embrace of overseas markets is only set to increase in the years ahead. The league has already voted to increase the number of games outside the US to 10 next year, while NFL commissioner Roger Goodell last month rekindled the age-old debate about the eventual establishment of an overseas franchise.
“At some point, there will be NFL teams outside the USA,” Goodell said in remarks to German media. “I have no doubt that this will happen one day.”
Peter O’Reilly, the NFL’s executive vice president of club business and international and league events, said the league had based its international expansion on “fan data, fan engagement and strategic opportunity in the market.”
“We look at where clubs are active and want to be,” O’Reilly told reporters. “That led us to Germany, then Brazil, then Spain, Ireland, France, now Australia, and then you’ve got a core set there.”
“We look at what could be next. What are parts of the world where there are opportunities, there is fandom, there is strategic opportunity?” he said. “And that’s how we work with it internally and with the ownership committee to see where we go next.”

Environmental Impact Assessment: From ‘Die-wan’ to a lifeboat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:14 UTC
01:41:14 KST

Releasing its latest demographic projections, the National Development Council last month predicted that Taiwan’s human population is set to shrink by 48 percent between now and 2075 — a collapse with undeniable economic fallout.
There’s no certainty that a smaller population will put less overall pressure on the country’s stressed environment (see “Will ‘peak people’ lead to a greener Taiwan?” in the Feb. 9, 2022 Taipei Times). But that doesn’t mean there won’t be opportunities to regain some of the exceptional biodiversity Taiwan enjoyed prior to the 20th century’s rapid industrialization and urbanization.
Taiwan has the expertise and wealth to restore ecosystems. And, thanks to rural depopulation, the country should soon have more land that can be given over to conservation or rewilding projects.
Photo courtesy of the Pheasant-Tailed Jacana Ecological Education Zone
Serious initiatives of this kind could ripple beyond Taiwan and have global value, exemplified by an ongoing project in the south of the country.
TAINAN’S JACANAS
Back in the late 1990s, when plans for Taiwan’s high-speed railway (HSR) were being finalized, environmentalists protested that the proposed route would likely destroy a key bird habitat.
Photo: Steven Crook
Ponds around Hulupi (葫蘆埤) in Tainan’s Guantian District (官田) were known to be the primary breeding grounds in Taiwan of the pheasant-tailed jacana (Hydrophasianus chirurgus), a bird notable both for its elegance and for its dwindling wild population. According to a 1998 survey, fewer than 50 jacanas remained.
Government agencies and conservation groups worked together to create what’s now known as the Pheasant-Tailed Jacana Ecological Education Zone (水雉生態教育園區). Getting the area’s farmers to stop putting out poisoned bait hasn’t been easy, but the local jacana population has stayed above 1,000 since 2016. What’s more, over the past decade bird enthusiasts in Kaohsiung’s Meinong District (美濃) have successfully created another jacana breeding ground (see “Not all gloom: two conservation success stories from Taiwan” in the June 22, 2022 Taipei Times). Before these interventions, the pheasant-tailed jacana was on the brink of disappearing.
The bird isn’t unique to Taiwan. Globally, the species isn’t immediately threatened; populations span South and Southeast Asia, with certain Indian wetlands supporting tens of thousands of individuals, earning it a “Least Concern” status on the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species.
Photo: Huang Ming-tang, Taipei Times
Yet local strongholds like Taiwan’s are becoming vital safeguards. Climate experts warn that parts of India may soon experience temperatures likely to kill birds as well as humans.
The pheasant-tailed jacana is more vulnerable to extreme heat than many avians, because their floating nests are exposed to the sun. Unlike most bird species, which practice biparental incubation, male pheasant-tailed jacanas handle 100 percent of the incubation and chick care. During the hottest hours, they must shield their eggs from solar heat; they cannot leave the nest to seek shade or cool down. If they get exhausted and dehydrated, they may succumb to heat stress.
Even if both parents survive, the chicks may not. Birds lack sweat glands, relying instead on respiratory evaporation (panting). When exposed to temperatures above 38 degrees Celsius, chicks younger than two weeks can quickly overheat or suffer irreversible organ damage.
Photo: Wang Hsiu-ting, Taipei Times
It wouldn’t take too many heatwaves across the Indian sub-continent — on top of the developmental pressures that are constantly chipping away at the species’ habitats in Vietnam and elsewhere — for Taiwan’s pheasant-tailed jacana strongholds to become critically important refugia (locations which support populations of a once more widespread species).
ANTEATERS, CATS AND TREES
Taiwan is already recognized as a modern refugium for the Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla), a critically endangered mammal species. Pangolin numbers elsewhere have crashed due to poaching for the animal’s meat (an expensive delicacy in China and Vietnam) and its scales (which are ground up into a traditional remedy for asthma and other ailments). In Taiwan, however, despite attacks by feral dogs, strong legal protection has helped the population grow from around 10,000 in 2004 to an estimated 15,000 in 2017.
Admirers of the clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa) say it may be possible to reintroduce the species to Taiwan’s foothills (see “Can Taiwan bring back the clouded leopard?” in the March 25, 2026 Taipei Times). A combination of ongoing deforestation and commercial poaching for its skin, teeth and bones has left the cat — categorized as “vulnerable” by the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species — embattled throughout China and Southeast Asia. But some of Taiwan’s indigenous people, for whom the clouded leopard has spiritual and cultural significance, have declared that they’d cherish the carnivore as a valued neighbor if it once again became part of their shared ecosystem.
Some of Taiwan’s most remarkable trees are gymnosperms, meaning their seeds aren’t enclosed inside ovaries or fruit, but exposed, often on the surface of cones. Among the country’s 28 native gymnosperms are the Taiwan catkin yew (Amentotaxus formosana) and the Taiwan cow-tail fir (Keteleeria davidiana var. formosana). The former is listed as a “valuable and rare” natural monument under the Cultural Heritage Preservation Act (文化資產保存法); the latter held that status until 2019, when the authorities decided that progress made by local scientists in inducing germination was sufficient to ensure the perpetuation of this species.
This success stands in stark contrast to the grim future facing gymnosperms in countries near Taiwan. A paper published June 20 in Communications Earth & Environment, alarmingly titled “Eastern and southern Asian gymnosperms are doomed to extinction under climate change,” warns that climate-driven habitat loss will leave “33 species facing possible extinction and 29 becoming highly vulnerable” by 2100.
One of the potential “long-term stable refugia for the survival of gymnosperm species” identified by the paper stretches across southern Taiwan. It includes Kenting National Park (墾丁國家公園) and Dawushan Nature Reserve (大武山自然保留區), but also large areas which, the paper acknowledges when discussing possible refugia throughout East and South Asia, “are currently dominated by land uses that are poorly compatible with biodiversity conservation [such as] cropland and urban land.”
Taiwan is no longer “Die-wan,” as it was branded in 1992 by the Environmental Investigation Agency. The UK-based campaigning group wanted to shame the country into cracking down on the rampant smuggling of rhino horns — which Taipei did after the US imposed limited trade sanctions. But if Taiwan is to become a lifeboat for multiple species, it’ll require sustained and purposeful government action. Demographic decline alone won’t create homes for these natural treasures.
Steven Crook, the author or co-author of four books about Taiwan, has been following environmental issues since he arrived in the country in 1991. He drives a hybrid and carries his own chopsticks. The views expressed here are his own.
A decade ago, Taiwanese television had an image problem. When representatives of Taiwan’s Public Television Service (PTS) traveled to Singapore to meet Netflix, they brought two dramas: A Touch of Green (一把青, 2015), a sweeping story of war, displacement and military families, and Wake Up (麻醉風暴, 2015), a tightly constructed medical thriller. They were not simply trying to sell programs. They were trying to change an idea of Taiwan. International perceptions of Taiwanese television, PTS executives recalled in interviews conducted for my joint research with Chairman Hu Yuan-hui (胡元輝), were still strongly associated with the idol dramas that had enjoyed enormous regional popularity
No matter where one sits on the political spectrum and who one blames for the ongoing struggles between the executive and legislative branches or the latest food scandal, there has been noticeable frustration with the way democratic institutions are functioning. Attempts to circumvent political opposition and institutional checks can begin a slide toward authoritarianism, even when presented as short-term solutions to gridlock. While that might solve problems in the short term, it inevitably evolves into a system that serves the rulers and the powerfully connected at the expense of the rights of regular folks. Spirox launches fast TGV crack inspection system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:14 UTC
01:41:14 KST

Semiconductor equipment supplier Spirox Corp (蔚華科技) has launched its first high-speed glass core substrate inspection system as it expands into next-generation packaging technologies, including panel-level packaging.
The company’s new optical inspection system can detect microcracks and debris accumulations, helping accelerate the volume production of glass core and through-glass via (TGV) technologies by improving yield rates, Spirox chairman Peter Chin (秦家騏) said at a technology forum in Hsinchu City yesterday.
Traditional optical inspection tools still struggle to detect tiny internal microcracks deep inside transparent glass at high speeds, the company said.
Photo: CNA
“We have attracted strong interest from Taiwan, Japan, the US and South Korean customers,” Chin said. “Almost all companies concentrating on developing glass-based technologies are approaching us.”
As artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance computing, and high-bandwidth memory continue to accelerate the development of advanced packaging technologies, glass core and TGV are emerging as key technologies for next-generation advanced packaging, Spirox said.
With major semiconductor firms planning to commercialize glass core and TGV technologies by 2028, engineering trials and process verifications next year would help fuel demand for Spirox’s advanced optical inspection systems, Chin said.
The equipment can also detect optical waveguides fabricated inside glass substrates using lasers, paired with novel optical structures such as glass couplers and glass bridges, Spirox CEO Paul Yang (楊燿州) said.
Spirox aims to sell dozens of the high-speed optical inspection tools next year for TGV and through-silicon via technologies, the company said.
The new system is critical for Spirox to transform itself from a semiconductor equipment distributor for other vendors to a semiconductor equipment developer, Yang said.
The strategic adjustment also plays an essential part in the company’s turnaround efforts. Spirox swung to a net profit of NT$13.64 million (US$432,535) last quarter from a loss of NT$103.95 million a year earlier.
The company has streamlined its equipment distribution business and recalibrated on own-brand equipment development, Yang said.
The company aims to boost the revenue share of own-brand equipment to 80 or 90 percent, he added.
“Spirox remains bullish on next year’s growth, driven by strong customer feedback on our inspection equipment,” Chin said.
The company gained significant traction among semiconductor manufacturers and market analysts after its name appeared on a validation results slide presented by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) at JPCA Show in June.
During the presentation, titled “Glass Substrate Development for CoWoS” (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate), TSMC announced a partnership with Japanese Ajinomoto buildup film substrate supplier Ibiden Co and Taiwan’s Innolux Corp (群創) to develop a glass core substrate.
Spirox helped Innolux validate the glass core substrate. The results showed significant improvements in warpage, thermal performance, power integrity and defect rates. The shift from wafer-based to panel-based processing aimed to overcome the physical limitations of traditional organic and silicon interposers.

Atopic dermatitis itchy and money drain: group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:12 UTC
01:41:12 KST

People with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis not only endure itchiness, but also have to spend a lot of money on treatments, the Atopic Dermatitis Patient Association told a news conference on Monday.
World Atopic Eczema Day is on Sept. 14 every year and the theme set for this year is “break the invisible burden,” highlighting the hidden emotional, social and physical struggles people with the condition have, the association said.
Atopic dermatitis is more than just dry and itchy skin, as people with moderate to severe conditions can experience chronic and relapsing flare-ups, as well as facing struggles such as undergoing treatment, financial burdens and psychological stress, said association chairman Chu Chia-yu (朱家瑜), a dermatologist at National Taiwan University Hospital.
Photo: Hou Chia-yu, Taipei Times
The association last year conducted a survey to assess the burdens of managing the disease among those with moderate to severe conditions, Chu said.
The poll showed that 72 percent of respondents had sought treatment for the disease from six or more doctors, with 46 percent having seen six to 10 doctors, while 18 percent had never been satisfied with their treatment, he said.
Twenty-eight percent spent more than NT$20,000 on skin treatments each month and 54 percent spent more than NT$5,000 per month on environmental controls such as mite eradication products, meaning that some might be spending NT$25,000 a month, he said.
Moreover, the disease can also cause poor quality of life and affect patients’ mental state, he said.
The study showed that when the disease was not effectively controlled, 88 percent of respondents rated their quality of life below 40 out of 100, citing poor sleep caused by itching, or appearance anxiety and social withdrawal due to skin flaking and redness, Chu said.
People with atopic dermatitis who are struggling with itchiness, sleep disruption or other conditions should not simply endure it or stop taking medication without consulting a doctor, but should discuss treatment options with a dermatologist, he added.
In an analysis of advanced treatments, the likelihood of skin-lesion improvement accounted for 43.8 percent of respondents’ decision weighting, while the likelihood of itch relief accounted for 16.53 percent, showing that people with the condition place greater emphasis on improving their appearance, he said.
A university student surnamed Wang (王) told the news conference that she would develop red, swollen and oozing sores all over her body, including her face, causing her to not even want to look in the mirror, let alone deal with people who do not understand her condition.
Another person with atopic dermatitis, surnamed Lai (賴), said that flare-ups would affect him from head to toe, and dealing with constant and intense itching and flaking would drain his energy.
Wang and Lai have found effective treatments after shared decisionmaking with their doctors and regained control over their lives, Chu said.

ASML wins over TSMC, Samsung for EUV machines as AI demand surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:09 UTC
01:41:09 KST

ASML Holding NV has won commitments from top chipmakers to use its latest semiconductor production gear, while embarking on a broader agreement to meet surging demand for more powerful artificial intelligence (AI) technology.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) and Samsung Electronics Co plan to adopt the Dutch company’s high numerical aperture (NA) extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment for high-volume manufacturing from 2030 and by 2028 respectively, joining Intel Corp in using machines that can cost US$400 million each.
TSMC is the leader in producing custom chips for the likes of Nvidia Corp and Apple Inc, while Samsung is the leading maker of memory chips.
Photo: Reuters
The four companies also agreed to an esoteric — yet critical — shift in the technology format for what are known as photomasks, a key component for producing semiconductors.
The group plans to move from the current standard of 6-inch photomasks to 12-inch versions, with the goal of boosting productivity and reducing costs as the industry races to keep up with soaring AI demand.
Photomasks are akin to the carved woodblocks used to print the same images repeatedly, except they are printing with light on silicon wafers.
While a shift to larger masks has long been considered complicated and expensive, the coordinated push offers the possibility of substantial benefits in chip production.
The new technology could increase throughput from high NA machines by 40 percent while simplifying the design process, ASML chief technology officer Marco Pieters said.
“That’s a huge opportunity, and of course that means a significant step in productivity,” Pieters said in an interview yesterday.
TSMC would adopt ASML’s high NA systems, based on current 6-inch masks, beginning in 2030.
The two companies aim to build a test line to produce 12-inch masks by 2031 as part of the process of having that technique begin use in production with high NA tools by 2033, TSMC said in a statement yesterday.
“TSMC has always believed in the power of collaboration to overcome technical barriers before they become economic barriers for the semiconductor industry,” TSMC chairman and CEO C.C. Wei (魏哲家) said in the statement.
Samsung plans to start using ASML’s high NA machines for computer memory by 2028.
It would “work closely with industry partners to develop the required mask technologies and supporting infrastructure,” the South Korean company said in a separate statement.
Intel, which has already taken delivery of high NA machines as it tries to make the transition from only making its own chips to being an outsourced provider of production, said it is already able to offer the benefits of the technology to prospective customers.
The company has been contributing to the push to shift to larger masks for more three years.

The authorities have launched 54 probes into suspected foreign election interference and other electoral fraud-related crimes to protect the integrity of the Nov. 28 local elections, the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau said yesterday.
Special agents launched investigations into illegal foreign campaign contributions, money laundering and election betting ahead of the “nine-in-one” elections, the bureau said.
The investigations resulted in 25 pretrial detentions, 70 suspects placed on bail, and the confiscation of NT$62.8 billion (US$2 billion) linked to suspected illegal cash flows used in breaking election laws, it said.
Photo: CNA
The bureau interviewed 559 people as potential suspects or witnesses, it added.
The investigations were part of the law enforcement effort to prevent foreign election interference, it said, adding that it is focusing on unlicensed money lending, election betting, and money launderers operating under shell corporations and virtual buyer groups.
Organizations and groups engaging in such activities often serve as conduits for funds used in election interference by Beijing, it said.
Another goal of the operation is to identify those who benefited from the Chinese government’s illegal campaign contributions, it said.
The bureau said it assigned 25 field offices to the effort, seizing NT$11.19 billion from unregistered moneylenders, NT$4.24 billion from alleged launderers and N$5.06 billion from alleged tax evaders.
The seizures included NT$153 million in cash, 521 bank accounts holding a total of NT$501 million, Tether cryptocurrency valued at US$2,184, 12 luxury cars valued at NT$23 million, luxury fashion accessories valued at NT$9.1 million, watches valued at NT$10 million and 35 properties valued at NT$101 million, the bureau said.
The properties and assets were deemed proceeds from suspected criminal activities, it said.
The bureau warned political candidates and members of the public against receiving or facilitating the transfer of suspicious funds from China or other countries.
Protecting elections’ integrity is a national security matter, and money laundering prevention is necessary to ensure the orderly functioning of the financial market, it added.
Separately yesterday, the High Prosecutors’ Office said that prosecutors uncovered 212 cases of illicit financial transactions intended to influence the elections, seizing more than NT$900 million in suspected criminal proceeds.
The office launched a crackdown on illicit financial flows nationwide from Aug. 17 to Friday last week to prevent illicit funds from influencing the elections, prosecutors said in a news release.
The operation uncovered 212 cases involving illicit financial flows and 588 people suspected of breaching the Banking Act (銀行法), the Money Laundering Control Act (洗錢防制法) and gambling provisions of the Criminal Code, they said.
Prosecutors detained 75 people, while 229 were released on bail, and the remainder were subject to other measures, including residence restrictions, it added.
Authorities seized about NT$909 million in suspected criminal proceeds in cash and bank accounts, as well as more than 390,000 Tether tokens, 20 vehicles and 850 electronic devices, such as mobile phones, tablets and computers, the office said.
They also seized 36 properties and more than 100 luxury items, including designer bags, watches and gold jewelry, it added.
