Crimea's tourism industry losses from Ukrainian attacks exceeded US$46m in January-June 2026
The losses suffered by the tourism industry in occupied Crimea in January-June 2026 exceeded RUB 4 billion (about US$46 million), according to data from Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
Source: Russian media outlet Verstka
Details: In the first six months of 2026, losses reported by tourism companies increased by 95.7% compared with the same period in 2025. Losses peaked in May, when they rose by almost RUB 850 million (US$9.8 million) in a single month.
Tourism companies earned 2.5 times less than the year before. The industry generated RUB 530 million (US$6.1 million) in January-June 2026, compared with almost RUB 1.3 billion (US$15 million) in the same period of 2025.
The deterioration in the figures came amid a mass refusal by Russians to visit the peninsula.
Official statistics show that the volume of paid services provided by tour operators in Crimea fell by almost 55% in July 2026 compared with July 2025, while the decline in Sevastopol was almost 73%.
The volume of paid services provided by hotels in Crimea fell by 74% compared with 2025, while in Sevastopol it fell by 10%.
Frequent Ukrainian attacks have caused problems with electricity and water supplies and fuel shortages during the tourist season on the peninsula.
In July, the Russian government allocated RUB 4.3 billion (US$49.6 million) to support the tourism industry in Crimea and Sevastopol. In August, the State Council of Crimea passed a law providing additional financial support for tourism companies.
Earlier, the Russian Union of Travel Industry proposed that the authorities introduce a moratorium until 2028 on bankruptcy proceedings, on-site inspections, debt collection and tax penalties for Crimean tourism businesses.
Background: In early September, it was reported that the grain harvest in Crimea is at risk, as local farmers are selling grain below cost.

German police arrest suspected power grid saboteur after manhunt

Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid
- Published
A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of carrying out a spate of sabotage attacks on Germany's electricity grid after spending several days on the run.
The suspect was carrying explosives when he was detained near the Weisweiler power plant in western Germany on Tuesday, police in Cologne said.
A tent in nearby undergrowth was also found to be rigged with further explosives, they added.
The suspect, named by German media as Daniel V, is believed to have written letters claiming responsibility for the attacks, which have taken place in Brandenburg and Saxony in the east as well North Rhine-Westphalia in the west.
Police said explosives found during the arrest were being examined by a bomb disposal expert, while officers were checking to see if any undiscovered devices had been set up in the surrounding area.
Prior to the suspect's arrest on Tuesday, police said they had found several launch devices on high-voltage lines near the Weisweiler plant on Monday afternoon, alongside "another confession letter".
A series of incidents across the grid in the last week have followed a similar pattern, with rockets used to shoot wires across high-voltage cables in order to cause short circuits.
The attacks have led to power-generating units at some plants being temporarily taken off the grid.
A statement from the Cologne Public Prosecutor's Office and Cologne Police on Tuesday did not provide further details on the suspect, or on the number and whereabouts of incidents he has been linked to.
German media have previously reported receiving two letters from the suspect claiming responsibility for the attacks. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said the handwritten letters contained information that had not yet been made public.
The letters were apparently signed with the first name Daniel, while his surname was kept anonymous, in line with German privacy rules. The letters also gave a residential address in the town of Gevelsberg.
Cologne Police had previously said it was searching for a 48-year-old suspect from the town in connection with the sabotage of electrical substations in three German states. Investigators had also said explosives were found during a search of the suspect's apartment.
In Saxony alone, police found 21 devices near high-voltage power lines last Friday and Saturday.
Interior Minister Armin Schuster has admitted it could have led to a regional blackout, but he has warned against jumping to conclusions.
"The way this deed was committed makes this case unusual, as well as the manner of the confession," he said.

Qatar bid to host 2036 Summer Olympics receives major new boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:56:31 UTC
00:56:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatar bid to host 2036 Summer Olympics receives major boost
The Arab League has backed Qatar's bid to host the 2036 Olympic and Paralympic Games, as the Gulf state steps up its campaign to bring the event to the Middle East for the first time.
The League's ministerial council approved its support at its 166th regular session in Cairo on Monday and called on member states to support Qatar's candidacy in international forums.
The council said the move was aimed at strengthening the Arab world's presence in international sport, according to Qatar News Agency.
Qatar formally confirmed in 2025 that it was in discussions with the International Olympic Committee (IOC) over hosting the 2036 Games.
It is expected to face significant competition. India, Indonesia, Turkey and Chile have all pursued bids, while South Korea's North Jeolla province has been selected as the country's candidate. Egypt has also said it intends to bid, while several other countries have previously expressed interest.
The IOC has said it aims to select the 2036 host in 2029. The contest is expected to formally take shape in March 2027, when the IOC executive board is due to select a shortlist of developed projects for further evaluation. A more intensive "targeted dialogue" phase is expected to begin in late 2028, before a final vote by IOC members in mid-2029.
Qatar is likely to emphasise its extensive sporting infrastructure and experience of staging major international events.
The country hosted the 2022 Fifa World Cup, becoming the first Arab country to stage the tournament, and has also hosted the Asian Cup and numerous world championships in Olympic sports.
Qatar's Olympic Committee has previously said that about 95% of the infrastructure required to stage the Games is already in place.
It is also due to host the Basketball World Cup in 2027 and the Asian Games in 2030, having previously staged the Asian Games in Doha in 2006.
Qatar has unsuccessfully sought to host the Olympics before, submitting bids for the 2016 and 2020 Games, which were awarded to Rio de Janeiro and Tokyo respectively.
No Middle Eastern country has hosted the Olympic Games.
In Asia, Japan has staged the Summer Olympics in Tokyo in 1964 and 2021, after the 2020 Games were delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic, while China hosted the event in Beijing in 2008.
The next Summer Olympics will be held in Los Angeles in 2028, followed by Brisbane in 2032.

Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
- Published
Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other countries covered by the American flag.
Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, showing the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered in stars and stripes. The entire landmass was labelled "United States of America".
Iceland's foreign minister said the post was "completely inappropriate".
Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries, including his push to acquire Greenland and calls to make Canada the America's 51st state.
His post of the map did not include a caption and preceded a flurry of posts of maps renaming the US state of New Mexico as "New America".
Responding to Trump's post, Iceland's Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called in US ambassador to Iceland Billy Long, who formally took up the post last month, local media reported.
When an ambassador is summoned, it typically means they are being called for a formal meeting, where the host country will express displeasure over their government's actions.
The post also drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said on Monday that the position of Greenland's government and people had been made clear.
"The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she told Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk.
"I hope no one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."
Trump's interest in Greenland has been a recurring theme on his social media accounts and in speeches since he took office again last year, claiming the island is necessary to the US to shore up its national security.
His post came shortly after the European Commission announced a €200m (£172m) investment in the Danish territory during a visit by Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Frederiksen.
The European Commission said its investment would focus on education, internet connectivity, the use of raw materials in the country and hydropower energy.
Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico "is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," after Trump's post.
"Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation," she wrote on social media.

Reported by
A Swiss court has handed Pierre Mirabaud, a former president of the Swiss Bankers Association and former partner at the private bank Mirabaud & Cie, a two-year suspended prison sentence after finding him guilty of foreign bribery and money laundering.
The Swiss Federal Criminal Court delivered its verdict late Tuesday morning, state broadcaster SRF reported.
According to the indictment, the 78-year-old former banker "continuously and systematically" funneled nearly 300 payments totaling 82.3 million Swiss francs ($101.7 million) to a senior Kuwaiti government official between 2000 and 2012. In exchange, the Kuwaiti official allegedly invested $595.2 million with the Geneva-based private bank.
Mirabaud, who chaired the Swiss Bankers Association from 2003 to 2009, pleaded guilty to making the illicit payments and admitted to his role in the corruption and money-laundering scheme.
During the hearing, Mirabaud expressed remorse. “I am here to take responsibility; that's why I accepted this procedure,” he said, according to public broadcaster RTS.
In an email to OCCRP, Mirabaud's attorney, Saverio Lembo, said his client had “fully cooperated with the judicial authorities” since the investigation began in 2012.
“Today he accepts responsibility for his actions, in accordance with the principles of individual responsibility, to which he has always been deeply committed,” Lembo wrote.
The Kuwaiti official, Fahad Al-Rajaan, who served as director general of Kuwait's Public Institution for Social Security (PIFSSI) from 1984 to 2012, was convicted in absentia in Kuwait in 2015 for corruption and embezzlement. He died in London in 2022.

How the EU Commission’s second-in-command plans to take on Big Tech, Big Oil and Beijing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:53:47 UTC
00:53:47 KST

BRUSSELS — Tax Big Oil, make Big Tech invest in renewables and protect Europe from climate disasters. Teresa Ribera’s post-summer policy wishlist isn’t short of ambitious ideas.
In a 90-minute interview with POLITICO, the European Commission’s vice president for the green transition and competition policy discussed how she sees China, data centers, climate disaster funding, and more.
Some of her comments give a glimpse of the EU executive’s plans for the coming months, while others showcase Ribera’s own priorities. Climate change remains her top concern, and she returned throughout the interview to the recent heat waves, wildfires and drought that have ravaged Europe. “This summer has been madness,” she said.
Advertisement
Two years into the job, the former Spanish ecological transition minister has also embraced the competitive aspect of her dual role, with her next big challenge being how to approach a potential breakup of search giant Google.
Here are the five key takeaways from the interview.
1. Brussels frets over climate costs
This summer has focused commissioners’ minds on the rising costs of climate change, said Ribera.
Friday’s Commission meeting on fall priorities kicked off with a discussion on global warming, and the tone was “consistent” on needing to better protect Europe against the effects of climate change, she said.
“On climate, there sometimes have been discussions on what is the right balance, to what extent is it compatible with competitiveness, and I think that it is increasingly clear that [climate action] is the only way forward in terms of competitiveness,” she argued, given that investments in curbing climate change are “lowering the cost” of future damages.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen “is sincerely committed to climate action and worried about the climate dimension,” Ribera said. “This summer has been such a big shock.”
Advertisement
Among the team of commissioners, she said, “there is a sense of serious concern and a sense of urgency on climate action.” But she acknowledged, “I don’t know to what extent it is consistent with the speed that would be required” to meet green goals.
2. Tax Big Oil to fund climate protection
The Commission is working on a proposal to better protect Europe against climate disasters, but Ribera is thinking one step ahead. Once that plan is presented, she said, the EU needs to start thinking about how to pay for measures to climate-proof the continent.
Last week, she told POLITICO that the EU should consider a bigger common budget, more joint debt or a levy on the profits of fossil fuel companies to raise the money. In this week’s interview, she doubled down on the idea of a windfall tax.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen “is sincerely committed to climate action and worried about the climate dimension,” Ribera said. | Olivier Matthys/EPA
While she pointed to a proposal for a global levy from United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, she also described a recent Spanish government proposal for a European fossil fuel tax as “interesting.”
“I had a friend working in an oil company saying that … a well-managed oil company is the most profitable business. A badly-managed oil company is the second-most profitable business,” she joked.
“But not so many people are getting these profits. And what we are already experiencing is that the impacts, the harms, the sorrow, the costs that are directly related to these profits are very high and are entirely socialized,” she added. “I think that it makes sense to open this discussion. I don’t know how far it can go.”
Advertisement
3. Make Big Tech pay for data centers’ energy needs
Ribera also worries about the environmental and societal impacts of large data centers proliferating in the EU. Grids and energy supply are already coming under strain, she noted.
Her preferred solution: Force tech giants to invest in renewable energy generation to power their data centers, rather than allowing them to freely draw from the grid.
“The companies behind this business are … concentrating market power and capacity in amounts that have not been perceived ever before. So, boldly speaking, they can be demanded to invest in what they may be needing and how it prevents additional conflicts with local communities,” she said.
Ribera pointed to a draft decree unveiled by the Spanish government last month that would require data centers to source 80 percent of their electricity from newly installed wind and solar as a good example. (Our Energy and Climate Pro subscribers can read more on that here.)
4. EU vs. Google
Speaking of Big Tech, Ribera is also in charge of the Commission’s pending decision on whether to insist on a breakup of Google after such a demand was ruled out in a recent court judgment in the U.S.
Ribera said that a consistent decision on both sides of the Atlantic would be preferable. “It’s always advisable to be sufficiently consistent, both for the companies, these global companies, the users, and the regulators,” she said.
Advertisement
But she didn’t show any signs of caving in to pressure coming from Washington to soften antitrust rules on Big Tech. Any decision, Ribera said, will be “based on our own capacities, assessments, and the compliance with our laws.” (Our Competition Pro subscribers can read more here.)
5. Talk to China but stick to red lines
Ribera has been known for a softer approach to China than many of her Commission colleagues. In this week's interview, she argued for a mix of dialogue and trade measures to cope with the challenges Beijing's manufacturing dominance poses to European industry.
“We need to find a way to address these imbalances” in trade with China, she said in the interview. At the same time, “I think that political dialogue is very important.”
That doesn’t mean the EU should roll over when it comes to defending its industries, Ribera insisted. “I think using also the strengths to defend the hard positions is important — we will not just allow anything.”
Brussels needs to figure out “where are fields where we can work [together with China], what are the elements of caution that we need to take into consideration … and where are the aspects where the political dialogue should complement or update the way we handle it.”

Laundry, backflips and panda suits: Humanoid robots take over IFA 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:51:50 UTC
00:51:50 KST

From doing the laundry to offering companionship and performing backflips, humanoid robots were everywhere at IFA 2026. Euronews took a closer look at what they can already do, and where the technology still falls short.
IFA is all about technology and innovation, with companies from around the world presenting their visions for the future.
In 2026, many of those visions include humanoid robots, and companies brought plenty of them to Berlin.
Across the exhibition halls, visitors repeatedly came across robots walking, waving, interacting with crowds or demonstrating individual tasks, with some being presented to European audiences for the first time.
"Alongside artificial intelligence, robotics is one of the key future topics at IFA 2026," Leif Lindner, CEO of IFA Management GmbH, said. He pointed to humanoids, physical AI and robotic systems for the home as examples of how quickly the technology is developing.
But beyond simply showing that robots can walk, talk or wave, companies are increasingly trying to demonstrate what they could actually be used for. With the trade fair drawing to a close, Euronews gathered some of the robotic highlights from this year's IFA.
Practical applications
Perhaps the most ambitious vision came from South Korean electronics company LG, which presented its idea of a "Zero Labor Home".
At the centre of its IFA presentation was CLOiD, LG's home robot, which the company used as the symbolic conductor of an "AI Orchestra" connecting appliances, entertainment systems and other devices across the home.
LG says its longer-term goal is to reduce the amount of household work people have to do, with robots and connected appliances taking over more everyday tasks.
Chinese home appliance and consumer electronics company Haier also focused on how robotics could be used around the home. At IFA, the company presented humanoid robots designed to interact with people and appliances, alongside cleaning and companion robots.
Another example came from US-based SwitchBot, which demonstrated a robot loading clothes into a washing machine.
The robot was able to pick up clothes, place them inside the machine and close it, showing one possible use for humanoid robots in the home. But the process was noticeably slow. So while the robot could take the laundry off your hands, for now, you would need plenty of patience.
Chinese company Pudu Robotics, meanwhile, is looking more towards commercial applications. The company has so far focused largely on service and cleaning robots, which it says are used in sectors including hospitality, retail, healthcare and logistics. At IFA, it also presented its PUDU D7 humanoid robot.
At its booth, the robot demonstrated relatively simple interactions. It could pick up objects on request, pose for pictures with visitors, take selfies from its own perspective and form a heart shape with its hands.
Such demonstrations remain a long way from robots independently, and quickly, handling complex everyday tasks. But they do offer an indication of where manufacturers see potential uses for humanoid robots beyond the exhibition floor.
Companions
But not every company is trying to make robots look or behave like humans. Some are moving away from the humanoid form altogether, developing smaller, often animal-inspired robots designed less as household helpers and more as companions.
Chinese electronics manufacturer TCL presented AiMe, an AI companion robot designed to interact with people and respond to voices, expressions and emotional cues.
The company says it can interact with users through conversations, games and storytelling, while remembering previous interactions over time. It can also be personalised and, with its rounded design and soft-looking appearance, resembles something closer to a teddy bear than a conventional robot.
A similar idea comes from Chinese company OlloBot with its OlloNi SS1, which it describes as a "Cyber Pet". The company says the small robot can learn from a user's voice, habits and interactions over time and adapt its responses accordingly.
Its appearance also deliberately moves away from the traditional image of a robot. With a rounded body and movements designed to mimic those of a pet, the SS1 is intended to feel more like a companion than a piece of technology.
Other manufacturers stuck more closely to companions people are already familiar with, taking inspiration from the animal world. MagicLab Robotics brought several humanoids to Berlin dressed in panda costumes, although their skills were less typical of their real-life counterparts, with the robots repeatedly performing backflips.
In fact, entertainment and spectacle were difficult to separate from the more practical ambitions surrounding humanoid robots at IFA.
Many companies used dancing, acrobatics and interactions with visitors to demonstrate what their machines could already do, even if those skills may not have an obvious place in everyday life.
Robots on stage
Nowhere was that more apparent than at IFA's Robot Show.
Humanoid robots and robotic pets came together on the runway to dance, perform Tai Chi, do backflips and even the splits.
Judging by the crowds, it was one of the most popular attractions at the trade fair. The area was packed with visitors, with cheers and applause accompanying the robots as they performed.
But the show also provided a reminder of how far the technology still has to go.
Some of the robots appeared noticeably unsteady after their performances. One that had just completed the splits looked particularly shaky when getting back onto its feet, while a robotic dog fell over during another demonstration.
The robots certainly managed to entertain the crowd. But for now, at least, they may not quite be ready for the big stage.

Germany to send Ukraine thousands more IRIS-T missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:51:44 UTC
00:51:44 KST

- Germany will supply Ukraine with several thousand more IRIS-T guided missiles, funded by the EU's 90 billion euro loan package, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said September 8.
- Germany separately pledged PAC-2 missiles from Bundeswehr stocks, while the EU agreed to buy 3.2 billion euros in Patriot missiles for Ukraine the same day.
Germany will supply Ukraine with several thousand more IRIS-T guided missiles, funded through the European Union’s 90 billion euro ($105 billion) loan package for Kyiv, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said September 8.
Pistorius made the announcement ahead of a video conference of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, the Ramstein-format meeting of Kyiv’s international backers, according to a correspondent for Ukrainian outlet Yevropeiska Pravda.
“I am glad that Ukraine will order several thousand more IRIS-T guided missiles, which will be financed through the EU’s defense loan for Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
The IRIS-T is a German medium-range surface-to-air missile system built by Diehl Defence, designed to intercept aircraft, drones and cruise missiles. Germany has supplied Ukraine with IRIS-T batteries and missiles since 2022 and has said it will continue deliveries in the coming years.
“The medium-range IRIS-T air defense system has been used in Ukraine very, very successfully,” Pistorius said.
“We continue uninterrupted deliveries of IRIS-T air defense systems, including guided missiles,” he added.
The purchase will draw on the EU’s 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine, which European leaders approved in December 2025 to cover Kyiv’s military and budget needs for 2026 and 2027. The loan is interest-free and backed by the EU’s common budget, after member states failed to agree on financing it through frozen Russian central bank assets instead.
Pistorius did not disclose the exact number of missiles Ukraine will order, their delivery timeline, or the total cost of the purchase.
Germany also announced separately at the September 8 Ramstein meeting that it would transfer PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from Bundeswehr stockpiles. The EU also agreed the same day to buy 3.2 billion euros worth of Patriot missiles for Ukraine.
Britain, for its part, is providing 100 million pounds ($135 million) for an air defense package under the PURL initiative, which funds Ukrainian purchases of U.S.-made weapons, ahead of the coming winter. That package includes Patriot missiles.

Syrians celebrate Yemen govt 'victories' over Houthis
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Syrians celebrate Yemeni govt 'victories' over Houthis on social media
Amid renewed fighting in Yemen between forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Iran-backed Houthis, some Syrians are seeing parallels with the rebel offensive which overthrew longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
The latest fighting in Yemen began with a Houthi offensive to take territory near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, but government forces have counterattacked on multiple fronts in recent days, seizing the strategic Hays district in Hodeida and launching an offensive in the Al-Jawf area. Dozens of Houthi fighters have reportedly surrendered.
The Houthis captured the Yemeni capital Sana'a and most of northern Yemen in 2014 and have remained in control there despite a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervening against them in 2015.
They have close ties to Iran and its allied groups, including Lebanon’s Hezbollah, and are accused of numerous human rights abuses, including arbitrary detention of political opponents, torture, and attacks on civilians.
Many Syrians have compared the Houthis to the regime of Bashar al-Assad, an authoritarian ruler also allied with Iran.
On social media, Syrians expressed their support for the Yemeni government through memes and images, some of them created with AI.
The Syrian Revolution 2011 page, which is associated with the early days of the Syrian uprising and, after 2024, became very supportive of current President Ahmed Al-Sharaa, shared a video of a Syrian fighter taking down a poster of Bashar al-Assad in 2024, accompanied by one of a Yemeni boy taking down a poster of Houthi leader Abdel Malik al-Houthi recently, captioned “from Syria to Yemen, victory is due to those peoples who do not surrender”.
It also shared an image of the well-known Damascene Sword monument in the Syrian capital’s Umayyad Square transformed into a traditional Yemeni dagger, with the news that the internationally recognised Yemeni government’s defence minister had given an order to "liberate Sanaa".
Syrian journalist Hadi Abdullah, who became well known during the uprising and is close to the current government, shared a picture of himself wearing traditional Yemeni dress and a dagger, saying, “Our Hearts are with Happy Yemen and its people”.
Many other Syrian activists and influencers shared similar photos of themselves wearing traditional Yemeni dress, apparently made with AI.
Some Syrians referred to Yemeni government operations against the Houthis as “Deterring Aggression”, the name which Syrian rebels gave to their lightning November-December 2024 offensive which overthrew Bashar al-Assad, although this name hasn’t been used by government forces.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government’s information minister, Muammar Al-Eriani, thanked Syrians for their support, according to Syria’s Halab Today TV.
Halab Today quoted him as saying, “We have followed with great pride and gratitude the popular campaign launched by Syrians on social media platforms, in solidarity with their brothers in Yemen.”
Eriani added that the Syrian social media campaign was “a profound expression of the bond of brotherhood between two peoples who have both tasted the bitterness of repression and the growing influence of Iran’s proxies.”
However, despite the solidarity, there are many differences between the current situation in Yemen and the one in Syria in 2024, with a victory by government forces over the Houthis, who appear much less dependent on external allies than the Assad regime, far from certain.

London police use tech to tackle masked phone snatchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:48:07 UTC
00:48:07 KST

London police use tech to tackle masked phone snatchers
London — Images of masked men riding along London's streets on mopeds or electric bikes and snatching phones straight out of the hand of unsuspecting tourists and locals have gone viral in recent years. The criminals have essentially taken advantage of new, quick but quiet transport technology to get a leg up on police.
The brazen robberies became such a problem in the U.K. capital that London's Metropolitan Police (the Met) developed a special task force — the Interceptors — specifically to combat the two-wheeled bandits. Nearly three years after the unit was established, police data indicate a positive downward trend.
During 2024, at the height of the phone snatching trend, there were 80,000 such offenses across London. As of July this year, 35,000 phones had been snatched, according to official statistics from the Met.
Police officials attribute that downward trend to the Interceptors. The specialist officers are trained in tactical pursuit and they operate across central London, specifically targeting phone thieves.
Cops and robbers, and drones and e-bikes
Taking a cue from their targets, the Interceptors use a combination of assertive on-the-ground policing and technology, including sophisticated cameras, drones and even officers on their own e-bikes, to track down and stop the thieves in their tracks.
They have focused on the central parts of London where tourists are ever-present, and where phone theft has been most frequent.
Dramatic police vehicle dash camera video shared with CBS News by the Met shows one of the techniques used by the Interceptors: crashing their own cars or e-bikes right into the suspected thieves to knock them off their wheels.
"We brought in new technology such as e-bikes … we brought in drones, we brought in Automatic Number Plate Recognition cameras. We've brought in all different levels of technology to hone down on how these criminals are operating," Commander Andy Featherstone, the Met's lead officer on phone theft, told CBS News.
He said when a report comes in that a phone has been stolen, "the drone can access the location in a matter of seconds," and then "you've got the eye in the sky, as it were."
"You've then got our Interceptors who are on the ground, and they can pursue and intercept the criminal in a much more safe way than perhaps before, where they would need to be in line of sight to do it and to be able to keep up with them to know where they're going," Featherstone said.
CBS News went along for a ride with the Interceptors and saw officers make two arrests after license plate recognition technology flagged a couple of mopeds with links to suspected crimes.
One of the arrests came after a minor driving a moped failed to stop when officers turned their lights on. A check by officers revealed that the young man had been suspected of phone snatching in London's Ladbroke Grove area just days earlier.
The bigger picture, and a bigger solution
Commander Featherstone told CBS News there are criminal networks behind some of the phone snatching gangs, and that London's police are becoming more effective at tracing the crimes to their roots.
"We discovered that there was an export market here," he said, adding that many of the stolen devices end up in North Africa or Asia, and China in particular, "where huge amounts of these phones are going there to be broken down as parts."
British police are now working with American tech giants including Apple and Alphabet to crack down on phone "jailbreaking" — hacking into the operating system to make a device usable by a new, unauthorized owner — to develop technology that ensures stolen devices are useless to anyone but their owner.
"When you remove the value of a stolen phone in the secondhand market, that is when we'll really break the back of this problem," Featherstone said.

Ukraine shows off its new Koral air defense systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:46:31 UTC
00:46:31 KST

- Ukraine publicly displayed a Koral surface-to-air missile launcher for the first time at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
- Ukroboronprom's image shows the missile launching from a self-propelled system on a Tatra truck chassis, built to intercept aircraft and ballistic targets.
Ukraine has publicly shown a launcher for its Koral surface-to-air missile for the first time, unveiling it at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland, a Militarnyi correspondent reported.
State defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom released an image showing a missile launch from a self-propelled launcher mounted on a Czech-made Tatra truck chassis. Ukraine’s defense industry has used Tatra chassis for other systems before, including the Buревій rocket launcher, so the choice fits an established pattern rather than marking something new on that front.
Ukroboronprom describes the missile as intended to intercept aircraft and ballistic targets as part of an air defense system. The developer says it can also be used in exceptional cases against ground or surface targets with a distinct radar signature, though that would be a secondary role rather than the system’s main job.
Koral has been in development since at least 2021, when state design bureau KB Luch first unveiled it as a medium-range interceptor. At the time, the bureau said the missile relied on already tested components, including its motor, seeker head, pulse correction engines, inertial navigation system and a non-contact proximity fuze, an approach meant to cut development time by reusing proven parts instead of building everything from scratch. KB Luch said in 2021 that the technical base for the system was about 70% complete, with financing identified as the main obstacle to finishing it.
Ukrainian officials have given inconsistent range figures over the years. KB Luch said in 2021 that Koral was designed to hit targets out to 30 km. Deputy Defense Minister Ivan Havryliuk cited a range beyond 100 km in 2023. Neither figure has been confirmed through independent testing data, and the discrepancy has not been publicly explained.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has said Koral is meant to eventually replace aging Soviet-era systems still in service, including the Buk and S-300PT, both of which date to the Cold War. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appeared alongside what was believed to be a Koral missile in an April 2026 video marking Ukraine’s defense industry holiday, the first time the missile itself, rather than a launcher, had appeared in public.
MSPO, formally the International Defence Industry Exhibition, runs September 8 to 11 in Kielce and is the largest defense trade fair in Central and Eastern Europe. This year marks its 34th edition.

Growth nearing 1% of GDP and higher revenues: what it means for the 2027 Budget Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:45:55 UTC
00:45:55 KST

According to economist Pietro Reichlin, speaking to Euronews, the 1% forecast "is realistic, but Italy remains last in the EU". Growth is not enough to widen the room for the 2027 budget, held back by structural flaws like low productivity and an ageing population.
The Italian economy could grow more than expected in 2026, approaching 1% of GDP.
That is the assessment of Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti, who on the closing day of the Teha Cernobbio Forum said that Italian GDP would exceed the 0.6% growth indicated in the government’s planning documents.
"For now we have secured 0.8%," the minister explained, adding that if the indicators continue to be favourable, "growth could come close to 1%."
For Pietro Reichlin, economist and professor at LUISS University, interviewed by Euronews, this is a "realistic estimate", but still not a result that allows us to speak of a turning point for the Italian economy. Growth remains held back by structural problems, from low productivity to unfavourable demographic trends.
It is not yet a new official government forecast, but the figure is significant because it comes on the eve of the drafting of the 2027 Budget Law and is accompanied by another positive signal for the public finances: rising tax revenues.
More growth, higher tax revenues
In the first seven months of 2026 the state recorded tax revenues of €346.1 billion, €9.4 billion more than in the same period of 2025, an increase of 2.8%, according to the bulletin (source in Italian) from the Finance Department of the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF).
"As GDP increases, revenues increase," the economist explains, a trend "accompanied by positive employment data". Higher employment and wages mean a broader tax base and therefore, under normal conditions, more income tax.
According to MEF estimates, between January and July 2026 direct taxes amounted to €200.7 billion (+€6.175 billion, or +3.2%) and indirect taxes totalled €145.5 billion (+€3.182 billion, or +2.2%).
Among the various items, personal income tax (Irpef) revenues came to €138.5 billion (+€3.7 billion, or +2.7%). VAT revenues totalled €100.3 billion (+€3.6 billion, or +3.8%).
Excise duties on energy products in the period January–July stood at €12.7 billion (-€1.2 billion, or -8.5%); in July alone they amounted to €2.2 billion, down 3% on July 2025, also as a result of temporary reductions introduced to limit the impact of higher energy prices.
Why Italy is still lagging behind other EU countries
Reichlin warns that "we should not celebrate the growth figure too much".
Looking at the international picture, he notes that the improvement is "fairly widespread" across the European Union, but that Italy "remains at the tail end, together with Germany and France".
"Growth, for example in Spain, is higher than ours," Reichlin says, stressing that the Italian figure is not "so brilliant", especially if we take into account the support provided by investment financed under the Pnrr.
According to the researcher, at the root of Italy’s backwardness there is a historical factor that dates back to the late 1990s: very low productivity. A feature shared with other peripheral EU countries.
In Reichlin’s view, part of Spain’s stronger growth is also linked to the large inflow of migrants, which has helped drive employment, a phenomenon common in southern European countries and one that also benefits Italy. But, the economist warns, employment growth "is not strong enough to allow us to offset" the problem of low productivity.
"So more work, more workers, but with little added value," he explains.
Without tackling this underlying issue, the professor argues, we cannot expect a corresponding increase in wages and a rise in prosperity.
What will change in the 2027 Budget Law
The higher revenues recorded in the first seven months of the year cannot automatically be regarded as resources available for next year’s Budget Law.
It will be necessary to determine how much of the increase in revenue is structural and can therefore be used to finance new measures in subsequent years.
If revenues perform better than expected, the economist warns that "we must not harbour illusions" regarding the 2027 budget. "To keep the public accounts in order, exit inflation and keep the deficit under control" or "to increase spending or adopt costly measures" revenues alone are not enough.
According to the professor, it will be a "very cautious budget law, because there is very little room for manoeuvre".
Besides productivity, growth is also undermined by the fact that "demographic trends are very unfavourable", he explains.
Italy is experiencing an ageing population and falling birth rates, and "this weighs on the public finances through the pension system, and also on the health service", causing public spending to rise naturally.
Reichlin concludes by saying that even if Italy managed to reduce the tax burden "especially on labour and businesses, as international organisations advise us", this would have a positive effect, but one major issue would remain unresolved. These measures would in fact have to be "offset by other sources of revenue, and it is not clear where these could come from".

Visite d'État de Lee Jae Myung, Président de la République de Corée.
France
Unknown Publisher

17:45:00 CEST
00:45:00 KST

Le Président de la République et Brigitte Macron ont accueilli le Président de la République de Corée, Lee Jae Myung, et son épouse Kim Hea Kyung pour une visite d'État en France du 8 au 9 septembre 2026.
Cette année marque les 140 ans des relations diplomatiques entre la France et la Corée.
Après la visite d’État en Corée du Président de la République en avril dernier, les deux dirigeants se sont retrouvés pour approfondir leurs convergences dans un contexte international instable et renforceront leur partenariat stratégique.
Les échanges ont permis de réaffirmer l’ambition des deux pays pour mettre pleinement en œuvre leur partenariat stratégique global, de faire le point sur les coopérations engagées en avril et d’ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives bilatérales. Des résultats significatifs sont attendus dans les domaines de la sécurité et de la défense, des technologies de pointe, de l’énergie et de la culture.
Les deux dirigeants ont évoqué également les crises internationales, notamment la situation dans la péninsule coréenne, la guerre d’agression russe en Ukraine et la situation au Moyen-Orient, dans l’objectif d'œuvrer à la stabilité, à la sécurité et au respect du droit international.
Revoir la déclaration conjointe :
9 septembre 2026 - Seul le prononcé fait foi
Déclaration conjointe du Président de la République et du Président de la République de Corée.
Emmanuel MACRON
Merci beaucoup et félicitations à tous les signataires de ces accords.
Monsieur le Président, cher Lee Jae Myung, Mesdames, Messieurs les ministres, Messieurs les ambassadeurs, Mesdames, Messieurs en vos grades et qualités. Cher Président, je suis très heureux de vous accueillir à Paris aujourd'hui pour votre visite d'État, vous-même, votre épouse et l'ensemble de votre délégation, avec de nombreux ministres et beaucoup d'entrepreneurs et d'artistes que nous avons vus hier.
2026 est une grande année pour la relation franco-coréenne puisque nous célébrons 140 ans de relations d'amitié entre nos deux pays. Cette relation déjà dense, nous avons eu l'occasion cette année de lui donner un nouvel élan. En effet, en avril dernier, j'étais à vos côtés pour une visite d'État à Séoul, et merci infiniment pour votre accueil si chaleureux. Puis, quelques semaines plus tard, vous veniez en France déjà, à Évian, à l'occasion du sommet du G7. C'est donc aujourd'hui notre troisième rendez-vous de haut niveau strictement bilatéral avec cette visite d'État.
Avant d'évoquer les discussions que le Président Lee et moi-même avons eues aujourd'hui, je voudrais rappeler que cette forte relation d'amitié s'est construite avec l'engagement du bataillon français sous le drapeau de l'ONU lors de la guerre de Corée, et n'a cessé de s'enrichir. Je vous remercie aussi infiniment de l'hommage que vous avez rendu ce matin aux anciens combattants et à l'Arc de Triomphe. Notre partenariat est un partenariat de confiance fondé sur cette histoire, des valeurs partagées, des intérêts communs aussi. Nous croyons ensemble dans la démocratie, les droits de l'homme, l'État de droit. Nous croyons ensemble dans le respect du droit international, dans le commerce libre et équitable. Au fond, c'est ce qui a nourri notre choix de rehausser notre partenariat en avril dernier pour en faire un partenariat stratégique global. C'est ce qui nourrit la relation entre nos deux pays et c'est ce qui, dans un moment de recomposition du monde et de bascule, fait que nous sommes convaincus l'un et l'autre que nous avons à défendre nos souverainetés réciproques, nos autonomies stratégiques respectives, et qu'ensemble, nous avons des actions communes à mener pour un Indopacifique apaisé et pour aussi des actions communes en matière de défense, de sécurité, de technologie, d'énergie, qui permettent d'améliorer notre souveraineté, notre indépendance, de coopérer de manière respectueuse et de ne tomber dans la vassalisation d'aucune grande puissance.
Cette « coalition des indépendants » à laquelle nous croyons est parfaitement illustrée par la relation bilatérale entre la Corée et la France. En effet, face à ces crises, nous avons une position commune. Nous constatons l'un et l'autre le soutien actif et désinhibé de la Corée du Nord à la guerre d'agression de la Russie en Ukraine, le soutien dont bénéficie Pyongyang en retour pour ses propres programmes militaires. Nous, nous partageons une vision commune d'un ordre international fondé sur le droit international et le système des Nations unies. Nos deux pays avancent aussi en étroite coordination face aux enjeux de sécurité et de stabilité. La République de Corée sait pouvoir compter sur le soutien constant de la France en faveur de la paix et de la stabilité de la péninsule. Je veux saluer ici votre constance, votre vision pragmatique. Ma conviction est très clairement qu'un chemin est possible suivant les axes que vous avez ouverts.
À ce titre, nous avons aussi longuement parlé des autres crises ensemble et des guerres qui se tiennent, je pense en particulier au Moyen-Orient. Nous avons également une vision partagée, celle qui consiste à défendre la liberté de navigation et le faire dans un contexte apaisé. Donc nous continuerons le travail commun pour proposer des solutions, comme d'ailleurs en avril dernier, nos deux pays étaient ensemble autour de la table lorsque nous avons, avec nos amis britanniques, lancé la première coordination pour une mission internationale ad hoc strictement pacifique pour la réouverture d'Ormuz. C'est dans ce cadre-là que nous continuerons d'avancer, de coordonner nos travaux pour pouvoir œuvrer ensemble à l'apaisement de cette région. En tout cas, les perspectives d'une mission multinationale strictement pacifique une fois un accord trouvé continuent de faire l'objet de travaux intenses.
Cette communauté de vues que nous avons encore pu constater ensemble l'un et l'autre à l'instant a nourri aussi des initiatives conjointes que nous avons décidé de prendre. La mission aérienne Pégase qui fera escale en République de Corée dans les jours qui viennent illustre en effet parfaitement notre volonté commune de renforcer notre relation de défense par des exercices stratégiques réguliers, des coopérations industrielles pour les équipements de défense, des échanges d'informations et l'amélioration aussi de l'interopérabilité de nos armées. Et l'accord révisé sur la protection des données classifiées signé aujourd'hui même entre nos ministères des Armées et de la Défense va contribuer à créer la confiance et la profondeur stratégique dont nos deux pays ont besoin. Vous l'avez compris, c'est donc une communauté de vues sur les grandes questions stratégiques et de défense que nous avons actée.
Mais cette vision-là, cette volonté de renforcer nos autonomies stratégiques ne s'arrête pas là. Nous avons aussi la volonté de prendre des initiatives sur la question de santé, de protection des océans, de gouvernance de l'intelligence artificielle, de protection de la jeunesse en ligne, de résorption des grands déséquilibres mondiaux, initiatives d'ailleurs pour beaucoup qui ont été lancées lors du G7 d'Évian auquel vous avez participé. S'agissant de la santé, la France rejoindra dans les prochains mois l'International Vaccine Institute, initiative de la Corée, et nous allons travailler ensemble pour préparer les grandes échéances comme la présidence coréenne du G20 en 2028 ou le sommet des océans à Busan en juin 2028.
Cette volonté commune d'œuvrer pour un multilatéralisme efficace s'est illustrée également parfaitement lors du Sommet Lumière que nous avons coprésidé à Saint-Paul-de-Vence hier et qui a permis de réunir une soixantaine de pays, organisations régionales et organisations internationales pour bâtir un multilatéralisme culturel, pour défendre la diversité de création, nos cinémas, nos animés et notre animation, nos jeux vidéo, pour protéger nos créateurs, nos acteurs, toutes celles et ceux qui font cette diversité, et pour bâtir aussi une plus grande compétitivité dans le secteur avec des initiatives communes que nous avons annoncées hier, en particulier l'initiative IRIS, le partenariat Lumière, ou ce que nous avons voulu faire ensemble avec d'autres partenaires pour l'éducation aux images et aux écrans.
La dynamique de notre relation s'illustre également par nos liens économiques et industriels. Plusieurs accords signés aujourd'hui le montrent. Le renforcement de nos relations s'inscrit en effet dans notre stratégie de renforcement de nos autonomies et nous voulons bâtir une vision commune et renforcer le lien entre nos acteurs dans les semi-conducteurs, dans l'intelligence artificielle, dans le quantique, en particulier, où nous avons la conviction que, là-dessus nous avons un destin commun. L'accord qui a été signé à l'instant entre Samsung et Mistral AI est de la plus haute importance à cet égard.
Nous avons aussi d'autres initiatives que nous voulons prendre. En matière de minerais critiques et de terres rares également, nous avons la volonté d'avancer, d'aller plus loin et de renforcer aussi nos indépendances. Et en matière de nucléaire civil, nous avons, grandes puissances nucléaires que nous sommes l'un et l'autre, avec des acteurs industriels importants, la volonté d'agir davantage ensemble. D'abord pour conforter et accompagner la dynamique, nous avons décidé de rehausser le niveau de notre dialogue nucléaire. L'accord signé entre Orano et KHNP montre l'importance justement d'un rapprochement dans l'amont du cycle nucléaire. Je veux ici dire combien nous soutenons les discussions entre nos industriels sur la question du traitement-recyclage des combustibles usés et une vision commune d'un aval du futur.
Ce qui s'est fait aussi en termes de propriété intellectuelle à l'instant et ce qui a été signé est de la plus haute importance pour favoriser les accords, là aussi, entre nos différents industriels dans tous les domaines. Nous serons dans un instant avec l'ensemble de nos chefs d'entreprise pour conclure le forum économique. Mais tout ça s'inscrit dans cette dynamique. Nous avons ensemble voulu passer un cap nouveau il y a quelques mois et, sur les technologies de pointe, très clairement, la coopération a pris une nouvelle dimension. Le protocole d'entente dans le domaine de l'IA et des technologies quantiques a été signé aujourd'hui, en plus de l'accord entre nos entreprises, et nous avons la volonté véritablement d'accélérer cela. Je veux ici vraiment remercier toutes celles et ceux qui ont permis cette accélération et cette concrétisation de ce que nous avions affirmé en avril dernier. Et encore une fois, les entreprises qui aujourd'hui ont signé cet accord entre Samsung et Mistral ont permis de passer un cap important dans la relation.L'excellence de la relation bilatérale en matière économique ne s'arrête pas là. Je pourrais citer les autres questions énergétiques, les questions de mobilité. Nous aurons l'occasion d'y revenir.
Enfin, je voudrais citer, pour conclure, l'extraordinaire dynamique des échanges humains et de nos liens culturels. Le cinéma français, la musique française, la création française est aimée dans votre pays comme la K-pop l'est dans le nôtre et comme le cinéma coréen, le Festival de Cannes, qui a confié à l'un de vos cinéastes la présidence il y a quelques semaines, l'a encore montré, aime votre cinéma. Les K-dramas, la K-pop font partie en effet de cette relation bilatérale. Le projet de lancement d'une nouvelle plateforme dédiée aux échanges entre les écosystèmes créatifs de nos deux pays, le France-Korea Creative Lab, qui sera partie intégrante du renouvellement de la lettre d'intention sur la coopération culturelle, permettra de consolider encore ce lien, comme nous l'avons illustré hier. Je dois dire ici que nous avons une même vision de l'importance de la culture et de l'art et une même conviction que c'est un secteur aussi économique à part entière où nous avons à défendre notre exception culturelle à l'un et à l'autre et la capacité à bâtir un modèle unique.
Enfin, pour encourager la coopération scientifique, un accord entre l'Université Paris-Saclay et le Korean Institute for Advanced Study dans les domaines des mathématiques et de la physique a été signé pendant votre visite et, là aussi, marque une étape importante de cette relation qui s'appuiera aussi sur une facilitation des échanges. Nous voulons plus d'échanges entre nos étudiants, nous l'avons réaffirmé l'un et l'autre, et nous voulons plus d'échanges aussi entre nos compatriotes. C'est aussi pour cela que j'ai le plaisir d'annoncer l'entrée en vigueur le 1ᵉʳ octobre de la révision de l'accord bilatéral visa vacances-travail qui permet de bénéficier du programme jusqu'à 35 ans et est un dispositif important pour la qualité de la relation bilatérale entre nos deux pays.
Voilà, je ne serai pas plus long, mais je veux ici dire combien, en quelques mois, nous avons su bâtir des partenariats nouveaux dans beaucoup de domaines d'avenir et que tout ça s'appuie sur une relation extrêmement confiante depuis des décennies. Tout ça, je crois, s'accélère aussi en pratiquant le reste du monde. Nous sommes bien placés l'un et l'autre pour savoir la valeur qu'ont des partenaires de confiance, fiables, respectueux de la souveraineté et de l'indépendance de l'ami, et qui ont une même vision de l'avenir. C'est ce qui lie la Corée et la France, et c'est ce qui fait que le désordre ambiant accélère la conviction que nous avons de devoir et de vouloir travailler l'un avec l'autre.
Merci infiniment, Président, pour cette visite d'État, pour votre présence depuis dimanche dans notre pays et jusqu'à demain soir, et pour la qualité des échanges que nous avons eus et des partenariats que nous avons signés. Merci beaucoup.
Une table-ronde économique a réuni ensuite des dirigeants d’entreprises françaises et coréennes autour de quatre grands axes :
- l’intelligence artificielle et le quantique,
- la transition énergétique,
- la santé,
- la décarbonation des mobilités et de l’industrie.

- list 4 of 4UK to hold off on deal ceding Chagos Islands amid US opposition
The Maldives government maintains that its own claim to the Chagos Islands is backed by historical ties and geographical proximity, being about 500km (310 miles) away while Mauritius is more than four times that distance.
These islands are home to the key UK-US military base on the island of Diego Garcia. It is the largest island in the archipelago, a strategic location in the middle of the Indian Ocean between Asia and Africa, and home to a military base that the UK leases to the US in a 99-year deal.
In his letter, Muizzu “expressed the Maldives’ concerns regarding the UK’s decision to proceed with the handover of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius”.
Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, had finalised a deal in May 2025 to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius. The multibillion-dollar agreement would allow the UK to maintain control of the strategically important US-UK airbase on Diego Garcia.
However, in his latest letter, Muizzu said he was “deeply disappointed” that the UK did not consult the Maldives when Starmer agreed to cede sovereignty of the archipelago to Mauritius, and urged Burnham to “rectify this oversight by your predecessor”.
Muizzu went on to highlight “the shared history and cultural ties between the Maldives and Chagos, as well as the Maldives’ longstanding support for major marine conservation and scientific research expeditions in the region”.
Last April, the UK set aside Starmer’s bill that would return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius due to a lack of support from United States President Donald Trump, as Mauritius promised to “spare no effort” to reclaim the archipelago.
A spokesperson of the UK’s Foreign Office was quoted on Tuesday by the Press Association news agency as saying that “the question of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago is a matter for the UK and Mauritius, which is why the previous government launched negotiations with Mauritius on the issue in 2022, rather than with the Maldives”.

Paris (France) (AFP) – Ferran Torres, whose goal against Argentina won the World Cup for Spain in July, leads a 30-man list for the men's Ballon d'Or revealed on Tuesday.
Issued on:
The 26-year-old who has since joined Paris Saint-Germain is one of six Spanish World Cup winners on the list, alongside 2024 laureate Rodri and last year's runner-up Lamine Yamal.
In the women's section, three-time winner Aitana Bonmati did not make the shortlist after breaking her leg midway through the season, but her former Barcelona team-mate Alexia Putellas, the winner in 2021 and 2022 and now a London City Lionesses player, is there.
Torres also won La Liga with Barcelona in May but is now teaming up with last year's Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele at PSG.
France international Dembele is one of nine PSG team-mates on the list to have won the Champions League in each of the last two years.
With Torres having joined the club, that makes it 10 current PSG players in total on the list.
Among them, Fabian Ruiz is the only player to have won the Champions League and World Cup in 2026.
Flying Georgian winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was one of the stars of PSG's successful Champions League defence, alongside Portuguese midfield pair Vitinha and Joao Neves, and all three are nominated.
Messi in for 17th time
Eight-time Ballon d'Or winner Lionel Messi received his 17th nomination, but his eternal rival Cristiano Ronaldo did not make the cut this time.
Messi helped inspire an ill-disciplined Argentina to the World Cup final, where they took almost 120 minutes to muster their first shot against Spain in a one-sided final.
England captain Harry Kane, who won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich, is included as is his French team-mate and wing wizard Michael Olise.
Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham earned his nomination with an impressive World Cup for England, scoring seven goals -- matching Erling Haaland's tally and beaten only by Messi (eight) and Kylian Mbappe, on 10.
Mbappe is there, after becoming the first player to win the World Cup golden boot a second time, while also scorching to the top of the tournament's all-time record scorer list.
Yamal is also nominated in for the Young Talent award, which he has won the last two years.
Vozinha, the 40-year-old who was one of the heroes of Cape Verde's fairytale World Cup run, has made the goalkeeper list.
Barcelona will also have a handful of contenders for the women's award.
Putellas is one of seven players who won the women's Champions League with the club in May to be on the list, including Poland's Ewa Pajor, who scored a brace in the 4-0 final victory over Lyon.
Three of the men's nominees play outside Europe. Messi is a MLS franchise Inter Miami and Sadio Mane and Julian Quinones play in Saudi Arabia.
The women's award spreads its net a little wider. Zambian Barbra Banda, who plays for Orlando Pride in South Africa, Mexican Scarlett Camberos who plays in her native country and Malawian Temwa Chawinga amd American Rose Lavelle, who play in the NWSL, on the list.
The winners will be announced in a ceremony at the London Palladium Theatre on October 26.

15:43:06 UTC

Under a government program extended for another year, children of Ukrainian veterans will have their contract-based tuition fully covered by the state for the 2026-27 academic year.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the extension of the program on Tuesday, Sept. 8, noting that the compensation applies to students at institutions of professional pre-higher and higher education.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
To apply, students must submit documents to their educational institutions, after which a certificate becomes available in the Diia app and must be confirmed within 20 calendar days.
The Diia app is a unified digital portal for public services that provides Ukrainian citizens with access to digital documents, such as payrolls, taxes, renewing driver’s licenses and applying for social assistance.
How the payment works
The Ministry of Veterans Affairs will transfer funds directly to the educational institution rather than to eligible students, according to Koretskyi.
Those who have already paid for tuition themselves – either in full or in part – will have those payments reimbursed by their school once the certificate is processed.
Part of broader wartime adjustments
The extension comes as Ukraine works through a broader set of wartime adjustments to both its education system and transport infrastructure.
Schools reopened on Sept. 1, with the government instructing local authorities to adopt new wartime measures, including avoiding mass gatherings and basing decisions on shelter access and evacuation speed.
EU Clears €3.2B Patriot Purchase for Ukraine Under €90B Loan
“Our task is to ensure that, despite the war, children have the opportunity to study safely and receive a quality education,” Koretskyi said on Aug. 31, while reviewing all matters related to the educational process, particularly shelters, meal arrangements and pay increases for education workers.
As Russia shifts its air attack tactics, combining and intensifying drone and missile strikes on civilian infrastructure, Kyiv has introduced a two-tier air raid siren system and updated transport schedules to keep the capital functioning even under repeated alerts.
On Monday, Sept. 7, Koretskyi said he had held an urgent meeting with government and Kyiv city officials over the capital’s ongoing transport collapse, with residents frequently getting stuck in traffic, unable to arrive home from work or reach hospitals.
“The economy must keep working, taxes must keep flowing into the budget, and people must keep receiving their salaries,” Koretskyi said in a separate statement on Sept. 3.
“The goal of all these changes is to protect people while also not allowing enemy attacks to paralyze cities,” he continued.
Local authorities are expected to conduct weekly reviews of the protective measures to adjust the response as attack patterns evolve.

Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia’s offensive, according to statistics verified by the United Nations.
In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people.
Zelensky told US news outlet Axios that the United States was pushing for a de-escalation ahead of winter and that Putin did not want to annoy Trump before the US midterm legislative elections in early November.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since launching its offensive in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as minus 20 deg C.

U.S. at Ramstein: allies must be prepared for Ukraine to need support for months and years to come
The U.S. official made the statement at the beginning of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting (otherwise known as Ramstein), according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“As President Trump has stated, our goal is lasting peace, and we are supporting every effort in that direction. From the standpoint of the Department of War, however, we cannot predict when this tragic war will end. As you all well know, Russia is reconstituting its forces and its defense-industrial capacity. We must be prepared for a protracted conflict and for Ukraine’s reequipments to persist in months and years ahead,” Colby said.
We must be prepared for other potential unforeseen situations. This reality makes assistance from Europe to Ukraine even more important, alongside accelerating rearmament and reindustrialization, Colby said.
In the his view, the priority should be to continue and increase the provision of Ukraine’s urgent battlefield needs through the PURL initiative.
“The continued flow of ammunition and critical capabilities is effective. It remains essential to enable Ukrainian forces to hold the front line and deny further Russian advances,” he stressed.
At the same time, Colby said, Europe should begin planning now for sustained procurement that will support both Ukraine’s long-term force regeneration and its own defense needs. The United States, as an Ally, must ensure that European investments in the defense-industrial base are integrated with and complement American investments. The Under Secretary emphasized the need to plan and implement investments on the basis of military effectiveness.
“In this frame, support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security by helping to rebuild Europe’s military strength and industrial capacity,” Colby noted.
He assured that the United States svg is ready to continue supporting these efforts. Through the Jumpstart program, the United States enables Allies and partners to procure capabilities for Ukraine, including air defense interceptors.
“Resourcing Ukraine’s defense, expanding production capacity, and building the forces and industrial base that Europe will need for the generation ahead – these actions demonstrate what allied-led defense looks like in practice, strengthening the credible deterrence that we are all pursuing as ‘NATO 3.0.’ We are confident that our allies can and will lead in supporting Ukraine’s self-defense and that this endeavor is highly correlating with Ukraine’s own battlefield success,” Colby said.
He welcomed the fact that European Allies are taking a leading role in providing for their own defense and are providing the bulk of support for Ukraine. According to him, this is “producing tangible results,” including the uninterrupted supply of U.S.-made weapons through the PURL initiative.
“Europe’s greater assumption of responsibility for its own defense is fully consistent with a strong and viable Ukrainian defense,” the Under Secretary stressed.
As reported, the 36th meeting of the Contact Group is being held virtually. Opening remarks were delivered by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, German Federal Minister of Defense Boris Pistorius, UK Secretary of State for Defense Wes Streeting, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara, and U.S. Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby.
Ahead of the Ramstein-format meeting, Ukraine submitted to NATO a list of urgent needs for air and missile defense systems.

In response, Shanmugam said the government took a serious view of sexual crimes and imposed stiff penalties, particularly when the victims were minors.

European Leagues extends EU complaint against FIFA to women’s football
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:40:03 UTC
00:40:03 KST

Halis Sunnetci
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
The European Leagues said Tuesday it extended its competition law complaint against FIFA to cover the women’s international match calendar and regulatory decisions related to women’s football.
The association said the extension was submitted to the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Competition, accusing FIFA of “abusive conduct” toward the women’s game.
The European Leagues, which represents professional football leagues across Europe, first filed the complaint with the European Commission in October 2024 alongside FIFPRO Europe and LaLiga.
The complaint focused on FIFA’s imposition of the men’s International Match Calendar, including the 2025 FIFA Club World Cup and 2026 FIFA World Cup.
It alleged that FIFA abused its dominant position under EU competition law and argued that an oversaturated calendar threatened players’ health and well-being as well as the sustainability of domestic competitions.
The extension comes after the European Leagues admitted 14 women’s professional leagues in June, including England’s Women’s Super League and the Scottish Women’s Premier League.
The European Leagues accused FIFA of following the same pattern of conduct identified in the men’s game, arguing that its dual role as regulator and competition organizer creates a conflict of interest.
It claimed FIFA uses its regulatory powers to favor its own competitions and commercial interests while failing to meaningfully engage with women’s professional leagues on calendar decisions.
The association said the conduct threatens the growth and financial sustainability of women’s professional leagues as well as players’ health and well-being.
It also said representatives of women’s professional leagues must be included in decision-making on calendar-related matters.
“The European Commission must now act to ensure that EU law is respected and that the future of women’s professional football is not determined unilaterally by FIFA,” it said.
The complaint comes amid wider pressure on FIFA President Gianni Infantino following the controversy about the now-abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which involved selling a minority stake in a new commercial entity controlling rights linked to FIFA competitions to private investors.
Infantino withdrew the proposal following widespread opposition, but UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and CONCACAF later accused him of breaking trust “through deception” and called for a fully independent review.
FIFA has previously said its 2023 international match calendar followed extensive consultation with stakeholders and maintained that it has the right to set parameters for its own competitions within agreed schedules.

Tunisian journalists protest after arrest of reporter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:39:26 UTC
00:39:26 KST

Breadcrumb
Tunisian journalists protest after arrest of reporter
Dozens of journalists protested in Tunisia on Tuesday over the arrest of a reporter on money-laundering charges, accusations his lawyer said were unfounded.
Mohamed Yousfi, editor-in-chief of the Alqatiba website, was detained on Friday when he arrived for a radio interview in capital Tunis and has been in custody since.
His lawyer, Hela Ben Salem, said Yousfi faced financial crime charges with prosecutors accusing him of receiving suspicious funds from abroad.
Ben Salem said at a press conference before the protest that the charges came under "anti-terror and illicit enrichment laws", but she said the case contained "no concrete evidence" of wrongdoing.
The National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT) said Yousfi's health deteriorated while in detention, after undergoing surgery for appendicitis following his arrest.
The SNJT also said members of his defence had to leave an interrogation to bring him medication as Yousfi was "screaming loudly from pain".
Press freedom groups have voiced concerns over civil liberties in Tunisia, where journalists, lawyers, opposition figures and activists have faced arrest and prosecution in recent years.
Zied Dabbar, head of the SNJT, told AFP that Yousfi's arrest came as part of a broader crackdown on journalists in Tunisia.
"We are faced with clear scenarios: prison, prosecution or exile," he said. "The authorities and the ruling establishment are repressing journalists."
Oussama Bouagila, North Africa director at Reporters Without Borders (RSF), said in a statement there was "nothing in the case to justify the continued detention of Yousfi".
"The accusation is based on a post that does not even mention his name, and his detention comes in the context of a smear campaign aimed at silencing him," said Bouagila, calling for his immediate release.
Alqatiba is an independent Tunisian media outlet known for investigative reporting and long-form coverage of political, economic, social and environmental issues.
Dabbar previously said Yousfi had been due to discuss water issues in Tunisia during the radio interview.
Water cuts have affected parts of Tunisia in previous summers, but this year's outages spread across much of the country, compounded by a shortage of bottled water.
Tunisia emerged as the only democracy of the Arab Spring demonstrations of 2011, but since President Kais Saied staged a sweeping power grab in 2021, rights groups have criticised a major rollback of freedoms.
Many, including journalists, currently stand behind bars or are facing prosecution also under a law Saied enacted in 2022 to prohibit "spreading false news".

Ribera ‘respectfully curious’ as to why a US judge spared Google
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:38:27 UTC
00:38:27 KST

BRUSSELS — The European Union should try to stay consistent with authorities elsewhere as it decides whether to order a breakup of Google’s advertising business, the bloc’s competition chief told POLITICO.
Teresa Ribera’s call for reflection marks a shift from the European Commission’s line a year ago that Google should break itself up, as the EU executive imposed a €2.95 billion fine for abuse of dominance in advertising. The U.S. search giant countered in November with a proposal of behavioral remedies only.
Her remarks on the need for regulatory alignment are especially significant as they come only days after a U.S. judge declined to force Google to sell its ad exchange.
Advertisement
“It’s always advisable to be sufficiently consistent, both for the companies, these global companies, the users and the regulators,” Ribera told POLITICO in an interview.
With the Trump administration threatening tariffs in response to EU enforcement while pursuing its own Big Tech crackdown, critics of America’s digital giants are starting to fear that pressure from an unpredictable U.S. could undermine Europe’s resolve to pursue its own agenda to rein in the dominant platforms.
The Commission has not yet seen the judge’s reasoning, which remains under seal, and Ribera said it was “respectfully curious” to read it.
Consistency is harder than it sounds.
President Donald Trump threatened a trade investigation into the EU within a day of Brussels fining Google €890 million in July under the Digital Markets Act. His trade representative, Jamieson Greer, has called the Commission’s recent actions on Android and Search a de facto forced technology transfer.
At the same time, U.S. courts have been imposing remedies in Big Tech cases that go further than some of the measures Brussels has pursued.
“Europe must follow its own path,” said Andreas Schwab, a German MEP with the center-right European People’s Party. “While we respect the independence of the American judiciary, behavioral measures alone have repeatedly proven insufficient to resolve structural conflicts of interest in digital markets.”
Watching the courts
Alignment is not only a problem when Washington retreats; it also arises when American courts go further than Brussels has been willing to.
In April 2025, a U.S. judge barred Apple from taking a commission on purchases made through external links in apps; the ban has applied to commissions on those sales in the U.S. since then.
Advertisement
In April 2025, a U.S. judge barred Apple from taking a commission on purchases made through external links in apps. | Annice Lyn/Getty Images
In Europe, where similar conduct drew a €500 million fine under the Digital Markets Act, the Commission in August accepted Apple’s revised terms, which will still allow the company to charge a fee on purchases made through external links.
“It’s a weird dynamic,” said Gene Burrus, global policy counsel for the Coalition for App Fairness, a developer group founded by Epic and Spotify. The wild card, he said, is a U.S. court acting in response to private litigation, with the U.S. government not part of it at all.
So far, in the major Google cases, U.S. courts have declined to order a breakup.
U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema found last April that Google had monopolized parts of the ad tech market, but then refused to order a divestiture.
In a separate case, Judge Amit Mehta similarly found that Google had operated an illegal search monopoly, then declined to make Google sell Chrome.
On this side of the Atlantic, the Commission has been left to grapple with the implications of both cases.
Ribera said a decision on possible remedies in Google’s advertising case would come in the next few months and would rest on “our own capacities, assessments, and the compliance with our laws.”
As for the Google search monopolization case, which does not have as direct a parallel in the EU, the Commission has nonetheless explored data-sharing remedies under the Digital Markets Act that would echo measures sought by U.S. authorities.
